  2. istio-cni not installed when needed: The default istioctl install doesn't include CNI. For PSA Restricted clusters, always add --set components.cni.enabled=true.
  3. GKE Autopilot restrictions: GKE Autopilot enforces strict pod security and requires istio-cni for sidecar injection.
  4. OpenShift default SCC: OpenShift's Security Context Constraints (SCC) restrict NET_ADMIN by default — istio-cni is required or custom SCC must be configured.
  5. kind cluster with default pod-security: Newer kind clusters enable PSA Restricted on kube-system, which may affect istio-init if pods are scheduled there.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-init The init container logs tell you EXACTLY why it failed. "Permission denied" = NET_ADMIN missing. "command not found" = image issue.
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> | grep -A10 "istio-init" Check the exit code: 1 = iptables failure, 126/127 = command not found/image issue.
kubectl get ns <ns> -o yaml | grep -A3 "pod-security" PSA enforce label with "restricted" means NET_ADMIN is blocked — install istio-cni.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Pod Security Admission Restricted profile blocks NET_ADMIN capability. The istio-init container requires NET_ADMIN to configure iptables for traffic capture. Solution: install istio-cni plugin which runs as a privileged DaemonSet on each node and handles iptables at the node level.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify the root cause — check init container logs kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-init "Permission denied" or "iptables: Permission denied" confirms NET_ADMIN is blocked.
2. Install istio-cni plugin istioctl install --set components.cni.enabled=true --set profile=default The CNI DaemonSet runs on every node with privileges and handles traffic capture without requiring NET_ADMIN on pods.
3. Verify istio-cni DaemonSet is running kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node One pod per node should be Running. Pods no longer need istio-init container.
4. Restart affected pods kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj With istio-cni installed, new pods skip istio-init entirely — iptables is handled at the node level.
5. (Alternative) Disable PSA for the namespace kubectl label ns <ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged --overwrite Only if istio-cni is not an option. This weakens security — istio-cni is the recommended approach.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Always install istio-cni in production. Starting with Istio 1.20+, istio-cni is the recommended default. It eliminates an entire class of injection failures and works with all pod security standards. Install it during your initial Istio setup — retrofitting later is more disruptive.
Check pod security standards before troubleshooting. kubectl get ns <ns> -o yaml | grep pod-security If you see "enforce: restricted", istio-init will fail. This is a 5-second check that saves hours of debugging.
istio-cni works differently from istio-init. With istio-cni, pods do NOT get an istio-init container. The iptables rules exist at the node level. This means kubectl exec into a pod won't show the iptables rules — you need to check the node itself.
kind and minikube users: install istio-cni from day one. Newer versions of kind (0.20+) and minikube enable PSA Restricted by default. If you're using your 6-cluster lab, install istio-cni on all clusters during initial Istio setup to avoid this issue entirely.
IC3
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC3
Sidecar Injected But Not Ready — Pod Shows 1/2 Ready, istio-proxy Failing

🔍 Symptom: The sidecar WAS injected (pod shows 2 containers), but kubectl get pods shows 1/2 READY — the istio-proxy container is not becoming Ready. The application container (Django) is Running and ready, but Envoy is stuck in Starting state, CrashLoopBackOff, or constantly restarting. The application can't communicate through the mesh because its Envoy proxy isn't functional.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  NAME                           READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
  anihpj-web-7d8f9-x             1/2     Running            0          5m
  anihpj-api-5c9b7-y             1/2     CrashLoopBackOff   15         5m

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-5c9b7-y -n anihpj -c istio-proxy --tail=20
  [warning][config] Failed to fetch certificate from SDS server
  [error] Envoy proxy is NOT ready: failed to get certificate

  kubectl describe pod anihpj-api-5c9b7-y -n anihpj | grep -A5 "istio-proxy"
  istio-proxy:
    State:          Waiting (CrashLoopBackOff)
    Last State:     Terminated (exit code 1)
    Reason:         Error
    Restart Count:  15
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. istiod unreachable or down: Envoy must connect to istiod via SDS (Secret Discovery Service) to get its mTLS certificates. If istiod is not running or unreachable, Envoy can't get certificates and stays not-ready. Check: kubectl get pods -n istio-system | grep istiod.
  2. Certificate issuance failure: istiod's CA cannot issue certificates — the root CA Secret (cacerts) may be corrupted or expired. Check istiod logs: kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod | grep -i "cert\|tls\|ca".
  3. Envoy proxy resource limits too low: The default proxy resources (CPU/memory) are insufficient — Envoy starts but gets OOMKilled immediately. Check: kubectl describe pod | grep -A2 "State.*OOMKilled". Fix: increase proxy resources via meshConfig.defaultConfig or pod annotations.
  4. Bootstrap configuration invalid: The Envoy bootstrap config (from istiod) contains errors. Envoy starts, loads bad config, and exits. Check kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy | grep "bootstrap\|config".
  5. DNS resolution failure for istiod: The pod cannot resolve istiod.istio-system.svc.cluster.local — CoreDNS is broken or network policy blocks DNS. Check: kubectl exec <pod> -c istio-proxy -- nslookup istiod.istio-system.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Time skew between node and istiod — certificate appears expired before it's even issued
  2. Custom EnvoyFilter or WasmPlugin causing Envoy crash — malformed filter configuration
  3. istiod Service port mismatch — the istiod Service was modified and Envoy connects to wrong port
  4. NetworkPolicy in istio-system blocking Envoy → istiod:15012 (xDS/SDS gRPC port)
  5. Envoy image corruption or wrong image tag — the injected sidecar image doesn't match istiod version
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Istio installed with demo profile on production: Demo profile has low resource defaults unsuitable for production workloads — Envoy OOMKills immediately.
  2. CA certificates not yet generated: On fresh install, istiod needs ~30 seconds to generate the self-signed root CA. Pods created during this window fail until CA is ready.
  3. Wrong trust domain configured: Custom trust domain mismatch between istiod config and what the injected Envoy expects.
  4. kubeadm cluster DNS issues: New kubeadm clusters may have CoreDNS not fully ready, causing istiod.istio-system DNS lookup to fail.
  5. Firewall on kubeadm node: The control plane node firewall may block pod-to-istiod communication on port 15012.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy --tail=50 Envoy logs tell you exactly what's wrong — "Failed to fetch certificate" = istiod/SDS issue, "OOM" = resource limits.
kubectl get pods -n istio-system | grep istiod istiod must be Running and Ready. If it's CrashLoopBackOff, fix istiod first — Envoy can't bootstrap without the control plane.
kubectl exec <pod> -c <app-container> -- nslookup istiod.istio-system Verify DNS resolution works from within the pod. If DNS is broken, Envoy can't find istiod.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: istiod is unreachable or not running. The Envoy sidecar must connect to istiod via SDS (port 15012) to fetch mTLS certificates during startup. Without certificates, Envoy is not ready and the pod shows 1/2. Always verify istiod health first when troubleshooting 1/2 pods.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify istiod is healthy kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod All istiod replicas must be Running and Ready. If not, fix istiod first.
2. Check Envoy logs for specific error kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy --tail=100 Look for: "Failed to fetch certificate" (istiod/SDS), "OOM" (resources), "bootstrap" (config).
3. If OOMKilled, increase proxy resources kubectl patch deploy <name> -n <ns> -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"annotations":{"sidecar.istio.io/proxyMemory":"256Mi"}}}}}' Default is ~128Mi; production workloads may need 256Mi-512Mi.
4. Verify DNS and network connectivity kubectl exec <pod> -c <app> -- nslookup istiod.istio-system.svc.cluster.local If DNS fails, check CoreDNS pods and network policies in istio-system.
5. Restart affected pods after fixing root cause kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj Once istiod is healthy and resources are sufficient, new pods start with 2/2 Ready.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
1/2 is always a data plane issue. The application container is fine — the problem is Envoy. Check Envoy logs first, then check istiod (control plane feeds Envoy its config). The app container being 1/1 is a good sign — focus on the proxy.
Resource limits are the silent killer. kubectl describe pod | grep OOMKilled Envoy memory scales with mesh size. A 500-service mesh without Sidecar scoping means every Envoy holds ~500 clusters — easily exceeding default 128Mi. Monitor and adjust.
Wait 30 seconds after installing Istio before deploying workloads. istiod needs time to generate the root CA on first install. Pods created during this window will fail because Envoy can't get certificates. Use istioctl verify-install to confirm readiness.
Check istiod first, always. 1/2 pods across multiple namespaces at the same time almost certainly means istiod is down or overloaded. Check kubectl get pods -n istio-system before debugging individual pods.
IC4
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC4
Sidecar SYNCED But Not Routing — proxy-status Shows STALE After Restart

🔍 Symptom: Pods show 2/2 Ready, injection appears successful, but istioctl proxy-status shows the Envoy as STALE on one or more xDS types (CDS, LDS, EDS, RDS). Configuration changes (VirtualService, DestinationRule) are not being applied to this pod. Traffic may be routing with stale config or not routing at all. The pod was recently restarted or the cluster experienced a network event.

  istioctl proxy-status
  NAME                          CDS     LDS     EDS     RDS     ISTIOD
  anihpj-web-xxx.anihpj         SYNCED  SYNCED  SYNCED  SYNCED  istiod-1
  anihpj-api-yyy.anihpj         STALE   STALE   STALE   STALE   istiod-1
  anihpj-db-0.anihpj            SYNCED  SYNCED  SYNCED  SYNCED  istiod-1

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-yyy -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep -i "stream\|grpc\|stale"
  [warning] gRPC config stream closed: connection timeout
  [warning] ADS stream to istiod.istio-system.svc:15012 broken
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Network interruption between Envoy and istiod: The gRPC stream (port 15012) was broken by a network blip, firewall rule, or istiod restart. Envoy tries to reconnect but may stay STALE for 30-60 seconds. Check: kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy | grep "stream\|grpc".
  2. istiod overloaded: Too many Envoys connecting simultaneously (e.g., after a mass pod restart). istiod's gRPC server can't handle the connection storm, and some Envoys stay STALE. Check istiod CPU/memory and scale up if needed.
  3. Envoy resource starvation: The Envoy sidecar doesn't have enough CPU to process xDS updates. Config pushes time out, and the stream breaks. Check kubectl top pod <pod> -c istio-proxy.
  4. NetworkPolicy blocking port 15012: A NetworkPolicy in the istio-system namespace blocks pod-to-istiod traffic on the xDS/SDS port. Check: kubectl get networkpolicy -n istio-system.
  5. istiod rolling update: During istiod rolling restart, existing Envoy gRPC streams are closed. Envoys reconnect to the new istiod pod, but there's a window where they show STALE before re-establishing the stream.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. DNS caching issue — Envoy resolves istiod to a stale IP after istiod pod IP change
  2. gRPC keepalive misconfiguration — aggressive timeouts causing premature stream closure on slow networks
  3. Node network MTU mismatch — large xDS config pushes exceed MTU and get fragmented/dropped
  4. Kubernetes Service mesh (kube-proxy) issues — istiod ClusterIP not routing correctly on certain nodes
  5. TLS handshake failures on xDS stream — certificate verification fails between Envoy and istiod
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Single istiod replica in production: With only 1 replica, any istiod restart causes ALL Envoys to go STALE simultaneously. Always run 2+ replicas for HA.
  2. kind cluster DNS instability: kind clusters sometimes have DNS resolution delays that cause istiod hostname resolution to fail intermittently.
  3. kubeadm control plane overload: Single-node kubeadm clusters run etcd + API server + istiod on the same node, causing resource contention during config pushes.
  4. CNI plugin delaying pod networking: The CNI (Calico/Cilium/Flannel) hasn't fully configured pod networking when Envoy tries to connect to istiod.
  5. Node clock skew across cluster: TLS certificates are time-sensitive — significant clock skew between nodes causes TLS handshake failures on xDS streams.
🔍 What to Look At:
istioctl proxy-status Shows which xDS types are STALE. All four STALE = gRPC stream broken. One STALE = specific config type issue.
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy | grep -E "stream|grpc|ads|stale" Envoy logs reveal the exact reason for stream breakage — connection timeout, TLS error, etc.
kubectl top pod -n istio-system -l app=istiod Check istiod CPU/memory. High usage (>80%) indicates overload — scale up or add HPA.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The gRPC stream between Envoy and istiod broke (network blip, istiod restart, or Envoy resource exhaustion). Envoy shows STALE until it reconnects and receives fresh config. Persistent STALE indicates a recurring network issue or istiod overload requiring more replicas.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Wait 60 seconds — temporary STALE may self-resolve After istiod restart or network blip, Envoy automatically reconnects within 30-60 seconds. Check proxy-status again before taking action.
2. Restart the affected pod kubectl delete pod <pod> -n <ns> Forces the Envoy to establish a fresh gRPC stream with istiod. New pod should show SYNCED within 10 seconds.
3. Scale up istiod for production HA kubectl scale deploy istiod -n istio-system --replicas=3 Multiple replicas ensure no single point of failure for xDS streams. Use HPA for auto-scaling.
4. Check for NetworkPolicy blocking port 15012 kubectl get networkpolicy -n istio-system -o yaml Ensure policies allow inbound traffic on port 15012 from all pod CIDRs.
5. Increase Envoy CPU resources if starved kubectl patch deploy <name> -n <ns> -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"annotations":{"sidecar.istio.io/proxyCPU":"500m"}}}}}' CPU-starved Envoys can't process xDS pushes fast enough, causing stream timeouts.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
STALE is a warning, not a crisis. STALE proxies still route traffic using their last-known configuration. Users are not affected unless the stale config is outdated. However, new routing changes won't apply until the proxy is SYNCED again.
Run at least 2 istiod replicas in production. kubectl scale deploy istiod -n istio-system --replicas=2 Single-replica istiod is the #1 cause of mass STALE events. If the only istiod restarts, every Envoy in the mesh goes STALE simultaneously.
Monitor proxy convergence time. istioctl proxy-status Add a health check that alerts if any proxy is STALE for > 2 minutes. This catches network issues and istiod overload before they impact config propagation.
Use pod anti-affinity for istiod replicas. Spread istiod pods across different nodes. If a node goes down, other istiod replicas continue serving xDS streams — preventing a complete mesh config outage.
IC5
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC5
Sidecar Injected Incorrectly — Wrong Image, Wrong Version, or Wrong Config

🔍 Symptom: The sidecar is injected but with unexpected behavior: the Envoy version doesn't match istiod, the proxy has too few resources, custom settings from the injection template are wrong, or the injection template ConfigMap has been corrupted. Pods show 2/2 Ready but mesh features (mTLS, metrics, routing) don't work correctly. istioctl proxy-config bootstrap shows unexpected configuration.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  NAME                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  anihpj-web-xxx           2/2     Running   0          5m
  (looks normal, but...)

  istioctl proxy-config bootstrap anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep ISTIO_VERSION
  ISTIO_VERSION: 1.20.0   ← istiod is 1.22.1! Version mismatch!

  kubectl get cm istio-sidecar-injector -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A5 "image:"
  image: docker.io/istio/proxyv2:1.20.0   ← WRONG image tag!

  kubectl logs anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | head -5
  [warning] mTLS negotiation failed: peer certificate expired
  [warning] Envoy version mismatch with control plane
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Injection template has wrong image tag: The istio-sidecar-injector ConfigMap specifies an old proxy image version. This happens after upgrading istiod but NOT updating the ConfigMap. Check: kubectl get cm istio-sidecar-injector -n istio-system -o yaml | grep image. Fix: reinstall or update the ConfigMap.
  2. Custom injection template overrides: Someone modified the injection template (e.g., to add custom labels, change resources, or add volumes) and introduced errors. The template is YAML — a single indentation error can silently change behavior.
  3. Multiple Istio revisions confusion: Namespace is labeled with istio.io/rev=canary but the ConfigMap for that revision has different settings than expected. During canary upgrades, the wrong revision's template may be applied.
  4. Helm values vs istioctl profile mismatch: Istio was installed with Helm using custom values, then someone ran istioctl install which overwrote the injection template with defaults.
  5. Proxy resource defaults too low for workload: The injection template specifies default CPU/memory that's insufficient for this workload's traffic volume — Envoy appears healthy but is silently throttled.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Pod-level annotations overriding injection template — sidecar.istio.io/proxyImage or proxyVersion set to wrong values
  2. Image pull policy is IfNotPresent but local cache has old version — new Envoy image is available but not pulled
  3. Custom CA bundle mounted incorrectly — Envoy has wrong trust anchors and can't verify certificates
  4. Environment variables in injection template not expanded correctly — references to ConfigMap/Secret values fail silently
  5. Init container resource limits in template too low — istio-init runs out of memory while configuring iptables
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Upgraded Istio but didn't upgrade CRDs: Control plane is new version but sidecars injected with old template — version mismatch and potential API incompatibility.
  2. Misconfigured revision tags: istio.io/rev=stable points to an old revision because the tag wasn't updated after upgrade.
  3. Air-gapped cluster with wrong registry mirror: The injection template references docker.io/istio/proxyv2 but the air-gapped registry has the image at a different path.
  4. kubeadm cluster using old cached images: containerd has cached an old proxyv2 image and the pull policy doesn't refresh it.
  5. minikube with stale image cache: minikube's internal image cache may serve an old proxy image even after `minikube image load` of a newer one.
🔍 What to Look At:
istioctl proxy-config bootstrap <pod> -n <ns> | grep -E "ISTIO_VERSION|image|proxy" Reveals the actual Envoy version and bootstrap settings loaded in the sidecar.
kubectl get cm istio-sidecar-injector -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -E "image:|version:" Check what image/version the injection template is configured to inject.
istioctl version Compare control plane version (istiod) vs data plane version (sidecars). Mismatch = injection template needs update.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The injection template ConfigMap (istio-sidecar-injector) has an outdated or incorrect proxy image tag, causing version mismatch between istiod and Envoy sidecars. This is the most common issue after Istio upgrades — istiod is upgraded but the injection template still references the old sidecar image.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify version mismatch istioctl version Shows control plane version AND data plane versions. Mismatch confirms the injection template needs updating.
2. Update the injection template (istioctl) istioctl install --set profile=default --set hub=<registry> --set tag=<version> Re-running install with correct version updates the injection ConfigMap and all sidecars on next restart.
3. Update the injection template (Helm) helm upgrade istio-base istio/base -n istio-system --set global.tag=<version> For Helm-based installs, upgrade the base chart to update the injection template.
4. Verify the fix on a test pod kubectl run test --image=nginx -n test --restart=Never New pods should now get the correct Envoy version. Check with istioctl proxy-config bootstrap.
5. Restart all application pods kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj Existing pods still have the old sidecar. Rolling restart replaces them with the correct version.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Always run istioctl version after upgrades. istioctl version This single command tells you whether control plane and data plane versions match. If they don't, your injection template is out of date and sidecars are running old Envoy.
Never manually edit the injection ConfigMap. The istio-sidecar-injector ConfigMap is managed by istioctl/Helm. Manual edits are overwritten on the next install/upgrade. Use IstioOperator or Helm values for customizations instead.
Use revision-based upgrades to avoid version confusion. Instead of updating the same ConfigMap, deploy a new revision. Label namespaces with istio.io/rev=<new-rev>. This cleanly separates old and new sidecar versions.
Pin the proxy image tag in production. Use explicit image tags (e.g., 1.22.1) rather than latest. This prevents unexpected sidecar version changes when the injection template is regenerated.

📌 IC6–IC10: Installation Profiles & Customization Issues

IC6
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC6
Demo Profile Used in Production — Resource Limits Too Low, Missing HA

🔍 Symptom: Istio was installed with istioctl install --set profile=demo on a production cluster. Pods are crashing with OOMKilled, istiod has only 1 replica (no HA), and addons (Kiali, Jaeger, Grafana) are deployed with low resource limits that can't handle production traffic. kubectl get pods -n istio-system shows many addon pods that shouldn't be in production. The demo profile is explicitly documented as "not for production use."

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system
  NAME                                    READY   STATUS       RESTARTS
  istiod-7d8f9-x                           1/1     Running      0
  istio-ingressgateway-abc                 1/1     Running      0
  istio-egressgateway-def                  1/1     Running      0
  kiali-ghi                                1/1     OOMKilled    12   ← Shouldn't be here
  jaeger-jkl                               1/1     OOMKilled    8    ← Shouldn't be here
  grafana-mno                              1/1     Running      0    ← Shouldn't be here
  prometheus-pqr                           1/1     OOMKilled    15   ← Shouldn't be here

  istioctl profile dump demo | grep -A5 "resources\|replicas"
  pilot.resources.requests.memory: 512Mi   ← Too low for production
  pilot.autoscaleMin: 1                    ← NO High Availability!
  gateways.istio-ingressgateway.autoscaleMin: 1  ← SPOF!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Wrong profile selected during install: The --set profile=demo flag was used instead of --set profile=default. The demo profile enables ALL features with minimal resources — designed for learning, not production. It includes Kiali, Jaeger, Grafana, and Prometheus that should be deployed separately in production.
  2. Following outdated quickstart guide: Many Istio tutorials use profile=demo for simplicity. Teams copy-paste the quickstart commands directly into production without understanding the implications.
  3. istiod running single replica: Demo profile sets autoscaleMin: 1 with no HPA — if istiod crashes, the entire mesh control plane is down. Production requires minimum 2 replicas.
  4. Addon resource limits too low: Kiali/Jaeger/Grafana/Prometheus from demo profile have minimal CPU/memory. Under production traffic, they OOMKill constantly — consuming node resources without providing value.
  5. No resource customization after install: Team assumes defaults are production-safe. The default profile provides production-ready base; demo explicitly does not.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm values override intended profile — someone set profile via istioctl but Helm values.yaml still specifies demo components
  2. CI/CD pipeline hardcoded demo profile — automated deployment script has demo profile baked in from initial testing
  3. Multiple Istio installations conflicting — demo and default profiles mixed, creating inconsistent component versions
  4. Air-gapped environment using cached demo images — proxyv2 image tagged as "demo" pulled from local registry
  5. Operator error selecting wrong kubeconfig context — installed demo on production cluster thinking it was dev
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New team unfamiliar with Istio profiles: First Istio deployment — demo profile seems "complete" with all features, team doesn't know it's unsuitable for production.
  2. kind/minikube profile carried to production: Team practiced on kind with demo profile, then ran the exact same command on the kubeadm production cluster.
  3. No architectural review before deployment: Istio was installed by a developer as part of a proof-of-concept that became production without platform team review.
  4. Cloud marketplace one-click install: Some cloud marketplaces deploy Istio with demo profile by default for quick evaluation — team didn't reconfigure for production.
  5. Missing production readiness checklist: No process exists to validate Istio configuration before production deployment.
🔍 What to Look At:
istioctl profile dump Shows the currently installed profile. If it says "demo," you're running a non-production configuration.
kubectl get pods -n istio-system Demo profile deploys kiali, jaeger, grafana, and prometheus pods. In production, these should be managed separately with appropriate resource limits.
kubectl get hpa -n istio-system Production should have HPA configured for istiod and ingress gateway. Demo profile typically has no HPA.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The demo profile was used for production installation. The demo profile is explicitly designed for learning/evaluation with ALL features enabled at minimal resource levels — it is NOT suitable for production workloads. The default profile provides a production-ready base; a custom IstioOperator YAML provides complete control.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify current profile and plan migration istioctl profile dump Confirm you're on demo. Plan to switch to default or create a custom IstioOperator YAML for production.
2. Migrate to production profile (in-place upgrade) istioctl install --set profile=default --set components.pilot.k8s.hpaSpec.minReplicas=2 Re-running install with default profile updates the control plane. Existing sidecars are unaffected — restart pods to pick up new proxy settings.
3. Deploy observability stack separately Remove Kiali, Jaeger, Grafana, Prometheus from the Istio install. Deploy them independently via their own Helm charts with production-appropriate resources. Or use --set addonComponents.kiali.enabled=false etc.
4. Configure HA for control plane istioctl install --set profile=default --set components.pilot.k8s.hpaSpec.minReplicas=2 --set components.pilot.k8s.hpaSpec.maxReplicas=5 Always run at least 2 istiod replicas. Configure HPA for automatic scaling under load.
5. Create a custom IstioOperator for full control For production, maintain an iop-production.yaml in Git with explicit settings for all components. Apply with istioctl apply -f iop-production.yaml. This ensures reproducible, auditable, version-controlled mesh configuration.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Demo is for demos. Default is for production. The demo profile includes everything — Kiali, Jaeger, Grafana, Prometheus, egress gateway — with minimal resources. Default includes ONLY istiod + ingress gateway with production-appropriate defaults. Start with default and add components intentionally.
Use IstioOperator YAML in Git, not CLI flags. istioctl apply -f iop-production.yaml A version-controlled IstioOperator file is auditable, reviewable, and reproducible. CLI flags like --set profile=demo are ephemeral — you can't tell what was installed 6 months ago.
Deploy observability tools separately from Istio. Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger, and Kiali are independent tools with their own scaling and availability requirements. Managing them via Istio's install couples their lifecycle to the mesh — upgrade Istio and your observability stack restarts. Deploy them independently.
Always run 2+ istiod replicas in any non-dev environment. Single istiod = single point of failure. If it crashes, no new sidecars can be injected and config changes stop propagating. The cost of a second replica is minimal; the cost of an istiod outage is massive.
IC7
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC7
istioctl and Helm Installation Conflict — Mixed Management Methods

🔍 Symptom: Istio was partially installed with Helm and partially with istioctl. The mesh has inconsistent component versions, missing resources, or conflicting configurations. helm list -n istio-system shows some charts installed, but istioctl verify-install reports missing components. Running istioctl install overwrites Helm-managed resources, and helm upgrade reverts istioctl changes. The two management methods are fighting each other.

  helm list -n istio-system
  NAME            NAMESPACE       STATUS          CHART           APP VERSION
  istio-base      istio-system    deployed        base-1.22.1     1.22.1
  istiod          istio-system    deployed        istiod-1.22.1   1.22.1

  istioctl verify-install
  ❌ Ingress Gateway Deployment: NOT FOUND   ← Helm didn't install this
  ❌ CRDs: 48 of 55 installed                 ← Some CRDs missing
  ✅ Istiod Deployment: 1/1 replicas available

  kubectl get deploy -n istio-system
  NAME                   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
  istiod                 1/1     1            1
  (ingress gateway missing — Helm charts need separate istio/gateway install)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Partial Helm install — only istio-base and istiod: Helm-based Istio installation requires MULTIPLE charts: istio/base, istio/istiod, and istio/gateway. Installing only the first two leaves the ingress gateway undeployed. Check: helm list -n istio-system — all three charts should be present.
  2. istioctl install overwrote Helm-managed resources: Running istioctl install on a Helm-managed cluster creates resources with different labels/annotations. Helm then detects drift and may revert changes on next helm upgrade.
  3. Team split — some use istioctl, some use Helm: Different team members manage Istio with different tools. The resulting configuration is inconsistent because istioctl and Helm use different defaults and templates.
  4. CRDs installed by istioctl but not Helm: istioctl installs CRDs automatically. Helm's CRD management is different — CRDs may need to be installed separately or managed by the base chart.
  5. Upgrade path confusion — Helm upgrade vs istioctl upgrade: The team doesn't know which tool to use for upgrades. Running both creates version mismatches between components.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Argo CD managing Istio with Helm, but manual istioctl commands were run — drift between GitOps and live state
  2. Helm release in different namespace — istio-base installed in default ns, gateway in istio-system
  3. Helm values.yaml missing gateway configuration — gateway chart installed but with wrong values resulting in no pods
  4. Custom CA certs managed differently — Helm mounts them via values, istioctl via Secret reference
  5. Multiple Helm releases for same component — istiod deployed twice with different release names
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New cluster setup with wrong docs followed: Team followed the Helm install guide but missed the gateway chart step (only installed istio-base and istiod).
  2. GitOps pipeline misconfigured: Argo CD Application only syncs istio-base and istiod charts — gateway chart was never added to the pipeline.
  3. Helm repo not updated: helm repo update wasn't run, so the latest chart versions aren't available — team tried istioctl as workaround.
  4. Air-gapped cluster with partial Helm charts: Only istio-base and istiod charts were mirrored to the air-gapped registry.
  5. kubeadm cluster with no Helm initially: Team installed Istio with istioctl, then later adopted Helm but didn't migrate — now both tools manage different parts.
🔍 What to Look At:
helm list -n istio-system Shows which Helm charts are installed. All three (istio-base, istiod, istio-gateway) should be present for a complete installation.
kubectl get deploy,svc -n istio-system Missing ingress gateway Deployment/Service confirms the gateway chart wasn't installed.
kubectl get crds | grep istio | wc -l Should show 55+ CRDs. Fewer means CRDs weren't fully installed — run istioctl install to add missing CRDs, or update Helm chart.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Istio was installed with Helm but only the istio-base and istiod charts were deployed — the gateway chart (istio/gateway) was missed. Helm-based Istio requires three separate chart installations for a complete mesh. Without the gateway chart, the ingress gateway is missing and external traffic cannot enter the mesh.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Decide on ONE management method — Helm or istioctl Pick one and stick with it. For GitOps workflows, Helm is preferred (Argo CD integration). For simpler setups, istioctl + IstioOperator is simpler.
2. If choosing Helm, install the missing gateway chart helm install istio-ingress istio/gateway -n istio-system --set service.type=LoadBalancer This deploys the ingress gateway Deployment, Service, and associated RBAC. Verify with helm list -n istio-system — all three charts should be present.
3. If choosing istioctl, uninstall Helm charts first helm uninstall istiod -n istio-system; helm uninstall istio-base -n istio-system; istioctl install --set profile=default Clean removal of Helm-managed resources before switching to istioctl. This prevents resource conflicts.
4. Verify complete installation istioctl verify-install Confirms all components are present: istiod Deployment/Service, ingress gateway, CRDs, webhooks, ConfigMaps, and RBAC.
5. Document the chosen installation method Write a runbook specifying Helm (with chart names and values) or istioctl (with IstioOperator YAML). Prevent future tool mixing by making the method explicit in team documentation.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Helm requires THREE charts. Don't forget the gateway. helm install istio-base istio/base -n istio-system helm install istiod istio/istiod -n istio-system helm install istio-ingress istio/gateway -n istio-system The most common Helm installation mistake is installing only istio-base and istiod, then wondering why there's no ingress gateway.
Never mix istioctl and Helm on the same cluster. They produce resources with different labels, annotations, and defaults. Mixing them creates configuration drift that breaks upgrades and causes unpredictable behavior. Choose ONE method per cluster.
Use Helm for GitOps (Argo CD/Flux), istioctl for simplicity. If your organization uses Argo CD or Flux for GitOps, Helm integrates natively. If you manage clusters manually or with simpler automation, istioctl + IstioOperator YAML is simpler and has built-in debugging (istioctl analyze, proxy-status).
Verify your installation after EVERY change. istioctl verify-install Run this after install, upgrade, Helm chart update, or any configuration change. It catches missing components before they cause production issues.
IC8
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC8
istio-cni Installed But Not Working — Pods Still Using istio-init, or Traffic Not Captured

🔍 Symptom: istio-cni was installed (istioctl install --set components.cni.enabled=true), but pods still have the istio-init init container, or traffic is not being captured by Envoy. kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node shows the CNI DaemonSet pods, but new application pods still show istio-init in their spec. Or, pods don't have istio-init but Envoy is not intercepting traffic — the iptables rules at the node level aren't working.

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node
  NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  istio-cni-node-xxx     1/1     Running   0          10m
  istio-cni-node-yyy     1/1     Running   0          10m

  kubectl get pod anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 "initContainers"
  initContainers:
  - name: istio-init          ← STILL PRESENT! CNI should eliminate this

  kubectl logs -n istio-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node --tail=20
  error: failed to add iptables rule: chain ISTIO_INBOUND already exists
  warning: conflict with existing iptables rules from Calico
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Injection template not updated after CNI install: Installing istio-cni updates the CNI daemon but doesn't automatically update the injection template. Existing pods or namespaces may still use the old template with istio-init. Fix: re-run istioctl install or restart istiod to regenerate the injection template.
  2. CNI plugin not in the CNI config directory: istio-cni installs its plugin binary and config to /etc/cni/net.d/ on each node. If another CNI (Calico, Cilium) manages this directory, istio-cni's config may be overwritten or not processed. Check node logs: journalctl -u kubelet | grep cni.
  3. CNI DaemonSet not running on all nodes: Some nodes have taints or nodeSelectors that prevent the istio-cni DaemonSet pod from scheduling. Pods on those nodes fall back to istio-init. Check: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node -o wide.
  4. CNI config not chained correctly: The istio-cni config must be processed BEFORE the primary CNI (Calico/Cilium). If the CNI config file ordering is wrong (lexicographic order in /etc/cni/net.d/), istio-cni is skipped.
  5. Existing pods not restarted after CNI install: istio-cni affects only NEW pods. Existing pods created with istio-init retain that init container until restarted.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Node iptables rules from previous CNI conflicting — old Calico/Cilium iptables rules interfere with istio-cni redirects
  2. istio-cni-node pod OOMKilled silently — CNI operations memory-intensive on large nodes
  3. SELinux blocking CNI operations — istio-cni needs privileges to write iptables rules and create network namespaces
  4. CNI config directory permissions wrong — /etc/cni/net.d not writable by istio-cni pod
  5. Race condition on node startup — kubelet starts pods before istio-cni DaemonSet pod is Ready on that node
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kubeadm with default CNI (Flannel/Calico): kubeadm clusters use a pod network CNI that may not chain correctly with istio-cni. Verify CNI chaining compatibility.
  2. kind cluster CNI directory restrictions: kind nodes have a specific CNI setup that may conflict with istio-cni's configuration.
  3. minikube with --cni flag: minikube started with a specific CNI may not support istio-cni chaining — check minikube CNI compatibility.
  4. GKE Autopilot restrictions: GKE Autopilot manages node networking and may not allow custom CNI plugins — istio-cni may not work as expected.
  5. Nodes running custom iptables rules: Security hardening scripts or custom firewall rules on nodes conflict with istio-cni's iptables modifications.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node -o wide One pod per node, all Running. Missing nodes = pods on those nodes won't get CNI-based traffic capture.
kubectl logs -n istio-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node --tail=50 CNI logs show iptables errors, CNI config conflicts, or permission issues.
kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -c "istio-init" Should return 0 if CNI is working — no istio-init container means CNI is handling traffic capture.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The injection template was not updated after installing istio-cni. Installing the CNI daemon is only half the process — the injection template must also be regenerated to exclude the istio-init container. Re-run istioctl install --set components.cni.enabled=true to update both the CNI DaemonSet AND the injection template.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify CNI DaemonSet is healthy on all nodes kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node -o wide Every node should have a Running CNI pod. If any node is missing, check taints/tolerations and nodeSelector.
2. Re-run install to update injection template istioctl install --set components.cni.enabled=true --set profile=default -y This updates the istio-sidecar-injector ConfigMap to exclude istio-init from the injection template.
3. Restart all application pods kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj New pods will be injected WITHOUT istio-init. Verify: kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep istio-init should return nothing.
4. Verify traffic capture on a test pod kubectl exec <pod> -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request GET /stats | grep "listener.*downstream_cx_total" Non-zero connection counts confirm Envoy is intercepting traffic via CNI rules.
5. Check CNI config on each node SSH to a node and check /etc/cni/net.d/ — the istio-cni config file should exist and be ordered before the primary CNI config.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Install istio-cni at initial Istio setup, not as an afterthought. Adding CNI later requires restarting every pod in the mesh — a disruptive operation in production. Enable CNI from day one, even if you don't think you need it yet.
CNI is becoming the default — learn it now. Newer Istio versions (1.22+) default to CNI-based traffic capture. The istio-init approach is being phased out. If you're starting fresh, install with CNI enabled.
Verify CNI on ALL nodes before considering it deployed. kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node -o wide A single node without the CNI pod means all pods on that node use istio-init fallback — inconsistent behavior across the cluster.
On your 6-cluster lab, test both approaches. Use istio-cni on kubeadm (production-like) and kind-cka-lab. Use istio-init on minikube (quick tests). Understanding both prepares you for any cluster configuration on the exam.
IC9
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC9
EnvoyFilter Breaking Mesh — Custom Configuration Causes Widespread Outages

🔍 Symptom: After applying an EnvoyFilter or WasmPlugin, services start failing across the mesh. Some pods return 503 errors, mTLS handshakes fail, or Envoy sidecars crash. istioctl analyze shows configuration errors related to the custom filter. Removing the EnvoyFilter restores service. The filter was applied mesh-wide (no workloadSelector) and the configuration is syntactically valid but semantically wrong for the current Envoy version.

  kubectl get envoyfilter,wasmplugin --all-namespaces
  NAMESPACE   NAME                    AGE
  istio-system custom-rate-limit      5m
  default     wasm-custom-auth        5m

  istioctl analyze --all-namespaces
  ❌ Error [IST0155] EnvoyFilter custom-rate-limit: configuration invalid
     for Envoy version 1.28 — field "typed_config" not recognized

  kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy | grep -i "filter\|reject\|wasm"
  [warning] Wasm service rejected config: failed to load plugin
  [error] EnvoyFilter config rejected: field not found in protobuf schema
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. EnvoyFilter applied mesh-wide without testing: The filter had no workloadSelector, so it applied to EVERY sidecar in the mesh. A bad filter configuration affects all services simultaneously. Always test with a targeted workloadSelector first.
  2. Envoy version incompatibility: The EnvoyFilter uses API fields that don't exist in the current Envoy version. EnvoyFilter is tightly coupled to Envoy's internal configuration schema — upgrading Istio can break filters written for older versions.
  3. WasmPlugin not available at specified URL: The OCI image or HTTP URL for the WASM module is inaccessible — Envoy can't download the plugin. The WasmPlugin is applied but silently fails because the binary can't be fetched.
  4. Filter priority conflict: The EnvoyFilter's insert position conflicts with Istio's built-in filters (e.g., trying to insert before the RBAC filter or HTTP connection manager). This causes Envoy to reject the entire listener configuration.
  5. Syntax valid, semantics wrong: The YAML passes kubectl validation and istiod accepts it, but Envoy rejects it at runtime because the protobuf structure doesn't match what Envoy expects. This is the most dangerous type — it applies silently and breaks traffic.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. WASM module OOM — the plugin compiled with memory leak slowly consumes all Envoy memory
  2. EnvoyFilter referencing a filter that was removed in newer Envoy version — filter chain name changed
  3. Multiple EnvoyFilters conflicting — two filters try to modify the same filter chain position
  4. WasmPlugin with CPU-intensive operation — custom auth hook does blocking I/O, starving Envoy worker threads
  5. OCI registry authentication failure — WasmPlugin can't pull the WASM binary due to missing imagePullSecrets
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Copy-pasted from older Istio version: EnvoyFilter YAML from Istio 1.18 applied to Istio 1.22 — API fields deprecated/removed between versions.
  2. Air-gapped cluster with no OCI registry: WasmPlugin references an external OCI registry that's not mirrored in the air-gapped environment.
  3. kind cluster with limited resources: WASM compilation or execution on kind nodes with limited CPU causes plugin load failures.
  4. Internet access blocked for egress: EnvoyFilter references external URLs that are blocked by cluster egress policies.
  5. New team learning EnvoyFilter: EnvoyFilter is powerful but complex — new adopters often apply broken configurations mesh-wide by accident.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get envoyfilter,wasmplugin --all-namespaces List all custom filters. Mesh-wide filters (no workloadSelector) affect every sidecar — these are the most dangerous.
istioctl analyze --all-namespaces Catches EnvoyFilter/WasmPlugin configuration errors BEFORE they break traffic. Run this before applying any custom filter.
kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy | grep -iE "filter|wasm|reject|config.*error" Envoy logs show exactly why a filter was rejected — version mismatch, missing field, load failure.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: An EnvoyFilter or WasmPlugin was applied mesh-wide (no workloadSelector) with configuration that is incompatible with the current Envoy version. EnvoyFilter is tightly coupled to Envoy's internal protobuf schema — what works in one Istio version may silently break in the next. Always test custom filters on a single workload before mesh-wide rollout.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Immediately remove the offending filter kubectl delete envoyfilter <name> -n <ns> This restores service immediately. Envoy hot-reloads the configuration without the broken filter.
2. Test with workloadSelector on a single deployment first Add workloadSelector: {labels: {app: test-app}} to limit the filter to a single deployment. Test thoroughly — metrics, mTLS, routing — before expanding scope.
3. Validate with istioctl analyze before applying istioctl analyze -f <filter-yaml> --all-namespaces Catches version incompatibilities and schema errors before the filter is applied to the cluster.
4. Prefer WasmPlugin over EnvoyFilter WasmPlugin is the modern, safer alternative. WASM modules are sandboxed (memory-safe) and version-independent. EnvoyFilter uses raw Envoy config that breaks across versions.
5. Use canary deployment for filter rollout Apply the filter to a canary namespace first, monitor for 24 hours, then expand to production. This limits blast radius if the filter is broken.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
EnvoyFilter is the escape hatch — use sparingly. 95% of use cases are covered by VirtualService, DestinationRule, and WasmPlugin. EnvoyFilter gives you raw access to Envoy's config — with great power comes great responsibility. If you can solve it with a standard CRD, do so.
Always use workloadSelector. Never apply mesh-wide. A mesh-wide EnvoyFilter without workloadSelector is a cluster-wide outage waiting to happen. One bad filter config breaks every sidecar in the mesh simultaneously.
Version-lock your EnvoyFilters with istio.io/rev. Annotate EnvoyFilters with the Istio revision they were tested against. When upgrading Istio, you know which filters need re-validation.
Practice filter rollback before you need it. kubectl delete envoyfilter <name> -n <ns> This single command is your emergency brake. Know it cold. When a bad filter breaks the mesh at 3 AM, you don't want to be searching documentation.
IC10
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC10
MeshConfig Corruption — istiod Won't Start or Behaves Unexpectedly

🔍 Symptom: istiod is CrashLoopBackOff or behaving unexpectedly after someone edited the istio ConfigMap in istio-system. The mesh configuration (meshConfig) has a YAML syntax error, an invalid field value, or a setting that conflicts with the installed components. kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod shows YAML parsing errors or configuration validation failures. Settings like outboundTrafficPolicy, accessLogFile, or defaultConfig were modified incorrectly.

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system | grep istiod
  istiod-7d8f9-x                           0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   12

  kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod --tail=30
  error: failed to parse mesh configuration
  yaml: line 15: did not find expected key
  invalid field "outbountTrafficPolicy" (typo: should be "outboundTrafficPolicy")
  fatal: mesh configuration validation failed — istiod cannot start

  kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml | head -30
  apiVersion: v1
  data:
    mesh: |
      accessLogFile: /dev/stdout
      outbountTrafficPolicy:    ← TYPO! "outbount" instead of "outbound"
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Manual kubectl edit introduced YAML error: Someone ran kubectl edit cm istio -n istio-system and made a typo — wrong indentation, misspelled field name, or invalid value. The ConfigMap is not validated until istiod restarts and tries to parse it.
  2. MeshConfig field name typo: Common misspellings: "outbountTrafficPolicy" (missing 'd'), "accessLogFile" misspelled, "enableAutoMtls" vs "enableAutoMtls" (case sensitivity). These are accepted by kubectl (ConfigMap is free-form YAML) but rejected by istiod.
  3. Indentation error in mesh config: The mesh config is a YAML string embedded in a ConfigMap. A single space of wrong indentation breaks the entire configuration. Use 2-space or 4-space indentation consistently.
  4. Conflicting settings with installed components: Setting a mesh config value that conflicts with the installed profile (e.g., disabling something the installed components expect).
  5. Missing backup before edit: No backup of the working ConfigMap was made before changes. The only way to recover is to remember the previous values or reinstall Istio.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Multiple people editing simultaneously — kubectl edit saves the last write, overwriting previous changes
  2. Copy-pasted mesh config from older Istio version — deprecated fields that are no longer valid
  3. IstioOperator and ConfigMap out of sync — IstioOperator sets one value, someone manually overrides in ConfigMap
  4. Encoding issue — non-ASCII characters accidentally introduced during edit (e.g., smart quotes from word processor)
  5. Istioctl install overwrites custom mesh config — running install resets ConfigMap to defaults, losing custom settings
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First Istio setup — team experimenting with mesh config: New users often edit the ConfigMap directly to understand settings, introducing errors.
  2. Following outdated blog post or tutorial: Mesh config format changed between Istio versions — old tutorials reference deprecated or renamed fields.
  3. kind cluster with resource constraints: istiod OOM during ConfigMap parsing — the error looks like config failure but is actually a resource issue.
  4. kubeadm cluster etcd issues: ConfigMap updates fail to persist to etcd, leaving istiod with partially written configuration.
  5. Automation script with hardcoded old values: An Ansible/Terraform/script applies an old mesh config that conflicts with the current Istio version.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod --tail=50 | grep -iE "parse|yaml|mesh|config.*error" istiod logs tell you the EXACT line and field that's invalid. The error message includes the problematic YAML key.
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml Visually inspect the mesh config for obvious typos, indentation errors, or invalid values.
diff <istioctl profile dump default> <kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}') Compare current ConfigMap against the default profile to identify custom changes that may be causing issues.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Manual editing of the istio ConfigMap introduced a YAML syntax error (typo, wrong indentation, or invalid field name). Kubectl accepts the ConfigMap update (it's free-form YAML), but istiod rejects it at startup because the mesh config fails validation. Always backup the ConfigMap before editing and validate the YAML syntax before restarting istiod.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Restore from backup (if you have one) kubectl apply -f istio-cm-backup.yaml Always backup the ConfigMap before editing: kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml > backup.yaml.
2. Fix the YAML error in the ConfigMap kubectl edit cm istio -n istio-system Correct the typo or indentation. Kill the istiod pod — it will restart and load the corrected config.
3. If no backup, reset to defaults and re-apply customizations istioctl install --set profile=default This regenerates the ConfigMap with default values. Then re-apply your custom settings (one at a time, verifying istiod starts after each).
4. Use IstioOperator for mesh config instead of ConfigMap Configure mesh settings in an IstioOperator YAML file in Git, applied via istioctl apply -f iop.yaml. This is auditable, version-controlled, and validated before application.
5. Validate mesh config syntax before applying kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | python3 -c "import sys,yaml; yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin); print('OK')" A quick YAML syntax check catches typos and indentation errors before they crash istiod.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
ALWAYS backup the ConfigMap before editing. kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml > istio-cm-$(date +%Y%m%d).yaml A 5-second backup saves hours of recovery. Make this a habit before every ConfigMap change.
Use IstioOperator, not kubectl edit, for mesh config. The IstioOperator API validates configuration before applying it. Direct ConfigMap editing bypasses all validation. For production, maintain an IstioOperator YAML in Git and apply with istioctl.
Validate YAML before applying. kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | yq eval A simple YAML parser catches syntax errors instantly. Add this to your pre-edit checklist.
Test mesh config changes on kind-cka-lab first. Your 6-cluster lab includes a dedicated kind-cka-lab cluster. Test ConfigMap changes there before applying to the kubeadm production cluster. If istiod crashes on kind, you've saved a production outage.

📌 IC11–IC15: Istio Upgrades & Version Management

IC11
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC11
In-Place Upgrade Fails — istiod CrashLoopBackOff After Upgrade

🔍 Symptom: You ran istioctl upgrade to move from Istio 1.21 to 1.22. The upgrade appeared to complete, but now istiod is in CrashLoopBackOff, the ingress gateway pods are stuck in Pending, and all new sidecars fail to inject. istioctl verify-install reports missing components. Running kubectl get pods -n istio-system shows the old istiod pod terminated but the new one won't start. The anihpj/jobpost application can't serve traffic because the mesh control plane is down.

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system
  NAME                                   READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
  istiod-7d8f9-new                       0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   12
  istiod-abc123-old                       1/1     Terminating        0
  istio-ingressgateway-xxx                1/1     Running            0

  kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod --tail=30
  error: failed to start: CRD "virtualservices.networking.istio.io"
         is missing required field "spec.address" in version v1beta1
  fatal: CRD validation failed — istiod cannot start with outdated CRDs

  istioctl verify-install
  ❌ CRDs: 48 installed, 55 required       ← 7 CRDs missing/outdated!
  ❌ Istiod Deployment: 0/1 replicas available
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CRDs not upgraded before istiod: Istio upgrades require updating CRDs BEFORE upgrading the control plane. Running istioctl upgrade without first applying new CRDs (istioctl manifest generate or helm upgrade base) causes istiod to fail because it expects new API fields that don't exist in old CRDs. Check: kubectl get crds | grep istio.
  2. Incompatible mesh config between versions: The mesh ConfigMap (istio in istio-system) contains settings from the old version that are deprecated or renamed in the new version. istiod reads the ConfigMap on startup and fails if it finds unknown fields.
  3. Webhook configuration not updated: The MutatingWebhookConfiguration and ValidatingWebhookConfiguration still reference the OLD istiod Service or old CA bundle. New istiod pods can't serve webhook requests because the webhook configuration points to terminated pods.
  4. Old envoy sidecars incompatible with new istiod: If the upgrade didn't update the injection template, existing sidecars run old Envoy versions that may not communicate correctly with the new istiod (xDS protocol changes between versions).
  5. New istiod can't write to existing resources: RBAC changes between Istio versions may revoke permissions the old ServiceAccount had. New istiod pods fail to reconcile existing VirtualServices/DestinationRules.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. etcd corruption during upgrade — ConfigMap/CRD writes partially committed, leaving inconsistent state
  2. New istiod image pull fails — the upgraded image tag doesn't exist in the registry or requires authentication
  3. PodDisruptionBudget blocking rollout — PDB minAvailable prevents old istiod from terminating for new one to start
  4. Resource quota exhausted in istio-system — new istiod exceeds namespace resource quota after upgrade
  5. NodeSelector/Affinity changes in new version — new istiod has different scheduling requirements and no nodes match
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Skipping multiple minor versions: Upgrading from Istio 1.18 directly to 1.22 — skipping versions is unsupported. Istio supports upgrades of at most ONE minor version at a time (1.21 → 1.22, not 1.18 → 1.22).
  2. Helm-based install upgraded with istioctl: Helm-managed Istio upgraded via istioctl upgrade — the two management methods conflict and leave inconsistent resource states.
  3. kind cluster resource starvation: The upgrade deploys new pods before old ones terminate — kind node runs out of CPU/memory, new istiod gets OOMKilled.
  4. kubeadm cluster API server version too old: New Istio CRDs require Kubernetes API features not available in older kubeadm clusters (e.g., v1 CRD structural schemas).
  5. Air-gapped cluster with stale images: The new Istio version images weren't mirrored to the air-gapped registry before upgrade was attempted.
🔍 What to Look At:
istioctl verify-install The single most important post-upgrade check. Shows exactly which components (CRDs, Deployments, webhooks) are out of sync with the expected version.
kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod --tail=50 | grep -iE "crd|deprecated|unknown field|version" istiod logs tell you the EXACT CRD or config field that's causing the failure. "CRD missing field" = CRDs not upgraded first.
kubectl get crds | grep istio | wc -l && istioctl manifest generate --set profile=default | grep -c "kind: CustomResourceDefinition" Compare installed CRD count vs expected count. Mismatch means CRDs weren't applied during upgrade.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: CRDs were not upgraded before the control plane. Istio upgrades MUST follow the sequence: 1) Upgrade CRDs first, 2) Upgrade control plane (istiod), 3) Upgrade data plane (sidecars). Running istioctl upgrade without first generating and applying new CRDs leaves istiod expecting API fields that don't exist in the old CRD definitions — istiod crashes because it can't validate resources.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Immediately roll back to previous version istioctl install --set profile=default --set hub=gcr.io/istio-release --set tag=1.21.0 Re-install the previous working version to restore the mesh control plane. This is an emergency rollback — the old CRDs are still in place and compatible.
2. Upgrade CRDs FIRST (the correct sequence) istioctl manifest generate --set profile=default --set tag=1.22.1 | grep -A1000 "kind: CustomResourceDefinition" | kubectl apply -f - Apply ALL new CRDs before upgrading istiod. Or use kubectl apply -f istio-1.22.1/manifests/charts/base/crds/.
3. Upgrade the control plane istioctl upgrade --set profile=default --set tag=1.22.1 With new CRDs in place, istiod starts successfully. Verify: istioctl verify-install.
4. Verify webhook configurations updated kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector -o yaml | grep "caBundle" The CA bundle should be updated to match the new istiod's certificate. If stale, restart istiod to regenerate webhook configs.
5. Restart application pods to upgrade sidecars kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj Existing pods still have old Envoy versions. Rolling restart injects new sidecars matching the upgraded control plane.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Remember the golden upgrade sequence: CRDs → Control Plane → Data Plane. This is non-negotiable. CRDs first (so the API knows about new fields), then istiod (the brain), then sidecars (the muscles). Skip any step and the mesh breaks. Write this on a sticky note.
Always upgrade ONE minor version at a time. Istio supports N→N+1 upgrades only. 1.18→1.22 requires four sequential upgrades: 1.18→1.19→1.20→1.21→1.22. Skipping versions is unsupported and will break the mesh.
Test upgrades on kind-cka-lab before production kubeadm. Your 6-cluster lab lets you practice the full upgrade sequence in isolation. Upgrade kind-cka-lab from 1.21→1.22, verify with istioctl verify-install, then apply the same procedure to kubeadm.
Always have a rollback plan before upgrading. istioctl install --set profile=default --set tag=<OLD_VERSION> Know the command to roll back to the previous version. If the upgrade fails, the mesh is down — you don't want to be reading docs at 3 AM.
IC12
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC12
Canary Upgrade Misconfigured — Revision Labels Wrong, Sidecars on Wrong Version

🔍 Symptom: You attempted a canary upgrade of Istio (deploying new revision alongside old) but namespaces aren't migrating correctly. Some pods in the anihpj namespace still run old sidecars, others get the new version — or worse, pods fail to inject entirely because istio.io/rev labels are misconfigured. istioctl proxy-status shows Envoys connecting to different istiod revisions. The mesh is fragmented: some services have new features, others don't, and mTLS between old and new Envoys may fail.

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system
  NAME                                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  istiod-stable-7d8f9                    1/1     Running   0
  istiod-canary-abc123                   1/1     Running   0

  kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels
  NAME     STATUS   LABELS
  anihpj   Active   istio.io/rev=canary   ← Should be "stable"!

  istioctl proxy-status
  NAME                          ISTIOD
  anihpj-web-xxx.anihpj         istiod-canary    ← Wrong: should be stable
  anihpj-api-yyy.anihpj         istiod-stable
  anihpj-db-0.anihpj            NONE              ← Injection FAILED!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Namespace labeled with wrong revision: istio.io/rev=canary was applied to the production namespace. The canary revision may not have all features validated yet. Check: kubectl get ns <ns> --show-labels. Fix: kubectl label ns <ns> istio.io/rev=stable --overwrite.
  2. Both istio-injection=enabled AND istio.io/rev set: The namespace has both labels. When istio-injection=enabled and istio.io/rev coexist, rev takes precedence. But if the revision doesn't exist, injection silently fails. Remove the conflicting istio-injection label.
  3. Canary revision not fully deployed: The istiod-canary deployment exists but its MutatingWebhookConfiguration isn't scoped correctly — the webhook namespaceSelector doesn't match the labels applied to the namespace.
  4. Revision tag misconfigured: istio.io/rev=canary is a TAG that points to an IstioRevision resource. If the IstioRevision or the tag isn't configured correctly, injection resolves to nothing — pods get NO sidecar.
  5. Default revision not set: No defaultRevision is configured in the IstioOperator. Namespaces WITHOUT an explicit istio.io/rev label get NO injection when only canary is deployed, because there's no default to fall back to.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Canary istiod uses different trust domain — mTLS between stable and canary Envoys fails because SPIFFE IDs differ
  2. Webhook failure policy is Fail — when canary istiod is unreachable, ALL pod creation in labeled namespaces fails
  3. IstioRevision resource not created — the canary revision was deployed via istioctl but the IstioRevision CR wasn't generated
  4. Pod-level annotation overrides namespace label — sidecar.istio.io/rev: stable on pod vs namespace label istio.io/rev=canary
  5. Old injection ConfigMap not cleaned up — istio-sidecar-injector ConfigMap from old version conflicts with revision-based injection
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First canary upgrade attempt: The team has never done a canary upgrade before and doesn't understand the revision labeling model — they applied the canary label to all namespaces by mistake.
  2. Multiple clusters with different revision states: In the 6-cluster lab, kind-cka-lab was upgraded to canary but kubeadm is still stable — someone applied the same namespace labels across clusters.
  3. Argo CD or Flux syncing old labels: GitOps tool reverts namespace labels to previous revision after manual change, causing oscillation between revisions.
  4. New cluster with only canary revision installed: The "stable" revision was never deployed — only canary exists, but the default revision tag points to "stable".
  5. kind cluster with multiple istiod revisions competing for limited resources — one istiod gets starved and stops serving xDS
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get ns <ns> --show-labels | grep "istio.io/rev\|istio-injection" Shows which revision label (if any) is applied. Both labels present = rev takes precedence. Neither = no injection (unless defaultRevision is set).
istioctl proxy-status Shows which istiod each Envoy is connected to. Mixed ISTIOD values indicate fragmented mesh — some sidecars on old revision, some on new.
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration -o yaml | grep -A10 "istio.io/rev" Verify each revision has its own webhook configuration with the correct namespaceSelector matching namespace labels.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The namespace istio.io/rev label points to a canary revision that may not be intended for production, or the label is mismatched with the deployed revisions. During canary upgrades, namespaces must be intentionally migrated from stable → canary one at a time. Accidentally labeling all namespaces with istio.io/rev=canary defeats the purpose of canary deployment and risks mesh fragmentation.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify all deployed revisions kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod -o wide Confirm both stable and canary istiod pods are Running. Note which revision is which.
2. Fix namespace labels — production uses stable kubectl label ns anihpj istio.io/rev=stable --overwrite Migrate production namespaces back to stable. Only test/canary namespaces should use the canary revision.
3. Remove conflicting istio-injection label kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection- When using revision-based injection, remove the old istio-injection=enabled label to avoid conflicts.
4. Restart pods to reconnect to correct istiod kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj Existing pods connected to istiod-canary will reconnect to istiod-stable after restart.
5. Set defaultRevision for safety istioctl install --set profile=default --set revision=stable --set defaultRevision=stable Namespaces without an explicit rev label will use the default revision. This prevents silent injection failures.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Canary upgrade is the SAFEST way to upgrade Istio. Deploy the new revision alongside the old one. Migrate ONE namespace at a time — test thoroughly, then move the next. If something breaks, flip the label back to stable. Zero-downtime rollback.
Never use both istio-injection AND istio.io/rev on the same namespace. kubectl label ns <ns> istio-injection- These labels conflict. istio.io/rev is the modern way; istio-injection=enabled is the legacy way. Pick one. When doing canary upgrades, use rev exclusively.
Always set a defaultRevision. Without it, namespaces with neither label get NO sidecar injection. With it, they gracefully fall back to the default revision. This single setting prevents a whole class of injection failures.
Practice canary upgrades on your 6-cluster lab. Use kind-cl1 as stable, deploy canary on kind-cl2. Practice migrating anihpj from stable → canary → stable. Master the revision labeling workflow before attempting in production kubeadm.
IC13
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC13
CRD Upgrade Skipped — API Version Conflicts After Istio Upgrade

🔍 Symptom: Istio was upgraded but CRDs were not applied first, or only partially applied. Existing Istio resources (VirtualServices, DestinationRules, Gateways) work with the old API version but new resources fail validation. kubectl apply -f virtualservice.yaml returns errors like "no matches for kind VirtualService in version networking.istio.io/v1alpha3" or validation errors about missing fields. The anihpj canary deployment VirtualService can't be applied because the API server doesn't recognize the new schema.

  kubectl apply -f istio/10-virtualservice-canary.yaml
  error: resource mapping not found for name: "anihpj-api-canary"
  namespace: "anihpj" from "istio/10-virtualservice-canary.yaml":
  no matches for kind "VirtualService" in version "networking.istio.io/v1"
  (available versions: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3, networking.istio.io/v1beta1)

  kubectl get crds | grep istio | sort
  authorizationpolicies.security.istio.io          2025-01-15T10:00:00Z
  destinationrules.networking.istio.io              2025-01-15T10:00:00Z
  envoyfilters.networking.istio.io                  2025-01-15T10:00:00Z
  gateways.networking.istio.io                      2025-01-15T10:00:00Z
  peerauthentications.security.istio.io             2025-01-15T10:00:00Z
  (virtualservices CRD shows v1beta1 but not v1!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CRDs not upgraded at all: The upgrade command was run but the CRD update step was completely skipped. Old CRDs only know about the old API versions (v1alpha3, v1beta1). New Istio resources use v1 — which doesn't exist in old CRDs. Check: kubectl get crd virtualservices.networking.istio.io -o yaml | grep -A5 "versions:".
  2. Partial CRD upgrade — only some CRDs applied: The CRD manifest was applied but some CRDs failed due to conflicts or timeouts. Check: kubectl get crds | grep istio — compare the count against the expected list from istioctl manifest generate.
  3. CRD conversion webhook not working: Newer Istio CRDs use conversion webhooks to support multiple API versions simultaneously. If the webhook is not configured or istiod is down, the API server can't convert between versions.
  4. Stored version mismatch: The CRD's storage version was updated but existing resources are stored in the old version. The API server can't serve them in the new version without conversion.
  5. Helm CRD management issue: Helm does NOT upgrade CRDs by default on helm upgrade (CRDs are a special resource class). The CRDs must be manually upgraded with kubectl apply -f base/crds/ before helm upgrade.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Custom resources stuck in terminating — old CRD version can't be removed because resources still reference it
  2. Multiple Istio operators installing CRDs — istioctl and Helm both tried to manage CRDs and one overwrote the other
  3. API server caching old CRD schema — after CRD upgrade, the API server cache hasn't invalidated yet (rare, resolves within minutes)
  4. CRD too large for etcd — Kubernetes has a 1MB limit per object; very large CRDs with many versions can exceed this
  5. RBAC preventing CRD updates — the user or ServiceAccount running the upgrade doesn't have permissions to modify CRDs
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kubeadm cluster with old Kubernetes version: Kubernetes versions before 1.22 may not support the CRD v1 structural schema — Istio CRDs require Kubernetes 1.22+.
  2. kind cluster with limited etcd: Applying 55+ CRDs simultaneously on a resource-constrained kind cluster may timeout or partially fail.
  3. GKE/AKS/EKS managed CRD limitations: Managed Kubernetes services may throttle CRD operations or have restrictions on CRD modification.
  4. GitOps reconciliation reverting CRDs: Argo CD or Flux has the old CRD manifests in Git and reverts the manual upgrade — CRDs must be updated in Git first.
  5. OpenShift SecurityContextConstraints blocking CRD operators — OpenShift requires specific SCC for CRD controllers.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get crd virtualservices.networking.istio.io -o yaml | grep -A10 "versions:" Shows which API versions are available. If v1 is missing, CRDs weren't upgraded. New Istio resources that use v1 will fail.
kubectl get crds | grep istio | wc -l Should match the expected count for your Istio version (typically 55+). Fewer = some CRDs failed to apply during upgrade.
kubectl api-resources | grep istio Lists all Istio API resources known to the API server. Compare against the Istio version's expected resource list.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: CRDs were not upgraded before or during the Istio upgrade. New Istio CRDs introduce new API versions (e.g., v1) and new fields. Without upgraded CRDs, the API server doesn't know about the new versions, and kubectl apply fails because the resource schema doesn't match. CRD upgrade is the FIRST step in any Istio upgrade — always before upgrading istiod.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Apply ALL CRDs from the new version kubectl apply -f https://github.com/istio/istio/releases/download/1.22.1/istio-1.22.1-crds.yaml Or download and apply: istioctl manifest generate --set profile=default | grep "kind: CustomResourceDefinition" -A10000 | kubectl apply -f -.
2. Verify all CRDs were applied kubectl get crds | grep istio | wc -l Compare against the expected count. Wait 30 seconds for CRDs to be fully registered before creating resources.
3. Check for conversion webhook health kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration,mutatingwebhookconfiguration | grep istio If istiod was restarted after CRD upgrade, webhooks should point to the running istiod.
4. Re-apply Istio resources with new API version kubectl apply -f istio/ -n anihpj Once CRDs support the new versions, re-apply your VirtualServices, DestinationRules, etc. They'll be stored in the new format.
5. For Helm installs, manually upgrade CRDs kubectl apply -f istio-1.22.1/manifests/charts/base/crds/ Helm does NOT automatically upgrade CRDs. This must be done manually before helm upgrade of istio-base/istiod.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
CRDs first. ALWAYS. No exceptions. Before any istioctl upgrade or helm upgrade, apply the CRDs. This is the #1 cause of failed Istio upgrades. Make CRD upgrade the first item in your upgrade runbook checklist.
Verify CRD count after upgrade. kubectl get crds | grep istio | wc -l A 5-second check that catches the most common upgrade failure. If the count is wrong, stop and investigate before proceeding with istiod upgrade.
Helm users: CRDs are YOUR responsibility. Unlike Deployments and ConfigMaps, Helm does not upgrade CRDs. The helm upgrade command skips CRDs entirely. You must manually apply the CRD YAML before upgrading the Helm charts.
Use istioctl manifest generate for CRD inspection. istioctl manifest generate --set profile=default > full-manifest.yaml This generates ALL resources including CRDs. Review the CRDs section to understand what new fields and API versions are being introduced in the upgrade.
IC14
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC14
Ambient Mode — Waypoint Proxy Not Working, ztunnel Failing

🔍 Symptom: Istio ambient mode was installed (istioctl install --set profile=ambient) instead of sidecar mode. The ztunnel DaemonSet is running, but traffic is not being intercepted, or L7 policies (AuthorizationPolicy, RequestAuthentication) are not being enforced. istioctl waypoint list shows no waypoint proxies. Application pods in the anihpj namespace don't have sidecars (which is expected in ambient), but their traffic isn't going through ztunnel either — services communicate directly without mTLS or policy enforcement.

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system
  NAME                                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  istiod-ambient-xxx                     1/1     Running   0
  ztunnel-yyy                            1/1     Running   0

  istioctl waypoint list
  No waypoint proxies found in any namespace   ← L7 policies won't work!

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  NAME                           READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  anihpj-web-xxx                 1/1     Running   0   ← No sidecar (ambient)
  (expected in ambient — but traffic must go through ztunnel!)

  kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=ztunnel --tail=10
  error: failed to create tunnel: permission denied
  warning: iptables rules not applied — node firewall blocking
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ztunnel not running on all nodes: ztunnel is a DaemonSet that must run on EVERY node. If a node is missing ztunnel (taints, nodeSelector, resources), pods on that node bypass the mesh entirely — no mTLS, no policies. Check: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=ztunnel -o wide.
  2. Waypoint proxy not deployed for namespace: Ambient mode handles L4 (mTLS, authZ) via ztunnel automatically, but L7 policies (HTTP routing, JWT auth) require a waypoint proxy. It doesn't deploy automatically — you must run istioctl waypoint apply -n <ns>.
  3. Namespace not labeled for ambient: Ambient uses istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient label instead of istio-injection=enabled. If the namespace isn't labeled, ztunnel won't redirect traffic from its pods. Check: kubectl get ns <ns> --show-labels.
