  4. CNI conflict with ztunnel iptables: ztunnel uses iptables to redirect pod traffic (similar to istio-init). If the existing CNI (Calico, Cilium) has conflicting iptables rules, ztunnel's redirects may not take effect.
  5. Mixed sidecar and ambient in same namespace: Some pods have sidecars (from old injection label), others rely on ambient. The sidecar and ztunnel both try to intercept traffic, creating routing loops or dropped connections.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. ztunnel OOMKilled on nodes with many pods — ztunnel is lightweight but hundreds of pods per node create many tunnels
  2. HBONE (HTTP-Based Overlay Network Encapsulation) port conflict — port 15008 used by ztunnel conflicts with another service
  3. Waypoint proxy resource starvation — waypoint is an Envoy deployment that needs sufficient CPU/memory for L7 processing
  4. DNS resolution inside ztunnel failing — ztunnel uses DNS for service discovery and can't resolve service names
  5. Ambient profile incomplete — installed with wrong profile or missing components (ztunnel DaemonSet not generated)
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Ambient is still alpha/beta: In older Istio versions, ambient mode is experimental. Features may be incomplete or buggy. Verify your Istio version fully supports ambient.
  2. kind cluster kernel version too old: ztunnel uses eBPF and modern kernel features — older kind node images may have kernels that don't support required features.
  3. kubeadm cluster with custom CNI: Custom CNI plugins that manage iptables directly may conflict with ztunnel's traffic capture mechanism.
  4. GKE/AKS/EKS ambient support: Managed Kubernetes services may not yet support ambient mode — ztunnel requires specific node-level permissions that managed services restrict.
  5. New team unaware ambient doesn't auto-create waypoints: Team assumes ambient "just works" like sidecar mode, but waypoint proxies for L7 must be explicitly deployed per namespace.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=ztunnel -o wide One ztunnel pod per node, all Running. Missing nodes = pods on those nodes have NO mesh protection.
istioctl waypoint list --all-namespaces Shows deployed waypoint proxies. Empty list = no L7 policy enforcement in any namespace.
kubectl get ns <ns> --show-labels | grep "dataplane-mode" Namespace must have istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient for ztunnel to intercept traffic from its pods.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Ambient mode requires explicit setup beyond just installing the profile. The namespace must be labeled with istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient, ztunnel must run on all nodes, and a waypoint proxy must be deployed for L7 policies. Unlike sidecar mode (which auto-injects), ambient has separate per-component setup steps that are easy to miss.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify ambient profile is installed correctly istioctl install --set profile=ambient --set tag=1.22.1 -y Installs istiod + ztunnel DaemonSet. Verify: kubectl get pods -n istio-system | grep ztunnel.
2. Label namespace for ambient data plane mode kubectl label namespace anihpj istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient This tells ztunnel to intercept traffic from pods in this namespace. Without it, pods bypass the mesh.
3. Verify ztunnel is intercepting traffic kubectl exec <ztunnel-pod> -n istio-system -- curl localhost:15020/stats | grep "inbound" Inbound connection stats show if ztunnel is successfully capturing pod traffic.
4. Deploy waypoint proxy for L7 policies istioctl waypoint apply -n anihpj --enroll-namespace Creates a waypoint proxy Deployment in the namespace and labels it for L7 traffic routing. Verify: istioctl waypoint list.
5. Restart pods to establish ztunnel tunnels kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj Existing pods may not have tunnels established. Restarting ensures all traffic flows through ztunnel.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Ambient is the future — learn it now. Istio ambient mesh eliminates sidecars entirely, reducing resource overhead by ~90%. It's the recommended path for new deployments in Istio 1.22+. Master both sidecar and ambient modes — the ICA exam may test ambient concepts.
Ambient L4 (ztunnel) is automatic. L7 (waypoint) is NOT. mTLS and L4 authorization work automatically via ztunnel. L7 policies (HTTP routing, JWT, rate limiting) require an explicit waypoint proxy deployment. This is the #1 ambient gotcha.
Test ambient on your 6-cluster lab. Use minikube for ambient mode experiments (easy reset). Compare sidecar vs ambient resource usage on kind-cka-lab. Practice switching anihpj between sidecar and ambient modes.
Don't mix sidecar and ambient in the same namespace. Ambient-mode namespaces should NOT have sidecar-injected pods. Remove istio-injection=enabled and use only istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient. Mixed pods cause traffic routing conflicts.
IC15
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC15
Multi-Revision Sidecars — Canary Upgrade Complete But Old Envoys Won't Upgrade

🔍 Symptom: A canary upgrade from Istio 1.21 to 1.22 was completed — all namespaces migrated to istio.io/rev=stable (which now points to 1.22). However, some pods in the anihpj namespace still run Envoy 1.21 sidecars. istioctl version shows a mix of data plane versions. The old sidecars still connect to the old istiod (which was supposedly removed), or worse — they can't get config updates because the old istiod is gone. New VirtualService rules don't apply to pods with old sidecars.

  istioctl version
  client version: 1.22.1
  control plane version: 1.22.1
  data plane version: 1.21.0 (13 proxies), 1.22.1 (7 proxies)  ← MIXED!

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  NAME                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  anihpj-web-xxx           2/2     Running   0          5m   ← New pod (1.22)
  anihpj-api-yyy           2/2     Running   0          3d   ← OLD pod (1.21)!
  anihpj-db-0              2/2     Running   0          5m   ← New pod (1.22)

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-yyy -c istio-proxy | grep -i "version\|istiod"
  [warning] Connected to istiod-stable.istio-system.svc (1.22.1)
  [warning] Version mismatch: proxy 1.21.0, control plane 1.22.1
  [warning] xDS stream: config may be incompatible
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Pods not restarted after namespace label change: The namespace label was changed from istio.io/rev=old to istio.io/rev=stable, but existing pods weren't restarted. Existing pods retain their original injected sidecar (old Envoy version) until recreated. Only NEW pods get the new sidecar. Fix: kubectl rollout restart deploy -n <ns>.
  2. StatefulSet pods not restarted: StatefulSets (like anihpj-db) are often forgotten during restart campaigns. They retain old sidecars indefinitely because StatefulSet pods aren't typically included in kubectl rollout restart deploy.
  3. Old istiod revision still running: After migrating namespaces to the new revision, the old istiod was not removed. Some Envoys still have long-lived gRPC connections to the old istiod. They don't switch to the new istiod until the old one is terminated.
  4. PodDisruptionBudget preventing restart: A PDB on the anihpj-api deployment prevents rolling restart from evicting old pods. The restart command appears to succeed but pods are never actually recreated.
  5. Stale xDS cache in old Envoys: Old Envoys with cached config keep serving traffic with outdated routes. Even after istiod upgrade, they don't fetch new config because the xDS stream error handling varies between Envoy versions.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Multiple namespace labels causing injection from wrong revision — istio-injection=enabled overrides istio.io/rev
  2. Sidecar resource with workloadSelector scoping specific pods to old revision — Sidecar CR overrides namespace label
  3. Immutable pods (Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets) — completed Job pods can't be "restarted" and retain old sidecars
  4. Image pull policy Always not set — node has cached old proxyv2 image and keeps using it even for new pods
  5. Custom injection template with hardcoded old version — someone modified the injector ConfigMap to pin a specific proxy version
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Cluster with many long-running pods: Production databases, message brokers, and stateful services may have uptime of weeks/months — they retain old sidecars long after an upgrade.
  2. kubeadm cluster with manual pod management: Pods managed outside Deployments/StatefulSets (bare pods, static pods) are never restarted automatically.
  3. kind cluster with limited resources: Restarting all pods simultaneously on kind exhausts resources — pods get stuck in Pending and never get new sidecars.
  4. Multiple teams managing different namespaces: The platform team migrated one namespace but didn't communicate to the anihpj team that they need to restart their pods.
  5. Air-gapped cluster with old proxyv2 image cached: The new proxy image wasn't pushed to the air-gapped registry, so new pods fall back to the cached old image.
🔍 What to Look At:
istioctl version The "data plane version" line shows how many proxies are on each version. Mixed versions = some pods haven't been restarted.
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.metadata.creationTimestamp}{"\n"}{end}' Shows pod ages. Old creation timestamps = pods that haven't been restarted since the upgrade.
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod If OLD revision istiod pods are still Running, some Envoys are still connected to them. Remove old revision.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Pods were not restarted after the namespace revision label was changed. Changing the istio.io/rev label only affects NEW pods created after the change. Existing pods retain their original injected sidecar version until they are deleted and recreated. A rolling restart of all deployments and statefulsets is mandatory after any revision label change.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Identify pods with old sidecars istioctl proxy-config bootstrap <pod> -n <ns> | grep ISTIO_VERSION Check the Envoy version in each pod. Any pod with old version needs restarting.
2. Restart Deployments (rolling) kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj Rolling restart creates new pods with the correct sidecar version. Old pods terminate gracefully.
3. Restart StatefulSets separately kubectl rollout restart sts -n anihpj StatefulSets are not included in deploy restart. Restart them explicitly — they restart one pod at a time in order.
4. Remove old istiod revision istioctl uninstall --revision=old Once all namespaces are migrated, remove the old istiod. This forces any remaining old Envoys to reconnect to the new istiod.
5. Verify uniform data plane version istioctl version All proxies should now show the same version. Zero proxies on old version = migration complete.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Restart pods is NOT optional after an upgrade. Changing the namespace label tells new pods which revision to inject — it does NOT change existing pods. Every upgrade must end with a full rollout restart of all workloads.
Check StatefulSets and DaemonSets separately. kubectl rollout restart sts -n <ns> kubectl rollout restart deploy only restarts Deployments. StatefulSets, DaemonSets, and bare pods must be restarted individually. These are the most commonly forgotten workloads.
Remove the old revision after migration is complete. Leaving old istiod pods running after all namespaces have migrated wastes resources and can cause subtle issues — Envoys may maintain connections to the old control plane indefinitely.
Use istioctl version as your upgrade completion check. This single command tells you if ANY proxy is still on the old version. Run it after every upgrade and restart campaign. Mixed data plane versions = incomplete upgrade.

📌 IC16–IC20: Advanced Installation & Configuration

IC16
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC16
Istio Uninstall Leaves Orphaned Resources — Pods Stuck, Traffic Broken

🔍 Symptom: Istio was uninstalled via istioctl uninstall or helm uninstall, but orphaned resources remain: MutatingWebhookConfigurations still reference the now-deleted istiod Service, CRDs still exist (preventing namespace cleanup), and sidecar-injected pods in the anihpj namespace are stuck in CrashLoopBackOff or Terminating because their istio-proxy containers can't connect to the removed control plane. The application is completely down because Envoy sidecars are failing but still attached to every pod.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  NAME                     READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
  anihpj-web-xxx           1/2     CrashLoopBackOff   45
  anihpj-api-yyy           1/2     CrashLoopBackOff   38
  anihpj-db-0              2/2     Running            0    ← Not injected (StatefulSet)

  kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration | grep istio
  istio-sidecar-injector          2d   ← STILL PRESENT after uninstall!

  kubectl get crds | grep istio
  (55 CRDs still installed)   ← Preventing clean namespace deletion!

  kubectl describe pod anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep -A5 "istio-proxy"
  State: Waiting (CrashLoopBackOff)
  Reason: Error — cannot connect to istiod.istio-system.svc:15012
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Pods not restarted BEFORE uninstall: Application pods still have istio-proxy containers injected. After control plane removal, these sidecars can't get certificates or config — they crash repeatedly. Always restart pods to remove sidecars BEFORE uninstalling Istio.
  2. MutatingWebhookConfiguration not cleaned up: istioctl uninstall may not remove the webhook. Future pod creation in labeled namespaces fails because the webhook tries to call the non-existent istiod. Check: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration | grep istio.
  3. CRDs not deleted after uninstall: Istio CRDs (VirtualService, DestinationRule, etc.) persist after uninstall. This prevents kubectl delete ns <ns> because the namespace contains custom resources with finalizers. CRDs must be deleted manually.
  4. Namespace labels not removed before uninstall: The anihpj namespace still has istio-injection=enabled. New pods would fail injection because istiod is gone. Labels must be removed before or immediately after uninstall.
  5. Istio CNI plugin still on nodes: istio-cni DaemonSet pods may persist after control plane removal. They continue to modify iptables, redirecting traffic to non-existent Envoy proxies — packets are blackholed.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm uninstall incomplete — istio-base chart left resources (CRDs, cluster roles) after istiod chart removed
  2. Finalizers on Istio resources blocking deletion — custom resources with istio finalizers can't be deleted without control plane
  3. ValidatingWebhookConfiguration blocking pod updates — webhook rejects pod modifications because istiod validation endpoint is gone
  4. Istio Secrets (cacerts, istio-ca-secret) persist in istio-system — namespace deletion blocked by remaining secrets
  5. RBAC ClusterRoleBindings for istiod ServiceAccount not removed — dangling RBAC references
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Test cluster cleanup gone wrong: Team uninstalled Istio from kind-cka-lab to start fresh but orphaned resources prevent clean reinstall.
  2. Istio reinstalled over orphaned resources: New install conflicts with old CRDs and webhooks — new istiod can't start because old resources exist.
  3. kubeadm cluster with manual Istio install: Installation done without istioctl (manual YAML apply) — no manifest to reference for clean uninstall.
  4. Namespace stuck in Terminating: anihpj namespace can't be deleted because it contains Istio custom resources with finalizers that call the removed control plane.
  5. minikube with leftover istio-cni: minikube node's iptables still has Istio redirect rules after uninstall — traffic to any port 15001 gets redirected to nothing.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration,validatingwebhookconfiguration | grep istio Webhooks should NOT exist after uninstall. If present, they'll interfere with pod creation and updates.
kubectl get crds | grep istio | wc -l Should return 0 after a clean uninstall. Non-zero means CRDs are orphaned — manual cleanup required.
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -c "istio-proxy" Count how many pods still have Envoy sidecars. These pods will break when the control plane is removed.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Application pods were not restarted to remove sidecars BEFORE Istio was uninstalled. The istioctl uninstall command removes the control plane but does NOT modify running pods. Sidecar-injected pods continue running with Envoy containers that crash because they can't reach istiod. The correct sequence is: 1) Remove namespace labels, 2) Restart all pods (removes sidecars), 3) Verify no istio-proxy containers, 4) THEN uninstall Istio.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Remove namespace injection labels immediately kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection- istio.io/rev- istio.io/dataplane-mode- Prevents new pods from attempting injection. Existing pods are already broken — they need restarting.
2. Restart all pods to remove sidecars kubectl rollout restart deploy,sts -n anihpj Without injection labels, new pods start WITHOUT sidecars. Application returns to normal (1/1).
3. Delete orphaned webhooks kubectl delete mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector; kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration istio-istio-system Removes webhooks that reference the deleted istiod — prevents future pod creation failures.
4. Delete Istio CRDs kubectl get crds | grep istio | awk '{print $1}' | xargs kubectl delete crd Removes all Istio custom resource definitions. This also deletes any remaining VirtualServices, DestinationRules, etc.
5. Clean up istio-system namespace kubectl delete ns istio-system After CRDs and webhooks are removed, the istio-system namespace can be deleted cleanly.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
REMOVE sidecars BEFORE uninstalling Istio. This is the single most important rule. Remove the namespace label, restart all pods, verify no istio-proxy containers remain, then uninstall. Skipping this step causes application outages.
istioctl uninstall is not a cleanup tool — it only removes what it installed. CRDs, webhooks, and injected sidecars are NOT removed by istioctl uninstall. You must manually clean these up. Create an uninstall runbook with all cleanup steps.
Practice clean uninstall on your 6-cluster lab. Use kind-cka-lab: install Istio, deploy anihpj, then practice the full uninstall sequence. Verify kubectl get crds | grep istio returns zero. Master this flow before you need it in production.
Check for istio-cni after uninstall. kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node istio-cni DaemonSet may persist after uninstall. It continues to modify node iptables — traffic gets redirected to non-existent proxies and is blackholed.
IC17
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC17
Custom CA Certificate Integration Fails — mTLS Broken Across Entire Mesh

🔍 Symptom: A custom CA certificate (intermediate CA or corporate PKI) was configured for Istio using the cacerts Secret. After the change, mTLS stops working cluster-wide. Envoy sidecars show "certificate verify failed" errors. istioctl proxy-status shows all proxies as STALE because they can't get valid certificates from istiod's SDS. The anihpj-web pod can't communicate with anihpj-api — 503 errors everywhere. Internal mesh traffic is completely broken.

  kubectl get secret cacerts -n istio-system
  NAME      TYPE     DATA   AGE
  cacerts   Opaque   3      10m

  kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod --tail=20 | grep -i "cert\|tls\|ca"
  error: failed to load CA certificate from cacerts Secret
  error: tls: failed to parse certificate: x509: unknown authority

  kubectl logs anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep -i "cert"
  [warning] SDS: failed to fetch certificate from istiod
  [error] mTLS handshake failed: certificate verification error
  [error] upstream connect error: TLS error: 268435648: certificate verify failed
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Missing or incorrect certificate chain: The cacerts Secret requires THREE entries: ca-cert.pem (root CA), ca-key.pem (private key), and cert-chain.pem (intermediate chain). Missing any of these, or incorrect order in the chain, causes istiod to reject the certificates. Check: kubectl get secret cacerts -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -E "ca-cert|ca-key|cert-chain".
  2. Certificate key mismatch: The private key (ca-key.pem) doesn't correspond to the certificate (ca-cert.pem). istiod validates that the key pair matches — if they don't, it falls back to the self-signed default CA (or fails). Verify: openssl x509 -in ca-cert.pem -noout -modulus | md5sum vs openssl rsa -in ca-key.pem -noout -modulus | md5sum.
  3. Root CA not trusted by Envoy bootstrap: The custom root CA must be included in the Envoy bootstrap configuration or the mesh trust domain. If Envoy sidecars don't trust the new root CA, they reject peer certificates from other sidecars signed by it.
  4. Certificate expired or not yet valid: The custom CA certificate has an expiration date in the past or a notBefore date in the future. istiod validates certificate validity at startup — expired certs cause it to fall back to auto-generated CA.
  5. Wrong Secret format/keys: The cacerts Secret must use specific keys: ca-cert.pem, ca-key.pem, cert-chain.pem. Using different key names (e.g., tls.crt, tls.key) means istiod doesn't find the certificates and silently generates its own.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Certificate chain order reversed — root CA must be last in chain, intermediate first
  2. ECDSA vs RSA algorithm mismatch — Envoy expects RSA but custom CA uses ECDSA (or vice versa)
  3. SAN (Subject Alternative Name) missing spiffe:// prefix — Istio SPIFFE IDs require specific URI SAN format
  4. Private key has passphrase — istiod cannot use encrypted private keys; must be decrypted before storing in Secret
  5. istiod restart didn't pick up new cacerts Secret — Secret was updated but istiod still uses cached old CA (restart istiod)
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Corporate PKI with non-standard certificate extensions: Enterprise CAs add custom X.509 extensions that Istio/Envoy doesn't recognize — certificate validation fails.
  2. Multi-cluster mesh with different CAs per cluster: kind-cl1 has CA-A, kind-cl2 has CA-B — cross-cluster mTLS fails because clusters don't share trust roots.
  3. kubeadm cluster using cert-manager: cert-manager manages the cacerts Secret but its renewal process uses different key names or format than Istio expects.
  4. Air-gapped cluster with internal CA: Internal CA certificate uses internal hostnames that external tools can't validate — confusing error messages.
  5. New team manually creating CA certs: OpenSSL commands executed incorrectly — wrong flags, missing extensions, incorrect key usage — resulting in technically invalid certificates.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get secret cacerts -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.ca-cert\.pem}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -text -noout Verify the certificate details — issuer, subject, validity dates, key usage. Check if it looks correct for a CA certificate.
kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod --tail=100 | grep -iE "cert|ca|tls|pki" istiod logs reveal exactly why the CA certificate was rejected — parse error, key mismatch, expired, or missing entry.
istioctl proxy-config secret <pod> -n <ns> Shows the certificate Envoy received from SDS. If it's the self-signed default (not your custom CA), the custom CA wasn't accepted.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The cacerts Secret is missing required keys or contains invalid certificates. Istio expects three specific keys: ca-cert.pem (root certificate), ca-key.pem (private key), and cert-chain.pem (intermediate chain). If any key is missing, has the wrong name, or contains an invalid certificate, istiod silently falls back to its auto-generated self-signed CA — and existing sidecars with old certificates can't validate against the new CA.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify cacerts Secret has all required keys kubectl get secret cacerts -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -E "^\s+[a-z].*:" Should show: ca-cert.pem, ca-key.pem, cert-chain.pem. Missing keys = istiod uses auto-generated CA.
2. Validate certificate files before creating Secret openssl verify -CAfile root-cert.pem intermediate-cert.pem; openssl rsa -in ca-key.pem -check -noout Verify the certificate chain is valid and the private key is unencrypted. istiod rejects encrypted keys and broken chains.
3. Create (or recreate) the cacerts Secret correctly kubectl create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system --from-file=ca-cert.pem --from-file=ca-key.pem --from-file=cert-chain.pem Use EXACT key names. Then restart istiod: kubectl rollout restart deploy/istiod -n istio-system.
4. Restart all sidecars to get new certificates kubectl rollout restart deploy,sts -n anihpj Existing sidecars have certificates from the old CA. Restarting forces them to fetch new certs from the custom CA.
5. Rollback if custom CA fails — delete cacerts and restart istiod kubectl delete secret cacerts -n istio-system; kubectl rollout restart deploy/istiod -n istio-system Without cacerts, istiod generates a new self-signed CA. Restart all sidecars to pick up new certificates.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
The cacerts Secret keys are CASE-SENSITIVE and EXACT. ca-cert.pem not ca-cert.pem.txt not cacert.pem. A single character wrong and istiod silently ignores your custom CA. Triple-check the key names.
Always test custom CA on a isolated cluster first. Use kind-cka-lab in your 6-cluster lab. Deploy the custom CA, verify mTLS works, then apply to kubeadm production. A broken custom CA breaks ALL mesh traffic — test before production.
Certificate rotation requires sidecar restart. When the root CA changes, all sidecars must be restarted to fetch new workload certificates. Plan for a full mesh restart during CA rotation — this is a disruptive operation.
istiod logs tell you EXACTLY what's wrong with your CA. kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod | grep -i "cert\|ca" Don't guess — the logs will say "failed to parse certificate," "key mismatch," or "missing cert-chain." Read them carefully before debugging.
IC18
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC18
Gateway Injection vs Manual Deployment Mismatch — Two Gateways, Conflicting Config

🔍 Symptom: The ingress gateway was deployed TWO ways simultaneously: once via the IstioOperator profile (auto-deployed with Istio install) and once via a manually created Gateway Deployment + Service. There are now TWO ingress gateway Deployments in istio-system fighting over the same Service. External traffic is intermittently routed to the wrong gateway pod, or the Gateway resource references a selector that matches both deployments. Inbound traffic to anihpj/jobpost is unreliable — sometimes works, sometimes returns 503.

  kubectl get deploy -n istio-system
  NAME                                   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
  istiod                                 1/1     1            1
  istio-ingressgateway                   1/1     1            1    ← Auto-deployed
  anihpj-ingress-gateway                 1/1     1            1    ← Manual!

  kubectl get svc -n istio-system | grep ingress
  istio-ingressgateway   LoadBalancer   10.96.1.100   <pending>
  (Both deployments target same labels: app=istio-ingressgateway)

  kubectl describe gw anihpj-gateway -n anihpj | grep selector
  Selector:  istio: ingressgateway   ← Matches BOTH deployments!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Gateway auto-deployed by IstioOperator + manual deployment: The default profile includes istio-ingressgateway. A separate team created their own gateway Deployment/Services with the same labels — both match the Gateway resource selector. Traffic is split unpredictably between them.
  2. Gateway injection enabled on manually deployed gateway: The manual gateway Deployment has sidecar.istio.io/inject: "true" — the gateway pod itself gets a sidecar injected. Now the gateway has an Envoy sidecar AND the gateway Envoy — double proxy causing routing loops.
  3. Service selector matches both gateway Deployments: The LoadBalancer Service has selector: app: istio-ingressgateway which matches both the auto-deployed AND manual gateway pods. External traffic is load-balanced across both — inconsistent behavior.
  4. Gateway resource name collision: Two Gateway resources in different namespaces reference the same selector: istio: ingressgateway — both gateways try to serve the same hostnames, creating configuration conflicts.
  5. Port conflict on the node: Both gateway Services try to use the same NodePort or the LoadBalancer allocates the same external IP to both — only one gets traffic.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm gateway chart installed AFTER istioctl — two gateways with different versions and configuration
  2. Custom gateway injection template conflict — manual gateway uses a different injection template than auto-deployed one
  3. Gateway pod anti-affinity rules clash — two gateways scheduled on same node but antiAffinity prevents co-location
  4. SDS certificate mismatch — auto-deployed gateway gets istiod certs, manual gateway has custom TLS Secret
  5. IngressGateway vs EgressGateway confusion — manual deployment used egress gateway image for ingress traffic
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Team didn't know Istio auto-deploys ingress gateway: New Istio users often create their own gateway deployment, not realizing the default profile already includes one.
  2. Multiple clusters with different gateway configurations: kubeadm uses auto-deployed gateway, kind-cl1 uses manual gateway — team copied the manual config to kubeadm.
  3. Gateway migration attempted but not completed: Team started migrating from auto-deployed to manual gateway but left both running during the transition.
  4. Terraform/IaC drift: Infrastructure-as-Code creates a gateway Deployment but the IstioOperator also deploys one — two sources of truth.
  5. New team testing gateway customization: Experimenting with gateway settings by creating a second deployment instead of modifying the existing one — both end up in production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get deploy,svc -n istio-system -l app=istio-ingressgateway Shows if there are multiple Deployments or Services with the same labels. More than one = conflict.
kubectl get gw --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -A2 "selector:" Shows which labels each Gateway resource uses to select gateway pods. Same label across multiple gateways = conflict.
kubectl get endpoints -n istio-system <svc-name> Shows which pod IPs are receiving traffic. More IPs than expected gateway pods = selector matching too broadly.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The default Istio installation auto-deploys an ingress gateway (istio-ingressgateway). A manual gateway Deployment was created with overlapping labels, causing the Gateway resource and LoadBalancer Service to match both deployments. External traffic is split randomly between two different gateway configurations, causing intermittent 503s and TLS failures for the anihpj/jobpost application.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Identify all gateway Deployments and Services kubectl get deploy,svc -n istio-system --show-labels | grep gateway List all gateway-related resources and their labels. Identify duplicates.
2. Choose ONE gateway approach and remove the other kubectl delete deploy anihpj-ingress-gateway -n istio-system If keeping the auto-deployed gateway, delete the manual one. Or disable the auto-deployed gateway in IstioOperator and keep the manual one.
3. Update Gateway resource selector to be specific kubectl patch gw anihpj-gateway -n anihpj --type merge -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"anihpj-ingress-gateway"}}}' Use unique, specific labels for your gateway to prevent accidental matching of other deployments.
4. Disable auto-deployed gateway if using custom one istioctl install --set profile=default --set components.ingressGateways[0].enabled=false If you're managing gateways manually, disable the auto-deployed one in the IstioOperator to prevent future conflicts.
5. Verify traffic flows to the correct gateway kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/<gateway> --tail=20 | grep "downstream_cx_total" Confirm only the intended gateway is receiving traffic. The duplicate should show zero connections.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Use unique labels for custom gateways. app: anihpj-ingress-gateway not app: istio-ingressgateway Never use the default Istio gateway labels for your custom gateway. A unique label prevents the Gateway resource from accidentally matching the wrong deployment.
Disable auto-deployed gateways if managing your own. Use --set components.ingressGateways[0].enabled=false during install. This prevents the dual-gateway problem entirely — Istio won't deploy one, and you deploy exactly what you need.
Never inject a sidecar into a gateway pod. The gateway IS an Envoy proxy. Injecting another Envoy as a sidecar creates a double-proxy situation — the sidecar intercepts traffic meant for the gateway Envoy, causing routing loops.
Check endpoints when debugging intermittent 503s. kubectl get endpoints -n istio-system If the endpoint list has unexpected IPs, your Service selector is matching pods it shouldn't. This is a quick way to catch duplicate gateway deployments.
IC19
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC19
IstioOperator Apply vs Install Conflicts — istioctl install Overwrites Custom IOP

🔍 Symptom: A custom IstioOperator YAML was carefully crafted and applied with istioctl apply -f iop.yaml. Later, someone ran istioctl install --set profile=default which overwrote the custom settings. Custom resource limits, HPA configurations, and gateway settings were replaced with defaults. The mesh was reconfigured without warning. Or, applying an IOP with istioctl apply doesn't take effect because a previous istioctl install created resources with a different owner reference.

  cat iop-production.yaml
  apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1
  kind: IstioOperator
  spec:
    profile: default
    components:
      pilot:
        k8s:
          hpaSpec:
            minReplicas: 3    ← Custom: 3 replicas
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: 2Gi     ← Custom: 2Gi memory

  istioctl install --set profile=default -y   ← Overwrites custom IOP!
  ✔ Istio core installed
  ✔ Istiod installed

  kubectl get hpa -n istio-system
  No resources found   ← HPA was removed! Custom minReplicas: 3 lost!

  kubectl get deploy istiod -n istio-system -o yaml | grep memory
  memory: 512Mi   ← Reset to default (was 2Gi)!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. istioctl install overwrites istioctl apply: istioctl install generates and applies a new manifest from CLI flags, ignoring any previously applied IstioOperator. istioctl apply uses the IOP file as the source of truth. Running install after apply replaces the IOP-managed configuration with CLI-flag defaults.
  2. Team doesn't know the difference between install and apply: install = generate from CLI flags (one-time). apply = reconcile from IOP file (continuous). Different team members use different commands, creating configuration oscillation.
  3. IOP file not in version control: The IstioOperator YAML was created ad-hoc and not stored in Git. When settings were overwritten by istioctl install, there was no record of the original custom configuration.
  4. Multiple IOP files with conflicting settings: Two different IOP files exist (iop-dev.yaml, iop-prod.yaml). Someone applied the wrong one, then someone else ran install to "fix" it — compounding the confusion.
  5. IOP applied to wrong cluster context: The custom IOP was applied to the wrong cluster (kubeadm vs kind-cka-lab). Later, istioctl install was run to "standardize" the configuration — effectively undoing the custom setup.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. IOP validation silently fails — istioctl apply reports success but some settings are rejected because they conflict with immutable fields
  2. Helm release secretly managing same resources — Helm upgrades overwrite IOP-applied settings because Helm owns the resources
  3. ArgoCD auto-sync reverts custom IOP — GitOps tool sees drift and syncs back to the Git-stored (default) configuration
  4. IstioOperator CRD version mismatch — IOP written for v1alpha1 but cluster has v1beta1; some fields silently ignored
  5. Partial apply — IOP changes only partially take effect because some components were manually modified and istioctl won't overwrite them without --force
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New team learning Istio configuration management: Team doesn't understand the difference between install/apply/upgrade and uses them interchangeably — each undoes the other's work.
  2. No established GitOps for Istio configuration: No single source of truth for mesh configuration — teams apply changes directly to the cluster without version control.
  3. kind cluster reset with different IOP: Kind cluster was deleted and recreated — the new install used default profile while the old one had a custom IOP that wasn't saved.
  4. kubeadm cluster manual experimentation: Team experimented with IOP settings directly on the production kubeadm cluster instead of testing on kind first.
  5. Missing runbook for Istio reinstallation: No documented procedure for reinstalling Istio with custom settings — when issues arise, team runs istioctl install --set profile=default as a "reset."
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get deploy istiod -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A5 "resources:" Check current resource limits. Compare against what the IOP specifies. Mismatch = IOP was overwritten.
git log --oneline iop-production.yaml Check Git history for the IOP file. If it doesn't exist in Git, the custom configuration was never version-controlled.
kubectl get events -n istio-system --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -20 Shows recent changes to istio-system resources — reveals who ran install/apply and when.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: istioctl install was run after a custom IstioOperator was applied, overwriting the custom configuration with defaults. istioctl install generates configuration from CLI flags only — it does not read or reconcile an existing IOP. The team didn't understand that install replaces configuration while apply reconciles it from a file.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Re-apply the custom IOP to restore settings istioctl apply -f iop-production.yaml This reconciles the mesh back to the custom configuration. Always use apply when you have an IOP file.
2. Store IOP in Git as the single source of truth git add iop-production.yaml && git commit -m "IstioOperator: production mesh config" Version-controlled IOP is auditable and recoverable. All mesh changes should go through Git, not direct CLI commands.
3. Use ONLY istioctl apply for IOP-managed clusters Ban istioctl install on clusters managed with IstioOperator. Document this in the team runbook. Install is for initial setup only.
4. Set up GitOps with ArgoCD or Flux Automatically reconcile the IOP from Git. Manual CLI changes are detected as drift and reverted — the IOP wins.
5. Verify mesh configuration matches IOP istioctl manifest generate -f iop-production.yaml | kubectl diff -f - Shows drift between the IOP-defined state and actual cluster state. Run periodically to detect unauthorized changes.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
istioctl install is for Day 0. istioctl apply is for Day 2. install = initial setup from CLI flags (no file, no version control). apply = ongoing management from IOP file (version-controlled, auditable). Never use install after the mesh is operational.
Your IOP file IS your mesh configuration. Treat it like production code. Store in Git, review changes via PR, test on kind-cka-lab before applying to kubeadm. The IOP defines resource limits, replica counts, gateway settings — losing it means losing your entire mesh configuration.
Always diff before applying. istioctl manifest generate -f iop.yaml | kubectl diff -f - See exactly what will change before it changes. This catches accidental overwrites and confirms your IOP is having the intended effect.
Label your clusters with their management method. Tag clusters as "IOP-managed" or "CLI-managed" so team members know which command to use. On IOP-managed clusters, istioctl install should be forbidden.
IC20
📦 CATEGORY 1: INSTALL/UPGRADE/CONFIG — Issue IC20
Air-Gapped Installation Failures — Images Not Mirrored, Proxy Config Wrong

🔍 Symptom: Istio was installed in an air-gapped (offline) environment — no direct internet access to docker.io/istio or gcr.io/istio-release. Pods in istio-system are stuck in ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull. The istiod pod can't start because the proxyv2 image is not available from the local registry. Sidecar injection fails because the istio/proxyv2 image reference in the injection template points to the public registry, not the internal one.

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system
  NAME                                   READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
  istiod-7d8f9-x                          0/1     ImagePullBackOff   12
  istio-ingressgateway-abc                0/1     ErrImagePull       8

  kubectl describe pod istiod-7d8f9-x -n istio-system | grep -A2 "Failed"
  Failed to pull image "docker.io/istio/pilot:1.22.1":
  dial tcp: lookup registry-1.docker.io: no such host

  kubectl get cm istio-sidecar-injector -n istio-system -o yaml | grep "image:"
  image: docker.io/istio/proxyv2:1.22.1   ← Public registry! Not air-gapped!

  curl -k https://internal-registry.local/v2/_catalog
  {"repositories":["istio/pilot","istio/proxyv2"]}   ← Images ARE mirrored
  ← But istioctl was configured with wrong hub!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Wrong --set hub during install: istioctl install was run without --set hub=internal-registry.local/istio. The default hub (docker.io/istio or gcr.io/istio-release) is used, which is unreachable from the air-gapped cluster. Images can't be pulled.
  2. Injection template still references public registry: Even if istiod was installed with the correct hub, the istio-sidecar-injector ConfigMap may still have the old public registry URL. Sidecar injection fails because Envoy images can't be pulled. Fix: reinstall with correct hub.
  3. Images not mirrored to internal registry: The istio/proxyv2, istio/pilot, and istio/operator images were never pushed to the internal registry. The air-gapped cluster has nowhere to pull them from. Check: skopeo list-tags docker://internal-registry.local/istio/pilot.
  4. Image tag mismatch after mirroring: Images were mirrored but with different tags (e.g., 1.22.1-prod instead of 1.22.1). istiod and istioctl look for the exact tag specified during install.
  5. Internal registry requires authentication: The internal registry needs imagePullSecrets, but the istio-system ServiceAccount or istiod ServiceAccount doesn't have them configured. Pods can't authenticate to pull images.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Internal registry TLS certificate not trusted — self-signed cert on registry causes HTTPS pull failures
  2. containerd/docker configured with wrong registry mirrors — mirror config points to old or incorrect registry URL
  3. Proxy settings not configured for Istio components — HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY env vars missing on istiod and gateways
  4. NetworkPolicy blocking pod-to-registry traffic — istio-system pods can't reach the internal registry subnet
  5. Registry storage full — image push succeeded previously but registry is now at capacity, pull fails silently
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kubeadm cluster in isolated VLAN: The kubeadm production cluster has no internet access by design (security requirement) — all images must come from the internal registry.
  2. Air-gapped cluster with no registry at all: New air-gapped environment — no internal registry has been set up yet. Images must be side-loaded via ctr image import on each node.
  3. kind cluster behind corporate proxy: kind nodes have Docker access but the registry mirror configuration in containerd is missing or incorrect.
  4. minikube with --registry-mirror not set: minikube uses its own Docker daemon — the registry mirror must be configured at minikube start, not during Istio install.
  5. Disconnected cluster with intermittent satellite link: Registry sync happens over slow/internittent link — some images synced, others failed silently.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod -n istio-system | grep -A3 "Failed\|ErrImagePull\|BackOff" Shows which registry the pod is trying to pull from. If it's docker.io or gcr.io, the hub wasn't configured for air-gap.
kubectl get cm istio-sidecar-injector -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -E "hub:|tag:|image:" Check what hub/tag the injection template is configured to use. Must match your internal registry.
curl -u user:pass https://internal-registry.local/v2/istio/pilot/tags/list Verify the required images and tags exist in the internal registry. Missing tags = images weren't fully mirrored.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Istio was installed without specifying the internal registry hub (--set hub=internal-registry.local/istio). The default hub points to public registries (docker.io/istio) which are unreachable from the air-gapped cluster. All Istio images fail to pull because the cluster cannot reach the internet.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Mirror Istio images to internal registry istioctl x precheck --hub=internal-registry.local/istio --tag=1.22.1 Download and push all required images: pilot, proxyv2, operator, etc. Verify with registry API.
2. Install with correct hub and tag istioctl install --set profile=default --set hub=internal-registry.local/istio --set tag=1.22.1 -y Override the default hub with your internal registry. All components will pull from this registry.
3. Configure imagePullSecrets if needed kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred -n istio-system --docker-server=internal-registry.local --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<pass> Add to ServiceAccount: kubectl patch sa istiod -n istio-system -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'.
4. Verify injection template uses internal registry kubectl get cm istio-sidecar-injector -n istio-system -o yaml | grep "hub:\|image:" Should now show internal-registry.local/istio instead of docker.io/istio. If not, reinstall.
5. Restart all pods to pull from internal registry kubectl rollout restart deploy -n istio-system; kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj Existing pods with old image references must be restarted to pull from the internal registry.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
--set hub is the MOST important flag for air-gapped installs. istioctl install --set hub=internal-registry.local/istio --set tag=1.22.1 Without this flag, Istio defaults to public registries. Every pod in istio-system and every injected sidecar will fail to pull images. This single flag makes or breaks air-gapped deployments.
Mirror ALL images, not just pilot and proxyv2. You need: pilot, proxyv2, operator, app (for addons), and any custom images your mesh uses. Use istioctl x precheck to list all required images for your profile.
Practice air-gapped install on your kind cluster. Create a local registry container, mirror images to it, and configure kind to use only the local registry. Practice the full air-gapped install flow — this is an increasingly common exam scenario.
Test image pull on one pod before full rollout. kubectl run test --image=internal-registry.local/istio/proxyv2:1.22.1 --restart=Never Verify the image is pullable before reinstalling the entire mesh. A quick test pod saves you from rolling back a failed mesh-wide reinstall.

🚦 Category 2: Traffic Ingress, Egress & Routing Troubleshooting (20 Issues)TR1-TR20

🟡 Traffic Management Issues — VirtualService, DestinationRule, Gateway, and Sidecar Resources

Traffic routing is the most visible part of the service mesh. When VirtualServices are misconfigured, DestinationRules have wrong subsets, or Gateways don't match, your users see 404s, 503s, or traffic going to the wrong service version. These issues require understanding the full request path: Gateway → VirtualService → DestinationRule → Envoy cluster → endpoint.

📌 TR1–TR5: VirtualService Routing Failures

TR1
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR1
VirtualService Not Routing — 404/503 When Accessing Service via Mesh

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService was created for the anihpj/jobpost API to route traffic by URL path, but requests return HTTP 404 or 503. The Kubernetes Service works fine when accessed directly (bypassing the mesh), but any request going through the Istio ingress gateway or mesh-internal routing fails. kubectl get vs -n anihpj shows the VirtualService exists, but istioctl analyze reports a configuration error. The route matches are not forwarding traffic to the correct destination.

  curl -H "Host: jobpost.com" http://<INGRESS_IP>/api/jobs
  HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found   ← VirtualService should match /api/*

  kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml
  spec:
    hosts:
    - anihpj-api
    http:
    - match:
      - uri:
          prefix: /api
      route:
      - destination:
          host: anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local   ← WRONG format!

  istioctl analyze -n anihpj
  ❌ Error [IST0101] VirtualService anihpj-api-vs: destination host
     "anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local" not found in mesh
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Wrong host format in destination: The VirtualService destination host uses FQDN (anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local) but Istio expects short names (anihpj-api) or namespace-qualified (anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local — correct but must match Service registry). The FQDN must exactly match what Istio's service registry knows.
  2. VirtualService hosts don't match Gateway: The VirtualService hosts field lists anihpj-api but the Gateway expects jobpost.com. Istio only applies VirtualService rules when the request's Host header matches one of the listed hosts.
  3. No routes match the request: The match conditions don't match the actual request. E.g., prefix: /api won't match /api/v1/jobs if there's a more specific match earlier in the route list that shadows it. Check route ordering.
  4. Destination host doesn't exist as a Kubernetes Service: The VirtualService routes to anihpj-api but there's no Service with that name in the mesh. The Service must exist and be registered in Istio's service registry. Check: kubectl get svc -n anihpj.
  5. VirtualService not in mesh gateway list: The Gateway resource has a hosts field but doesn't include * or the specific host the VirtualService expects. Add "*" to the Gateway hosts or list the specific hostname.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. VirtualService in wrong namespace — Gateway selects VS from specific namespaces, but the VS is in a namespace not included in the Gateway's selector
  2. Port mismatch — VirtualService routes to port 80 but the Service listens on 8080
  3. HTTP redirect loop — VirtualService has a redirect rule that creates an infinite redirect chain
  4. Mirror/directResponse rule intercepting before route — a catch-all mirror or directResponse rule eats all traffic before reaching actual destinations
  5. Multiple VirtualServices for same host — two VS define conflicting rules for the same host; only one wins (deterministic but unexpected)
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New mesh with no VirtualService experience: First-time Istio users expect Kubernetes Services to "just work" through the mesh — they don't realize VirtualServices are needed for advanced routing.
  2. kind cluster DNS differences: CoreDNS on kind resolves service names differently, causing hostname format issues that don't occur on kubeadm.
  3. Gateway deployed but not associated with VirtualService: The Gateway exists but its hosts field doesn't include the hostname the VirtualService expects.
  4. Missing default route fallback: The VirtualService has only specific matches (e.g., /api/v1, /api/v2) but no catch-all route — unmatched paths return 404.
  5. Service not in service registry due to label mismatch — Istio discovers services by pod labels; if labels don't match, the service isn't registered.
🔍 What to Look At:
istioctl analyze -n <ns> The most important diagnostic tool for routing issues. Catches host mismatch, missing services, invalid route weights, and conflicting configurations.
istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n <ns> -o json | grep -A20 "anihpj-api" Shows the actual Envoy route table. Confirms whether the VirtualService was translated into Envoy routes correctly.
kubectl get svc -n <ns> Verify the destination Service exists and its name matches the host in the VirtualService. Istio can't route to non-existent Services.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The VirtualService uses a destination host that doesn't match the Istio service registry. Either the host is in FQDN format that Istio doesn't recognize, or the Kubernetes Service doesn't exist. Always use the short Service name (anihpj-api) or namespace-qualified (anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local) — never guess the host format; verify with istioctl proxy-config clusters.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Run istioctl analyze to identify the exact error istioctl analyze -n anihpj Pinpoints configuration problems: invalid hosts, missing services, conflicting routes. Fix what it reports first.
2. Fix the destination host to match service registry Change host: anihpj-api (short name) or verify FQDN matches exactly. Use istioctl proxy-config clusters to see how Istio registers the service.
3. Verify VirtualService host matches Gateway host kubectl get gw -A -o yaml | grep -A5 "hosts:" The Gateway's hosts list must include the hostname in the VirtualService's hosts list. Add "*" for broad matching during testing.
4. Check route match ordering Istio evaluates routes in ORDER — the first match wins. Ensure specific paths come before general ones. Add a catch-all route as the LAST entry with no match conditions.
5. Test with a simple route first Replace complex routing with a single route to anihpj-api:8080. If traffic flows, the destination is correct — then incrementally add match conditions and verify each one.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Always run istioctl analyze after creating any traffic resource. istioctl analyze -n <ns> This single command catches 90% of VirtualService and DestinationRule configuration errors before they affect users. Make it part of your deploy pipeline.
Use short host names in VirtualService destinations. host: anihpj-api Short names are unambiguous within a namespace. FQDNs are fragile — they break if the cluster domain changes or DNS configuration differs between clusters.
Understand route ordering — first match wins. VirtualService routes are evaluated sequentially. A catch-all at position 1 shadows all routes below it. Always put specific routes first and generic routes last.
Use proxy-config routes to see what Envoy actually has. istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n <ns> The VirtualService YAML is your intent — the Envoy route table is what actually executes. Always verify the two match. If they don't, your VirtualService isn't being applied.
TR2
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR2
DestinationRule Not Applied — Load Balancing Ignored, Subsets Not Found

🔍 Symptom: A DestinationRule was created to define subsets (v1, v2) and configure load balancing, but traffic continues to use round-robin to all pods. Subset routing from the VirtualService fails with "no healthy upstream" or 503 errors. istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> shows only the default cluster — no subset clusters (e.g., outbound|8080|v1|anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local) exist. The anihpj canary deployment (v2) is unreachable because the subset doesn't resolve to any endpoints.

  kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml
  spec:
    host: anihpj-api
    subsets:
    - name: v1
      labels:
        version: v1.0      ← Pod labels use "app-version: v1"!
    - name: v2
      labels:
        version: v2.0      ← Label mismatch!

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-api --show-labels
  NAME              READY   LABELS
  anihpj-api-v1-xxx 2/2     app=anihpj-api,app-version=v1
  anihpj-api-v2-yyy 2/2     app=anihpj-api,app-version=v2

  istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "anihpj-api.*v1"
  (no output — subset clusters not created! Label mismatch means no endpoints for v1/v2)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Subset labels don't match pod labels: The DestinationRule defines labels: {version: v1} but pods have app-version: v1. Istio subsets filter pod endpoints by EXACT label match — if no pods match, the subset has zero endpoints and returns 503. Check: kubectl get pods -l <dr-labels>.
  2. DestinationRule host doesn't match VirtualService host: The DR specifies host: anihpj-api but the VS routes to host: anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local. Host names must match between VS and DR — Istio applies DR settings by host name.
  3. DestinationRule in wrong namespace: A DestinationRule for host: anihpj-api must be in the same namespace as the Service, or its exportTo field must include the VirtualService's namespace. DR in wrong namespace = setting not applied.
  4. TrafficPolicy not taking effect: The DR sets trafficPolicy: {loadBalancer: {simple: LEAST_REQUEST}} but traffic still uses ROUND_ROBIN. The DR host doesn't match the VS destination, so the policy is never applied.
  5. Multiple DestinationRules for same host: Two DRs define settings for host: anihpj-api. Only ONE DR is applied per host — the oldest or the one with the most specific match. The other DR is silently ignored.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Subset name typo in VirtualService — VS references subset "v-1" but DR defines "v1"
  2. DR has exportTo restricting visibility — set to "." (current namespace only) but VS is in a different namespace
  3. Connection pool settings too restrictive — maxConnections: 1 and all connections are in use, causing 503
  4. TLS settings in DR conflict with PeerAuthentication — DR specifies ISTIO_MUTUAL but PA sets PERMISSIVE
  5. WorkloadSelector in DR filtering wrong pods — DR applies only to specific workloads, not the ones the VS routes to
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First time using subsets: Team creates DestinationRule with subsets but doesn't realize labels must match pod labels exactly — including case sensitivity.
  2. Canary deployment with different label schema: The v2 deployment uses version: canary while v1 uses app-version: v1 — inconsistent labeling breaks subset routing.
  3. kind cluster with multiple Istio revisions: DR created in revision "stable" but VS is in revision "canary" — resources in different revisions don't interact.
  4. kubeadm cluster with manual pod labeling: Labels applied manually via kubectl instead of being set in Deployment spec — pods get inconsistent labels on restart.
  5. Copy-pasted DR from older Istio version: DestinationRule API changed between versions — labels field format or behavior may differ.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l <dr-subset-labels> Test if any pods match the subset labels. Zero pods = subset is empty and will always return 503.
istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> | grep "subset\|v1\|v2" Shows if subset clusters were created. Missing subset clusters = labels don't match or DR not applied.
kubectl get dr -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A10 "host:\|labels:\|exportTo:" Verify the DR host matches the VS host, labels match pod labels, and exportTo allows cross-namespace access.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The DestinationRule subset labels don't match the actual pod labels. Istio creates endpoint groups for each subset by filtering pods whose labels match exactly. If no pods match (e.g., version: v1 in DR but app-version: v1 on pods), the subset has zero healthy endpoints — and any VirtualService routing to that subset returns 503 with "no healthy upstream."
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify pod labels match DR subset labels kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-api --show-labels Copy the exact label key:value from the pod output. Update the DR to use the identical labels.
2. Fix DestinationRule subset labels kubectl edit dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj Change labels: {version: v1} to labels: {app-version: v1}. Save — the change takes effect within seconds.
3. Verify subsets now have endpoints istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "anihpj-api.*v1" Should now show endpoint counts for v1 and v2 subsets. Non-zero endpoints = subset routing is working.
4. Test subset routing with VirtualService curl -H "Host: jobpost.com" http://<INGRESS_IP>/api/jobs If the VS routes to subset v1 or v2, the response should come from the correct deployment version.
5. Add consistent labels to all Deployments Standardize pod labels across all versions of a service. Use version: v1 in Deployment spec labels to ensure all pods of that version share the same subset label.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Labels are the contract between DestinationRule and pods. Check pod labels FIRST when a subset returns 503. It's almost always a label mismatch — the DR says version: v1 but pods have app-version: v1. Use kubectl get pods --show-labels religiously.
Use consistent label schemas across all services. Standardize on version for all services or app-version for all — don't mix. Inconsistent labels cause confusing, hard-to-debug subset failures that shift from service to service.
Check proxy-config clusters — not the DR YAML. istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> The DR YAML shows your intent. The Envoy cluster list shows reality. If a subset cluster doesn't exist in Envoy, your DR isn't working — regardless of what the YAML says.
Only one DestinationRule per host is applied. If you have two DRs for the same host, only one wins. Merge them into a single DR with multiple subsets and traffic policies. Multiple DRs for the same host is a common silent failure.
TR3
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR3
Gateway Not Listening — External Traffic Never Enters the Mesh

🔍 Symptom: The Istio ingress gateway is deployed and running, a Gateway resource is configured with the correct host, and a VirtualService routes to the anihpj-web service. But external traffic never reaches the application — curl http://<EXTERNAL_IP> returns connection refused or times out. The LoadBalancer Service shows EXTERNAL-IP: <pending> indefinitely, or the external IP is assigned but port 80/443 is not listening. Inside the cluster, the Gateway appears correctly configured.

  kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system
  NAME                   TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)
  istio-ingressgateway   LoadBalancer   10.96.100.1    <pending>     80:30080/TCP

  curl http://<NODE_IP>:30080/ -H "Host: jobpost.com"
  curl: (7) Failed to connect: Connection refused   ← Port not listening!

  kubectl get gw anihpj-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml
  spec:
    selector:
      app: anihpj-ingress   ← No pod has this label!
    servers:
    - port:
        number: 80
        protocol: HTTP
      hosts:
      - "jobpost.com"
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Gateway selector doesn't match any gateway pod: The Gateway resource's selector field (e.g., app: anihpj-ingress) must match the labels on the ingress gateway Deployment pods. If no pods match, the Gateway config is never loaded by any Envoy. Check: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l <selector>.
  2. Ingress gateway Service not type LoadBalancer: The istio-ingressgateway Service type is ClusterIP — external traffic can't reach it. Must be LoadBalancer (cloud) or NodePort (bare metal). Check: kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system.
  3. Gateway port not open on Service: The Gateway resource defines port 443 but the istio-ingressgateway Service only exposes ports 80 and 15021. istiod can't configure Envoy to listen on a port the Service doesn't expose. Service ports must match Gateway ports.
  4. No external IP assigned (bare metal / kind): LoadBalancer Services on bare metal or kind clusters get <pending> EXTERNAL-IP indefinitely. Use NodePort (service.type: NodePort) or install MetalLB for LoadBalancer support.
  5. Firewall/network blocking ingress port: The node's firewall or security group blocks the NodePort (e.g., 30080). Traffic reaches the node but is dropped before reaching the kube-proxy. Check: netstat -tlnp | grep 30080 on the node.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Gateway HTTPS but TLS certificate Secret missing — TLS listener fails to start because cert can't be loaded
  2. Ingress gateway pod not scheduled — node taints or resource constraints prevent gateway pod from starting
  3. Multiple Gateway resources with same selector — conflicting configurations cause Envoy to reject one or both
  4. Gateway namespace not included in istiod's discovery — istiod doesn't watch the namespace where the Gateway is defined
  5. Host header mismatch — curl sends Host header that doesn't match any Gateway host, so no route matches
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kind cluster — no LoadBalancer support: kind clusters can't provision external LoadBalancer IPs. Use service.type: NodePort or install MetalLB for the ICA exam scenarios.
  2. kubeadm cluster on single node: NodePort works but localhost may not route to the NodePort — use the node's actual IP address.
  3. Docker Desktop interfering: Docker Desktop's networking can block NodePort traffic on Windows/Mac — use kubectl port-forward for testing.
  4. minikube tunnel not running: minikube LoadBalancer Services require minikube tunnel to assign EXTERNAL-IP — without it, IP stays <pending>.
  5. Cloud provider firewall rules not configured: AWS Security Groups, GCP Firewall Rules, or Azure NSG blocking the ingress port — even though the Service has an external IP.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l <gateway-selector> If no pods match the Gateway selector, the Gateway config is never loaded. The default selector is istio: ingressgateway.
kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A10 "ports:" Verify the Service ports include the ports defined in the Gateway resource. Mismatched ports = Envoy can't listen.
istioctl proxy-config listeners <gateway-pod> -n istio-system Shows which ports the gateway Envoy is actually listening on. If the expected port is missing, the Gateway config didn't apply.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Gateway resource's selector doesn't match any ingress gateway pod. The default Istio ingress gateway pod has labels istio: ingressgateway and app: istio-ingressgateway. If the Gateway resource specifies a different selector (e.g., app: anihpj-ingress), no gateway pod loads the configuration, and the listener is never created. The fix is to match the Gateway selector to the actual gateway pod labels.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. List gateway pods and their labels kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway --show-labels Note the exact labels on the running gateway pod. The Gateway resource selector must match these labels.
2. Fix Gateway selector to match pod labels kubectl edit gw anihpj-gateway -n anihpj Change selector: {app: anihpj-ingress} to selector: {istio: ingressgateway}. Save — gateway listeners appear within seconds.
3. Verify Service type and external IP kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system For bare metal/kind: change to NodePort. For cloud: verify LoadBalancer provisioned an IP. For minikube: run minikube tunnel.
4. Verify gateway Envoy listeners istioctl proxy-config listeners <gateway-pod> -n istio-system | grep "80\|443" Confirms the gateway Envoy is actually listening on the expected ports.
5. Test external access curl -H "Host: jobpost.com" http://<NODE_IP>:<NODEPORT>/ Should return the anihpj-web page. If not, check firewall/security groups on the node.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
The Gateway selector MUST match the gateway pod labels. This is the #1 Gateway misconfiguration. The default selector is istio: ingressgateway. If you change it, you must also change the gateway Deployment labels to match — or your Gateway resource does nothing.
On bare metal and kind, use NodePort — not LoadBalancer. LoadBalancer requires a cloud controller or MetalLB. Without one, EXTERNAL-IP stays <pending> forever. NodePort works on every cluster type. For the ICA exam, know both patterns.
Service ports and Gateway ports must match. If your Gateway defines port 8443 but the Service only has ports 80, 443, and 15021 — the Gateway will never listen on 8443. The Service is the network boundary; the Gateway configures what happens inside it.
Use proxy-config listeners to see what's actually listening. istioctl proxy-config listeners <gateway-pod> -n istio-system Don't assume your Gateway YAML is working — verify it by checking the actual Envoy listeners. If the port isn't in the listener list, the Gateway config didn't apply.
TR4
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR4
TLS Misconfiguration — Gateway HTTPS Fails, TLS Handshake Errors

🔍 Symptom: The Istio ingress gateway is configured for HTTPS with a TLS certificate, but clients receive TLS handshake errors, SSL protocol errors, or ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR in the browser. curl -v https://jobpost.com shows "tlsv1 alert unknown ca" or "no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name." The TLS Secret exists in the namespace, but the Gateway resource's credentialName or serverCertificate field doesn't reference it correctly, or the certificate is invalid.

  curl -v https://jobpost.com/
  * TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS alert, unknown CA (560)
  * SSL certificate problem: self signed certificate
  curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: self signed certificate

  kubectl get gw anihpj-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A15 "tls:"
  tls:
    mode: SIMPLE
    credentialName: anihpj-tls-cert

  kubectl get secret anihpj-tls-cert -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -E "^\s+[a-z].*:"
  tls.key:    (present)
  tls.crt:    (present)
  ← Missing ca.crt! For mutual TLS or custom CA, ca.crt is required

  kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway | grep -i "tls\|cert\|ssl"
  [warning] TLS secret "anihpj-tls-cert" not found in namespace "anihpj"
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. TLS Secret in wrong namespace: The Gateway resource references credentialName: anihpj-tls-cert but the Secret exists in a different namespace. The Secret MUST be in the same namespace as the Gateway resource, or in istio-system for cross-namespace access. Check: kubectl get secret -n <gateway-ns>.
  2. TLS Secret wrong format: Istio expects Kubernetes TLS Secrets with specific keys: tls.crt (certificate chain) and tls.key (private key). Using different key names like cert.pem or key.pem means the Gateway can't find the certificate. Check: kubectl get secret <name> -o yaml | grep -E "^\s+[a-z]".
  3. Certificate CN/SAN doesn't match hostname: The TLS certificate's Common Name or Subject Alternative Names (SANs) don't include the hostname in the Gateway (jobpost.com). Browsers and clients reject the certificate because the hostname doesn't match.
  4. Gateway TLS mode mismatch: SIMPLE mode expects standard TLS (server cert). MUTUAL requires client certificates (mTLS). PASSTHROUGH passes TLS through without termination. Wrong mode = handshake failure.
  5. Gateway port protocol mismatch: The Gateway server defines port 443 with protocol: HTTP instead of protocol: HTTPS. istiod doesn't apply TLS configuration to HTTP ports — only to HTTPS or TLS protocol ports.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Private key encrypted with passphrase — Envoy cannot use encrypted private keys; must be decrypted
  2. Certificate expired or not yet valid — Envoy checks validity dates; expired certs are rejected at startup
  3. Certificate chain incomplete — only server cert is provided, intermediate CA cert missing from tls.crt
  4. Multiple Gateway resources with same port and host — TLS configuration conflict between two Gateways
  5. SDS (Secret Discovery Service) not working — istiod can't push the Secret to the gateway Envoy because SDS connection is broken
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Self-signed cert in production: Team generated a self-signed certificate with openssl for testing, then deployed to production. Browsers reject self-signed certs with security warnings.
  2. Let's Encrypt/cert-manager integration not set up: No automated certificate management — certs expire and aren't renewed, causing sudden TLS failures.
  3. kind cluster with port forwarding: Testing HTTPS via kubectl port-forward — the forwarded port doesn't support TLS correctly; use NodePort instead.
  4. kubeadm cluster with self-signed CA: Internal CA not trusted by external clients — external browsers reject the certificate chain.
  5. minikube IP changes after restart: TLS certificate issued for a specific IP, but minikube IP changes on restart — certificate hostname no longer matches.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get secret <name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -text -noout | grep -E "Subject:|DNS:" Verify the certificate's subject and SAN entries match the hostname the Gateway expects. Mismatch = TLS handshake failure.
kubectl get gw <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A10 "tls:" Check TLS mode, credentialName, and that the port protocol is HTTPS (not HTTP). Wrong protocol = TLS config ignored.
kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway | grep -iE "tls|cert|secret|sds" Gateway logs show Secret loading errors, TLS handshake failures, and certificate validation issues.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The TLS Secret referenced by the Gateway (credentialName) either doesn't exist in the same namespace, has the wrong key format, or contains a certificate whose SAN/CN doesn't match the Gateway's hostname. Istio gateways use SDS (Secret Discovery Service) to load TLS certs — if the Secret isn't found or is invalid, the TLS listener fails to start and clients get handshake errors.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify TLS Secret exists in the Gateway namespace kubectl get secret anihpj-tls-cert -n anihpj Secret must exist and have DATA=2 (tls.crt + tls.key). Missing = create it from your certificate files.
2. Validate certificate matches hostname echo | openssl s_client -servername jobpost.com -connect <IP>:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep DNS Check that the SAN includes the Gateway hostname. If not, regenerate the certificate with the correct SAN.
3. Create TLS Secret with correct keys kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls-cert -n anihpj --cert=fullchain.pem --key=privkey.pem Uses the standard tls.crt and tls.key keys. Include the full certificate chain (server cert + intermediate) in the cert file.
4. Ensure Gateway port protocol is HTTPS kubectl edit gw anihpj-gateway -n anihpj Change protocol: HTTP to protocol: HTTPS for TLS ports. Port protocol determines whether TLS configuration is applied.
5. Verify TLS listener is active istioctl proxy-config listeners <gateway-pod> -n istio-system -o json | grep -A5 "443" The listener should show TLS context with the Secret name. Missing TLS context = Secret not loaded.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
The TLS Secret MUST be in the SAME namespace as the Gateway resource. This is the #1 TLS configuration error. Unlike VirtualServices (which can reference services cross-namespace), TLS Secrets are namespace-scoped to the Gateway. Always create the Secret in the Gateway's namespace.
Use cert-manager for automated TLS. Manual certificate management is error-prone — certs expire, SANs are wrong, chains are incomplete. cert-manager automates issuance and renewal of TLS certificates from Let's Encrypt, Vault, or internal CAs.
Always include the full certificate chain in tls.crt. Server certificate FIRST, then intermediate CA certs, then root CA (optional). Wrong order or missing intermediates cause "unknown CA" errors on some clients but not others — maddening to debug.
Test TLS with openssl s_client, not curl. openssl s_client -connect <IP>:443 -servername jobpost.com Shows the full TLS handshake, certificate chain, and any errors. Much more diagnostic information than curl's "SSL certificate problem."
TR5
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR5
HTTP Route Order Conflict — First Match Shadows Other Routes, Wrong Traffic Distribution

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService has multiple HTTP routes with match conditions: a canary route (5% to v2), a specific path route (/api/admin → v1), and a default catch-all. However, the canary route always gets 100% of traffic, or the /api/admin path never matches. The route order in the VirtualService causes one route to shadow others. Istio evaluates routes in ORDER — the FIRST matching route wins. If the catch-all is listed first, no other route ever matches.

  kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml
  spec:
    hosts:
    - anihpj-api
    http:
    - route:                          ← Route 1: Catch-all (NO match!)
      - destination:
          host: anihpj-api
          subset: v1
        weight: 100
    - match:                           ← Route 2: Canary — NEVER REACHED!
      - headers:
          canary:
            exact: "true"
      route:
      - destination:
          host: anihpj-api
          subset: v2
    - match:                           ← Route 3: Specific path — NEVER REACHED!
      - uri:
          prefix: /api/admin
      route:
      - destination:
          host: anihpj-api
          subset: v1
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Catch-all route listed FIRST: A route with NO match conditions matches ALL requests. If it's the first route, it immediately wins — no subsequent route is ever evaluated. Always put catch-all routes LAST.
  2. Weighted routing before specific matches: A 90/10 traffic split with a header match positioned BEFORE the specific path routes. All traffic (even with matching headers) hits the weighted split first and is distributed.
  3. Exact match vs prefix match ordering: An exact: /api match appears before prefix: /api/admin. Both match /api/admin, but the exact match wins because it comes first — even though prefix would be more appropriate.
  4. Header match conditions too broad: A header match like regex: ".*" or present: true for a common header matches ALL requests, shadowing subsequent routes.
  5. Mirror route consuming traffic: A mirror rule at position 1 with no match redirects all traffic to the mirror destination — the original route and all subsequent routes are effectively bypassed.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Multiple VirtualServices for same host — different VS define conflicting routes; the one with the oldest creation timestamp wins
  2. Route has redirect/fault/directResponse — non-routing actions at position 1 intercept all traffic
  3. Weight total not 100 — weighted routes with sum != 100 cause unpredictable distribution
  4. Case sensitivity in match — uri: exact: /API vs actual path /api; HTTP paths are case-sensitive in Istio matching
  5. Query parameter matching not supported — match on query params requires regex on uri, not a separate match field
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New to Istio routing model: Team assumes VirtualService uses "best match" or "longest prefix" like other proxies — Istio uses "first match wins," which is counterintuitive for Kubernetes users accustomed to Ingress.
  2. Copy-pasted routes from example: Copied a VirtualService example that had catch-all first without understanding route ordering implications.
  3. Generated VirtualService from tool: A YAML generator or Helm template produces routes in alphabetical order, not priority order — catch-all ends up first.
  4. kind cluster testing with curl: Testing routes with curl without proper Host headers — match conditions that rely on headers silently fail.
  5. Iterative route addition without reordering: New routes appended to the end of the VirtualService — if they should take priority, they must be moved to the top.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vs <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A2 "http:" | head -30 Review route order visually. Routes with NO match condition (catch-all) must be LAST. Specific matches should come first.
