istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n <ns> -o json | grep -B5 -A10 "match\|route" Shows the Envoy route table. The first route config is the one that always wins for matching requests.
curl -v -H "canary: true" http://<SVC>/api/admin Test with specific headers/paths to verify which route captures the request. Compare against expected behavior.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: A catch-all route (no match conditions) is listed FIRST in the VirtualService. Since Istio evaluates routes in order — first match wins — the catch-all consumes every request, and no subsequent specific routes ever match. The correct order is: most specific matches first, then progressively broader matches, with the catch-all LAST.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Review route order — most specific MUST come first Reorder routes: 1) Exact path matches, 2) Prefix path matches, 3) Header-based matches, 4) Weighted distribution, 5) Catch-all (no match).
2. Move catch-all to the LAST position kubectl edit vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj Cut the catch-all route (no match conditions) and paste it as the last http route. All specific routes will now be evaluated first.
3. Verify each route matches its intended traffic curl -v http://<SVC>/api/admin && curl -v -H "canary: true" http://<SVC>/api/jobs Each request should hit the correct route. Use different paths/headers to test all routes.
4. Add a catch-all at the end (if missing) Always include a catch-all route as the LAST entry. Without it, unmatched requests return 404. With it, they fall through to a default destination.
5. Use istioctl analyze to detect ordering issues istioctl analyze -n anihpj Istio 1.20+ can detect shadowed routes — routes that can never match because a preceding route always captures the same traffic.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
First match wins. ALWAYS. This is non-negotiable. Every Istio user trips over this. Routes are evaluated top-to-bottom — the FIRST matching route wins and no others are checked. Specific→General is the only correct ordering.
Always put a catch-all as the LAST route. A route with NO match conditions is a catch-all. If it's not last, it shadows everything below it. If you don't have a catch-all at the end, add one — unmatched requests return 404.
Use istioctl proxy-config routes to see actual evaluation order. istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n <ns> The VirtualService YAML shows the route list — the Envoy route table shows the evaluation order. Verify they're the same. If a route is missing from Envoy, it's being shadowed.
Add comments in your VirtualService YAML for route ordering. Label each route with its priority: "# PRIORITY 1: Admin routes", "# PRIORITY 2: Canary header", "# LAST: Catch-all". This prevents reordering mistakes during edits.

📌 TR6–TR10: Egress & External Traffic

TR6
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR6
Egress Traffic Blocked — External API Calls Fail from Inside Mesh

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api service inside the mesh tries to call an external payment API (api.payment-gateway.com), but the request fails with connection refused or times out. By default, Istio blocks ALL outbound traffic to external hosts — only hosts explicitly allowed via ServiceEntry or meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy can be reached. Envoy sidecars are blocking the outbound connection because the external host is not in the mesh's service registry.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-api -- curl -v https://api.payment-gateway.com
  curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer
  (Envoy is blocking — external host not in mesh registry)

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep "payment-gateway"
  [warning] Unknown cluster: outbound|443||api.payment-gateway.com
  [error] No route to external host: blocked by default outboundTrafficPolicy

  kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep outbound
  outboundTrafficPolicy:   # empty = ALLOW_ANY or REGISTRY_ONLY?
  (REGISTRY_ONLY blocks all external traffic by default)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. REGISTRY_ONLY outboundTrafficPolicy mode: The default mesh config sets outboundTrafficPolicy.mode: REGISTRY_ONLY, which blocks ALL traffic to hosts not registered in Istio's service registry. External APIs are not registered by default — they must be explicitly added via ServiceEntry. Fix: create ServiceEntry or change mode to ALLOW_ANY.
  2. No ServiceEntry for the external host: A ServiceEntry resource declaring api.payment-gateway.com as an external service was never created. Without it, Envoy refuses to route traffic to that hostname. Check: kubectl get serviceentry -n anihpj.
  3. ServiceEntry has wrong resolution: resolution: NONE (default, uses DNS) may not work if CoreDNS can't resolve the external hostname. Change to resolution: DNS or STATIC with explicit IP endpoints.
  4. ServiceEntry ports don't match: ServiceEntry defines port 80 but the application calls https:// on port 443. Ports must match — Istio creates separate clusters per port. Check: kubectl get se -o yaml | grep -A5 "ports:".
  5. Sidecar resource restricting egress: A Sidecar resource with egress field may restrict which hosts a workload can access, even if a ServiceEntry exists globally. The Sidecar overrides the global registry for that workload.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. DNS resolution failure inside pod — /etc/resolv.conf has wrong nameserver or search domain
  2. TLS origination not configured — ServiceEntry has HTTP but the external API requires HTTPS; need TLS origination
  3. NetworkPolicy blocking egress from pod to external IP on port 443
  4. Egress gateway misconfigured — traffic routed through egress gateway but the gateway's ServiceEntry is wrong
  5. ServiceEntry location field wrong — MESH_EXTERNAL vs MESH_INTERNAL affects routing behavior
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First Istio deployment — team unaware REGISTRY_ONLY is default: Kubernetes Services reach external endpoints by default; Istio blocks them by default. This is the #1 surprise for new Istio users.
  2. kind cluster with Docker network isolation: Docker's internal networking blocks kind pods from reaching certain external IPs even without Istio.
  3. Corporate proxy required: External traffic must go through an HTTP proxy — ServiceEntry doesn't configure proxy settings; requires EnvoyFilter or mesh config.
  4. kubeadm cluster with restrictive firewall: Node-level firewall blocks outbound HTTPS to external APIs, appearing as an Istio issue.
  5. Air-gapped cluster — external APIs literally unreachable: No internet connectivity at all; ServiceEntry won't help — need local API mock/stub.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep -A2 "outboundTrafficPolicy" REGISTRY_ONLY = blocks external by default. ALLOW_ANY = allows all external. Switch to ALLOW_ANY for quick testing.
kubectl get serviceentry --all-namespaces | grep "payment-gateway" ServiceEntry must exist for each external host in REGISTRY_ONLY mode. Missing = traffic blocked.
istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> | grep "payment-gateway" If a cluster for the external host doesn't exist in Envoy, the ServiceEntry didn't register correctly.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Istio's default outboundTrafficPolicy: REGISTRY_ONLY blocks all external traffic. The external payment API host (api.payment-gateway.com) is not registered in the mesh service registry. A ServiceEntry must be created to whitelist the external host, or the outbound policy must be changed to ALLOW_ANY for less restrictive egress.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create ServiceEntry for the external host kubectl apply -f - <<EOF ... apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1 kind: ServiceEntry ... spec: hosts: [api.payment-gateway.com] ports: [{number: 443, protocol: HTTPS}] resolution: DNS ... EOF Registers the external host in Istio's registry. Envoy now creates a cluster for it and allows traffic.
2. Verify cluster appears in Envoy istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj | grep "payment-gateway" After ServiceEntry is created, Envoy should show outbound|443||api.payment-gateway.com within seconds.
3. (Alternative) Change to ALLOW_ANY mode istioctl install --set meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy.mode=ALLOW_ANY Allows all external traffic without ServiceEntries. Less secure but simpler for development environments.
4. Test external connectivity kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-api -- curl -v https://api.payment-gateway.com Should now succeed. If not, check ServiceEntry ports and resolution mode.
5. For TLS origination, add TLS settings to ServiceEntry If the external API needs TLS but the app uses HTTP, configure TLS origination in DestinationRule referencing the ServiceEntry host.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
REGISTRY_ONLY is the production default — know it well. ALLOW_ANY is easy but insecure (allows all egress). REGISTRY_ONLY requires explicit ServiceEntries — more work but gives you complete control and audit trail of external dependencies.
ServiceEntry = your external API catalog. Every external API your mesh services call should have a ServiceEntry. This documents dependencies, enables observability, and gives you control over egress security.
Use resolution: DNS for dynamic IPs, STATIC for fixed IPs. DNS = Istio resolves the hostname periodically (handles IP changes). STATIC = you provide IPs (faster, no DNS dependency). NONE = original dest IP is used (for transparent pass-through).
Check the Envoy cluster list — not the ServiceEntry YAML. istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> If the external host isn't in the cluster list, traffic is blocked — regardless of what your ServiceEntry YAML says. Always verify.
TR7
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR7
Traffic Shifting Weight Wrong — Canary Gets 100% Instead of 10%

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService is configured to split traffic 90% to v1 (stable) and 10% to v2 (canary), but monitoring shows v2 receiving 100% of traffic or v1 receiving nothing. The anihpj canary deployment is accidentally serving all production users. The VirtualService YAML looks correct — two destinations with weights — but Istio normalizes weights differently than expected, or one destination's host/subset doesn't resolve to any endpoints, causing the other to get all traffic.

  kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A15 "route:"
  route:
  - destination:
      host: anihpj-api
      subset: v1
    weight: 90
  - destination:
      host: anihpj-api
      subset: v2
    weight: 10

  istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "anihpj-api.*v2"
  outbound|8080|v2|anihpj-api.anihpj.svc   WEIGHTED: weight 100 ← NORMALIZED!
  outbound|8080|v1|anihpj-api.anihpj.svc   WEIGHTED: weight 0   ← ZERO!

  kubectl get endpoints anihpj-api -n anihpj
  NAME          ENDPOINTS
  anihpj-api    10.244.1.5:8080,10.244.1.6:8080   ← Both v1 and v2 pods
  ← But DestinationRule subsets: v1 has NO matching pods (label mismatch)!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Subset with zero endpoints gets 0%: If subset v1 has no healthy pods (label mismatch, all pods failing health checks), Envoy removes it from load balancing. The 90% weight is redistributed to the remaining destinations — v2 gets 100%.
  2. Weight normalization misunderstanding: Istio normalizes weights to percentages. Weights of {90, 10} → 90%/10%. But if both destinations route to the SAME cluster (same host + subset), the weights effectively resolve to 100% to that cluster. Duplicate destination entries cause issues.
  3. DestinationRule subsets incorrect: Both v1 and v2 subsets in the DestinationRule have the SAME labels — both select the same pods. The VirtualService weight is applied to identical endpoint groups, resulting in 100%/100% (all traffic to both — the first matching route wins).
  4. Route order issue with weighted routing: A header-based match route BEFORE the weighted route captures all canary traffic. The header route sends 100% to v2, then remaining traffic hits the 90/10 split — but all canary-intended traffic was already consumed.
  5. Pod readiness probe failing on v1: v1 pods are unhealthy (failing readiness probe). Istio removes them from the load balancing pool. v2 pods are healthy, so they receive all traffic despite the 90/10 weight configuration.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Only one destination in the route — forgot to add the v2 destination to the weighted list
  2. Weight field missing — Istio assigns equal weight to all destinations if weight field omitted
  3. TrafficPolicy in DestinationRule overrides VS weight — DR loadBalancer setting conflicts with weight-based routing
  4. HPA scaled v1 to 0 — v1 deployment scaled down accidentally, leaving only v2 pods
  5. Service selector changed — Service points only to v2 pods after a label update
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First canary deployment: Team sets up weighted routing but doesn't understand that weights distribute to healthy endpoints only — if v1 is down, v2 gets everything.
  2. kind cluster with limited resources: v1 pods can't start due to resource limits on kind — effectively all traffic goes to v2.
  3. Mirroring vs shifting confusion: Team configured mirror instead of route — traffic is duplicated to v2 instead of shifted.
  4. kubeadm cluster with manual pod scaling: v1 replicas manually set to 0 during testing and never restored.
  5. multi-cluster mesh — v2 pods in kind-cl2 are healthy but v1 pods in kubeadm are down, skewing the weight distribution across clusters.
🔍 What to Look At:
istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> | grep -E "v1|v2" | grep WEIGHTED Shows the ACTUAL weights Envoy is using after normalization. If v1 shows weight 0, its endpoints are unhealthy.
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l <subset-labels> Verify pods exist for each subset. Zero pods = that subset gets 0% of traffic.
kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns> Shows all pod IPs behind the Service. Compare against subset pod IPs to verify both subsets have endpoints.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: One of the DestinationRule subsets (v1) resolves to zero healthy endpoints — either pods don't match the subset labels, or pods are failing health checks. Envoy removes the zero-endpoint subset from load balancing and redistributes its weight to the remaining destinations — v2 gets 100% instead of the intended 10%. Weight-based routing requires ALL subsets to have at least one healthy endpoint.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify each subset has healthy pods kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-api,app-version=v1 Each subset label combination must return at least one Running pod. Zero = fix labels or scale up.
2. Fix DestinationRule subset labels to match pods kubectl edit dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj Ensure subset labels EXACTLY match pod labels. Use kubectl get pods --show-labels to verify.
3. Verify weights in Envoy clusters istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n anihpj -o json | jq '.[] | select(.name | contains("anihpj-api")) | {name, weight: .load_assignment.endpoints[0].lb_endpoints[0].load_balancing_weight}' Confirms actual weight distribution. Should show ~90 for v1 and ~10 for v2.
4. Ensure v1 Deployment has at least 1 replica kubectl scale deploy anihpj-api-v1 -n anihpj --replicas=1 Weighted routing requires at least one pod in each subset. Scale up if needed.
5. Test canary routing with a loop for i in {1..100}; do curl -s http://<SVC>/api/jobs | grep "version"; done | sort | uniq -c 100 requests should show ~90 from v1 and ~10 from v2. Note: Istio weights are approximate, not exact.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Zero healthy endpoints = zero traffic. Always. If a subset has no pods (or pods are unhealthy), its weight is redistributed to other destinations. A 90/10 split becomes 0/100 if the 90% subset is empty. This is the most common cause of "canary taking all traffic."
Verify endpoints — not just the VS YAML. kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns> The VirtualService defines intent. The actual endpoint list determines reality. If v2 has 3 endpoints and v1 has 0, the weights don't matter — v2 gets everything.
Weights are approximate, not exact. Envoy uses weighted round-robin — it's statistically accurate over many requests, not exact per-request. 100 requests at 10% weight might give 7 or 13 to the canary, not exactly 10.
Use consistent labels for canary deployments. Every version of a service should use the same label key (version: v1, version: v2). Don't mix version, app-version, and track across deployments — it makes subset configuration fragile.
TR8
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR8
Header-Based Routing Not Working — All Traffic Goes to Default Route

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService is configured to route requests with end-user: internal header to v2 (internal API) and all other traffic to v1 (external API). But ALL requests — even those with the matching header — go to v1. The header match never fires. curl -H "end-user: internal" http://anihpj-api/api/jobs returns v1 content instead of v2. The header match condition is either syntactically wrong, case-sensitive, or in the wrong position in the route list.

  curl -H "end-user: internal" http://anihpj-api/api/jobs
  {"version":"v1"}   ← Expected v2!

  kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "match:"
  - match:
    - headers:
        end-user:           ← Missing value specification!
          exact: internal   ← Should be under "end-user", not sibling!
    route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api
        subset: v2

  istioctl analyze -n anihpj
  ❌ Error [IST0138] VirtualService anihpj-api-vs: header match
     "end-user" has no match type (exact, prefix, regex, or present)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Header match missing type: Header matches require a type field (exact, prefix, regex, or present). If the type is missing or on the wrong indentation level, the match is invalid and silently skipped. Correct format: headers: {end-user: {exact: "internal"}}.
  2. Case sensitivity: HTTP headers are case-insensitive per RFC 7230, but the match VALUE is case-sensitive in Istio. exact: "Internal" won't match internal. Use lowercase values or regex (regex: "(?i)internal") for case-insensitive matching.
  3. Header-based route AFTER catch-all: The header match route is positioned AFTER a catch-all route. Since the catch-all matches first, the header route is never evaluated. Move the header route BEFORE the catch-all.
  4. Header not sent by client/app: The application or curl command doesn't actually send the header. Typos in the header name (enduser vs end-user) or HTTP libraries stripping custom headers. Verify with curl -v or proxy access logs.
  5. Multiple header match conditions AND logic: Multiple headers in a single match are ANDed — ALL must match. If the route requires both end-user: internal AND version: canary, requests with only one header don't match.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Gateway stripping headers — some gateways/proxies remove custom headers before forwarding
  2. Header value with special characters — regex match needed for values containing colons, slashes, or spaces
  3. match vs match (singular vs plural) — correct field is - match: (list), not - matches:
  4. Port in host header — Host: anihpj-api:8080 vs just anihpj-api; header match on host won't work if port is included
  5. Envoy not receiving the header — sidecar's iptables rules strip or modify certain headers
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New to Istio header matching: Team assumes header match is like Kubernetes ingress annotations — Istio's YAML structure is different and more strict about match types.
  2. kind cluster with curl testing: curl on kind nodes behaves differently — some headers are filtered by the Docker network stack.
  3. Service mesh testing with browser: Browser sends many headers automatically (User-Agent, Accept, etc.) that can accidentally match or interfere with route matching.
  4. Copy-pasted header match from older API version: v1alpha3 vs v1beta1 VirtualService API — header match syntax changed between versions.
  5. kubeadm cluster with nginx ingress: Team confused Kubernetes Ingress header annotations with Istio VirtualService header match syntax.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vs <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A15 "match:" Check header match syntax: each header must have a type (exact/prefix/regex/present). Check indentation — the type must be nested under the header name.
curl -v -H "end-user: internal" http://<SVC>/ Use -v to verify the header is actually sent in the request. Look at the request headers printed by curl.
istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n <ns> -o json | grep -A10 "headers" Shows the Envoy route config with header matchers. Verify the header match is present and correctly structured.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The header match in the VirtualService is missing a match type (exact, prefix, regex, or present), or the type is at the wrong YAML indentation level. Istio requires each header to specify HOW to match: exact string, prefix, regex, or just check if the header is present. Without the type, the match is invalid and the route is silently skipped.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Fix header match syntax Correct format: - match: - headers: {end-user: {exact: "internal"}}. Ensure the match type is nested under the header name, not at the same level.
2. Move header-based route BEFORE the catch-all Reorder routes: header match first, then weighted routes, then catch-all last. First match wins — headers must be checked before the catch-all.
3. Verify header is being sent kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request GET /stats | grep "downstream" Check if envoy is receiving the header. Or enable access logging to see all headers on each request.
4. Test with a simpler match first Use headers: {end-user: {present: true}} to match ANY request with the header, without checking the value. Then refine to exact/regex.
5. Use istioctl analyze to catch syntax errors istioctl analyze -n anihpj Detects invalid header match configurations, missing match types, and route shadowing.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Every header match needs a type: exact, prefix, regex, or present. Just listing the header name is not enough. Istio must know HOW to match the value. Missing type = invalid match = route skipped. istioctl analyze catches this.
Use present: true for simple feature flags. headers: {canary: {present: true}} When you just need to check if a header exists (not its value), use present: true. Simpler than exact and works regardless of the header value.
Header matching + route ordering = most common confusion. Headers are checked in route order. If your header route is after the catch-all, it never fires. Always put header-based routes FIRST in the VirtualService.
Use regex for case-insensitive matching. headers: {end-user: {regex: "(?i)internal"}} HTTP headers are case-insensitive in names, but Istio matches values case-sensitively. Use regex with (?i) flag for case-insensitive value matching.
TR9
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR9
TCP Routing Misconfiguration — Non-HTTP Traffic Dropped or Routed Wrong

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-db PostgreSQL service uses TCP (not HTTP) on port 5432. A VirtualService and Gateway are configured for TCP routing, but database connections fail with connection refused or time out. istioctl proxy-config listeners shows the TCP listener exists, but no TCP proxy filter is attached. Or, the VirtualService uses HTTP route rules that don't apply to TCP traffic — TCP routes require a separate tcp: section, not http:.

  kubectl get vs anihpj-db-vs -n anihpj -o yaml
  spec:
    hosts:
    - anihpj-db
    http:              ← WRONG! PostgreSQL is TCP, not HTTP!
    - route:
      - destination:
          host: anihpj-db
          port:
            number: 5432

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-api -- nc -zv anihpj-db 5432
  nc: connect to anihpj-db port 5432 (tcp) failed: Connection refused

  kubectl get gw anihpj-db-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 "tcp:"
  (no TCP section — Gateway only has HTTP servers)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. TCP route defined under http section: VirtualService has separate sections for HTTP (http:), TCP (tcp:), and TLS (tls:). TCP services like PostgreSQL, Redis, MySQL must use the tcp: section. Rules under http: only apply to HTTP/1, HTTP/2, and gRPC traffic.
  2. Gateway server protocol wrong: The Gateway resource defines server port 5432 with protocol: HTTP. For TCP services, the protocol must be TCP or TLS. HTTP protocol on a TCP port means the Gateway expects HTTP traffic — TCP connections fail.
  3. No TCP listener on Gateway: The Gateway resource doesn't include a server block for the TCP port. Only ports defined in the Gateway are opened on the gateway proxy Envoy — if port 5432 isn't listed, it's not listening.
  4. VirtualService host doesn't match Gateway host: TCP VirtualService has hosts: [anihpj-db] but the Gateway expects hosts: ["*"] or anihpj-db. Host mismatch = VirtualService not bound to Gateway.
  5. TCP match conditions incorrectly specified: TCP VirtualService supports match on source labels, gateways, and destination ports — but NOT on headers, URI, or HTTP methods. Using HTTP match syntax in TCP routes silently fails.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Health check on TCP port failing — Envoy health check probes the TCP port and marks the cluster as unhealthy
  2. DestinationRule with HTTP-specific settings applied to TCP — connectionPool.http settings don't affect TCP traffic
  3. SNI passthrough not working — TLS traffic to anihpj-db needs TLS protocol in both Gateway and VirtualService
  4. Multiple TCP VirtualServices for same port — only one takes effect; the others are silently ignored
  5. Envoy TCP proxy filter not loaded — custom EnvoyFilter may have removed or modified the TCP proxy filter chain
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First time routing TCP through Istio: Most tutorials focus on HTTP routing. Team doesn't know TCP routes use a different VS section and Gateway protocol.
  2. kind cluster with database behind Istio: anihpj-db is a StatefulSet with PostgreSQL — connecting through the mesh requires proper TCP configuration.
  3. Database connection pooling confusion: Application uses connection pooling (pgbouncer) on a different port — VirtualService must account for both ports.
  4. kubeadm cluster with external database: PostgreSQL runs outside the cluster — TCP routing through ServiceEntry requires different configuration than in-mesh services.
  5. TLS termination at Gateway for TCP — Team expects Gateway to terminate TLS for TCP traffic, but TCP protocol passes through; use TLS protocol.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vs <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -E "^( http:| tcp:| tls:)" Check which section the routes are under. TCP services must use tcp: section, not http:.
kubectl get gw <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -B2 -A5 "port:" Verify server port protocol is TCP (not HTTP) for non-HTTP services. Gateway protocol determines how Envoy handles the connection.
istioctl proxy-config listeners <pod> -n <ns> | grep -A5 "5432" Shows if a TCP listener exists on port 5432. Missing listener = Gateway or VirtualService didn't create it.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The VirtualService defines the PostgreSQL database route under the http: section instead of tcp:. HTTP route rules (header matching, URI prefix, weighted routing) don't apply to TCP traffic. TCP services must use the tcp: section with a single destination per route. Additionally, the Gateway server port must use protocol: TCP (not HTTP) for non-HTTP backends.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Move TCP route to tcp section Remove the database route from http: and add it under tcp:: tcp: - match: - port: 5432 route: - destination: {host: anihpj-db, port: {number: 5432}}.
2. Fix Gateway server protocol to TCP kubectl edit gw anihpj-gateway -n anihpj Change protocol: HTTP to protocol: TCP for port 5432. Or add a new server block for TCP if routing through the ingress gateway.
3. Verify TCP listener is created istioctl proxy-config listeners <gateway-pod> -n istio-system | grep 5432 Should show a TCP listener on 0.0.0.0:5432 with a TCP proxy filter.
4. Test database connectivity kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-api -- psql -h anihpj-db -U postgres -c "SELECT 1" Should connect successfully through the mesh. Verify with istio-proxy access logs or connection counters.
5. For TLS-encrypted database, use tls section If PostgreSQL uses TLS, use tls: section in VirtualService and protocol: TLS in Gateway. The TLS VirtualService supports SNI-based routing.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
TCP traffic uses tcp: section, not http:. Every VirtualService has three route sections: http:, tcp:, and tls:. HTTP routes go under http, TCP (PostgreSQL, Redis, MySQL) under tcp, and TLS passthrough under tls. Wrong section = completely ignored.
Gateway protocol determines how Envoy handles the connection. HTTP = L7 HTTP routing (path, headers, etc.). TCP = L4 TCP proxy (no HTTP parsing). TLS = SNI-based passthrough. Mismatch between Gateway protocol and VirtualService section = connection failure.
For databases, TCP routing through mesh is normal. PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB — all use TCP. Configure them with tcp: VirtualService routes. This enables mTLS, metrics, and access logging for database traffic without changing the application.
istioctl proxy-config listeners shows all listeners. istioctl proxy-config listeners <pod> -n <ns> If the TCP port isn't in the listener list, your Gateway or VirtualService didn't create it. Fix the configuration — not the pod.
TR10
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR10
Sidecar Resource Too Restrictive — Workload Can't Reach Dependencies

🔍 Symptom: A Sidecar resource was applied to optimize the anihpj-web Envoy configuration by limiting which services it knows about. But now anihpj-web can't reach anihpj-api — 503 errors, "no healthy upstream." The Sidecar resource's egress field restricts which hosts the workload can connect to, and anihpj-api was accidentally omitted. Even though a VirtualService exists for anihpj-api, the Sidecar's restrictive egress list prevents the Envoy from creating a cluster for it.

  kubectl get sidecar anihpj-web-sidecar -n anihpj -o yaml
  spec:
    egress:
    - hosts:
      - "./anihpj-db.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
      - "./redis.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
      ← MISSING: anihpj-api!
    workloadSelector:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web

  curl http://anihpj-api/api/jobs (from anihpj-web pod)
  HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
  upstream connect error: no healthy upstream

  istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "anihpj-api"
  (no output — Sidecar doesn't allow Envoy to know about anihpj-api!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Dependency omitted from Sidecar egress hosts: The Sidecar's egress.hosts list explicitly enumerates allowed outbound connections. Missing anihpj-api means Envoy doesn't create a cluster for it — connections fail with "no healthy upstream." Add the missing host.
  2. Wrong host format in Sidecar: The Sidecar uses ./anihpj-db.anihpj.svc.cluster.local (FQDN with ./ prefix) but anihpj-api is referenced as anihpj-api (short name). The format must match what Istio's service registry uses.
  3. Sidecar workloadSelector too broad: The selector matches ALL workloads in the namespace (app: anihpj-web), applying the restrictive egress to more pods than intended. Pods that need to reach different services are blocked.
  4. No wildcard for namespace: The Sidecar lists individual hosts instead of ./* (all services in current namespace). When a new service is added to the namespace, the Sidecar must be manually updated — easy to forget.
  5. Ingress side missing: The Sidecar defines egress but forgets to define ingress for inbound traffic. Without ingress, the workload's Envoy may not accept inbound connections on expected ports.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Sidecar applied to istio-system namespace — affects istiod and gateway pods, breaking the entire mesh
  2. Multiple Sidecars with same workloadSelector — only one takes effect; the restrictive one may win unpredictably
  3. Sidecar not applied because workloadSelector labels changed — pods label mismatch means Sidecar doesn't apply
  4. Default Sidecar (istio-system) overrides namespace-local Sidecar — global Sidecar has broader scope
  5. Sidecar import/export confusion — exportTo on DestinationRule conflicts with Sidecar egress
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First time using Sidecar resource: Team applies Sidecar to optimize Envoy memory usage but inadvertently breaks service connectivity by being too restrictive.
  2. Large mesh with many services: In a 50+ service mesh, manually listing every dependency in the Sidecar is error-prone — a missing host is almost guaranteed.
  3. kind cluster testing Sidecar optimization: Team tests Sidecar on kind and accidentally applies the restrictive config to production kubeadm.
  4. New microservice added after Sidecar created: A new service (anihpj-notifications) was added to the namespace but the Sidecar wasn't updated to include it.
  5. Copy-pasted Sidecar from another namespace: Sidecar from namespace-A copied to namespace-B — hosts reference services in namespace-A that don't exist in namespace-B.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get sidecar -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A20 "egress:" Check the egress hosts list. Every service the workload needs to reach must be listed explicitly or covered by a wildcard.
istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> | grep -c "outbound" Without Sidecar: 50+ clusters. With restrictive Sidecar: 5-10 clusters. Count the clusters — missing services = missing clusters.
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l <sidecar-selector> Verify which pods the Sidecar is affecting. If the selector is too broad, more pods are restricted than intended.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Sidecar resource's egress.hosts list doesn't include all services the workload depends on. The anihpj-api service was omitted, so Envoy doesn't create an outbound cluster for it — connections fail with 503. Sidecar is a powerful optimization tool but requires knowing ALL dependencies upfront. Even one missing host breaks service connectivity.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add missing dependency to Sidecar egress kubectl edit sidecar anihpj-web-sidecar -n anihpj Add "./anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local" to the egress hosts list. Envoy creates the cluster within seconds.
2. Use wildcards for simpler management Replace individual hosts with "./*" (all services in current namespace) + "istio-system/*" (control plane). Easy to maintain as services change.
3. Verify clusters are created istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "anihpj-api" Should now show outbound|8080||anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local.
4. Test connectivity kubectl exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-web -- curl -s http://anihpj-api/api/jobs Should return job listings. If still 503, check that the host format matches the cluster list.
5. Consider removing Sidecar if not needed kubectl delete sidecar anihpj-web-sidecar -n anihpj Sidecar is an optimization — not a requirement. If managing the host list is too error-prone, remove the Sidecar and let Envoy know about all services.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Sidecar is an optimization — only use it when you need it. In small meshes (<20 services), Sidecar adds complexity without significant benefits. In large meshes (100+ services), it dramatically reduces Envoy memory usage. Apply it selectively when you actually need the optimization.
Use ./* for your namespace, not individual hosts. hosts: ["./*"] This lets the workload reach ALL services in its own namespace. Add external namespaces only when cross-namespace communication is needed. Much simpler than maintaining a host list.
Check the cluster count after applying Sidecar. istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> | grep -c "outbound" Without Sidecar: 50+. With restrictive Sidecar: exactly the number of hosts you listed + istiod/system. If the count is wrong, your host list is incomplete.
Update Sidecar when adding new services. Every new microservice added to the namespace is invisible to workloads with restrictive Sidecars until you update the egress list. Make Sidecar updates part of your service deployment checklist.

📌 TR11–TR13: Traffic Mirroring, Redirects & Rewrites

TR11
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR11
Traffic Mirroring Not Working — No Traffic Copied to Canary

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService is configured to mirror 100% of production traffic to a canary deployment (v2) for testing, but zero traffic reaches the canary. The mirror destination shows no requests. The VirtualService YAML has mirror configured, but the canary pods show no incoming connections. The mirror is silently ignored — perhaps because the mirror destination uses a subset with no healthy endpoints, or the mirror percentage is formatted incorrectly.

  kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A8 "mirror:"
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api
        subset: v1
    mirror:
      host: anihpj-api
      subset: v2
    mirrorPercentage:           ← Missing value field!
      (empty — defaults to 0%)

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-v2-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-api | wc -l
  0   ← No requests reaching the canary!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. mirrorPercentage value missing or zero: mirrorPercentage.value defaults to 0 if not specified. Must set mirrorPercentage: {value: 100.0} to mirror all traffic. The field requires the nested value key — just writing mirrorPercentage: 100 is invalid YAML for Istio.
  2. Mirror destination subset has no healthy pods: The mirror destination's subset (e.g., v2) resolves to zero endpoints. Envoy silently drops mirrored traffic when the mirror cluster has no healthy endpoints — no error, just zero traffic.
  3. Mirror destination host unreachable: The mirror destination hostname doesn't resolve in the mesh registry. Envoy skips mirroring to unreachable hosts without logging an error.
  4. Mirror on wrong route: The mirror is configured on the LAST route entry, but a catch-all route above it captures ALL traffic. The route with mirror is never evaluated. Mirror must be on the route that actually processes traffic.
  5. mirror vs mirror (singular/plural): Using mirrors: (plural, wrong) instead of mirror: (singular, correct). The Istio API uses singular mirror — plural is silently ignored.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Firewall blocking mirrored traffic — mirror destination on a different subnet that's not reachable
  2. mTLS failing for mirrored traffic — mirror destination requires mTLS but the mirrored request doesn't have the correct identity
  3. Mirrored response causes confusion — the mirror destination returns errors that are logged but not propagated
  4. Sidecar resource blocking mirror destination — egress restriction prevents Envoy from creating cluster for the mirror host
  5. HTTP method restrictions — mirror destination only accepts POST but mirrored traffic includes GET/HEAD requests that the backend rejects
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First time using traffic mirroring: Team expects mirror to "just work" but doesn't realize it requires the mirror destination to be a running, reachable service with matching endpoints.
  2. kind cluster with canary not deployed: Mirror destination v2 was defined but the canary Deployment was never created — zero pods, zero traffic mirrored.
  3. Mirror vs shadow vs fork confusion: Team uses terminology from other service meshes; Istio uses "mirror" specifically and its API differs from other implementations.
  4. kubeadm cluster with canary in different namespace: Mirror references host in a different namespace — cross-namespace mirror requires FQDN.
  5. Mirror for TCP traffic: TCP VirtualService doesn't support mirror — only HTTP routes can mirror. Team tries mirroring PostgreSQL traffic.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vs <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A10 "mirror" Verify mirrorPercentage.value is set to a non-zero number. Missing value field = 0% mirrored.
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l <mirror-subset-labels> Mirror destination must have at least one healthy pod. Zero pods = mirror silently drops traffic.
istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n <ns> -o json | grep -A10 "mirror" Shows the Envoy route with mirror configuration. Verify mirror is present in the actual Envoy config.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: mirrorPercentage.value was not set or is set to 0. The Istio mirror API requires mirrorPercentage: {value: 100.0} — just specifying the mirror destination without the percentage value results in 0% traffic mirrored. Additionally, the mirror destination subset must have healthy endpoints — if all pods in the canary subset are down, mirrored traffic is silently dropped.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set mirrorPercentage.value explicitly Add mirrorPercentage: {value: 100.0} to the VirtualService route. 100.0 mirrors ALL traffic; use 10.0 for 10% mirroring.
2. Verify mirror destination has healthy pods kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-api,app-version=v2 At least one Running and Ready pod. If none, deploy the canary or scale up.
3. Ensure mirror is on the active route Mirror must be configured on the route that actually matches traffic. If you have multiple routes, mirror must be on the one that processes requests.
4. Verify mirror in Envoy route config istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n anihpj -o json | grep -B5 -A15 "request_mirror_policies" Confirms the mirror policy is present in Envoy's actual configuration, not just the VirtualService YAML.
5. Test with canary pod logs kubectl logs -f <canary-pod> -n anihpj Mirrored requests appear as normal HTTP requests. If logs stay empty, mirroring isn't working.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
mirrorPercentage.value is mandatory — not optional. Without it, mirroring defaults to 0%. Always set mirrorPercentage: {value: 100.0}. The nested value key is required — top-level mirrorPercentage: 100 is invalid.
Mirror silently drops traffic if the destination is unhealthy. No logs, no errors, no warnings. If the mirror subset has zero healthy pods, your mirrored traffic vanishes. Always verify mirror destination health before relying on it.
Use mirror for dark launches, not canary deployments. Mirror sends a COPY of traffic to the canary — the canary's response is discarded. Use it for testing with real traffic (dark launch). Use weight-based routing for canary deployments where the canary's response matters.
Mirror uses the SAME headers as the original request. The mirrored request keeps the original Host header. If your canary expects a different host, it may reject the request. Add -host: canary header handling on the canary side or adjust routing.
TR12
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR12
HTTP Redirect Loop — Infinite 301/302 Redirects

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService is configured to redirect HTTP→HTTPS or old-URL→new-URL, but clients get stuck in an infinite redirect loop — ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS in the browser. The redirect rule creates a chain where each redirect points to a URL that matches another redirect rule. Or, the redirect authority includes a port that the Gateway doesn't serve, causing the client to reconnect and trigger the same redirect again.

  curl -v http://jobpost.com/
  HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
  Location: https://jobpost.com/
  (redirect to HTTPS)

  curl -v -L https://jobpost.com/
  HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
  Location: https://jobpost.com/   ← Same URL! Infinite loop!

  kubectl get vs anihpj-web-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "redirect:"
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /
    redirect:
      uri: /
      authority: jobpost.com       ← Redirects to itself on port 80!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. HTTPS redirect loop on HTTPS Gateway: A redirect rule on the HTTPS Gateway (port 443) redirects to HTTPS, but the redirect target matches the same Gateway and redirect rule — infinite recursion. The redirect rule must only exist on the HTTP Gateway (port 80), not HTTPS.
  2. Redirect authority missing scheme: redirect: {authority: "jobpost.com"} doesn't specify HTTPS. The client is redirected to http://jobpost.com which hits the same redirect rule again. Must use redirect: {authority: "jobpost.com", redirectCode: 301} and configure the HTTP Gateway to redirect to HTTPS explicitly.
  3. Redirect to same URL: The redirect.uri: / redirects to the same path (/). Combined with authority: jobpost.com, the client is sent to http://jobpost.com/ which matches the same VirtualService route — infinite loop.
  4. Port mismatch in redirect: Redirect authority is jobpost.com:8080 but the Gateway only serves port 80. The client gets redirected to port 8080, which doesn't exist, and the client retries — hitting the same redirect rule.
  5. Multiple VirtualServices with conflicting redirects: Two VS define redirect rules for the same host — one redirects to HTTPS, the other redirects back to HTTP. The client oscillates between them.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Redirect with capture groups creating recursive pattern — regex capture in redirect.uri that matches the new URL
  2. Application-level redirect conflicting with Istio redirect — Django returns 301, Istio returns 301, they point at each other
  3. Browser caching redirect — 301 is permanent; browser caches the redirect and perpetuates the loop even after the rule is fixed
  4. Redirect code 308 (Permanent Redirect) caching more aggressively than 301
  5. CDN or external load balancer redirecting independently — two layers of redirect fighting each other
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First HTTPS redirect setup: Team copies the HTTP→HTTPS redirect example but applies it to the HTTPS Gateway instead of HTTP Gateway — infinite loop.
  2. kind cluster with port-forward confusion: Port-forward to port 80 redirects to HTTPS :443, but port-forward doesn't support HTTPS — loop.
  3. kubeadm cluster with multiple Gateways: HTTP and HTTPS served from different Gateway resources — redirect references the wrong one.
  4. TLS termination at cloud LB: Cloud Load Balancer terminates TLS and forwards HTTP to Istio — Istio sees HTTP and redirects to HTTPS, but the LB expects HTTP.
  5. New team testing redirect with browser: Browser 301 caching makes debugging redirect loops extremely confusing — use curl -v instead.
🔍 What to Look At:
curl -v http://<HOST>/ 2>&1 | grep -E "Location:|HTTP/" Shows the redirect chain. Each Location header tells you where the client is being sent. Same URL = loop.
kubectl get vs --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -B5 -A10 "redirect:" Find all redirect rules across all VirtualServices. Check if multiple VS redirect to conflicting URLs.
kubectl get gw --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -B5 -A10 "hosts:" Verify Gateway host configuration. Redirect should exist on HTTP Gateway (80), not HTTPS Gateway (443).
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The HTTP→HTTPS redirect rule was applied to the HTTPS Gateway or the redirect destination matches the same route. HTTP→HTTPS redirect must ONLY exist on the HTTP Gateway (port 80) and redirect to https://jobpost.com — which is served by a DIFFERENT Gateway server (port 443) with a different VirtualService that does NOT have the redirect rule. Both Gateways can exist in the same Gateway resource as separate server blocks.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Configure HTTP→HTTPS redirect on HTTP Gateway only Create a Gateway with TWO server blocks: one for port 80 (HTTP with redirect) and one for port 443 (HTTPS with actual routing). Only the HTTP server has the redirect VirtualService.
2. Use separate VirtualServices for HTTP and HTTPS VS-http: has the redirect rule. VS-https: has the actual routing rules (no redirect). Both bind to the same Gateway but different server ports.
3. Verify redirect target doesn't match any redirect rule curl -v -L http://jobpost.com/ The final response should be 200 (not 301). If it's still a redirect, the HTTPS Gateway also has a redirect rule.
4. Clear browser cache after fixing redirect 301 redirects are cached by browsers. After fixing, open in incognito/private mode or use curl to verify.
5. Use 302 (Temporary) for testing redirectCode: 302 302 redirects are not cached by browsers, making debugging easier. Switch to 301 (Permanent) only when the redirect is verified correct.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
HTTP→HTTPS redirect goes on port 80, never on 443. One Gateway resource, TWO server blocks: port 80 serves the redirect VS, port 443 serves the real routing VS. If you put the redirect on the HTTPS server, every HTTPS request redirects to HTTPS — infinite loop.
Use two separate VirtualServices for HTTP redirect and HTTPS routing. VS-http: redirect rule only. VS-https: actual routes (no redirect). Clean separation prevents accidental redirect loops from route ordering issues.
Always debug redirects with curl, not a browser. curl -v -L http://jobpost.com/ curl shows every redirect step. Browsers cache 301 redirects permanently — making debugging impossible after the first request. Always test redirects with curl first.
Anihpj/jobpost HTTPS redirect is a common exam scenario. You'll likely need to configure HTTP→HTTPS redirect for jobpost.com on the ICA exam. Practice on your 6-cluster lab: HTTP Gateway on port 80 → redirect to HTTPS → HTTPS Gateway on 443 → VirtualService → anihpj-web.
TR13
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR13
URL Rewrite Not Working — Backend Gets Wrong Path

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService is configured to rewrite /api/v2/jobs to /jobs before forwarding to the backend, but the backend receives the original path (/api/v2/jobs) instead of the rewritten path (/jobs). The backend returns 404 because it doesn't have a route for /api/v2/jobs. The rewrite rule is syntactically correct but placed on the wrong match, or the rewrite doesn't apply to the matched route.

  curl http://anihpj-api/api/v2/jobs
  HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found   ← Backend expects /jobs, not /api/v2/jobs

  kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "rewrite:"
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /api/v2
    rewrite:
      uri: /
    route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -- tail -5 /var/log/access.log
  GET /api/v2/jobs HTTP/1.1 404   ← Backend still sees original path!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Rewrite on wrong route: The rewrite is configured on one route but traffic matches a DIFFERENT route (e.g., catch-all). Rewrite only applies to the specific route it's configured on — if traffic hits another route, no rewrite happens.
  2. Prefix rewrite removes too much or too little: rewrite: {uri: "/"} replaces the ENTIRE matched path with "/". For /api/v2/jobs, the prefix /api/v2 is matched, and the URI is rewritten to / + the remaining path /jobs → //jobs (double slash). Use rewrite: {uri: " "} (empty) or "/api/v1".
  3. Rewrite field name typo: Using rewriteUri: or urlRewrite: instead of the correct rewrite: with nested uri:. Wrong field name = rewrite silently ignored.
  4. Rewrite with exact match doesn't work as expected: uri: {exact: "/api/v2/jobs"} with rewrite: {uri: "/jobs"} — the entire path is replaced. Prefix match allows partial replacement; exact match replaces everything.
  5. Rewrite + redirect conflict: The route has BOTH rewrite and redirect. Only one takes effect — redirect overrides rewrite. The backend sees the redirect target, not the rewritten path.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Application-level path handling — Django/nginx in the container has its own URL routing that may conflict with Istio rewrite
  2. Multiple rewrite routes for same prefix — only the first matching route's rewrite applies
  3. Rewrite with authority change — rewriting both path and host requires separate authority field in rewrite
  4. Query parameters not preserved during rewrite — by default, query params are preserved; if they disappear, a custom EnvoyFilter may be stripping them
  5. Gateway stripping before VirtualService — Gateway-level configuration may strip path prefix before VirtualService matching
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First time using URL rewrite: Team assumes rewriting is automatic but doesn't understand prefix vs exact match behavior with rewrite.
  2. API version migration: Moving from /api/v1 to /api/v2 — rewrite should map v2 paths to v1 backend paths, but the mapping logic is reversed.
  3. kind cluster testing with curl paths: curl with trailing slashes behaves differently — /api/v2/jobs vs /api/v2/jobs/ match different prefixes.
  4. kubeadm cluster with nginx-ingress background: Team familiar with nginx rewrite rules (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target) — Istio's rewrite syntax is different.
  5. Multiple VirtualService layers: Gateway VS rewrites path, then internal VS also rewrites — double rewrite causing unexpected results.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vs <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A12 "rewrite:" Verify rewrite is on the correct route and the uri value is correct. Check that rewrite and redirect aren't both present.
istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n <ns> -o json | grep -A5 "prefix_rewrite\|regex_rewrite" Shows the actual rewrite configuration in Envoy. If missing, the rewrite rule didn't apply.
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy | grep "rewrite\|route" Proxy logs show if the route with rewrite was matched and how the path was transformed.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The rewrite is on a route that doesn't match the incoming traffic, OR the rewrite is set to uri: "/" which creates a double-slash path (//jobs) because the prefix match strips /api/v2 and prepends / before the remaining /jobs. Use rewrite: {uri: "/api/v1"} to map v2 paths to v1 backend paths, or use an empty string to strip the prefix entirely.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify rewrite is on the correct route Ensure the match conditions on the route with rewrite actually match your traffic. Test the match independently by removing rewrite and checking if the route is hit.
2. Fix rewrite URI for prefix match For prefix /api/v2, use rewrite: {uri: "/api/v1"} to map v2→v1 paths. The matched prefix is replaced with the rewrite URI; the remainder of the path is appended.
3. Remove conflicting redirect on same route If the route has both redirect and rewrite, remove one. They can't coexist on the same route.
4. Test with curl and verify path received curl -v http://anihpj-api/api/v2/jobs && kubectl logs <backend-pod> -n anihpj --tail=2 Backend logs should show the rewritten path (/api/v1/jobs), not the original (/api/v2/jobs).
5. Use istioctl proxy-config routes for verification istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n anihpj -o json | jq '.[] | select(.match) | {match, rewrite: .route.rewrite}' Confirms the rewrite configuration is correctly loaded by Envoy.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Prefix rewrite replaces the matched prefix — the rest of the path is appended. prefix: /api/v2 + rewrite: {uri: "/api/v1"} on path /api/v2/jobs → backend receives /api/v1/jobs. The matched prefix is REMOVED and the rewrite URI is PREPENDED.
Use rewrite: {uri: " "} to just strip the prefix. If you want /api/v2/jobs → /jobs, use an empty space or omit the uri field entirely. rewrite: {} strips the matched prefix without adding anything.
Rewrite is per-route, not per-VirtualService. If you have 5 routes and only 1 has rewrite, only traffic matching that 1 route gets rewritten. Traffic matching other routes gets the original path.
Verify with the backend, not the proxy. The Envoy config shows what SHOULD happen. The backend logs show what ACTUALLY arrived. Always check both — a rewrite that looks correct in Envoy may still surprise the backend.

📌 TR14–TR15: Multi-Cluster & Advanced Routing

TR14
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR14
Multi-Cluster Service Routing — Cross-Cluster Calls Failing

🔍 Symptom: Istio is configured for multi-cluster mesh (kind-cl1, kind-cl2, kind-cl3 in your 6-cluster lab). A Service on kind-cl1 needs to call a Service on kind-cl2 via Istio's multi-cluster routing. But cross-cluster requests fail with 503 Service Unavailable or timeout. The remote Service is not appearing in the local cluster's service registry, or the ServiceEntry for the remote cluster has incorrect endpoints or resolution mode.

  kubectl --context kind-cl1 exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -- curl http://anihpj-api.kind-cl2/api/jobs
  HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
  upstream connect error: no healthy upstream for anihpj-api.kind-cl2

  istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "kind-cl2"
  outbound|8080||anihpj-api.kind-cl2   HEALTHY: 0   ← Zero endpoints!

  kubectl --context kind-cl1 get serviceentry -n anihpj
  NAME              HOSTS                       LOCATION   RESOLUTION
  anihpj-api-cl2    anihpj-api.kind-cl2          MESH_INTERNAL   STATIC
  (STATIC resolution but no endpoints configured!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ServiceEntry with STATIC resolution but no endpoints: resolution: STATIC requires explicit endpoints (IP addresses). If endpoints are missing or incorrect, the cluster has zero healthy entries. Check: kubectl get se -o yaml | grep -A10 "endpoints:".
  2. Cross-cluster network connectivity broken: Pods on kind-cl1 can't reach pod IPs on kind-cl2 because the kind networks are isolated. Multi-cluster routing requires network connectivity between clusters — VPN, VPC peering, or flat network.
  3. DNS resolution cross-cluster failing: resolution: DNS relies on the local cluster's CoreDNS to resolve the remote hostname. If CoreDNS can't resolve anihpj-api.kind-cl2, the cluster has zero endpoints.
  4. mTLS trust domain mismatch: kind-cl1 uses trustDomain: cluster1.local and kind-cl2 uses trustDomain: cluster2.local. Cross-cluster mTLS requires a shared trust domain or explicit SPIFFE federation. Without it, TLS handshake fails.
  5. Gateway-based multi-cluster not configured: The east-west gateway on kind-cl2 is not deployed or the ServiceEntry doesn't route through it. Multi-cluster requires either flat network (direct pod-to-pod) or gateway-based (pod → local gateway → remote gateway → remote pod).
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. ServiceEntry port mismatch — remote service listens on 8080 but ServiceEntry defines port 80
  2. Remote cluster istiod not exposing services — exportTo: . (local only) on the remote service's resources
  3. Cross-cluster load balancing weight zero — all endpoints in remote cluster weighted to 0 by DestinationRule
  4. NetworkPolicy blocking inter-cluster traffic — pod-to-pod network policy on kind-cl2 blocks inbound from kind-cl1 CIDR
  5. Istio CA certificates not shared — separate root CAs means cross-cluster mTLS verification fails
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First multi-cluster mesh setup: Team configures ServiceEntry but doesn't realize the underlying network must also allow cross-cluster communication.
  2. kind clusters with isolated Docker networks: Each kind cluster uses a separate Docker network — pods on kind-cl1 can't reach kind-cl2 without a Docker network connection.
  3. kubeadm + kind hybrid: kubeadm cluster (bare metal) can't route to kind cluster (Docker NAT) — network layers incompatible.
  4. kind-cl1/2/3 multi-cluster lab: The 6-cluster lab's kind-cl1, cl2, cl3 are designed for multi-cluster testing but network isolation must be solved first.
  5. Remote cluster service not exposed: Services default to exportTo: * but someone changed it to exportTo: . — service not visible to other clusters.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl --context kind-cl2 get svc,endpoints -n anihpj Verify the remote service exists and has healthy endpoints. Cross-cluster routing can't reach a service that doesn't exist.
istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> | grep -E "HEALTHY|endpoint" Shows if the remote cluster has healthy endpoints. Zero = ServiceEntry endpoints wrong or network unreachable.
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -- ping <remote-pod-ip> Basic network connectivity test. If ping fails, the underlying network doesn't support cross-cluster pod communication.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The ServiceEntry for the remote cluster uses resolution: STATIC but has no endpoints configured, or the configured endpoint IPs are not reachable from the local cluster's pod network. Cross-cluster routing requires both Istio configuration (ServiceEntry/DestinationRule) AND underlying network connectivity (pod IPs must be routable across clusters).
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify remote service exists and is healthy kubectl --context kind-cl2 get pods,svc,endpoints -n anihpj The remote service must be running with healthy endpoints before cross-cluster routing can work.
2. Fix ServiceEntry endpoints or resolution For STATIC: add correct pod IPs. For DNS: ensure CoreDNS resolves the remote hostname. For gateway-based: configure LOCALITY_LB and egress gateway.
3. Verify cross-cluster network connectivity kubectl --context kind-cl1 run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- ping <kind-cl2-pod-ip> If pings fail, configure Docker networking to allow inter-cluster communication or set up a VPN/VPC peering.
4. For kind clusters, use host network or MetalLB kind clusters can be connected via a shared Docker network. Create all kind clusters on the same network in your 6-cluster lab for multi-cluster testing.
5. Verify mTLS trust across clusters Multi-cluster mTLS requires shared trust domain (cluster.local by default) or explicit SPIFFE trust bundle federation.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Multi-cluster = Istio config + network connectivity. Both must work. ServiceEntry configures Istio's view of the remote service. But the network must also allow pod-to-pod IP routing. If pings fail between clusters, no amount of Istio configuration will make cross-cluster calls work.
Use DNS resolution for dynamic remote endpoints. resolution: DNS lets Istio resolve the hostname periodically — better than STATIC for remote services that may change IPs. But DNS must be configured to resolve across clusters.
Your 6-cluster lab is perfect for multi-cluster practice. kind-cl1, cl2, cl3 are designed for multi-cluster scenarios. Practice cross-cluster ServiceEntry, east-west gateway, and locality-based load balancing across them.
Start with flat network multi-cluster before gateway-based. Flat network (pods can ping each other directly) is simpler. Gateway-based (traffic goes through east-west gateways) adds latency but works for isolated networks. Master flat network first.
TR15
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR15
Locality Load Balancing Fails — Traffic Not Staying in Same Region/Zone

🔍 Symptom: Locality-based load balancing is configured to keep traffic within the same region/zone (e.g., prefer pods on kind-cl1 for clients on kind-cl1). But traffic is randomly distributed across all clusters regardless of locality. The failoverPriority or localityLbSetting in the DestinationRule is not taking effect. Cross-region latency is high because requests are going to pods in remote clusters instead of local ones.

  kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A15 "localityLbSetting\|failover"
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      localityLbSetting:          ← Present but empty!
        (no distribute or failover configured)
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5

  kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep "topology.kubernetes.io/region\|zone"
  (no region/zone labels on kind nodes)

  istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep -A5 "locality"
  (no locality weights assigned — all endpoints equal weight)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. localityLbSetting empty or missing distribution: The localityLbSetting is present but doesn't have distribute or failover fields. Without explicit distribution rules, Istio uses equal-weight distribution across all localities. Must specify distribute: [{from: "us-east/*/*", to: {...}}].
  2. Nodes not labeled with region/zone: Istio determines pod locality from the node's topology.kubernetes.io/region and topology.kubernetes.io/zone labels. If nodes don't have these labels, all pods are in the same (empty) locality — locality LB has no effect. Check: kubectl get nodes --show-labels.
  3. All endpoints in same locality: If all pods are in the same region/zone (e.g., single-cluster deployment), locality LB correctly has nothing to distinguish — all traffic stays local because there's only one locality.
  4. localityLbSetting on wrong DestinationRule: The locality setting is on the DR for anihpj-api but traffic is routed via a different hostname that uses a different DR without locality settings.
  5. Outlier detection removing local endpoints: Local pods are failing health checks (outlier detection ejects them), forcing traffic to remote localities. The locality LB prefers local but local endpoints are all ejected — falls back to remote.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Mesh config locality settings override DR — global meshConfig.localityLbSetting conflicts with per-DR settings
  2. Envoy version doesn't support locality LB — older Envoy versions lack full locality-aware load balancing
  3. Distribute "from" field doesn't match actual pod localities — from: "us-east/*/*" but pods are in "us-east-1/a"
  4. Failover configured but no healthy endpoints in failover locality — failover chain broken
  5. Weighted routing overriding locality — VirtualService weight-based routing takes precedence over locality preferences
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Single-cluster lab — all 6 clusters are independent: Each cluster only has nodes in one locality. Locality LB works across zones within a cluster, not across separate clusters.
  2. kind clusters don't have region/zone labels by default: Must manually label kind nodes with kubectl label node <name> topology.kubernetes.io/region=us-east --overwrite.
  3. kubeadm single-node cluster: Only one node — all pods are in the same locality. Locality LB has no effect.
  4. Misunderstanding locality vs multi-cluster: Team thinks locality LB routes between clusters — it routes between zones/regions within the SAME control plane.
  5. First locality LB configuration — team expects automatic locality-aware routing without explicit distribute/failover rules.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep "region\|zone" Nodes must have topology.kubernetes.io/region and topology.kubernetes.io/zone labels for locality LB to work.
kubectl get dr <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A20 "localityLbSetting" Check that distribute or failover rules are explicitly defined. Empty localityLbSetting = no effect.
istioctl proxy-config endpoints <pod> -n <ns> --cluster "outbound|8080||anihpj-api" -o json | grep -A10 "locality" Shows the locality of each endpoint and any weight biases applied by locality LB.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The DestinationRule's localityLbSetting is present but empty — no distribute or failover rules are configured. Without explicit distribution rules, Istio treats all localities equally and uses standard load balancing. Additionally, kind/kubeadm nodes may not have topology.kubernetes.io/region and zone labels, so Istio can't distinguish pod localities.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Label nodes with region and zone kubectl label node <name> topology.kubernetes.io/region=us-east topology.kubernetes.io/zone=us-east-1a --overwrite Repeat for all nodes, using appropriate region/zone values per cluster.
2. Configure localityLbSetting with distribute rules Add distribute: [{from: "us-east/*/*", to: {"us-east/*/*": 80, "us-west/*/*": 20}}]. This keeps 80% of traffic in us-east and sends 20% to us-west for failover readiness.
3. Add failover rules for resilience Add failover: [{from: "us-east", to: "us-west"}, {from: "us-west", to: "us-east"}]. When all local endpoints are unhealthy, traffic fails over to the other region.
4. Verify endpoint locality in Envoy istioctl proxy-config endpoints <pod> -n anihpj --cluster "outbound|8080||anihpj-api" -o json | jq '.[] | {locality, weight}' Should show different weights for endpoints in different localities based on the distribute rules.
5. Test with traffic generator across localities Send requests from pods in different regions and verify they prefer local endpoints. Monitor with Kiali's locality graph.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Nodes MUST have region/zone labels for locality LB. kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep topology Without these labels, Istio sees all pods as co-located and locality LB does nothing. This is the #1 reason locality LB doesn't work — unlabeled nodes.
Distribute controls traffic split. Failover controls fallback. distribute = how traffic is split between localities under normal conditions. failover = where traffic goes when the local locality is completely unhealthy. Both are optional — configure what you need.
Locality LB works within a single control plane. It distributes traffic across zones/regions in the SAME mesh. For multi-cluster with separate control planes, use ServiceEntry + traffic distribution instead.
Label your 6-cluster lab nodes with regions. kubeadm = us-east-1a, kind-cka-lab = us-east-1b, kind-cl1 = us-west-2a, etc. This lets you practice locality LB across your lab clusters.

📌 TR16–TR20: Egress Gateway & External TLS Origination

TR16
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR16
Egress Gateway Not Routing — External Traffic Still Goes Direct

🔍 Symptom: An egress gateway was deployed to control all outbound traffic from the mesh to external services, but traffic is bypassing the egress gateway entirely. Pods are connecting directly to external APIs instead of going through the designated egress gateway. The egress gateway shows zero connections. The ServiceEntry, VirtualService, and DestinationRule for egress routing exist but aren't redirecting traffic through the gateway.

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway
  NAME                                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  istio-egressgateway-xxx                1/1     Running   0

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -- curl -v https://api.payment-gateway.com
  (traffic goes DIRECT to api.payment-gateway.com — not through egress gateway!)

  kubectl get se external-payment -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 "resolution\|location"
  resolution: DNS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL     ← Correct, but no egress gateway binding!

  kubectl get vs,dr -n anihpj -l "egress=true"
  No resources found   ← Missing VirtualService to redirect through gateway!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Missing VirtualService to redirect through egress gateway: A ServiceEntry alone only registers the external host. A VirtualService is needed to redirect traffic matched by that ServiceEntry TO the egress gateway. Without it, Envoy routes directly to the external host.
  2. Gateway resource not selecting egress gateway pods: The Gateway resource defines the egress gateway but its selector doesn't match any egress gateway pod labels. Check: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l <selector>.
  3. DestinationRule for TLS origination missing: Egress traffic to HTTPS sites needs a DestinationRule to configure TLS origination from the egress gateway. Without it, the gateway forwards plain HTTP — external HTTPS endpoint rejects it.
  4. Sidecar egress field not allowing egress gateway: The workload's Sidecar resource restricts egress to only certain hosts — the egress gateway host is not listed. Envoy can't route through the gateway because the Sidecar blocks it.
  5. ServiceEntry resolution NONE with egress gateway: resolution: NONE uses the original destination IP — it can't be redirected through an egress gateway. Must use resolution: DNS so the gateway can resolve the hostname.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Egress gateway namespace mismatch — Gateway resource in different namespace than egress gateway pods
  2. Port mismatch between ServiceEntry and Gateway — SE defines port 80 but Gateway only has port 443 open
  3. Egress gateway certificate issues — gateway can't establish TLS to external host because its own cert is invalid
  4. ALLOW_ANY mode bypasses egress gateway — meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy.mode: ALLOW_ANY lets traffic go directly
  5. NetworkPolicy blocking pod→egress gateway traffic on port 15443 (default egress TLS port)
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Egress gateway not installed: Default Istio profile does NOT include egress gateway. Must install explicitly: --set components.egressGateways[0].enabled=true.
  2. First egress gateway setup — team creates ServiceEntry but doesn't know VirtualService is also needed to force traffic through gateway.
  3. kind cluster with egress gateway resource constraints: Egress gateway pod can't start due to resource limits on kind — no gateway, all traffic goes direct.
  4. kubeadm cluster firewall: Egress gateway pod on kubeadm can't reach external APIs due to node firewall — appears as gateway not working.
  5. Multi-cluster egress — egress gateway on kind-cl1 routes traffic for services on kind-cl2, creating circular routing.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway Egress gateway pods must be Running. If not, install with --set components.egressGateways[0].enabled=true.
kubectl get vs,dr,se -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A5 "gateways:\|egress" VirtualService must specify gateways: [mesh, istio-egressgateway] to route through egress gateway.
istioctl proxy-config clusters <egress-pod> -n istio-system | grep "payment-gateway" Egress gateway Envoy should have a cluster for the external host. Missing = ServiceEntry not reaching the gateway.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The egress gateway is deployed but a VirtualService to redirect traffic THROUGH it was never created. ServiceEntry registers the external host in the mesh registry. But to force traffic through the egress gateway, a VirtualService must match the host and route it to gateways: [mesh, istio-egressgateway]. Without this VirtualService, Envoy sidecars route directly to the external host — bypassing the egress gateway entirely.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify egress gateway is installed and running kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway Install if missing: istioctl install --set components.egressGateways[0].enabled=true.
2. Create VirtualService to redirect through gateway VS with gateways: [mesh, istio-egressgateway] and route to the external host. This forces Envoy sidecars to route through the gateway, not directly.
3. Create DestinationRule for TLS origination DR for the external host with tls: {mode: SIMPLE, credentialName: ...}. Configures the egress gateway to originate TLS to the external API.
4. Create Gateway resource for egress Gateway resource selecting istio: egressgateway with server blocks for the external ports. This opens the ports on the egress gateway Envoy.
5. Verify traffic flows through gateway kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway --tail=20 | grep "payment-gateway" Egress gateway logs should show connections to the external host. If empty, traffic is still bypassing the gateway.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Egress gateway needs THREE resources: ServiceEntry + VirtualService + DestinationRule. ServiceEntry = register the host. VirtualService = redirect through gateway. DestinationRule = configure TLS origination. ALL THREE are required for a complete egress gateway setup.
Switch to REGISTRY_ONLY mode when using egress gateway. ALLOW_ANY mode lets traffic bypass the egress gateway directly. REGISTRY_ONLY forces all external traffic through the registry — and the registry routes through the egress gateway. Always use REGISTRY_ONLY with egress gateways.
Egress gateway is a security control, not a performance optimization. It adds latency (extra hop). Use it when you need: centralized egress IP, audit logging of all external calls, or controlled access to external services. For simple egress, ServiceEntry alone is sufficient.
Test egress with and without gateway on your 6-cluster lab. Deploy the payment-gateway mock service, then test direct ServiceEntry vs egress-gateway-routed access. Observe the difference in proxy-config clusters and access logs.
TR17
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR17
TLS Origination Fails — External HTTPS Call Rejected

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api pod calls an external payment API via HTTP (http://api.payment-gateway.com), but the external API requires HTTPS. A DestinationRule is configured for TLS origination (Istio upgrades the HTTP call to HTTPS), but the call fails with TLS handshake error or the external API rejects the connection. The TLS origination is either misconfigured, using the wrong TLS mode, or missing the CA certificate for the external API.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -- curl -v http://api.payment-gateway.com/pay
  curl: (35) error:1408F10B:SSL routines:ssl3_get_record:wrong version number

  kubectl get dr external-tls-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "tls:"
  trafficPolicy:
    tls:
      mode: SIMPLE          ← SIMPLE requires trusting the external CA!
    portLevelSettings:
    - port:
        number: 443
      tls:
        mode: SIMPLE
        (no caCertificates or credentialName!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. SIMPLE TLS mode without CA certificates: mode: SIMPLE makes Envoy originate TLS, but Envoy must verify the external server's certificate. Without caCertificates or credentialName, Envoy uses its default trust store — which may not include the external API's CA. Use mode: SIMPLE with caCertificates: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt.
  2. MUTUAL TLS mode when external API expects standard TLS: mode: MUTUAL sends a client certificate to the external API. If the external API doesn't expect mTLS, it rejects the connection. Most public APIs use standard (SIMPLE) TLS.
  3. Port mismatch — TLS on wrong port: The DestinationRule configures TLS on port 80 (HTTP) but the external API serves HTTPS on port 443. The TLS origination is applied to the wrong port — the connection to port 80 fails.
  4. SNI not set for external host: The external API uses SNI (Server Name Indication) to serve multiple certificates on the same IP. Without sni: api.payment-gateway.com in the DestinationRule, the TLS handshake may get the wrong certificate.
  5. DestinationRule host doesn't match ServiceEntry: TLS origination DR for host: *.payment-gateway.com but ServiceEntry has hosts: [api.payment-gateway.com]. Wildcard vs exact hostname mismatch — TLS origination not applied.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. External API uses self-signed certificate — Envoy rejects it unless caCertificates includes the self-signed cert
  2. TLS version mismatch — external API only supports TLS 1.2 but Envoy negotiates TLS 1.3
  3. Cipher suite mismatch — external API requires specific ciphers not in Envoy's default cipher list
  4. Client certificate required by external API — need MUTUAL mode with client certificate Secret
  5. HTTP protocol mismatch — app sends HTTP/1.1 but external expects HTTP/2 over TLS (h2)
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First TLS origination setup: Team knows about TLS origination but doesn't realize the need for caCertificates or credentialName.
  2. Air-gapped cluster with internal CA: External API's certificate is signed by a corporate CA — Envoy's default trust store doesn't include it.
  3. kind cluster testing with mock API: Mock API uses self-signed cert — Envoy rejects unless caCertificates explicitly trusts the self-signed cert.
  4. kubeadm cluster with custom trust store: Node's CA bundle is customized — Envoy's default trust path may not exist.
  5. TLS origination through egress gateway: Two layers of TLS — sidecar→gateway (mTLS) + gateway→external (TLS origination) — configuration complexity doubles.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get dr <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A15 "tls:" Check TLS mode, SNI, caCertificates, credentialName. Missing CA = Envoy can't verify external server certificate.
istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> -o json | grep -A10 "transport_socket_matches\|tls_context" Shows the TLS configuration Envoy is using. Verify the TLS context is applied to the correct cluster.
