kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy | grep -iE "tls.*error\|cert.*error\|ssl" Envoy logs show TLS handshake errors, certificate verification failures, and protocol mismatches.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: TLS origination is configured with mode: SIMPLE but no caCertificates or credentialName is specified. Envoy must verify the external API's TLS certificate using a trust anchor. Without an explicit CA certificate, Envoy uses its default trust store — which may not include the CA that signed the external API's certificate, especially for private APIs or corporate PKI environments.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add caCertificates to the DestinationRule trafficPolicy: {tls: {mode: SIMPLE, caCertificates: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt}} Uses the system CA bundle on the Envoy container. For custom CAs, mount the CA cert via Secret and reference the path.
2. Set SNI to match the external hostname tls: {mode: SIMPLE, sni: api.payment-gateway.com} Ensures Envoy sends the correct SNI during TLS handshake. Some servers require SNI to serve the correct certificate.
3. For mTLS, use MUTUAL mode with client certificate tls: {mode: MUTUAL, clientCertificate: /etc/certs/client.pem, privateKey: /etc/certs/client-key.pem} Only use MUTUAL if the external API explicitly requires client certificates.
4. Verify TLS origination is applied istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n anihpj -o json | jq '.[] | select(.name | contains("payment")) | .transport_socket_matches' Should show TLS context with the correct SNI and CA certificate configuration.
5. Test external connectivity through TLS origination kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj -c anihpj-api -- curl -v http://api.payment-gateway.com/pay The app sends HTTP; Envoy originates HTTPS. Should return the external API's response.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
SIMPLE = standard TLS. MUTUAL = client certificates. 99% of external APIs use SIMPLE TLS (just verify the server). MUTUAL is for APIs that require client certificates — much rarer. Know the difference.
Always set SNI when originating TLS. sni: api.payment-gateway.com SNI tells the external server which certificate to present. Without it, you may get the wrong certificate — or the server may reject the connection entirely.
TLS origination upgrades HTTP to HTTPS transparently. Your application code stays unchanged — it calls HTTP URLs. Istio's Envoy intercepts and upgrades to HTTPS. This is one of the most powerful features of the service mesh.
Test TLS origination on anihpj-api → payment gateway. Set up a mock HTTPS server on minikube, configure TLS origination so anihpj-api calls HTTP but the mock receives HTTPS. This is a classic ICA exam scenario.
TR18
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR18
Ingress Gateway SDS Certificate Not Loading — TLS Listener Fails

🔍 Symptom: The ingress gateway is configured for TLS with a Kubernetes Secret referenced via credentialName. But the TLS listener fails to start — istioctl proxy-config listeners shows the port but no TLS context. Gateway logs show "Secret not found" or "SDS: failed to fetch certificate." Clients get connection reset or TLS handshake errors. The Secret exists, but the gateway can't read it because of RBAC, namespace, or SDS configuration issues.

  kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway | grep -i "sds\|secret\|cert"
  [warning] SDS: failed to fetch secret "anihpj-tls-cert" from istiod
  [error] TLS listener on 0.0.0.0:443 failed to start: no certificate

  kubectl get secret anihpj-tls-cert -n anihpj
  NAME               TYPE                DATA   AGE
  anihpj-tls-cert    kubernetes.io/tls   2      10m

  kubectl auth can-i get secret anihpj-tls-cert -n anihpj --as=system:serviceaccount:istio-system:istio-ingressgateway-service-account
  no   ← RBAC: gateway ServiceAccount can't read Secret in anihpj namespace!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Secret in different namespace than Gateway: The Gateway resource is in istio-system but the TLS Secret is in anihpj. By default, gateways can only read Secrets in their own namespace. The Secret must either be in the same namespace as the Gateway, or RBAC must allow cross-namespace Secret access.
  2. RBAC: gateway ServiceAccount lacks Secret read permission: The ingress gateway's ServiceAccount doesn't have RBAC to read Secrets in the namespace where the TLS certificate lives. Check: kubectl auth can-i get secret <name> -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:istio-system:istio-ingressgateway-service-account.
  3. Secret type wrong — not kubernetes.io/tls: Istio SDS expects TLS Secrets with type kubernetes.io/tls and keys tls.crt + tls.key. Opaque Secrets or Secrets with different keys are silently ignored by SDS.
  4. Secret doesn't exist or was deleted and recreated: The Secret was accidentally deleted and recreated with a different UID — SDS caches the old Secret reference and doesn't pick up the new one until the gateway pod is restarted.
  5. SDS connection from gateway to istiod broken: The gateway Envoy connects to istiod via SDS (part of xDS on port 15012). If the xDS stream is broken, the gateway can't fetch certificate updates. Check: istioctl proxy-status for the gateway pod.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Gateway annotation missing — some Istio versions require annotation to enable SDS for gateways
  2. Certificate in Secret expired — SDS loads the Secret but Envoy rejects the expired certificate
  3. Multiple Secrets with similar names — Gateway references credentialName "tls-cert" but the Secret is "tls-certs"
  4. SDS resource temporarily unavailable — istiod restarting during Secret update causes brief SDS outage
  5. Gateway Deployment has wrong SDS socket path — UDS socket for SDS not mounted correctly in the gateway container
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First time using TLS with Gateway: Team creates Secret in the application namespace (where everything else lives) but Gateway is in istio-system — namespace mismatch.
  2. kind cluster with Gateway in different namespace: Testing Gateway in non-default namespace — Secret must be co-located or RBAC configured.
  3. kubeadm cluster with strict RBAC: Default RBAC doesn't allow cross-namespace Secret access — must explicitly create Role/RoleBinding.
  4. cert-manager creating Secrets in cert-manager namespace: Certificates auto-generated but in the wrong namespace for the Gateway to access.
  5. Multi-tenant cluster — team A's Gateway can't read team B's namespace Secrets by design.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get secret <name> -n <ns> Verify the Secret exists, has type kubernetes.io/tls, and has DATA=2 (tls.crt + tls.key).
kubectl auth can-i get secret <name> -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:istio-system:istio-ingressgateway-service-account Checks if the gateway ServiceAccount has RBAC permission to read the Secret. "no" = RBAC issue.
kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway | grep -iE "sds|secret|cert" Gateway logs show exactly why the Secret can't be loaded — namespace, RBAC, not found, or invalid format.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The TLS Secret is in a different namespace than the Gateway resource, and the ingress gateway's ServiceAccount doesn't have RBAC permission to read Secrets in that namespace. SDS (Secret Discovery Service) requests the Secret from istiod, but istiod can't access it due to Kubernetes RBAC restrictions — the gateway TLS listener fails because it can't load the certificate.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Move Secret to same namespace as Gateway kubectl get secret anihpj-tls-cert -n anihpj -o yaml | sed 's/namespace: anihpj/namespace: istio-system/' | kubectl apply -f - Co-locating the Secret with the Gateway resource avoids all RBAC issues.
2. Or grant RBAC for cross-namespace access Create Role in the Secret's namespace allowing get,list,watch on Secrets. Create RoleBinding for the gateway ServiceAccount.
3. Verify Secret type is kubernetes.io/tls kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls-cert -n istio-system --cert=cert.pem --key=key.pem Recreate the Secret with the correct type and keys. Opaque Secrets are ignored by SDS.
4. Restart gateway pod to clear SDS cache kubectl rollout restart deploy istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system If the Secret was recreated, the gateway may have cached the old reference. Restart forces SDS to re-fetch.
5. Verify TLS listener is active istioctl proxy-config listeners <gateway-pod> -n istio-system -o json | grep -B5 -A10 "tls_context" TLS context should show the certificate chain from the Secret. Missing = Secret still not loaded.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Put TLS Secrets in the SAME namespace as the Gateway resource. This eliminates 95% of SDS/certificate issues. If the Gateway is in istio-system, the Secret goes in istio-system. Period.
Use kubernetes.io/tls type for TLS Secrets. kubectl create secret tls ... This command creates the correct Secret type with the correct keys. Never manually craft TLS Secrets with kubectl create secret generic.
Gateway logs + kubectl auth can-i = your TLS debugging toolkit. Gateway logs say what failed. kubectl auth can-i confirms why. Together they solve any TLS Secret issue in minutes.
SDS is how gateways get TLS certs — understand it. SDS (Secret Discovery Service) is part of the xDS protocol. Gateways don't mount Secrets as files — they fetch them from istiod via gRPC. This is why RBAC and namespace matter so much.
TR19
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR19
gRPC Routing Fails — HTTP/2 vs HTTP/1.1 Protocol Mismatch

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api has a gRPC endpoint that a client service calls through the mesh. But gRPC calls fail with protocol errors, streaming responses are broken, or clients get HTTP 1.1 426 Upgrade Required. The VirtualService is configured with http: routes, but gRPC requires specific HTTP/2 configuration. Envoy is treating the gRPC connection as HTTP/1.1, breaking gRPC's requirement for HTTP/2 transport.

  grpcurl -plaintext anihpj-api:50051 anihpj.JobService/ListJobs
  ERROR: Code: Unavailable Message: upstream connect error
  or HTTP/1.1 426 Upgrade Required (Envoy treating gRPC as HTTP/1.1)

  kubectl get vs anihpj-grpc-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -B2 -A10 "http:"
  http:
  - match:
    - port: 50051
    route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api
        (no gRPC-specific configuration!)

  kubectl get dr anihpj-grpc-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 "http2\|h2"
  (no http2ProtocolOptions or h2 configuration)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. gRPC port not configured for HTTP/2: The DestinationRule doesn't specify trafficPolicy.connectionPool.http.h2UpgradePolicy: DEFAULT or the port-level settings for HTTP/2. Envoy treats the connection as HTTP/1.1 by default — gRPC (which requires HTTP/2) fails. Add http2ProtocolOptions: {} on the port.
  2. Gateway protocol HTTP instead of GRPC or HTTP2: The Gateway server defines the gRPC port with protocol: HTTP. Should be protocol: GRPC or HTTP2 for proper gRPC/HTTP2 handling.
  3. VirtualService matches on HTTP paths: gRPC routes via VirtualService must use match: [{port: 50051}] or exact path matches, not HTTP-specific match conditions (headers, URI prefix). HTTP path matches don't apply to gRPC requests.
  4. gRPC service name mismatch: gRPC uses /package.Service/Method paths. The VirtualService must match these paths explicitly, or use port-based routing. Path prefixes like /anihpj. must match the gRPC method paths exactly.
  5. Upstream connection uses HTTP/1.1: Even if the Gateway accepts HTTP/2, the connection from Gateway to backend may be HTTP/1.1. The DestinationRule must specify trafficPolicy.connectionPool.http.h2UpgradePolicy for the backend connection.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. gRPC-Web vs gRPC confusion — gRPC-Web requires different routing and doesn't support bidirectional streaming
  2. TLS termination breaks HTTP/2 — TLS terminated at Gateway but backend only supports HTTP/1.1
  3. Max request size too small — gRPC streaming messages exceed default limits for request body size
  4. Timeout too short — default 15s timeout kills long-lived gRPC streams; increase for streaming RPCs
  5. EnvoyFilter modifying HTTP connection manager — custom filter removes HTTP/2 support from the filter chain
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First gRPC service in the mesh: All existing services use HTTP/1.1 REST. gRPC is the first HTTP/2 service — team doesn't know about HTTP/2 configuration requirements.
  2. kind cluster testing gRPC with grpcurl: grpcurl behaves differently than production gRPC clients — TLS and HTTP/2 negotiation may differ.
  3. anihpj-api gRPC endpoint added after initial setup: gRPC was added to the existing API service — VirtualService was not updated for gRPC routing.
  4. Service port naming convention: Istio auto-detects protocol from port name (grpc-* or http2-*). If the port is not named following conventions, Istio defaults to HTTP/1.1.
  5. kubeadm cluster with gRPC health checking: gRPC health probes require specific configuration — standard HTTP health checks don't work for gRPC services.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get svc anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 "ports:" If the port is named grpc-api or grpc-web, Istio auto-detects gRPC/HTTP2. If named http, it defaults to HTTP/1.1.
kubectl get dr <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A10 "http2\|h2Upgrade\|trafficPolicy" Check for HTTP/2 protocol options in the DestinationRule. Missing = Envoy uses HTTP/1.1 to the backend.
istioctl proxy-config listeners <pod> -n <ns> | grep -A5 "HttpConnectionManager\|http2" Shows if the listener's HTTP connection manager is configured for HTTP/2 support.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The gRPC service's port is not named with the grpc- prefix (e.g., grpc-api), or the DestinationRule doesn't specify HTTP/2 protocol options. Istio determines the protocol from the Service port name: names starting with grpc- or http2- are treated as HTTP/2; all others default to HTTP/1.1. Without HTTP/2, gRPC connections fail because gRPC requires HTTP/2 transport.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Name the Service port with grpc- prefix Change port: {name: http-api, number: 50051} to port: {name: grpc-api, number: 50051}. Istio auto-detects HTTP/2 for grpc-* named ports.
2. Add HTTP/2 protocol to DestinationRule trafficPolicy: {connectionPool: {http: {h2UpgradePolicy: DEFAULT}}} Forces HTTP/2 upgrade for the upstream connection. Also set http2MaxRequests: 1000 for gRPC connection concurrency.
3. Configure VirtualService with port-based routing match: [{port: 50051}] Port-based matching is simpler than path-based for gRPC. Avoid HTTP path matching for gRPC routes.
4. Increase timeouts for streaming RPCs Set timeout: 0s (no timeout) for long-lived gRPC streams or set an appropriate value (300s+) for streaming endpoints.
5. Test gRPC routing with grpcurl grpcurl -plaintext -authority anihpj-api anihpj-api:50051 list Should list gRPC services. If it fails with protocol error, HTTP/2 is not configured correctly.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Name your gRPC ports with grpc- prefix. It's not optional. port: {name: grpc-api, number: 50051} This single naming convention tells Istio to treat the port as HTTP/2/gRPC. Without it, gRPC fails. This is the #1 gRPC-on-Istio mistake.
gRPC = HTTP/2. REST = HTTP/1.1. Envoy must know which is which. Envoy's HTTP connection manager handles HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 differently. gRPC over HTTP/1.1 fails with protocol errors because streaming and trailers don't exist in HTTP/1.1.
Use port-based routing for gRPC, not path-based. gRPC paths are /Package.Service/Method — complex to match. Port-based routing (match: [{port: 50051}]) is simpler and more predictable.
gRPC streaming needs timeout: 0s. Istio's default 15s timeout kills streaming gRPC calls midway. For streaming endpoints, set timeout: 0s (infinite) or a very large value.
TR20
🚦 CATEGORY 2: TRAFFIC INGRESS/EGRESS/ROUTING — Issue TR20
VirtualService Not Applied — Gateway Bound But No Effect

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService is bound to a Gateway (via gateways: field), the Gateway is correctly configured with matching hosts, the ingress gateway pod is running, but the VirtualService routes are not taking effect. Traffic enters the gateway but returns 404 or is routed to the wrong destination. istioctl proxy-config routes on the gateway pod shows the old routes or no routes at all for the configured host. The VirtualService YAML is valid but istiod is not pushing the configuration to the gateway Envoy.

  kubectl get vs anihpj-web-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 "gateways:"
  gateways:
  - anihpj-gateway     ← Gateway exists, VS bound, but routes don't apply!

  istioctl proxy-config routes <gateway-pod> -n istio-system -o json | grep "jobpost.com"
  (no output — gateway has NO routes for jobpost.com!)

  kubectl get gw anihpj-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 "hosts:"
  hosts:
  - "anihpj.com"        ← VS expects "jobpost.com"!
  (host mismatch between Gateway and VirtualService)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Gateway hosts don't include VirtualService hosts: The Gateway's hosts list must include the hostname(s) listed in the VirtualService's hosts. If Gateway has hosts: ["anihpj.com"] but VS has hosts: ["jobpost.com"], the VS is never activated. Gateway hosts act as a filter — only matching VS hosts are processed.
  2. Gateway in wrong namespace: The VirtualService references gateways: [anihpj-gateway] but the Gateway resource is in a different namespace. Gateways referenced by short name must be in the same namespace as the VirtualService. Use anihpj-gateway.istio-system for cross-namespace.
  3. istiod not watching VirtualService namespace: istiod's meshConfig.discoverySelectors restricts which namespaces it watches. The anihpj namespace may not be in the discovery list — VS resources in that namespace are ignored.
  4. VirtualService not in mesh gateways list: The VS references gateways: [mesh] but the Gateway needs it to reference istio-ingressgateway. Or vice versa — referencing gateways: [istio-ingressgateway] but mesh-internal traffic expects mesh.
  5. Multiple VirtualServices for same host conflict: Two VS define routes for jobpost.com. Only one is applied to the gateway — the oldest by creation timestamp. The other VS is silently ignored.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Gateway selector changed after VS created — gateway pods no longer match the Gateway resource selector
  2. VirtualService has no http/tcp/tls routes — empty VS binds to Gateway but has nothing to route
  3. istiod config push delayed — large mesh with many configs; propagation takes 30+ seconds
  4. VirtualService exportTo restricts visibility — VS exported only to "." (same namespace) but Gateway is in istio-system
  5. Gateway resource has no servers defined — empty Gateway resource, nothing to bind to
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First VirtualService + Gateway setup: Team creates both resources but doesn't understand the host matching requirement — Gateway hosts must include VS hosts.
  2. kind cluster with multiple Gateways: Two Gateway resources select the same gateway pod — conflicting configurations, neither works correctly.
  3. kubeadm cluster with namespace restrictions: istiod configured to only watch istio-system — VS in anihpj namespace not discovered.
  4. Gateway in one namespace, VS in another: Cross-namespace Gateway binding requires FQDN reference — team used short name.
  5. Copy-pasted Gateway from tutorial: Tutorial's Gateway has hosts: ["*"] — works for all hosts. Team changed it to a specific host but forgot to match the VS host.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get gw <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A5 "hosts:" Gateway hosts list must include the VirtualService's hosts. If VS has hosts: [jobpost.com], Gateway must have hosts: ["jobpost.com"] or "*".
kubectl get vs <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A3 "gateways:\|hosts:" Check the gateways field (binds to Gateway resource) and hosts field (must match Gateway hosts).
istioctl proxy-config routes <gateway-pod> -n istio-system --name http.8080 -o json | jq '.[].virtualHosts[].name' Shows which virtual hosts are actually configured on the gateway. Missing host = VS not applied.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Gateway resource's hosts list does not include the hostname defined in the VirtualService. The Gateway's hosts act as a filter — istiod only applies VirtualService configurations for hosts that match an entry in the Gateway's hosts list. If Gateway has hosts: ["anihpj.com"] and the VS has hosts: ["jobpost.com"], the gap causes the VS to be silently ignored by the gateway.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Align Gateway hosts with VirtualService hosts Ensure kubectl get gw -o yaml | grep hosts: includes the same hostnames as kubectl get vs -o yaml | grep hosts:. Use "*" in Gateway to match all hosts during testing.
2. Verify Gateway is in same namespace as VirtualService kubectl get gw -n <vs-namespace> If Gateway is in a different namespace, reference it as gateways: [<name>.<namespace>] in the VirtualService.
3. Run istioctl analyze for configuration validation istioctl analyze -n anihpj Detects Gateway-VirtualService host mismatches, namespace issues, and binding problems automatically.
4. Check gateway routes in Envoy istioctl proxy-config routes <gateway-pod> -n istio-system If routes for the host are missing, the VS is not bound. If they exist but are wrong, the VS has incorrect routing rules.
5. Use wildcard during initial setup, then restrict Set Gateway hosts: ["*"] initially to confirm the VirtualService routes work. Then progressively restrict to specific hostnames.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Gateway hosts and VirtualService hosts MUST align. Think of Gateway hosts as the "allowed list." If the VS host isn't in the Gateway's list, the VS never activates. This is the #1 reason a perfectly valid VS has no effect.
Use istioctl proxy-config routes on the GATEWAY, not the sidecar. For ingress traffic problems, check the gateway Envoy's routes — not the application pod's sidecar. The gateway is where ingress config is applied.
Cross-namespace Gateway references need the namespace suffix. gateways: [anihpj-gateway.istio-system] Short name only works if the Gateway is in the same namespace as the VirtualService. For cross-namespace, append .<ns>.
Start with hosts: ["*"] and restrict later. Wildcard matching ensures the VirtualService binds. Once routing works, restrict Gateway hosts for security. Incremental configuration is safer than trying to get everything right at once.

🛡️ Category 3: Traffic Resilience & Destination Rules Troubleshooting (15 Issues)TP1-TP15

🟡 Resilience Issues — Circuit Breaking, Retries, Timeouts, Fault Injection, Outlier Detection

Traffic resilience protects your services from cascading failures. When circuit breakers trip too early, retries amplify load, or timeouts are too aggressive, your mesh can make services LESS reliable instead of more. These issues require understanding how Envoy enforces resilience policies at the connection and request level.

📌 TP1–TP5: Circuit Breaking & Connection Pool Issues

TP1
🛡️ CATEGORY 3: TRAFFIC RESILIENCE/POLICIES — Issue TP1
Circuit Breaker Tripping Too Early — 503 Errors Under Normal Load

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api service returns HTTP 503 errors under what appears to be normal load. Requests are rejected before reaching the backend. The DestinationRule has circuit breaker settings, but they're too restrictive — maxConnections: 1 or maxRequestsPerConnection: 1 causes Envoy to reject requests after the first connection. The circuit breaker is doing its job, but the thresholds are set for a low-traffic test environment, not production.

  curl http://anihpj-api/api/jobs
  HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
  upstream connect error: no healthy upstream

  kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A15 "connectionPool:"
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 1        ← Only 1 connection allowed!
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 1
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 1  ← Requests queued, then rejected!

  istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "anihpj-api.*circuit"
  circuit_breakers: max_connections: 1, max_pending_requests: 1
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Circuit breaker limits too low for production: maxConnections: 1 allows only one TCP connection to the backend. Any concurrent request gets a 503. Test environment values (maxConnections: 1, maxRequestsPerConnection: 1) were copied to production. Multiply by at least 100x for production.
  2. Connection pool exhausted: http1MaxPendingRequests: 1 means only 1 request can queue while waiting for a connection. All other requests are immediately rejected with 503. Increase pending request capacity.
  3. maxRequestsPerConnection too low: Setting 1 forces Envoy to create a new connection for every request — adding connection overhead that slows everything down. Use 0 (unlimited) or a high value for HTTP/1.1 keep-alive.
  4. Circuit breaker on wrong host: The DestinationRule's circuit breaker is on host: anihpj-api but the VirtualService routes to a different hostname — the circuit breaker doesn't apply to the actual traffic.
  5. HPA not scaling backend: The circuit breaker limits connections to protect the backend, but the backend has HPA that could handle more traffic. Circuit breaker thresholds should match HPA max capacity.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Circuit breaker inherited from mesh config — global meshConfig.connectionPool settings are too restrictive
  2. Outlier detection ejecting all endpoints — circuit breaker doesn't trip; outlier detection removed all healthy hosts
  3. Connection timeout too short — connections are opened but timeout before completing; new requests get queued and rejected
  4. HTTP/2 max concurrent streams reached — 1 connection with limited streams blocks all additional requests
  5. Sidecar resource limiting Envoy's connection pool — Sidecar egress settings restrict concurrent outbound connections
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Test environment values copied to production: maxConnections: 1 was set for testing circuit breaker behavior — accidentally committed to production config.
  2. kind cluster resource constraints: Circuit breaker set low because kind nodes can't handle many connections — same values deployed to kubeadm production unnecessarily.
  3. First circuit breaker configuration: Team configures circuit breaking but misunderstands the units — thinks maxConnections: 1000 is "1000 connections" but it's actually the envoy default.
  4. kubeadm cluster with small DB backend: Circuit breaker set for PostgreSQL (limited connections) but applied to the API service (which can handle many more).
  5. Copy-pasted DR from another service: Circuit breaker from database service (conservative) copied to API service (high traffic) — completely wrong thresholds.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get dr <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A20 "connectionPool:" Check tcp.maxConnections and http.maxRequestsPerConnection. Values of 1 = circuit breaker is throttling ALL traffic.
istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> -o json | jq '.[] | select(.name | contains("anihpj-api")) | .circuitBreakers' Shows the actual circuit breaker thresholds loaded in Envoy. Compare against actual traffic volume.
istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n <ns> | grep "circuit_breaker\|pending" Envoy stats show how many requests are being rejected by circuit breakers — non-zero = thresholds too low.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The DestinationRule's connection pool settings (maxConnections: 1, maxRequestsPerConnection: 1) are too restrictive for production traffic. These values were likely set for testing and never updated. Every concurrent request beyond the first is rejected with 503 by Envoy's circuit breaker, even though the backend service is perfectly healthy and capable of handling more connections.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set production-appropriate circuit breaker limits Use maxConnections: 1000, http1MaxPendingRequests: 100, maxRequestsPerConnection: 0 (unlimited). Adjust based on actual backend capacity.
2. Remove circuit breaker temporarily to verify kubectl patch dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/trafficPolicy/connectionPool"}]' If 503s disappear, the circuit breaker was the cause. Then add back with proper thresholds.
3. Monitor circuit breaker stats istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n anihpj | grep "upstream_rq_pending_overflow\|upstream_cx_overflow" Non-zero overflow counters mean your circuit breaker thresholds are still too low.
4. Match circuit breaker to backend capacity Set maxConnections to ~80% of the backend's actual connection limit. Set maxRequestsPerConnection: 0 for HTTP keep-alive (browsers reuse connections).
5. Use outlier detection alongside circuit breaking Circuit breakers limit connections; outlier detection removes unhealthy endpoints. Use both for defense in depth — don't rely on circuit breakers alone.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
maxConnections: 1 is a testing value, never production. This value effectively makes your service single-threaded through the mesh. Every concurrent request gets 503. For production, start at 1000 and tune down based on observed capacity.
Remove circuit breakers first to isolate 503s. If you're getting 503s and circuit breakers are configured, remove them temporarily. If the 503s stop, you have your answer. Then add back with proper thresholds.
Check Envoy stats for circuit breaker trips. istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n <ns> | grep "overflow\|breaker" Envoy exposes counters for every circuit breaker action. Non-zero = circuit breaker is actively rejecting traffic.
Different services need different circuit breaker thresholds. PostgreSQL: 20-100 connections. Redis: 100-1000. HTTP API: 1000+. Don't copy-paste the same DestinationRule across all services — tune per backend.
TP2
🛡️ CATEGORY 3: TRAFFIC RESILIENCE/POLICIES — Issue TP2
Retry Storm Amplifying Load — Retries Overwhelm Backend

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService is configured with automatic retries (3 attempts) for the anihpj-api service. During a brief backend slowdown, the retries create a retry storm: each failed request triggers 2 more retries, tripling the load on an already-struggling backend. The backend crashes completely under the amplified load. Istio's retry budget and timeout settings are too aggressive, turning a minor hiccup into a full outage.

  kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "retries:"
  retries:
    attempts: 3
    perTryTimeout: 10s        ← Each retry waits 10s!
    (no retryOn specified — retries on ANY error!)

  kubectl top pod -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-api
  NAME              CPU    MEMORY
  anihpj-api-v1-xxx  95%    800Mi   ← Overloaded by retry storm!

  istioctl proxy-config stats anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "retry\|upstream_rq"
  upstream_rq_retry: 15234           ← 15K retries in minutes!
  upstream_rq_retry_overflow: 8923   ← Retry budget exceeded!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Too many retry attempts: attempts: 3 means 1 original + 2 retries = 3x load amplification. During a slowdown, every request generates 3x the normal traffic — overwhelming the backend. Reduce to attempts: 1 or 2 for critical services.
  2. No retryOn condition specified: Without retryOn, Envoy retries on ALL errors — including 4xx client errors that retry can't fix. Specify retryOn: 5xx,reset,connect-failure to only retry on server errors and connection failures.
  3. perTryTimeout too long: perTryTimeout: 10s means each retry attempt can take 10 seconds. With 3 attempts, a single request can hold resources for 30s — starving other requests. Reduce to 2s or 3s.
  4. No retry budget configured: Istio supports retryBudget to limit the percentage of retries relative to total requests. Without it, there's no cap on retry amplification. Set retryBudget: {budgetPercent: 20, minRetriesPerSecond: 10}.
  5. Retry on non-idempotent endpoints: POST /api/jobs creates a new job — retrying on failure may create duplicate jobs. Retries should only be configured for idempotent methods (GET, HEAD, PUT). POST with side effects should NOT be retried.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. All upstream endpoints failing — retries go to the same failing endpoints because no healthy alternatives exist
  2. Circuit breaker not configured — no limit on total concurrent requests to the backend; retries add to the pool without bound
  3. Retry on timeout causing cascading delays — backend is slow, retries add more slow requests, total latency explodes
  4. HTTP/2 multiplexing amplifying retries — single HTTP/2 connection carries hundreds of streams; retry affects all of them
  5. Application-level retry on top of Istio retry — Django app also has retry logic; retry-on-retry creates exponential amplification
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First retry configuration: Team enables retries without understanding amplification — 3 attempts on a slow backend = 3x the traffic, making it slower.
  2. kind cluster with limited resources: Backend runs out of CPU on kind — retries amplify the problem instead of helping.
  3. Copy-pasted retry config from tutorial: Tutorial's attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 10s is for demonstrating the feature — not for production.
  4. kubeadm cluster with database bottleneck: anihpj-api depends on PostgreSQL — retries on API level don't help if the database is the bottleneck.
  5. Retries enabled during incident: Team adds retries during an outage hoping to "fix" it — retries make the outage worse by tripling load.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vs <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A10 "retries:" Check attempts, perTryTimeout, and retryOn. High attempts + no retryOn + long timeout = retry storm.
istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n <ns> | grep "retry" Envoy retry counters show how many retries are happening. High numbers relative to total requests = storm.
kubectl top pod -n <ns> Backend resource usage spikes during retry storms. If CPU/memory is maxed during normal request rates, retries are amplifying load.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The VirtualService retry configuration uses attempts: 3 without a retryOn condition or retryBudget limit. This causes Envoy to retry EVERY failed request (including 4xx client errors) up to 2 additional times, tripling the load on an already-struggling backend. Without a retry budget to cap the retry percentage, there's no limit on amplification — a minor slowdown becomes a full outage.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Limit retries to 1 or 2 attempts retries: {attempts: 2, perTryTimeout: 2s} 1 original + 1 retry = 2x amplification at most. Keep perTryTimeout short (2s) so retries fail fast.
2. Add retryOn to only retry on server errors retryOn: "5xx,reset,connect-failure,refused-stream" Only retry on server errors and connection failures. Never retry on 4xx (client errors) — they'll fail again.
3. Configure retry budget retries: {attempts: 2, retryBudget: {budgetPercent: 20, minRetriesPerSecond: 10}} Limits retries to 20% of total requests. Prevents retry amplification beyond the budget.
4. Remove retries for non-idempotent endpoints Create separate VirtualService routes for GET (with retries) and POST/PUT/DELETE (without retries). Retrying a POST can create duplicate resources.
5. Monitor retry stats in production istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n anihpj | grep "retry" Alert if retry rate exceeds 10% of total requests — indicates backend issues that retries aren't solving.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Retries multiply load. Always use a retry budget. attempts: 3 without a budget = your backend sees 3x traffic when things go wrong. The budget limits retries to a percentage of healthy traffic — preventing the death spiral.
Never retry POST requests unless you're sure they're idempotent. POST /api/jobs creates a new job posting. Retrying it creates duplicates. Separate your VirtualService routes: GET routes get retries, POST routes don't.
Retries are NOT a fix for slow backends. If the backend is slow, retries make it slower by adding more load. Fix the backend first, then add retries for transient failures (network blips, connection resets).
Practice retry storms on your 6-cluster lab. Set attempts: 10 on anihpj-api, add a 5s delay, then send 100 requests. Watch the retry storm in Envoy stats and Kiali graphs. Understanding this failure mode is critical for the ICA exam.
TP3
🛡️ CATEGORY 3: TRAFFIC RESILIENCE/POLICIES — Issue TP3
Timeout Too Short — Long-Running Requests Killed Prematurely

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-api has an endpoint that generates reports (takes ~30 seconds). But requests to this endpoint always fail with HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout after exactly 15 seconds. The VirtualService or DestinationRule has a timeout: 15s that kills the request before the backend can respond. Envoy is enforcing the timeout at the proxy level — the backend completes the work successfully, but the response is discarded because the upstream connection was reset.

  curl http://anihpj-api/api/reports/generate
  HTTP/1.1 504 Gateway Timeout                        (after exactly 15s)
  upstream request timeout

  kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 "timeout:"
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /api/reports
    timeout: 15s              ← Kills reports after 15s!

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-api | grep "report"
  Report generation completed in 28s  ← Backend finishes, but response is lost!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. One-size-fits-all timeout too short: A blanket timeout: 15s is applied to ALL routes, including long-running report generation. Different endpoints have different latency profiles — reports need 60s, health checks need 5s. Use route-specific timeouts.
  2. Global mesh timeout overriding route timeout: meshConfig.defaultConfig.proxyMetadata or global timeout settings apply to all requests, even if individual routes have longer timeouts. The global timeout is the hard limit.
  3. Envoy's default 15s timeout: If no timeout is specified, Envoy defaults to 15 seconds. Any endpoint taking longer than 15s gets 504. You must explicitly set longer timeouts for long-running endpoints.
  4. Timeout on wrong route: The timeout: 15s is on the catch-all route, but the report route has no timeout override — it inherits the catch-all's timeout.
  5. gRPC streaming timeout: gRPC streaming RPCs can run indefinitely — a 15s timeout kills the stream midway. Set timeout: 0s (infinite) for streaming endpoints.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. perTryTimeout in retries shorter than total timeout — retry timeout kills request before overall timeout is reached
  2. Upstream connection idle timeout — connection closed during long request processing
  3. Load balancer timeout upstream — cloud LB or external proxy has its own timeout shorter than Istio's
  4. HTTP/2 stream timeout — HTTP/2 stream-level timeout closes the stream while the TCP connection is still open
  5. Application-level timeout inside Django — Gunicorn/uWSGI has its own worker timeout that kills the worker
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First long-running endpoint in the mesh: All previous endpoints respond in <1s. The report endpoint is the first that takes 30s — no timeout override configured.
  2. kind cluster with slow I/O: Report generation is slow on kind due to limited disk I/O — what takes 10s in production takes 30s on kind, exceeding default timeout.
  3. Default 15s timeout unknown to new users: Team assumes Istio passes requests through without timeout — unaware of the 15s default.
  4. kubeadm cluster with database latency: PostgreSQL query takes 20s due to missing index — request times out at Envoy level before DBA can fix the query.
  5. Copy-pasted VirtualService with timeout inherited from another service's config.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vs <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -B5 -A5 "timeout:" Check timeout on each route. Routes without explicit timeout inherit Envoy's default 15s.
istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n <ns> -o json | jq '.[].virtualHosts[].routes[] | {match: .match, timeout: .route.timeout}' Shows the actual timeout value applied to each route in Envoy.
curl -v -m 60 http://anihpj-api/api/reports/generate Test with a longer client timeout. If the server still returns 504 at 15s, Istio timeout is the cause.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The VirtualService has a timeout: 15s (or relies on Envoy's 15s default) applied to the report generation endpoint. Long-running requests that take 30s are killed by Envoy at the 15s mark — the backend completes successfully but the Envoy proxy has already reset the upstream connection and returned 504 to the client.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set route-specific timeout for long endpoints timeout: 60s Add a separate route for /api/reports/* with a longer timeout (60s+). Put it BEFORE the catch-all route.
2. Set global timeout to a reasonable default timeout: 30s Increase the default timeout globally via meshConfig or set on the catch-all route. 15s is too aggressive for most real-world APIs.
3. Use timeout: 0s for streaming/infinite endpoints gRPC streaming, WebSockets, and SSE endpoints should use timeout: 0s (disabled). These connections can be long-lived.
4. Verify timeout in Envoy config istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n anihpj -o json | jq '.[].virtualHosts[].routes[] | {timeout: .route.timeout}' Confirm the long timeout is actually applied to the correct route.
5. Match application-level timeouts If Django/Gunicorn has a 45s worker timeout, set Istio timeout to 50s — slightly longer to let the app timeout first, giving better error messages.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
15s is Envoy's default — know it, override it. Every route without an explicit timeout gets 15 seconds. If your API has a 30-second endpoint, you MUST set timeout: 30s or longer. This is the #1 cause of mysterious 504 errors.
Use route-specific timeouts, not one global value. GET /api/health → 5s. POST /api/reports → 120s. Different endpoints, different latency profiles. Configure timeouts per route group for precise control.
Never set timeout: 0s globally. Disabling timeouts completely means a dead backend holds connections forever — eventually exhausting all Envoy file descriptors. Only use 0s for specific streaming endpoints.
Istio timeout should be slightly LONGER than app timeout. If Django times out at 30s, set Istio at 35s. This way, the app returns a proper error message instead of Envoy returning a generic 504.
TP4
🛡️ CATEGORY 3: TRAFFIC RESILIENCE/POLICIES — Issue TP4
Fault Injection Not Working — No Errors or Delays Injected

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService is configured to inject 50% HTTP 500 errors and 2s delays to test the anihpj-web frontend's resilience. But no errors or delays occur — all requests succeed with normal latency. istioctl proxy-config routes shows the fault filter is present, but it's not triggering. The fault injection percentage is formatted incorrectly, or the fault filter is on a route that doesn't match any traffic.

  kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "fault:"
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /api/test
    fault:
      abort:
        percentage:            ← Wrong format!
          value: 50            ← Should be 50.0 (float)!
        httpStatus: 500
      delay:
        percentage:
          value: 100           ← Should be 100.0!
        fixedDelay: 2s

  curl http://anihpj-api/api/test
  HTTP/1.1 200 OK    ← No fault injected!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Percentage value must be float (50.0 not 50): Istio YAML requires percentage: {value: 50.0} — the decimal point is required for YAML float parsing. Integer 50 may be parsed as 0% or silently ignored. Always use 50.0 format.
  2. Fault on wrong route: The fault is configured on a route with specific match conditions that don't match the test traffic. Test hitting /api/jobs but fault is on /api/test — never triggered.
  3. Fault after catch-all: The fault route is AFTER the catch-all route. Traffic is captured by the catch-all before reaching the fault route — fault never fires.
  4. Both abort and delay configured on same route: Istio evaluates abort before delay. If abort triggers, delay is not applied. If the abort percentage is low and delay is high, most requests see neither.
  5. Fault injection on gateway-bound VS only: Fault injection works on gateways: [mesh] (internal traffic) but the VS is bound to gateways: [istio-ingressgateway] — only external traffic gets faults, not internal mesh traffic.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. fault vs faults (singular/plural) — using faults: (plural) silently ignored; must use fault: (singular)
  2. Delay format wrong — fixedDelay: 2 (missing "s" suffix) interpreted as nanos, not seconds
  3. HTTP status code out of range — httpStatus: 600 (invalid HTTP status) causes the filter to be rejected
  4. Fault injection disabled in mesh config — global setting disables fault injection for the entire mesh
  5. EnvoyFilter overriding fault filter — custom filter removes or repositions the fault injection filter in the chain
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First fault injection test: Team creates fault injection but doesn't realize percentage must be float (50.0) — integer values silently fail.
  2. kind cluster testing resilience: Fault injection configured but test traffic uses a different URL path than the fault route matches.
  3. kubeadm cluster with production caution: Team creates fault injection but sets percentage to 0 "just to be safe" — forgetting to increase it for actual testing.
  4. Fault injection on TLS traffic: Delay injection on TCP/TLS routes behaves differently than on HTTP routes — delay may not be applied as expected.
  5. New team testing chaos engineering: Fault injection is step 1 in chaos engineering — misunderstanding of percentage format is extremely common.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vs <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A10 "fault:" Verify percentage values have decimal point (50.0). Integer (50) = interpreted as 0 in some YAML parsers.
curl -v http://<SVC>/<matching-path> 2>&1 | grep "HTTP/" Test with the exact path that matches the fault route. If you get 200, the fault isn't triggering.
istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n <ns> -o json | grep -A10 "fault" Shows the actual fault filter configuration in Envoy. Check percentage and check which route it's on.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The fault injection percentage.value is specified as an integer (50) instead of a float (50.0). Istio's YAML parser requires float format for percentage values — integer 50 may be silently interpreted as 0%, causing the fault filter to be present in Envoy's configuration but never triggering. Always use percentage: {value: 50.0} with the decimal point.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Fix percentage to float format percentage: {value: 50.0} Always include the decimal point. 50.0 = 50%, 0.5 = 0.5%, 100.0 = 100%.
2. Verify fault route matches test traffic Ensure the route's match conditions match the URLs you're testing. Use a simple prefix match (uri: {prefix: /}) for initial testing.
3. Move fault route BEFORE catch-all Reorder routes: fault injection route first, then normal routes, then catch-all. The fault must be evaluated before the catch-all captures traffic.
4. Test fault injection with a loop for i in {1..20}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://anihpj-api/api/test; done With 50% fault injection, ~10 out of 20 requests should return the fault HTTP status (e.g., 500).
5. Start with 100% injection for testing percentage: {value: 100.0} Use 100% to confirm the fault is working at all. Then reduce to the desired percentage for resilience testing.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Always use 50.0, never 50. The YAML float requirement is the #1 fault injection gotcha. Integer percentages are silently treated as 0%. Always include the decimal point.
Test fault injection at 100% first. If 100% injection doesn't work, 50% won't either. Validate the mechanism at 100%, then adjust the percentage for realistic chaos testing.
Fault injection is for testing ONLY. Never leave fault injection enabled in production. Add a comment banner to your VS YAML: # WARNING: FAULT INJECTION ENABLED — REMOVE BEFORE PRODUCTION.
Use fault injection on your 6-cluster lab for chaos engineering practice. Inject 500s and delays on anihpj-api and observe how anihpj-web handles them. This is a core ICA exam scenario — knowing how to configure AND verify fault injection.
TP5
🛡️ CATEGORY 3: TRAFFIC RESILIENCE/POLICIES — Issue TP5
Outlier Detection Ejecting Healthy Pods — False Positive Evictions

🔍 Symptom: Outlier detection (also called "circuit breaker" in Envoy terms) is configured to evict pods that return 5 consecutive 5xx errors. But healthy pods are being evicted — pods with zero errors are removed from the load balancing pool. The anihpj-api service has 3 replicas but only 1 is receiving traffic; the other 2 are marked unhealthy. istioctl proxy-config endpoints shows endpoints with eject status even though the pods are perfectly healthy.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-api
  NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  anihpj-api-v1-a   2/2     Running   0        ← Healthy!
  anihpj-api-v1-b   2/2     Running   0        ← Healthy!
  anihpj-api-v1-c   2/2     Running   0        ← Healthy!

  istioctl proxy-config endpoints anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "anihpj-api"
  10.244.1.5:8080  HEALTHY     weight: 1.0
  10.244.1.6:8080  EJECTED     weight: 1.0   ← WHY?
  10.244.1.7:8080  EJECTED     weight: 1.0   ← WHY?

  kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A15 "outlierDetection:"
  outlierDetection:
    consecutive5xxErrors: 5
    interval: 10s
    baseEjectionTime: 30m        ← Ejected for 30 MINUTES!
    maxEjectionPercent: 100       ← 100% of pods can be ejected!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. consecutive5xxErrors too low: consecutive5xxErrors: 1 or 2 causes a single error burst to eject a pod. Transient errors (network blip, brief GC pause) are misinterpreted as pod failure. Use 5 or higher for production.
  2. baseEjectionTime too long: baseEjectionTime: 30m means an ejected pod stays out of the pool for 30 minutes — even if it recovered immediately. Use 30s to 5m for faster recovery.
  3. maxEjectionPercent too high: maxEjectionPercent: 100 allows Envoy to eject ALL pods. If all pods are ejected, the service is completely down. Set to 50 or lower to ensure at least half the pods always remain in the pool.
  4. 5xx from health checks counted as errors: If the health check endpoint returns 5xx (due to application bug), outlier detection ejects pods based on health check failures — not actual traffic errors. Health check failures should not count toward outlier detection.
  5. interval too short: interval: 1s evaluates errors too frequently — a single slow second with 3 errors triggers ejection. Use 10s or longer to smooth out transient spikes.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. consecutiveGatewayErrors vs consecutive5xxErrors confusion — gateway errors (502, 503, 504) are different from 5xx from the backend
  2. Split horizon — different Envoy sidecars have ejected different pods based on their local error view
  3. TCP-level errors triggering ejection — connection failures counted as 5xx equivalent by Envoy
  4. Outlier detection on a DestinationRule that also has circuit breaker — both interact unpredictably
  5. Pod restart causing false positive — when a pod restarts, Envoy sees connection failures until the pod is ready
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First outlier detection configuration: Team copies settings from docs without understanding the implications — baseEjectionTime: 30m is documentation default but inappropriate for most services.
  2. kind cluster with flaky network: Docker network on kind occasionally drops packets — Envoy counts these as 5xx errors and ejects healthy pods.
  3. kubeadm cluster with rolling updates: During deployment rollouts, terminating pods return 5xx — outlier detection ejects them before they're gracefully terminated.
  4. New team unaware of outlier detection defaults: Outlier detection is NOT enabled by default — if it's ejecting pods, someone configured it with overly aggressive settings.
  5. Canary deployment confusing outlier detection: Canary pod (v2) returns different response codes that look like errors to the caller — outlier detection ejects the canary.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get dr <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A15 "outlierDetection:" Check all outlier detection parameters: threshold, interval, baseEjectionTime, maxEjectionPercent.
istioctl proxy-config endpoints <pod> -n <ns> --cluster "outbound|8080||anihpj-api" -o json | jq '.[] | {address, health, weight}' Shows which endpoints are ejected and their health status in Envoy's view.
istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n <ns> | grep "outlier_detection" Envoy stats showing how many ejections have occurred and how many are currently active.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Outlier detection thresholds are too aggressive: consecutive5xxErrors is set too low (1-2), baseEjectionTime is too long (30m), and maxEjectionPercent is too high (100%). A single transient error burst can eject healthy pods for 30 minutes — and with 100% max ejection, all pods can be evicted, causing a complete service outage. Outlier detection should protect against genuinely failing pods, not react to normal traffic fluctuations.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Adjust outlier detection thresholds Use consecutive5xxErrors: 7, interval: 30s, baseEjectionTime: 60s, maxEjectionPercent: 33. These are safer defaults that eject only truly failing pods and recover quickly.
2. Remove outlier detection temporarily kubectl patch dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/trafficPolicy/outlierDetection"}]' If all pods return to HEALTHY status, outlier detection was the cause. Re-add with safer thresholds.
3. Monitor outlier detection stats istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n anihpj | grep "ejections\|outlier" Track ejection counts over time. Zero is ideal; frequent ejections indicate either flaky pods OR too-aggressive thresholds.
4. Set maxEjectionPercent to 50% or lower Never allow outlier detection to eject more than 50% of pods. This ensures at least half the capacity remains available even during an ejection event.
5. Configure per-endpoint health checks separately Use Kubernetes readiness probes for pod health, not outlier detection. Outlier detection should complement health checks, not replace them.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Outlier detection is NOT enabled by default. If it's active, someone configured it. Check your DestinationRules. Outlier detection doesn't appear magically — it requires explicit configuration. If pods are being ejected unexpectedly, look for the DR that's causing it.
Start with conservative outlier detection. consecutive5xxErrors: 5, baseEjectionTime: 30s, maxEjectionPercent: 33. Observe for a week, then tighten if needed. It's easier to make thresholds stricter than to explain why healthy pods were ejected in production.
maxEjectionPercent: 100 is a disaster waiting to happen. This setting allows outlier detection to eject EVERY pod. If all pods are ejected, your service is down. Always cap at 50% or lower.
Use istioctl proxy-config endpoints to see ejection state. istioctl proxy-config endpoints <pod> -n <ns> --cluster <cluster> This shows you the exact view Envoy has of each endpoint — HEALTHY, EJECTED, or TIMEDOUT. It's the ground truth for outlier detection debugging.

📌 TP6–TP10: Rate Limiting, Load Balancing & Session Affinity

TP6
🛡️ CATEGORY 3: TRAFFIC RESILIENCE/POLICIES — Issue TP6
Rate Limiting Not Working — External API Calls Not Throttled

🔍 Symptom: A rate limiting EnvoyFilter or WasmPlugin was deployed to limit calls to the external payment API to 10 requests per second. But the external API reports thousands of requests per minute — rate limiting is not enforcing the limit. The EnvoyFilter configuration is valid but the rate limit service is unreachable, or the filter doesn't match the traffic. The anihpj-api is hammering the payment gateway, risking API key revocation or cost overruns.

  kubectl get envoyfilter rate-limit-filter -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A15 "rate_limit"
  - applyTo: HTTP_FILTER
    match:
      context: GATEWAY
      (matches GATEWAY context — but traffic is mesh-internal!)

  kubectl get svc ratelimit -n istio-system
  NAME        TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      PORT(S)
  ratelimit   ClusterIP   10.96.50.100    8081/TCP   ← Service exists

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=ratelimit
  No resources found   ← Rate limit SERVER not deployed!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Rate limit service (Redis + ratelimit server) not deployed: Istio's built-in rate limiting requires an external rate limit service (e.g., the official ratelimit server with Redis backend). The EnvoyFilter references this service, but it's not running — all requests pass through unchecked. Deploy the rate limit server and Redis.
  2. EnvoyFilter context mismatch: The filter is applied to context: GATEWAY but traffic flows through context: SIDECAR_OUTBOUND (mesh-internal). The filter never sees the traffic. Use context: ANY or match the correct context.
  3. Rate limit descriptor rules don't match: The rate limit configuration specifies descriptor_key: "header" with descriptor_value: "x-user-id", but traffic doesn't have this header. No matching descriptor means no limiting — all requests pass.
  4. Rate limit service unreachable: The ratelimit Service exists but its endpoint IPs are wrong or the service is crash-looping. Envoy can't reach the rate limit server — fail-open behavior allows all traffic through.
  5. Race condition on fail-open: By default, if the rate limit service is unreachable, Envoy FAILS OPEN (allows all traffic). This prevents outages but means rate limiting silently stops working. Configure failure_mode_deny: true for strict enforcement.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Rate limit gRPC port mismatch — EnvoyFilter references port 8081 but ratelimit service listens on 8080
  2. Redis backend for rate limiter not configured — ratelimit server running but has no storage backend
  3. EnvoyFilter applied to wrong listener — inserted in inbound chain but traffic is outbound; or vice versa
  4. Rate limit configuration ConfigMap not mounted — ratelimit server has no rules to enforce
  5. TLS between Envoy and ratelimit service failing — gRPC connection over TLS with invalid certificates
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First rate limiting setup: Team deploys EnvoyFilter but doesn't realize Istio doesn't include a rate limit server — it must be deployed separately.
  2. kind cluster without Redis: Rate limiting requires Redis for counters — Redis not deployed on kind, ratelimit server has no persistence.
  3. kubeadm cluster with strict egress: The rate limit server needs to call Redis on port 6379 — blocked by NetworkPolicy.
  4. WasmPlugin rate limiting vs EnvoyFilter: Newer Istio versions support Wasm-based rate limiting; team used old EnvoyFilter approach that requires external server.
  5. Misunderstanding Istio rate limiting architecture: Team assumes VirtualService has a rate limit field — it doesn't. Rate limiting requires EnvoyFilter + external service.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=ratelimit The rate limit server must be Running. If no pods, rate limiting is silently doing nothing (fail-open).
kubectl get envoyfilter -A -o yaml | grep -A5 "context:\|rate_limit" Verify the EnvoyFilter matches the correct traffic context (SIDECAR_OUTBOUND for mesh-internal, GATEWAY for ingress).
istioctl proxy-config listeners <pod> -n <ns> -o json | grep -A10 "rate_limit\|envoy.filters.http.ratelimit" Shows if the rate limit filter is actually loaded in Envoy's filter chain.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The rate limit service (the external gRPC server that Envoy calls for rate limiting decisions) is not deployed or is unreachable. Istio does NOT include a rate limit server — it provides the EnvoyFilter mechanism but the actual rate limit server (usually the official envoy ratelimit service + Redis) must be deployed separately. By default, fail-open behavior allows all traffic through when the rate limit server is down.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Deploy the rate limit server and Redis Deploy the official envoy ratelimit service with Redis backend. Use the reference deployment from Istio's samples: samples/ratelimit/rate-limit-service.yaml.
2. Configure rate limit rules in ConfigMap Define descriptor rules: which headers/paths to rate limit, the unit (per-minute, per-second), and the request count limit.
3. Fix EnvoyFilter context to match traffic Use context: SIDECAR_OUTBOUND for mesh-internal rate limiting or context: ANY for both gateway and sidecar traffic.
4. Set failure_mode_deny: true Configure the rate limit filter to fail-closed if the rate limit server is unreachable. Trade-off: prevents rate limit bypass but can cause outages if ratelimit server is down.
5. Verify rate limiting with a load test Send 100 requests in rapid succession with the matching descriptor (header/path). Only the configured limit should succeed; the rest should return 429.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Istio does NOT include a rate limit server. You must deploy it. The EnvoyFilter is just the CLIENT side. The actual rate limiting decisions come from an external gRPC service. Without it, rate limiting silently does nothing.
Fail-open is the default — your rate limiting can silently stop. If the rate limit server goes down, Envoy allows ALL traffic through. Monitor the rate limit server's health as carefully as the mesh itself.
Use WasmPlugin for simpler rate limiting in newer Istio. Istio 1.22+ supports Wasm-based rate limiting that doesn't require an external server. This is the future direction — simpler deployment, fewer dependencies.
Rate limit the payment API on your 6-cluster lab. Deploy the ratelimit service on kubeadm, configure an EnvoyFilter, and verify that anihpj-api can't exceed 10 req/s to the mock payment gateway. This is a common ICA advanced scenario.
TP7
🛡️ CATEGORY 3: TRAFFIC RESILIENCE/POLICIES — Issue TP7
Load Balancer Algorithm Ignored — Always Round Robin Despite LEAST_REQUEST Setting

🔍 Symptom: A DestinationRule configures loadBalancer: {simple: LEAST_REQUEST} to distribute traffic to the backend with the fewest active requests. But monitoring shows traffic is still distributed round-robin — all pods receive equal requests regardless of their current load. The load balancer setting is either not applied to the correct host, overridden by another DestinationRule, or incompatible with other traffic policies.

  kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 "loadBalancer:"
  loadBalancer:
    simple: LEAST_REQUEST
  (looks correct, but...)

  kubectl get dr anihpj-api-global -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A3 "loadBalancer:"
  loadBalancer:
    simple: ROUND_ROBIN     ← Global DR overrides namespace DR!

  istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "anihpj-api.*LbPolicy"
  LbPolicy: ROUND_ROBIN    ← Not LEAST_REQUEST!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Global DestinationRule overriding namespace DR: A DestinationRule in istio-system (global scope) for the same host overrides the namespace-local DR. Global DRs take precedence — the namespace DR's LEAST_REQUEST is silently ignored. Check: kubectl get dr --all-namespaces | grep anihpj-api.
  2. LEAST_REQUEST not supported for TCP services: simple: LEAST_REQUEST only works for HTTP services. TCP services silently fall back to ROUND_ROBIN. If the Service port is named tcp (not http), LEAST_REQUEST is ignored.
  3. ConsistentHash missing hash key: consistentHash: {} without httpHeaderName, httpCookie, or useSourceIp — empty hash config fallbacks to ROUND_ROBIN.
  4. Load balancer on wrong host: The DR specifies host: anihpj-api but the VS routes to host: anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local. Host mismatch = DR settings not applied.
  5. Locality LB overriding simple LB: localityLbSetting is configured — locality-aware load balancing takes precedence over simple LB policy when locality settings are present.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. RING_HASH requires minimum ring size — too small ring with few endpoints behaves like ROUND_ROBIN
  2. MAGLEV vs RING_HASH confusion — both are consistent hash but MAGLEV requires table size config
  3. LEAST_REQUEST with weighted routing — VirtualService weight overrides LB algorithm for the initial distribution
  4. Envoy version doesn't support the LB algorithm — older Envoy versions only support ROUND_ROBIN, LEAST_REQUEST, RANDOM
  5. Outlier detection interacting with LB — ejected endpoints can't receive requests, making distribution appear unbalanced
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First load balancer configuration: Team assumes setting simple: LEAST_REQUEST is enough — doesn't know about global DR precedence.
  2. kind cluster with few replicas: With 2 pods, LEAST_REQUEST and ROUND_ROBIN are indistinguishable — both distribute traffic evenly.
  3. kubeadm cluster with service port naming: Port named api instead of http-api — Istio treats it as TCP, ignoring HTTP-specific LB algorithms.
  4. Copy-pasted DR with wrong host: DR from service-A copied for service-B but host not updated — LB settings applied to wrong service.
  5. Session affinity (consistent hash) used but cookie/header not sent by client: No affinity key = random distribution despite hash configuration.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get dr --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -B5 -A10 "host: anihpj-api" Check for global DRs (in istio-system) that may override namespace-scoped DRs.
kubectl get svc <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A5 "ports:" Port names starting with http- or grpc- enable HTTP LB algorithms. Plain tcp or custom names = TCP only.
istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n <ns> -o json | jq '.[] | select(.name | contains("anihpj-api")) | .lbPolicy' Shows the actual LB policy Envoy is using. ROUND_ROBIN when LEAST_REQUEST was configured = overridden.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: A global DestinationRule (in istio-system) for the same host overrides the namespace-local DestinationRule's load balancer settings. Istio merges DR settings hierarchically: mesh-level (istio-system) DRs take precedence over namespace-level DRs. The namespace DR setting LEAST_REQUEST is silently overridden by the global DR's ROUND_ROBIN.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Check for conflicting global DestinationRules kubectl get dr --all-namespaces | grep anihpj-api If a DR in istio-system exists for the same host, it overrides your namespace DR. Delete or modify it.
2. Move LB settings to the global DR If a global DR exists, add the load balancer config there. Or delete the global DR and let the namespace DR control LB settings.
3. Name Service ports with http- or grpc- prefix Rename ports: {name: http-api, port: 8080}. This enables HTTP-specific LB algorithms including LEAST_REQUEST.
4. Verify LB policy in Envoy clusters istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n anihpj -o json | jq '.[] | select(.name | contains("anihpj-api")) | {lbPolicy}' Should now show LEAST_REQUEST instead of ROUND_ROBIN.
5. For consistent hash, specify httpHeaderName or httpCookie consistentHash: {httpHeaderName: "x-user-id"}. Without a hash key, consistent hash degenerates to round robin.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Global DRs in istio-system override namespace DRs. This is by design — mesh-wide policies take precedence. Always check kubectl get dr --all-namespaces when LB settings aren't working as expected.
Port naming determines available LB algorithms. http-* or grpc-* port names → HTTP LB algorithms (LEAST_REQUEST, RING_HASH, MAGLEV). Plain tcp → ROUND_ROBIN only. Name your ports correctly.
LEAST_REQUEST is ideal for mixed-duration workloads. If some API calls take 50ms and others take 5s, LEAST_REQUEST keeps the fast pods from being overloaded while slow requests are in flight. ROUND_ROBIN doesn't account for request duration.
Session affinity (consistentHash) requires a unique key per user. Use httpHeaderName: "x-user-id" or httpCookie: {name: "session", ttl: 3600s}. All requests from the same user go to the same pod — useful for stateful services.
TP8
🛡️ CATEGORY 3: TRAFFIC RESILIENCE/POLICIES — Issue TP8
Connection Pool Exhaustion — Ports Running Out Under Load

🔍 Symptom: Under high load, the anihpj-web frontend starts getting "Cannot assign requested address" errors or connections fail with EADDRNOTAVAIL. This is a TCP connection pool exhaustion issue — the Envoy sidecar is running out of ephemeral ports for upstream connections. The connection pool settings are either too restrictive or the default values are insufficient for high-traffic services making many outbound connections.

  kubectl exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- ss -s
  Total: 16384 (kernel 16384)
  TCP:   16345 (established 16200, closed 45)
  (Almost all 16K ephemeral ports are in use!)

  istioctl proxy-config stats anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "upstream_cx"
  upstream_cx_total: 150000
  upstream_cx_overflow: 12300    ← 12K connections rejected!
  upstream_cx_connect_timeout: 8900

  kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 "connectionPool:"
  (no connection pool configured — using defaults!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No connection pool limits configured: Without explicit connection pool settings, Envoy uses defaults that may not be appropriate for high-traffic services. The absence of limits doesn't mean "unlimited" — it means defaults that can still exhaust ephemeral ports.
  2. HTTP keep-alive not configured: Without maxRequestsPerConnection set to keep connections alive, Envoy creates a new TCP connection for every HTTP request — rapidly consuming ephemeral ports for high-RPS services.
  3. Too many upstream clusters: Each upstream service creates separate connection pools. 50 services × 100 connections each = 5000 connections — quickly approaching the ~16K ephemeral port limit per Envoy.
  4. Connection idle timeout too long: Default idle timeout holds connections open for 1 hour. High-churn services accumulate dead connections that consume ports without being used.
  5. Sidecar resource scoping not used: The Envoy knows about ALL services in the mesh (50+ clusters), each with its own connection pool. Without Sidecar resource to limit known services, connection pools multiply unnecessarily.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Node-level ephemeral port exhaustion — not Envoy, the Linux kernel is running out of ports for the entire node
  2. TIME_WAIT sockets accumulating — connections in TIME_WAIT state consume ports for 60-120s after closing
  3. DNS resolution creating extra connections — each DNS lookup creates a temporary connection if not cached
  4. Health checks creating connections — frequent health checks open/close connections rapidly, fragmenting the port pool
  5. Circuit breaker interaction — circuit breaker opens, connections reset, new connections created; rapid cycling exhausts ports
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Large mesh on kind cluster: 50 services in the mesh = 50+ clusters per Envoy. kind's resource limits make connection pool exhaustion more likely.
  2. kubeadm cluster with many services: The anihpj namespace has 5 services, but the Envoy knows about ALL namespaces (default) — hundreds of unnecessary clusters.
  3. New team unaware of Sidecar resource: Sidecar resource limits which services Envoy knows about, dramatically reducing connection pools and memory.
  4. High-traffic test without connection pooling: Load testing on kind without configuring connection pool limits — test overwhelms the proxy.
  5. Linux default ephemeral port range (32768-60999): Only ~28K ports available; high-connection services may need sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range expanded.
🔍 What to Look At:
istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n <ns> | grep "upstream_cx" Check upstream_cx_total, upstream_cx_overflow, and upstream_cx_connect_timeout. Overflow = connections rejected.
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy -- curl localhost:15000/clusters | grep -c "outbound" Counts how many upstream clusters Envoy is managing. High count (>50) = consider Sidecar resource scoping.
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy -- ss -s Shows total TCP connections. Near 16384 = ephemeral port exhaustion imminent.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No connection pool limits are configured, and Envoy's default behavior opens new connections aggressively. High-throughput services create thousands of upstream connections, exhausting the ~16K ephemeral ports available to the Envoy process. Without connection pool configuration (maxConnections, maxRequestsPerConnection) and HTTP keep-alive, each request may open a new TCP connection — rapidly consuming the limited port range.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Configure connection pool limits connectionPool: {tcp: {maxConnections: 100, connectTimeout: 10s}, http: {http1MaxPendingRequests: 100, http2MaxRequests: 1000, maxRequestsPerConnection: 0}} Limits max connections while allowing connection reuse (maxRequestsPerConnection: 0 = unlimited reuse).
2. Enable HTTP keep-alive with connection reuse Set maxRequestsPerConnection: 0 (unlimited) for HTTP/1.1 — one connection handles many requests instead of one-per-request.
3. Use Sidecar resource to limit known services Create a Sidecar resource with egress: [{hosts: ["./*", "istio-system/*"]}]. Limits Envoy to only know about necessary services — dramatically reduces cluster count.
4. Reduce idle timeout for connections connectionPool: {tcp: {idleTimeout: 300s}} Close idle connections after 5 minutes instead of the default 1 hour. Frees up ports faster.
5. Increase ephemeral port range if needed sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="1024 65535" Kernel-level change to increase available ports from ~28K to ~64K. Use as a last resort.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Sidecar resource is the best connection pool optimization. Limiting Envoy to only known services (via Sidecar egress hosts) reduces clusters from 50+ to 5-10. Fewer clusters = fewer connection pools = fewer ports. This is the single most effective optimization.
Connection pool limits are about PROTECTION, not restriction. Setting maxConnections: 100 doesn't limit throughput — with keep-alive, 100 connections handle thousands of RPS. It protects the proxy from port exhaustion.
Monitor upstream_cx_overflow — it's your early warning. istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n <ns> | grep "overflow" Non-zero overflow counters mean connections are being rejected. Tune connection pool limits BEFORE overflow reaches production levels.
Practice connection pool tuning on your 6-cluster lab. Use a load generator against anihpj-api, observe connection counts with ss -s, tune pool limits, and watch upstream_cx stats. This is a hands-on ICA scenario.
TP9
🛡️ CATEGORY 3: TRAFFIC RESILIENCE/POLICIES — Issue TP9
Failover Not Triggering — Traffic Not Redirected to Backup Cluster

🔍 Symptom: A DestinationRule is configured with trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.localityLbSetting.failover to redirect traffic to a backup cluster (kind-cl2) when the primary cluster (kind-cl1) fails. But when all pods in kind-cl1 are stopped, traffic does NOT fail over — requests return 503 Service Unavailable instead of being routed to the healthy backup. The failover chain is configured but not taking effect because the primary endpoints are "ejected" (via outlier detection) rather than "absent."

  kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A20 "failover:"
  localityLbSetting:
    failover:
    - from: us-east
      to: us-west
  (failover configured — but not triggering!)

  kubectl --context kind-cl1 scale deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj --replicas=0
  (primary cluster pods removed)

  curl http://anihpj-api/api/jobs
  HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable   ← No failover to kind-cl2!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Failover requires ALL primary endpoints to be unhealthy: Locality failover only triggers when 0% of endpoints in the primary locality are healthy. If even ONE endpoint is healthy, traffic stays local. Outlier detection may have ejected the endpoint but it's still "present" — failover doesn't trigger. All pods must be deleted or truly unhealthy.
  2. Failover localities don't match pod localities: from: us-east must match the node labels where primary pods run. If nodes are labeled us-east-1 (with sub-region), the failover rule from: us-east may not match. Locality format is <region>/<zone>/<sub-zone>.
  3. No healthy endpoints in failover locality: The failover target (us-west) has no healthy pods either. Both localities are empty — 503 is the only possible response.
  4. ServiceEntry not configured for cross-cluster: Failover between clusters requires ServiceEntries to register the remote cluster's services. If kind-cl2's service is not registered via ServiceEntry on kind-cl1, failover has no destination to route to.
  5. Outlier detection conflict with failover: Outlier detection ejects pods (making them unavailable locally), but failover only considers locality health — it doesn't know about ejected pods. Traffic stays in the primary locality even with all endpoints ejected.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Failover priority chain broken — us-east fails to us-west, but us-west fails to us-east (circular with no base)
  2. Multiple failover rules conflicting — two DRs with different failover chains; only one takes effect
  3. Locality format mismatch — from: us-east/*/* vs from: us-east (wildcard vs exact format)
  4. Failover only works with distribute — failover without distribute configuration may not be evaluated
  5. Network connectivity to failover locality broken — cross-cluster network route doesn't exist
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First cross-cluster failover setup: Team deploys failover config but doesn't understand that all endpoints must be gone — not just unhealthy.
  2. kind cluster nodes without locality labels: kind nodes don't have topology.kubernetes.io/region labels — all pods are in empty locality; failover can't distinguish.
  3. Single-cluster testing failover: Testing failover within a single kind cluster — expected to route to another cluster that isn't connected.
  4. kubeadm cluster with misconfigured locality: Node labels set incorrectly — region=us-east-1 instead of topology.kubernetes.io/region=us-east-1.
  5. Failover testing by scaling down: Team scales Deployment to 0 to test failover — but endpoint deletion is not the same as endpoint health failure for Envoy.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep "topology.kubernetes.io/region" Verify nodes have correct region/zone labels matching the failover configuration.
istioctl proxy-config endpoints <pod> -n <ns> --cluster <cluster> -o json | jq '.[] | {locality, healthStatus}' Shows endpoint localities and health. All must be unhealthy in primary before failover triggers.
kubectl --context kind-cl2 get pods,svc -n anihpj Verify the failover destination has running pods. Empty failover destination = 503.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Failover only triggers when ALL endpoints in the primary locality are absent or unhealthy. Scaling a deployment to 0 removes the endpoints, but existing Envoy configurations may still have cached endpoints that are "ejected" rather than "absent." Additionally, cross-cluster failover requires ServiceEntries to register remote services — without them, the failover destination has no endpoints to route to.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Label all nodes with correct region/zone kubectl label node <name> topology.kubernetes.io/region=us-east topology.kubernetes.io/zone=us-east-1a --overwrite Must use the standard Kubernetes topology labels. Failover uses these to determine pod locality.
2. Create ServiceEntry for remote cluster services Register kind-cl2's services on kind-cl1 via ServiceEntry. Without it, failover has no destination endpoints in the to locality.
3. Verify failover destinations have healthy pods kubectl --context kind-cl2 get pods -n anihpj The failover target must have at least one healthy pod. Both localities empty = 503.
