Use kubectl create secret tls — never create TLS Secrets manually. This command creates the correct Secret type with the exact key names SDS expects. Manual Secret creation is the #2 cause of SDS failures.
Default cert served = SDS didn't load your cert. If openssl shows CN=istiod.istio-system.svc, your custom cert wasn't loaded. Check Secret namespace, type, and RBAC first.
Gateway logs are your best friend for TLS debugging. kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway | grep -i "sds\|secret\|cert" They tell you exactly why a Secret wasn't loaded: not found, wrong type, RBAC denied, or invalid format.
SW7
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW7
External Authorization (ext-authz) Fails — gRPC Service Unreachable

🔍 Symptom: An AuthorizationPolicy is configured to delegate authorization decisions to an external gRPC authorization service (OPA, custom authz). But ALL requests are blocked with 403 Forbidden — even requests that should be allowed. The external authorization service is unreachable from Envoy, or the gRPC connection between Envoy and the ext-authz service fails. Envoy defaults to DENY when the ext-authz service is unavailable (fail-closed).

  kubectl get authorizationpolicy ext-authz-policy -n anihpj -o yaml
  spec:
    action: CUSTOM
    provider:
      name: opa-ext-authz
    rules: [{}]

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep -i "ext_authz\|extauthz"
  [error] ext_authz: gRPC connection to opa-ext-authz:9191 failed: connection refused

  kubectl get svc opa-ext-authz -n anihpj
  NAME            TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      PORT(S)
  opa-ext-authz   ClusterIP   10.96.60.100    9191/TCP

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=opa-ext-authz
  No resources found   ← ext-authz service NOT deployed!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Ext-authz service not deployed: The AuthorizationPolicy references provider.name: opa-ext-authz but the actual gRPC authorization service (OPA, custom authz server) is not running. Envoy can't connect — defaults to DENY (fail-closed). Deploy the ext-authz service first.
  2. Ext-authz provider not configured in mesh config: The extensionProviders section in the istio ConfigMap must define the ext-authz service (name, service address, port, timeout). Without this configuration, Envoy doesn't know where to send authz requests.
  3. gRPC connection timeout too short: Default ext-authz timeout is 600s, but if the service is slow (>10ms), concurrent requests queue and timeout — Envoy denies them.
  4. Port mismatch between config and service: Mesh config defines ext-authz on port 9191 but the actual service listens on port 9000. gRPC connection fails — all requests denied.
  5. Fail-open vs fail-closed misconfiguration: Default is fail-closed (DENY when ext-authz is unreachable). For testing, set failOpen: true to ALLOW requests when the service is down — but never in production.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. TLS between Envoy and ext-authz failing — mutual TLS required but certs not configured
  2. Ext-authz service returning errors — service is reachable but returns gRPC INTERNAL errors; Envoy defaults to DENY
  3. NetworkPolicy blocking Envoy→ext-authz traffic on gRPC port
  4. Ext-authz service not in mesh registry — ServiceEntry needed if ext-authz is external to the mesh
  5. Envoy sidecar resource blocking ext-authz — egress Sidecar doesn't include the ext-authz service host
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First ext-authz setup: Team creates AuthorizationPolicy with CUSTOM action but doesn't deploy the actual authorization service — all traffic blocked.
  2. kind cluster with OPA: OPA deployed but meshConfig extensionProvider not updated — Envoy doesn't know where to send authz requests.
  3. kubeadm cluster with custom authz service: Custom gRPC authz service crashes under load — fail-closed means ALL requests denied during outage.
  4. New team confused by ext-authz architecture: AuthorizationPolicy is just the CONFIG — the actual authz service is a separate deployment that must be running.
  5. Mesh config extensionProvider typo: Provider name in ConfigMap (opa-authz) doesn't match AuthorizationPolicy reference (opa-ext-authz).
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A20 "extensionProviders:" Verify the ext-authz provider is configured with correct name, service, and port. Missing = Envoy can't route authz requests.
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l app=<ext-authz-app> The ext-authz service must be Running. Check logs: is it listening on the expected gRPC port?
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy | grep -i "ext_authz" Envoy logs show ext-authz connection status, gRPC errors, and authorization decisions.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The external authorization service (gRPC server) referenced by the AuthorizationPolicy's CUSTOM provider is not deployed or is unreachable. Envoy's ext-authz filter makes a gRPC call to the external service for every request — if the service is down, Envoy defaults to DENY (fail-closed), blocking ALL traffic to the protected workload.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Deploy the ext-authz service (OPA, custom, etc.) Deploy the gRPC authorization server with the correct labels and service. Verify it's Running and listening on the configured port.
2. Configure extensionProvider in mesh config extensionProviders: [{name: opa-ext-authz, envoyExtAuthzGrpc: {service: opa-ext-authz.anihpj.svc.cluster.local, port: 9191}}] Must be in the istio ConfigMap under mesh.extensionProviders. Restart istiod after changes.
3. Verify gRPC connectivity from Envoy to ext-authz kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- curl -v telnet://opa-ext-authz:9191 Envoy must be able to reach the ext-authz service. Check NetworkPolicies and service endpoints.
4. Set failOpen for testing (remove for production) failOpen: true In the extensionProvider config. When true, requests are ALLOWED if ext-authz is unreachable. Use for testing only.
5. Monitor ext-authz health as critical infrastructure If ext-authz goes down and failOpen is false, the protected service is completely unavailable. Treat ext-authz with the same SLO as the mesh control plane.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
AuthorizationPolicy CUSTOM = YOU must provide the authorization service. Istio provides the FILTER that calls your service. You must deploy and configure the actual gRPC authorization server. Without it, CUSTOM action blocks everything (fail-closed).
Extension providers are configured in the mesh ConfigMap, not the AuthorizationPolicy. The AuthorizationPolicy just references the provider NAME. The actual gRPC connection details (service, port, timeout) are in the istio ConfigMap under mesh.extensionProviders.
ext-authz is a critical path dependency. If ext-authz is down and failOpen is false, ALL requests to protected workloads are blocked. This makes ext-authz as critical as the database. Design for high availability.
Start with failOpen: true during development. This prevents ext-authz outages from blocking all traffic while you're still iterating on the authorization logic. Switch to failOpen: false only after production validation.
SW8
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW8
CUSTOM AuthorizationPolicy Without Provider — All Requests Denied

🔍 Symptom: An AuthorizationPolicy with action: CUSTOM was created but no provider is specified. ALL requests to the anihpj-api service are blocked with 403 Forbidden. The policy matches all traffic (empty rules) and CUSTOM action without a provider defaults to DENY — effectively creating a "deny all" policy. Even internal health checks and metrics endpoints are blocked.

  kubectl get authorizationpolicy custom-deny -n anihpj -o yaml
  spec:
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app: anihpj-api
    action: CUSTOM            ← No provider specified!
    rules: [{}]               ← Matches ALL traffic → ALL denied!

  curl http://anihpj-api/health
  HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
  RBAC: access denied (CUSTOM action with no provider defaults to DENY)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CUSTOM action without provider defaults to DENY: When action: CUSTOM has no provider field, or the provider name is empty/misspelled, Istio treats it as DENY for all matching requests. This is the default fail-safe behavior.
  2. Provider name typo: provider: {name: "ext-authz"} but the mesh config has name: "ext-authz-service". Provider name must match exactly — typo means "no provider found" → DENY.
  3. Empty rules matches ALL: rules: [{}] applies the CUSTOM action to every request. Without specific from/to/when conditions, all traffic hits the CUSTOM action — which without a provider means all traffic is denied.
  4. Provider defined in AuthorizationPolicy but not in mesh config: The provider must be registered in BOTH the AuthorizationPolicy AND the istio ConfigMap extensionProviders. Policy-only without mesh config registration → provider not found → DENY.
  5. Multiple CUSTOM policies with different providers — only one provider is evaluated; the other policies default to DENY
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CUSTOM policy applied mesh-wide — all services in all namespaces blocked by one bad policy
  2. Provider configured but ext-authz returns gRPC error — error responses treated as DENY by Envoy
  3. Health check paths caught by CUSTOM — no exception for /health or /ready; probes fail
  4. Policy created before provider deployed — ordering issue; policy active before ext-authz is ready
  5. CUSTOM + DENY + ALLOW policy mix — CUSTOM without provider overrides ALLOW policies
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First CUSTOM AuthorizationPolicy: Team creates the policy but doesn't realize a provider must be explicitly configured — assumes "CUSTOM" means "custom logic" not "external service."
  2. kind cluster with partial ext-authz setup: Mesh config has extensionProvider but AuthorizationPolicy has no provider field — mismatch.
  3. kubeadm cluster upgrade broke extensionProviders: Istio upgrade changed ConfigMap format — provider configuration lost.
  4. Copy-pasted CUSTOM policy without understanding: Policy YAML copied from docs but provider section not included.
  5. New team confusing CUSTOM action with custom conditions: Team thinks CUSTOM means "custom match conditions" — it actually means "delegate to external service."
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get authorizationpolicy <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A3 "action:\|provider:" CUSTOM action must have a provider field referencing a registered extension provider. Missing = DENY.
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep -A20 "extensionProviders" Verify the provider name referenced in the policy exists in the mesh config. Mismatch = DENY.
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy | grep -i "ext_authz.*fail\|provider.*not found" Envoy logs show if the provider was not found or if ext-authz calls are failing.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The AuthorizationPolicy uses action: CUSTOM without specifying a provider field, or the provider name doesn't match any extension provider configured in the mesh ConfigMap. When CUSTOM action can't find a provider, Istio defaults to DENY for all matching requests — effectively creating a cluster-wide block on the targeted workload.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add provider field to AuthorizationPolicy provider: {name: opa-ext-authz} Must match the name field of an extension provider in the mesh ConfigMap.
2. Register provider in mesh ConfigMap In istio ConfigMap: extensionProviders: [{name: opa-ext-authz, envoyExtAuthzGrpc: {service: ..., port: 9191}}].
3. Temporarily delete CUSTOM policy to restore service kubectl delete authorizationpolicy custom-deny -n anihpj Immediately restores traffic while you fix the provider configuration.
4. Add health check exceptions to CUSTOM policy Add a rule with to: [{operation: {notPaths: ["/health", "/ready"]}}] to exclude probes from CUSTOM evaluation.
5. Test CUSTOM policy on non-production namespace first Apply CUSTOM policies to a test namespace before production. CUSTOM without provider = complete service outage for the targeted workload.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
CUSTOM without provider = DENY. This is the #1 CUSTOM policy mistake. If you see 403s immediately after creating a CUSTOM policy, check the provider field first. Missing provider defaults to blocking ALL traffic.
Provider name must match in both AuthorizationPolicy AND mesh ConfigMap. Double registration required. Typo in either place = provider not found = DENY. Use the exact same string in both locations.
Always exclude health check paths from CUSTOM evaluation. CUSTOM policies without health check exceptions cause pods to fail probes and CrashLoop. Add notPaths: ["/health", "/ready"] to every CUSTOM policy.
Test CUSTOM policies on kind-cka-lab before kubeadm production. A bad CUSTOM policy blocks ALL traffic to the targeted service. Test the full ext-authz chain on your lab cluster before production rollout.
SW9
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW9
SPIFFE Identity Not Propagated — Source Principal Empty in AuthorizationPolicy

🔍 Symptom: An AuthorizationPolicy ALLOW is configured to permit requests based on source principal (SPIFFE identity). But the policy never matches — requests are blocked even from the correct source. istioctl proxy-config secret shows the source pod HAS a valid certificate, but Envoy logs show the incoming request has an empty or missing principal. The issue is that the source pod is using plaintext (not mTLS), so no SPIFFE identity is presented in the connection.

  kubectl get authorizationpolicy allow-api-to-db -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 "principals:"
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/anihpj-api"]

  kubectl logs anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep -i "rbac"
  rbac access denied: source principal is empty
  (connection is plaintext — no SPIFFE identity!)

  kubectl get peerauthentication -n anihpj
  No resources found   ← No mTLS enforcement → traffic is plaintext!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No PeerAuthentication enforcing mTLS: Principal-based AuthorizationPolicy requires mTLS to extract the SPIFFE identity. Without PeerAuthentication (STRICT or PERMISSIVE), connections are plaintext and have no principal — ALLOW never matches. Enable mTLS first.
  2. DestinationRule DISABLE overriding mTLS: PeerAuthentication is STRICT but a DestinationRule has tls.mode: DISABLE for the target host — connection is plaintext, principal is empty.
  3. Trust domain mismatch: Source has SPIFFE ID spiffe://custom-trust-domain/ns/anihpj/sa/anihpj-api but AuthorizationPolicy expects cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/anihpj-api. The trust domain prefix must match.
  4. Source pod not in mesh: The source pod doesn't have an Envoy sidecar — it connects directly without mTLS. No sidecar = no certificate = no principal. Verify sidecar injection on the source.
  5. AuthorizationPolicy expects principal but PERMISSIVE mode allows plaintext: With PERMISSIVE, some traffic uses mTLS (has principal) and some is plaintext (no principal). ALLOW fails for plaintext connections intermittently.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. mTLS certificate expired on source — certificate invalid, connection falls back to plaintext in PERMISSIVE mode
  2. External workload (VM) connecting — VM has no SPIFFE identity unless registered via WorkloadEntry
  3. Istio-proxy crash on source — sidecar down, connection goes directly from app with no principal
  4. TCP service with no protocol detection — Envoy can't determine if it's HTTP; mTLS may not be negotiated
  5. Gateway-originated traffic — Gateway presents its own SPIFFE identity, not the original client's identity
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First principal-based AuthorizationPolicy: Team creates ALLOW with principals but doesn't enable mTLS — policy never matches, all traffic blocked.
  2. kind cluster with default PERMISSIVE: New Istio installs are PERMISSIVE — some traffic uses mTLS, some doesn't; intermittent authz failures.
  3. kubeadm cluster with mixed mTLS: Some namespaces STRICT, some PERMISSIVE — principal available from STRICT namespaces only.
  4. New team testing AuthorizationPolicy without mTLS: Team doesn't realize principal-based policies REQUIRE mTLS — spends hours debugging policy YAML.
  5. Multi-cluster mesh with different trust domains: Principal format differs between clusters — cross-cluster authz fails on principal mismatch.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get peerauthentication -A At minimum, PERMISSIVE must be enabled for principals to exist. STRICT guarantees all traffic has principals. No PA = no mTLS = empty principals.
kubectl logs <dest-pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy | grep "source principal is empty\|peer certificate" Envoy logs show whether the incoming connection has a peer certificate (mTLS) or is plaintext (no principal).
istioctl proxy-config secret <source-pod> -n <ns> -o json | jq '.[].certificateChain' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep URI Extract the actual SPIFFE ID from the source certificate. Compare against the principal in AuthorizationPolicy.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No PeerAuthentication is configured to enable mTLS. Principal-based AuthorizationPolicies require mTLS to extract the source's SPIFFE identity from the TLS certificate. Without mTLS (even PERMISSIVE), connections are plaintext and have no principal — the ALLOW policy can never match, and all requests are blocked by implicit DENY.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Enable PeerAuthentication (at least PERMISSIVE) kubectl apply -f - <<EOF ... apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1 kind: PeerAuthentication metadata: name: default namespace: anihpj spec: mtls: {mode: STRICT} ... EOF STRICT guarantees all traffic has mTLS and principals. PERMISSIVE allows both — use STRICT for production authz.
2. Remove any DestinationRule TLS DISABLE kubectl get dr -A -o yaml | grep -B5 "mode: DISABLE" DR DISABLE overrides PeerAuthentication — remove or change to ISTIO_MUTUAL.
3. Verify principal matches between source cert and policy istioctl proxy-config secret <source-pod> -n anihpj Copy the exact SPIFFE ID into the AuthorizationPolicy principal field. Match including trust domain prefix.
4. Verify source pod has sidecar injected kubectl get pod <source> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep "istio-proxy" Without a sidecar, the pod connects directly — no certificate, no principal. Label the namespace for injection.
5. Test with STRICT mTLS to guarantee principals Set mesh-wide STRICT temporarily to confirm authz works. Then relax to PERMISSIVE if needed. This isolates principal vs policy issues.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Principal-based AuthorizationPolicy REQUIRES mTLS. No exceptions. Without mTLS, there's no certificate, no SPIFFE ID, and the principal is empty. Your ALLOW policy can never match. Always enable PeerAuthentication before creating principal-based authz.
Use STRICT during authz development and testing. PERMISSIVE can hide issues — some traffic works, some doesn't, depending on whether mTLS was negotiated. STRICT removes the ambiguity: either all traffic has principals, or none does.
Trust domain is part of the principal. Don't forget it. cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/anihpj-api includes the trust domain. Custom trust domains change the first segment. Account for this in AuthorizationPolicy.
Empty principal in Envoy RBAC logs = plaintext connection. If you see "source principal is empty" in destination Envoy logs, the source is connecting without mTLS. Fix PeerAuthentication, not the AuthorizationPolicy.
SW10
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW10
Multi-Cluster mTLS Trust — Cross-Cluster Certificate Validation Fails

🔍 Symptom: Istio is deployed across kind-cl1 and kind-cl2 with multi-cluster mesh. Services on kind-cl1 can't communicate with services on kind-cl2 — all cross-cluster requests fail with TLS handshake errors. The clusters use different root CAs, or the trust domain is different between clusters. Envoy on kind-cl1 doesn't trust the certificate presented by the Envoy on kind-cl2 because the signing CA is different.

  kubectl --context kind-cl1 exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -- curl https://anihpj-api.kind-cl2/api/jobs
  curl: (35) SSL connect error: certificate verify failed

  kubectl logs anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep -i "cert\|tls.*error"
  [error] TLS error: certificate verification failed: x509: certificate signed
          by unknown authority (cluster2-ca)

  kubectl --context kind-cl1 get cm istio-ca-root-cert -n istio-system
  (only kind-cl1 root cert — kind-cl2 CA not trusted!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Separate root CAs per cluster: Each cluster has its own self-signed root CA. Cluster-A's Envoy doesn't trust certificates signed by Cluster-B's CA. Must share a common root CA or exchange CA certificates between clusters.
  2. Trust domain mismatch: kind-cl1 uses cluster.local and kind-cl2 uses cluster2.local. SPIFFE IDs from different trust domains are not trusted by default. Must configure trust domain aliases or use a shared trust domain.
  3. Cluster-A's CA cert not distributed to Cluster-B: The istio-ca-root-cert ConfigMap in istio-system must be shared across clusters. Cluster-A's Envoys need Cluster-B's root CA to validate Cluster-B's workload certificates.
  4. Cross-cluster ServiceEntry not configured: Multi-cluster routing requires ServiceEntry to register remote services. Without it, the destination host isn't in the mesh registry — Envoy can't route, and TLS may not be negotiated correctly.
  5. Different Istio versions between clusters: Certificate formats or trust mechanisms changed between Istio versions — cross-version mTLS may fail. Both clusters should run the same Istio version.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Cluster-B's CA certificate expired — CA rotation happened on one cluster but not the other
  2. Intermediate CA vs root CA — one cluster has intermediate CA; the other cluster doesn't trust it
  3. Custom CA on one cluster only — one cluster uses custom corporate CA; other uses self-signed Istio CA
  4. East-west gateway TLS termination — gateway terminates TLS but re-originates with different certificate
  5. mTLS PERMISSIVE on one cluster — allows plaintext fallback; cross-cluster uses plaintext unexpectedly
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First multi-cluster mesh setup: Team installs Istio on both clusters independently — each gets its own self-signed CA; cross-cluster mTLS fails.
  2. kind-cl1 and kind-cl2 lab setup: Two kind clusters with separate CAs — must manually exchange root certs for multi-cluster mTLS.
  3. kubeadm + kind hybrid mesh: Different Kubernetes distributions with different CA management — cert exchange more complex.
  4. New team unaware of cross-cluster CA exchange: Assumes multi-cluster mesh "just works" — doesn't realize root CA must be shared or exchanged.
  5. Six-cluster lab with isolated clusters: Each of the 6 clusters has its own CA — multi-cluster mTLS requires explicit CA trust configuration.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl --context kind-cl1 get cm istio-ca-root-cert -n istio-system -o yaml | grep "root-cert" Check which root certificates are trusted. Should include BOTH cluster CAs for multi-cluster mTLS.
istioctl proxy-config secret <pod> -n <ns> -o json | jq -r '.[].certificateChain.inlineBytes' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -issuer Shows which CA signed the workload certificate. Different issuers across clusters = CA trust issue.
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy | grep -i "certificate signed by unknown\|verify failed" Envoy logs tell you exactly which CA is untrusted — look for "signed by unknown authority" messages.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The two clusters use different root CAs (each cluster's Istio generated its own self-signed CA during installation). Cluster-A's Envoys don't trust certificates signed by Cluster-B's CA because Cluster-A doesn't have Cluster-B's root certificate in its trust bundle. Multi-cluster mTLS requires either a shared root CA across all clusters or explicit CA certificate exchange via the istio-ca-root-cert ConfigMap.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Exchange root CA certs between clusters kubectl --context kind-cl2 get cm istio-ca-root-cert -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.root-cert\.pem}' | kubectl --context kind-cl1 create cm cluster2-ca -n istio-system --from-file=root-cert.pem=/dev/stdin Export Cluster-B's root cert and import it into Cluster-A. Repeat in reverse for Cluster-B.
2. Configure trust domain aliases In mesh config: trustDomainAliases: ["cluster2.local"]. Allows Cluster-A to trust SPIFFE IDs from Cluster-B's trust domain.
3. Or use a shared root CA during installation Generate one CA, create cacerts Secret on all clusters before installing Istio. All clusters share the same root of trust.
4. Verify cross-cluster certificate trust kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -- openssl s_client -connect <remote-svc>:443 2>&1 | grep "Verify return code" Should show "Verify return code: 0 (ok)" — certificate is trusted after CA exchange.
5. Create ServiceEntries for cross-cluster services Multi-cluster routing requires ServiceEntry on each cluster to register remote services. Without it, Envoy can't route — even if TLS trust is configured.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Multi-cluster mTLS requires shared trust. This doesn't happen automatically. Each Istio install generates its own CA. For multi-cluster mesh, you MUST either share a root CA or exchange certificates between clusters. This is the #1 multi-cluster security pitfall.
Shared root CA at install time is the cleanest approach. Create one CA, generate the cacerts Secret, and deploy it to all clusters BEFORE installing Istio. All workloads trust each other natively.
Your 6-cluster lab is perfect for practicing CA exchange. Exchange root certs between kind-cl1 and kind-cl2. Configure trust domain aliases. Verify cross-cluster mTLS with openssl s_client. This is an advanced ICA scenario.
Same Istio version on all clusters avoids certificate format mismatches. Certificate formats and trust mechanisms evolve between Istio versions. Keep all clusters on the same version for predictable cross-cluster mTLS behavior.

📌 SW11–SW12: Gateway Security & Certificate Management

SW11
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW11
Gateway mTLS Passthrough Fails — Backend Doesn't Receive Client Certificate

🔍 Symptom: The ingress gateway is configured for MUTUAL TLS (mTLS passthrough), requiring clients to present certificates. But the backend anihpj-api service never receives the client certificate — the X-Forwarded-Client-Cert header is missing or empty. The gateway terminates mTLS but doesn't forward the client certificate information to the backend, preventing the application from identifying the client.

  curl -v --cert client.pem --key client-key.pem https://jobpost.com/api/jobs
  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  (X-Forwarded-Client-Cert header missing!)

  kubectl get gw anihpj-gateway -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A10 "tls:"
  tls:
    mode: MUTUAL
    credentialName: jobpost-tls-cert
    (no forwardClientCertificate: true!)

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-api | grep "X-Forwarded"
  (no client certificate headers in application logs)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. forwardClientCertificate not enabled in Gateway: The Gateway TLS configuration must include topology.istio.io/forwardClientCertDetails: SANITIZE or set forwardClientCertificate: true. Without it, the gateway terminates mTLS but drops the client cert info.
  2. DestinationRule not configured to propagate headers: Even if Gateway forwards client cert, the DestinationRule for the backend must not strip custom headers. Check if trafficPolicy.tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL preserves headers.
  3. Client certificate not validated by Gateway: Gateway MUTUAL mode requires credentialName pointing to a CA certificate. If CA cert is wrong, the gateway rejects the client cert — but the error is opaque to the backend.
  4. Header stripped by sidecar: The anihpj-api sidecar Envoy may strip X-Forwarded-Client-Cert as an untrusted header. Must configure the sidecar to trust headers from the gateway.
  5. Wrong TLS mode on gateway server: The gateway server port must have protocol: HTTPS (not HTTP) and tls.mode: MUTUAL. HTTP protocol on the port means TLS config is ignored.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. numTrustedProxies not set — Envoy doesn't know Gateway is a trusted proxy; strips its headers
  2. Client cert has no SAN — Forward-Client-Cert uses SAN for identity; empty SAN = empty header
  3. Multiple gateways chained — first gateway forwards cert, second gateway strips it
  4. HTTP/2 multiplexing — multiple streams on one connection; client cert only sent on first stream
  5. EnvoyFilter modifying headers — custom filter removes or overrides Forwarded-Client-Cert
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First mTLS Gateway with client cert forwarding: Team configures MUTUAL TLS but doesn't know forwardClientCertificate is a separate setting.
  2. kind cluster testing mTLS: Self-signed client certs used for testing — Gateway validates but backend doesn't receive the identity.
  3. kubeadm cluster with corporate PKI: Client certs from corporate CA — SAN format differs from what the application expects.
  4. New team debugging missing client identity: Application shows "anonymous user" — debugging application code instead of Gateway TLS config.
  5. Copy-pasted Gateway config without forwardClientCertificate — common in Istio examples that focus on SIMPLE mode.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get gw <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A15 "tls:" Check for mode: MUTUAL AND forwardClientCertificate configuration. Both must be present.
curl -v --cert client.pem --key client-key.pem https://<host>/ 2>&1 | grep -i "x-forwarded-client-cert" Check if the header is present in the response (echo server) or backend application logs.
istioctl proxy-config listeners <gateway-pod> -n istio-system -o json | grep -A10 "forward_client_cert" Shows if the gateway Envoy is configured to forward client certificate details to the backend.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Gateway TLS configuration enables MUTUAL mode (requiring client certificates) but doesn't enable forwardClientCertificate. The gateway validates the client certificate but doesn't forward the client's identity to the backend service. The X-Forwarded-Client-Cert header is never set, so the application can't identify the authenticated client.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Enable forwardClientCertificate in Gateway TLS Add topology.istio.io/forwardClientCertDetails: SANITIZE to the Gateway's TLS configuration. This forwards the client cert's URI SAN as X-Forwarded-Client-Cert header.
2. Configure numTrustedProxies on sidecar Set numTrustedProxies: 1 via mesh config or pod annotation. Tells the sidecar Envoy that the gateway is a trusted proxy — headers from it are not stripped.
3. Verify header reaches backend kubectl exec <backend-pod> -n anihpj -- env | grep X-Forwarded-Client-Cert Or check application logs. The header should contain the client's SPIFFE ID or URI SAN.
4. Ensure DestinationRule preserves custom headers Check that DR for the backend doesn't strip X-Forwarded-* headers. ISTIO_MUTUAL mode preserves headers; DISABLE may strip them.
5. Update application to read X-Forwarded-Client-Cert The header contains the URL-encoded client certificate. Parse it to extract the client identity for authentication/authorization in the application.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
MUTUAL TLS validates the client. forwardClientCertificate shares the identity. These are two SEPARATE settings. MUTUAL = requires client cert. forwardClientCertificate = passes client identity to backend. Both are needed for end-to-end client auth.
numTrustedProxies = 1 when behind a single Istio gateway. This tells Envoy "trust the previous hop." Without it, the sidecar strips X-Forwarded-* headers as potentially spoofed. Set to the number of proxies in front of the service.
X-Forwarded-Client-Cert contains the URL-encoded PEM certificate. Not just the SAN. Your application needs to URL-decode and parse the PEM to extract the full client identity. Libraries exist for this in most languages.
Test mTLS passthrough on your 6-cluster lab with client certs. Generate client/server certs, configure MUTUAL on the Gateway, enable forwardClientCertificate, and verify the anihpj-api receives the client identity. This is an advanced ICA security scenario.
SW12
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW12
Certificate Rotation Fails — Old Cert Still Served After Update

🔍 Symptom: The TLS certificate for jobpost.com was updated in the Kubernetes Secret (new cert + key), but the ingress gateway is still serving the OLD certificate. Clients see the old expiry date and some report certificate errors after the old cert expires. The Secret was updated 10 minutes ago, but SDS hasn't picked up the change — or the gateway pod needs to be restarted to reload the certificate from SDS.

  openssl s_client -connect jobpost.com:443 -servername jobpost.com 2>&1 | openssl x509 -noout -dates
  notBefore=Jan  1 00:00:00 2025 GMT
  notAfter =Dec 31 23:59:59 2025 GMT    ← OLD cert! New one expires 2026!

  kubectl get secret jobpost-tls-cert -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A2 "tls.crt"
  tls.crt: (new cert data — updated 10 minutes ago)

  kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway | grep -i "sds.*secret\|cert.*update"
  (no SDS update events — gateway still has old cert in memory!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Gateway pod not restarted after Secret update: SDS caches certificates in memory. Some Istio versions require a gateway pod restart to pick up Secret changes — SDS watches for Secret updates but caching may prevent immediate reload. Restart: kubectl rollout restart deploy istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system.
  2. Secret updated incorrectly — new cert appended, not replaced: kubectl create secret tls with --dry-run -o yaml | kubectl apply -f - may merge old and new data. Use kubectl delete secret <name> && kubectl create secret tls ... for clean replacement.
  3. SDS watching wrong namespace: The gateway pod watches Secrets in its own namespace. If the Secret was updated in a different namespace (where the Gateway resource was created), SDS doesn't see the change.
  4. Multiple gateway replicas — some still have old cert: Rolling restart didn't complete or some pods stuck with old cert. All gateway pods must be restarted to serve the new certificate uniformly.
  5. Certificate chain order wrong in new Secret: New tls.crt has server cert first, but intermediate CA cert missing or in wrong order. SDS loads the cert but Envoy rejects it — falls back to old cached cert or default cert.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. SDS connection to istiod broken — certificate updates not pushed from istiod to gateway Envoy
  2. cert-manager renews cert but Secret name changes — Gateway still references old Secret name
  3. Private key doesn't match new certificate — Envoy rejects the mismatch, keeps serving old cert
  4. SDS polling interval not reached — SDS watches for Secret changes but may have a polling delay
  5. Gateway Deployment uses Secret as file mount (not SDS) — mount not updated until pod restart
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First certificate rotation: Team updates Secret and expects instant propagation — doesn't know about SDS caching or pod restart requirements.
  2. kind cluster with cert-manager: cert-manager auto-renews but Gateway doesn't auto-reload — scheduled restart needed.
  3. kubeadm cluster with manual cert rotation: Team manually updates cert but forgets to restart gateway pods — old cert served until expiry.
  4. New team debugging cert with openssl: Openssl shows old cert; team checks Secret (new) and assumes network/CDN caching — actually SDS cache on gateway.
  5. Multi-cluster gateway rotation: Cert rotated on kind-cl1 gateway but kind-cl2 gateway still has old cert — inconsistent across clusters.
🔍 What to Look At:
openssl s_client -connect <IP>:443 -servername <host> 2>&1 | openssl x509 -noout -dates Shows the certificate ACTUALLY being served. Compare dates against what's in the Secret.
kubectl get secret <name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates Shows the certificate IN the Secret. If dates differ from what's served, SDS hasn't reloaded.
kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway --tail=50 | grep -i "sds\|cert\|secret.*update\|warm" Gateway logs show SDS updates. Look for "SDS: new secret" or "certificate updated" messages.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The TLS Secret was updated with a new certificate, but the ingress gateway pod has not been restarted. SDS (Secret Discovery Service) fetches certificates at gateway startup and caches them. While SDS can watch for Secret changes, the gateway Envoy may hold the old certificate in memory until a pod restart triggers a full SDS refresh. Always restart gateway pods after rotating TLS certificates.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Restart gateway pods to reload certificates kubectl rollout restart deploy istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system Forces SDS to re-fetch all Secrets. New certificate is served within seconds of pod restart.
2. Verify Secret has correct new certificate kubectl get secret jobpost-tls-cert -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject Confirm the correct certificate is in the Secret BEFORE restarting the gateway.
3. Verify private key matches certificate diff <(openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -modulus) <(openssl rsa -in key.pem -noout -modulus) Mismatched key = Envoy rejects the cert and serves the old one. No output = keys match.
4. Verify all gateway replicas serve new cert for i in {1..3}; do openssl s_client -connect <IP>:443 -servername jobpost.com 2>&1 | openssl x509 -noout -dates; sleep 1; done With multiple replicas, ensure every connection gets the new certificate. Inconsistent = some pods not restarted.
5. Set up automated cert rotation Use cert-manager to auto-renew and a cron job or tool like istioctl proxy-refresh to restart gateways after renewal. Manual rotation always fails eventually.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Always restart gateway pods after TLS certificate rotation. SDS caching means the old certificate may be served indefinitely until a restart. Make gateway restart part of your certificate rotation runbook — never skip it.
Verify the cert in the Secret BEFORE restarting the gateway. Restarting with a bad cert = gateway serves NO cert or the default. Check dates, subject, and key match before the restart.
Use openssl to compare served cert vs Secret cert. If dates differ, the gateway hasn't picked up the new Secret. If dates match but the cert is wrong, the Secret itself has the wrong content.
Automate certificate rotation from day one. Manual rotation is error-prone: wrong cert in Secret, forgotten restart, mismatched keys. cert-manager + automated gateway restart eliminates these failure modes.

📌 SW13–SW15: Workload Identity & Trust Domain

SW13
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW13
Workload Onboarding Fails — VM Can't Join Mesh via WorkloadEntry

🔍 Symptom: A VM or external host is being onboarded to the Istio mesh via WorkloadEntry and WorkloadGroup. The VM runs the istio-proxy sidecar, but it can't connect to istiod or can't get certificates. The proxy starts but fails to bootstrap — logs show "failed to connect to istiod" or "certificate request failed." The VM is network-reachable but the mesh trust isn't established because the VM's identity isn't recognized by the control plane.

  ssh vm-worker "sudo journalctl -u istio-proxy -n 20"
  [error] Failed to connect to istiod.istio-system.svc:15012
  [error] Certificate request failed: no matching WorkloadEntry found
  [error] Bootstrap failed: cannot join mesh without identity

  kubectl get workloadentry vm-worker -n anihpj
  NAME        AGE   ADDRESS
  vm-worker   10m   192.168.1.100

  kubectl get workloadgroup vm-group -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "template:"
  template:
    labels:
      app: vm-worker        ← WorkloadEntry MUST match these labels!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. VM cannot reach istiod: The VM proxy must connect to istiod.istio-system.svc:15012 for xDS and SDS. If the VM is outside the Kubernetes cluster network, it can't resolve or reach the ClusterIP Service. Use a Gateway or NodePort to expose istiod externally.
  2. WorkloadEntry labels don't match WorkloadGroup: The WorkloadEntry's labels must match the WorkloadGroup's template.labels. Mismatch = istiod doesn't recognize the VM as part of the group and won't issue certificates.
  3. VM proxy bootstrap config missing: The istio-proxy on the VM needs a bootstrap file pointing to the correct istiod address, trust domain, and discovery address. Wrong bootstrap = proxy can't find the control plane.
  4. istiod not exposed for external access: By default, istiod only listens on the internal ClusterIP. VM onboarding requires exposing istiod via an east-west gateway or a LoadBalancer/NodePort service.
  5. Network firewall blocking port 15012: VM-to-istiod communication over port 15012 (xDS/SDS gRPC) is blocked by firewall or security group rules between the VM network and Kubernetes pod network.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. WorkloadEntry address incorrect — VM IP changed after WorkloadEntry creation; istiod looks for old IP
  2. TLS certificate on VM expired — VM proxy has stale bootstrap cert; can't establish gRPC to istiod
  3. VM DNS not resolving istiod.istio-system.svc — CoreDNS only accessible from within the cluster
  4. WorkloadGroup not created before WorkloadEntry — WorkloadEntry references non-existent WorkloadGroup
  5. Istio version mismatch — VM proxy version doesn't match cluster istiod version; xDS protocol incompatibility
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First VM onboarding to mesh: Team follows VM onboarding guide but misses the step to expose istiod externally — VM can't reach control plane.
  2. kind cluster with external VM: Docker network isolation prevents external VMs from reaching kind's ClusterIP services — need host network or NodePort.
  3. kubeadm cluster with on-premise VM: VM in the same data center but different VLAN — network must allow VM→pod communication.
  4. Multi-cluster mesh with VM: VM onboarded to kind-cl1 needs to communicate with services on kind-cl2 — ServiceEntry + cross-cluster routing needed.
  5. New team confused by WorkloadEntry vs ServiceEntry: WorkloadEntry registers a WORKLOAD (VM). ServiceEntry registers a SERVICE (external API). Different purposes.
🔍 What to Look At:
ssh vm-worker "curl -v telnet://<istiod-ip>:15012" Verify basic network connectivity from VM to istiod xDS port. Connection refused = istiod not exposed externally.
kubectl get workloadentry <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A5 "labels:" Check labels match WorkloadGroup template labels. Mismatch = istiod won't recognize the VM as part of the mesh.
ssh vm-worker "cat /etc/istio/config/mesh" | grep -E "discoveryAddress|istiod" Verify the bootstrap config points to the correct istiod address. Wrong address = proxy can't bootstrap.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The VM cannot reach istiod for xDS/SDS services. By default, istiod only exposes port 15012 on its internal ClusterIP — unreachable from outside the Kubernetes cluster. VM onboarding requires exposing istiod externally via an east-west gateway or a dedicated LoadBalancer/NodePort Service. Without network connectivity to istiod, the VM proxy cannot bootstrap, get certificates, or receive mesh configuration.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Expose istiod for external access Create an east-west gateway or expose istiod via kubectl expose deploy istiod -n istio-system --type=NodePort --port=15012. VM proxy connects to this external endpoint.
2. Generate correct bootstrap config for VM istioctl x workload entry configure -f workloadgroup.yaml -o /tmp/bootstrap Generates the correct bootstrap files with the right discovery address, trust domain, and certificates.
3. Ensure WorkloadEntry labels match WorkloadGroup The labels in WorkloadEntry must exactly match the template.labels in WorkloadGroup. Mismatch = istiod doesn't issue certificates to the VM.
4. Verify VM can reach istiod on port 15012 ssh vm-worker "nc -zv <istiod-nodeport-ip> 15012" Basic connectivity test. Must succeed before the proxy can bootstrap and join the mesh.
5. Check VM proxy logs for bootstrap errors ssh vm-worker "sudo journalctl -u istio-proxy -f" Proxy logs detail every step of the bootstrap process — certificate request, xDS connection, config reception.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
VM onboarding = network connectivity + identity registration. Two independent requirements: 1) VM must reach istiod (network), 2) WorkloadEntry must match WorkloadGroup (identity). Both must work — fix them independently.
Use istioctl x workload entry configure — never build bootstrap manually. This command generates all files: bootstrap, certificates, mesh config. Manual bootstrap creation is extremely error-prone.
Test VM onboarding on your 6-cluster lab. Use minikube or kubeadm to simulate a VM (a pod without Istio injection), register it via WorkloadEntry, and verify it joins the mesh. This is the most advanced mesh expansion scenario.
WorkloadEntry = one instance. WorkloadGroup = template for many. WorkloadEntry registers a SINGLE VM instance. WorkloadGroup defines the template (labels, service account) for auto-registration of multiple VMs.
SW14
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW14
AuthorizationPolicy IP-Based Blocking — Wrong CIDR Blocks Legitimate Traffic

🔍 Symptom: An AuthorizationPolicy DENY rule blocks traffic from specific IP ranges (e.g., blocking external office IPs from accessing the database). But legitimate internal traffic is also blocked because the pod CIDR overlaps with the blocked IP range, or the ipBlocks field catches the Envoy sidecar's egress IP instead of the original source IP. Services within the mesh can't reach each other.

  kubectl get authorizationpolicy block-external-ip -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "ipBlocks:"
  - from:
    - source:
        ipBlocks: ["10.0.0.0/8"]     ← Pod CIDR is 10.244.0.0/16 → BLOCKED!

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -- curl anihpj-db:5432
  curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer
  (internal pod IP falls within blocked 10.0.0.0/8 range!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CIDR block too broad — includes pod network: ipBlocks: ["10.0.0.0/8"] blocks the entire 10.x.x.x range, including the pod CIDR (10.244.0.0/16). Internal pods are blocked alongside external IPs. Use more specific CIDRs.
  2. ipBlocks matches Envoy egress IP, not original source: In some configurations, the source IP seen by the destination Envoy is the SOURCE ENVOY's IP (after NAT), not the original application pod IP. IP-based rules match the wrong address.
  3. DENY ipBlocks without ALLOW for pod CIDR: The DENY blocks a broad range. An ALLOW policy for the pod CIDR should permit internal traffic — but if ALLOW is missing or has incorrect CIDR, internal traffic is blocked.
  4. IPv4 vs IPv6 mismatch: Policy specifies IPv4 CIDRs but traffic arrives via IPv6 (dual-stack cluster). The ipBlocks rule never matches IPv6 traffic — or matches everything unexpectedly.
  5. X-Forwarded-For header used incorrectly: Envoy uses the original source IP (layer 4), not the X-Forwarded-For header (layer 7). If your logic depends on X-Forwarded-For, ipBlocks won't match as expected.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Remote ipBlocks with non-mesh traffic — ipBlocks only works for mesh-internal traffic with mTLS
  2. notIpBlocks logic inverted — DENY with notIpBlocks blocks everything EXCEPT the specified range
  3. Multiple AuthorizationPolicies merging ipBlocks — union of all policies applies unexpectedly
  4. NAT on the node changes source IP — real source IP lost before reaching Envoy
  5. IPv6-only cluster with IPv4 ipBlocks — rules don't apply; all traffic passes or all traffic blocked
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First IP-based AuthorizationPolicy: Team blocks a "suspicious" IP range but accidentally includes the pod network — entire mesh goes down.
  2. kind cluster with custom pod CIDR: Pod CIDR configured differently from default — ipBlocks written for default CIDR don't match.
  3. kubeadm cluster with multiple networks: Pod network, service network, and host network — IP-based rules need to account for all source networks.
  4. New team confusing ipBlocks with network policy: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy and Istio AuthorizationPolicy ipBlocks work at different layers — different source IP semantics.
  5. Copy-pasted CIDR from firewall rules: Firewall CIDRs include pod network — same rules applied to AuthorizationPolicy break internal traffic.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl cluster-info dump | grep -E "cluster-cidr|service-cluster-ip-range|pod-network-cidr" Find the pod CIDR. Ensure ipBlocks don't overlap with the pod network. Overlap = internal traffic blocked.
kubectl logs <dest-pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy | grep -i "rbac.*denied.*ip\|source.ip" Envoy RBAC logs show the source IP of blocked requests. Verify it matches what you expect.
kubectl get authorizationpolicy -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A5 "ipBlocks:\|notIpBlocks:" Check all policies for ipBlocks. Multiple policies merge — one broad DENY blocks everything.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The ipBlocks CIDR range is too broad and includes the Kubernetes pod CIDR. For example, 10.0.0.0/8 blocks ALL 10.x.x.x addresses — including the pod network (10.244.0.0/16). Every pod in the mesh falls within the blocked range, so all internal mesh traffic is denied. IP-based rules must use specific CIDRs that exclude the pod and service networks.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Find the exact pod CIDR kubectl get nodes -o yaml | grep podCIDR Use the exact pod CIDR. Create ALLOW rules for this range before creating DENY rules for external IPs.
2. Use specific CIDRs for DENY rules Replace 10.0.0.0/8 with 203.0.113.0/24 (the actual external IP range). Always use the narrowest possible CIDR.
3. Add ALLOW for internal pod and service CIDRs ALLOW 10.244.0.0/16 (pod network) and 10.96.0.0/12 (service network). Internal traffic is explicitly permitted before DENY rules apply.
4. Use principals instead of ipBlocks for mesh-internal traffic For mesh services, use principals or namespaces — more reliable than IP-based rules. IP rules are best for external (non-mesh) traffic.
5. Test with a temporary permissive policy kubectl delete authorizationpolicy block-external-ip -n anihpj If traffic resumes, the IP block was the cause. Re-add with corrected CIDRs.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Never use /8 CIDRs in AuthorizationPolicy ipBlocks. They almost certainly overlap with your pod or service network. Use /24 or /16 at most, and always verify against the actual pod CIDR.
ipBlocks is for external (non-mesh) traffic. Use principals for mesh traffic. Mesh services have SPIFFE identities — more precise than IP addresses. Reserve ipBlocks for blocking external actors without mesh identities.
ALLOW internal traffic FIRST, then DENY external traffic. Explicitly ALLOW your pod CIDR and service CIDR before creating any DENY rules. This prevents accidentally blocking your own infrastructure.
Check Envoy RBAC logs for the actual source IP being evaluated. The source IP Envoy sees may differ from what you expect (NAT, proxy hops). Always verify with logs before writing IP-based rules.
SW15
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW15
Istio CA Certificate Expiry — All Workloads Lose mTLS Simultaneously

🔍 Symptom: At a specific date/time, ALL mTLS traffic in the mesh fails simultaneously. Workload certificates are expired because the Istio self-signed root CA has a 1-year default expiry. Sidecars can't get new certificates because the CA itself is expired. The entire mesh security layer collapses — all STRICT mTLS connections fail, and even PERMISSIVE connections may degrade because certificate renewal stops working.

  kubectl get secret istio-ca-secret -n istio-system -o yaml | grep "root-cert"
  (root CA certificate present)

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- openssl s_client -connect anihpj-db:5432 2>&1 | grep "verify error"
  verify error:num=10:certificate has expired
  verify error:num=10:certificate has expired   ← ALL certs expired!

  kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod | grep -i "ca\|cert.*expir"
  error: root CA certificate expired (2026-01-01)
  fatal: cannot issue workload certificates — CA is invalid
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Self-signed root CA expired: Istio's auto-generated CA cert has a 1-year expiry. After 1 year, the CA can't issue new workload certificates, and existing certs start expiring. Workload certificates (24h default TTL) expire within 24 hours of CA expiry.
  2. No CA rotation plan: Team deployed Istio and never planned for CA rotation. 365 days later, the mesh security collapses without warning. CA rotation must be performed BEFORE the root CA expires.
  3. Workload certs expire before rotation completes: Workload certificates have a 24h TTL. If CA rotation takes longer than 24h, the last certificates issued by the old CA expire before new CA starts issuing.
  4. Custom CA with short expiry: A custom CA (corporate PKI) was used with a short expiry policy. The corporate CA expired — Istio can't issue workload certs because the intermediate CA is expired.
  5. Certificate chain broken during rotation: During CA rotation, the old CA cert is removed before all workloads have transitioned to the new CA. Some workloads still have old-CA-issued certs that are no longer trusted.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. System clock skew between nodes — certificates appear expired on nodes with wrong time
  2. istiod timezone mismatch — CA issues certs with UTC time; node checks against local timezone
  3. Intermediate CA expired but root CA valid — chain validation fails at intermediate level
  4. Cert-manager auto-renewal failed silently — cert-manager couldn't renew; certificates expired unnoticed
  5. Workload cert TTL set too short — custom workload cert TTL of 1h means certs expire before CA rotation completes
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Istio installed ~365 days ago: The default CA expiry is 1 year. Many production clusters hit this exactly 365 days after initial deployment.
  2. kind cluster test environment: Test cluster CA expired — no one monitors test cluster certs; sudden failure surprises everyone.
  3. kubeadm production cluster: Production CA expired at 3 AM — no monitoring alert configured for CA expiry. Site-wide outage.
  4. New team unaware of CA lifecycle: Istio "just worked" for a year — no one documented CA rotation procedure. Emergency scramble when certs expire.
  5. Multi-cluster mesh with different CA ages: kind-cl1 CA expires 3 months before kubeadm CA — cascading failures across clusters.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get secret istio-ca-secret -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.root-cert\.pem}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates Check the root CA certificate expiry date. If within 30 days, plan immediate rotation.
istioctl proxy-config secret <pod> -n <ns> -o json | jq -r '.[].certificateChain.inlineBytes' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates Check workload certificate expiry. Should be within 24h of current time (default TTL). Expired = CA issue.
kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod | grep -iE "ca.*expir|cert.*invalid|failed to sign" istiod logs confirm if the CA is expired and cannot issue new certificates.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Istio self-signed root CA certificate has expired (default 1-year validity). The CA can no longer sign new workload certificates, and existing workload certificates (24h TTL) expire within a day. All mTLS connections fail because workloads can't present valid certificates. This is a predictable, calendar-based failure that requires proactive CA rotation every 365 days.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Check CA certificate expiry immediately kubectl get secret istio-ca-secret -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.root-cert\.pem}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates If expired, proceed to CA rotation. If within 30 days, schedule rotation immediately.
2. Perform CA rotation (self-signed CA) kubectl delete secret istio-ca-secret -n istio-system && kubectl rollout restart deploy/istiod -n istio-system Deleting the CA secret forces istiod to generate a new self-signed CA. Then restart all workloads to get new certs.
3. Restart all workloads to get new certificates kubectl rollout restart deploy,sts -n anihpj All workloads need new certificates signed by the new CA. Rolling restart across all namespaces.
4. For custom CA, renew the CA certificate Generate new CA cert+key, create/update the cacerts Secret in istio-system, restart istiod. Restart all workloads.
5. Set up monitoring and alerting for CA expiry Monitor the root CA cert expiry date. Alert at 60 days, critical alert at 30 days. Automate CA rotation well before expiry.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Istio's default CA expires in 365 days. Calendar this. NOW. This is not optional. Every Istio installation will hit this. Set a calendar reminder for day 300. CA rotation takes planning — don't wait until day 364.
CA rotation requires restarting EVERY workload. Plan for it. All sidecars need new certificates signed by the new CA. This means a full mesh restart. Schedule it during a maintenance window and communicate widely.
Check your CA expiry RIGHT NOW on every cluster. kubectl get secret istio-ca-secret -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.root-cert\.pem}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates Run this on all your clusters today. You might be closer to expiry than you think.
Use a custom CA with longer expiry for production. The default 1-year self-signed CA is fine for dev/test. For production, use a custom CA (corporate PKI or cert-manager) with 5+ year validity and automated rotation.

🔍 Category 5: Troubleshooting Control Plane & Configuration (10 Issues)TC1-TC10

🟣 Control Plane Issues — istiod, Webhooks, CRDs, and Configuration Sync

When the control plane fails, the entire mesh is affected. istiod crash, webhook configuration errors, and config sync failures cascade to every sidecar. These issues require understanding xDS protocol, istiod internals, and the mesh configuration lifecycle.

📌 TC1–TC3: istiod Debugging & Configuration Sync

TC1
🔍 CATEGORY 5: TS CONTROL PLANE — Issue TC1
istiod CrashLoopBackOff — Control Plane Won't Start

🔍 Symptom: istiod is in CrashLoopBackOff — the mesh control plane is completely down. No new sidecars can be injected, existing sidecars can't get config updates, and istioctl proxy-status shows all proxies as STALE. The anihpj/jobpost application still serves traffic (existing sidecars have cached config), but any changes to VirtualServices or DestinationRules are not applied.

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system
  NAME                      READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
  istiod-7d8f9-x            0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   25

  kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod --tail=30
  error: failed to initialize mesh configuration
  error: CRD validation failed: field "address" not recognized
  fatal: cannot start — invalid configuration detected

  istioctl proxy-status
  NAME                          STATUS
  anihpj-web-xxx.anihpj         STALE (istiod unreachable)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Invalid mesh ConfigMap: The istio ConfigMap has YAML syntax errors, deprecated fields, or invalid values. istiod reads the mesh config at startup — if it's invalid, istiod crashes. Check: kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml for typos.
  2. Outdated CRDs after upgrade: istiod was upgraded but CRDs were not. New istiod expects new CRD fields that don't exist — validation fails at startup. Run: istioctl verify-install.
  3. Resource limits too low (OOMKilled): istiod runs out of memory during startup (loading CRDs, building config). Increase memory limits or reduce mesh size. Check: kubectl describe pod for OOMKilled.
  4. Webhook configuration conflict: MutatingWebhookConfiguration or ValidatingWebhookConfiguration points to a non-existent istiod Service or has invalid CA bundle. istiod tries to reconcile webhooks and fails.
  5. Conflicting IstioOperator or Helm values: Multiple installation methods (istioctl + Helm) created conflicting resources. istiod can't determine which configuration is authoritative — crashes on startup validation.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. etcd corruption — Istio resources (VS, DR) partially written; istiod can't parse them
  2. istiod image pull failed — new image not available; old pod terminated; new pod can't start
  3. RBAC changes — istiod ServiceAccount lost permissions to list/watch CRDs
  4. PodSecurityPolicy/PSA blocking — istiod needs specific capabilities to write webhook configs
  5. Node disk pressure — ephemeral storage full on node where istiod is scheduled
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New Istio installation on resource-constrained cluster: kind or minikube with limited memory — istiod OOMKilled during initial CRD loading.
  2. Multi-revision istiod conflict: Two istiod revisions (stable + canary) fighting over webhook configurations — one crashes.
  3. kubeadm cluster etcd latency: Single-node etcd on kubeadm — slow etcd responses cause istiod startup timeouts.
  4. Mesh config edited without validation: Team directly edits istio ConfigMap without YAML validation — typo crashes istiod on next restart.
  5. New team running istioctl install over existing Helm installation — resource conflicts crash istiod.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod --tail=50 istiod logs tell you EXACTLY why it crashed — invalid ConfigMap, missing CRDs, OOM, or permission denied.
kubectl describe pod -n istio-system -l app=istiod | grep -A5 "State:\|OOMKilled\|Error" Check exit reason: OOMKilled = resources, Error = config issue, CrashLoopBackOff = persistent failure.
istioctl analyze --all-namespaces Even with istiod down, istioctl analyze can check configuration files locally for errors that would crash istiod.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The istio ConfigMap in istio-system has invalid YAML or unrecognized fields, causing istiod to fail during mesh configuration initialization. istiod parses the mesh config at startup — any syntax error, typo in field names, or deprecated value causes a fatal error. The control plane cannot start until the ConfigMap is fixed.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Read istiod logs to identify the exact error kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod --tail=100 | grep -iE "error|fatal|invalid|failed" The first error message usually tells you exactly what's wrong — ConfigMap, CRD, or webhook.
2. If ConfigMap error, restore from backup or fix YAML kubectl edit cm istio -n istio-system Fix typos, remove invalid fields. Or restore: istioctl install --set profile=default regenerates the ConfigMap.
3. If CRD error, upgrade CRDs istioctl manifest generate --set profile=default | grep "kind: CustomResourceDefinition" -A1000 | kubectl apply -f - Applies all CRDs required by the current Istio version. Restart istiod after CRD update.
4. If OOMKilled, increase istiod memory limits kubectl patch deploy istiod -n istio-system -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"discovery","resources":{"limits":{"memory":"4Gi"}}}]}}}}' Large meshes (200+ services) may need 2-4Gi for istiod. Monitor with kubectl top pod.
5. If all else fails, reinstall Istio istioctl install --set profile=default -y Reinstall regenerates all control plane resources. Sidecars are unaffected — they reconnect after istiod starts.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
istiod logs are your first stop. Always. The exact reason for the crash is in the logs. Don't guess — read the first ERROR or FATAL line. It tells you whether it's ConfigMap, CRD, webhook, or OOM.
Backup the istio ConfigMap before ANY edit. kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml > backup.yaml A single character typo crashes istiod. Always backup. Always validate YAML syntax before saving.
Existing sidecars survive istiod crashes. Sidecars cache their last configuration. The mesh continues routing traffic even with istiod down. New sidecars and config changes are blocked, but existing services remain functional.
Run 2+ istiod replicas in production. Pod anti-affinity + 2 replicas means one istiod crash doesn't take down the control plane. The surviving replica handles xDS and webhooks while the crashed one restarts.
TC2
🔍 CATEGORY 5: TS CONTROL PLANE — Issue TC2
Webhook Not Called — Sidecar Injection Webhook Fails Silently

🔍 Symptom: Pods are created in a namespace labeled istio-injection=enabled, but the sidecar is never injected. No errors in pod events — the pod starts normally with 1/1 containers. The MutatingWebhookConfiguration exists, but it's not being called by the API server. The webhook's namespaceSelector doesn't match the namespace labels, or the webhook's CA bundle is invalid, causing the API server to silently skip it.

  kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector -o yaml | grep -A10 "namespaceSelector:"
  namespaceSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: istio-injection
      operator: In
      values: ["enabled"]         ← Correct
    - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
      operator: NotIn
      values: ["istio-system","kube-system"]   ← Excludes system namespaces

  kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels
  NAME     LABELS
  anihpj   istio-injection=enabled,kubernetes.io/metadata.name=anihpj
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Webhook CA bundle invalid or expired: The caBundle in the MutatingWebhookConfiguration must contain a valid CA certificate that the API server trusts. If the CA bundle is wrong, the API server can't verify the webhook's TLS connection and silently skips it.
  2. Webhook failurePolicy: Ignore: If the webhook's failurePolicy is Ignore (the default), the API server silently skips the webhook when it fails — pods start without sidecars and no error is reported. Change to Fail to surface errors.
  3. istiod Service not reachable from API server: The webhook's clientConfig.service points to istiod.istio-system.svc:443. If the API server can't reach this Service (network, firewall, DNS), the webhook call fails silently.
  4. namespaceSelector doesn't match: The webhook's namespace selector expects istio-injection: enabled but the namespace has istio-injection=enabled (label key=value format). Selectors use matchLabels or matchExpressions — verify syntax.
  5. Webhook not updated after istiod restart: After istiod pod restart, the webhook's clientConfig.caBundle may be stale. istiod should update it automatically, but if it doesn't, the API server rejects the webhook's TLS certificate.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. API server admission control ordering — another MutatingWebhook runs first and modifies the pod; Istio webhook skipped
  2. ObjectSelector on webhook — webhook configured to only inject pods with specific labels
  3. Webhook timeout too short — API server times out waiting for istiod response; skips injection
  4. NetworkPolicy blocking API server → istiod:443 — webhook traffic blocked by policy
  5. Multiple istio-sidecar-injector webhooks — duplicate webhook configurations; one works, one doesn't
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New cluster — webhook not yet activated: After fresh Istio install, webhook may not be immediately active — wait 30s and try again.
  2. kind cluster API server configuration: kind's API server may have custom admission plugin ordering that affects webhook execution.
  3. kubeadm cluster firewall: Control plane node firewall blocks API server → istiod communication on port 443 (webhook port).
  4. New team checking pod events: With failurePolicy: Ignore, there are NO events indicating webhook failure. Team assumes injection label is wrong.
  5. Istio uninstalled and reinstalled: Old webhook configuration persisted; new istiod didn't update it — CA bundle mismatch.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector -o yaml | grep -A5 "caBundle\|failurePolicy\|namespaceSelector" Check CA bundle, failure policy, and namespace selector. Ignore policy + bad CA = silent failure.
kubectl get ns <ns> --show-labels Verify the namespace has the exact label the webhook's namespaceSelector expects.
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver | grep -i "webhook\|istio\|inject" API server logs show webhook call attempts, failures, and timeouts. Critical for debugging silent webhook issues.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The MutatingWebhookConfiguration's failurePolicy is Ignore (default), and the webhook call to istiod is failing — due to invalid CA bundle, unreachable istiod Service, or TLS certificate mismatch. The API server silently skips the failed webhook and creates the pod without the sidecar. No errors are logged in pod events, making this extremely difficult to detect without checking API server logs.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Check API server logs for webhook errors kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver --tail=100 | grep -i "istio\|webhook\|inject" API server logs show "failed to call webhook" or "x509: certificate signed by unknown authority" — the real error.
2. Regenerate webhook configuration kubectl rollout restart deploy/istiod -n istio-system istiod regenerates the MutatingWebhookConfiguration with current CA bundle and service reference on startup.
3. Temporarily set failurePolicy: Fail for debugging kubectl patch mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector --type json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/webhooks/0/failurePolicy","value":"Fail"}]' With Fail policy, API server rejects pod creation if webhook fails — making the error visible. Revert to Ignore for production.
4. Verify API server can reach istiod kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never -- nc -zv istiod.istio-system.svc 443 If the API server can't reach istiod:443 (webhook port), the webhook call always fails.
5. Check namespace labels match webhook selector kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection=enabled --overwrite Re-apply the label to ensure it matches. Check: kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
API server logs are the ONLY place to debug webhook failures. Pod events show nothing when failurePolicy is Ignore. The API server logs have the definitive answer: why the webhook was skipped or failed.
failurePolicy: Ignore is a silent killer. It's the default for a reason (prevents webhook outages from blocking pod creation), but it means injection failures are invisible. Use Fail during debugging.
Restarting istiod regenerates all webhook configs. If you suspect CA bundle or webhook configuration issues, restarting istiod is the fastest fix — it regenerates webhooks with current certificates.
This is one of the hardest issues to detect without API server access. On managed Kubernetes (GKE, EKS, AKS), you may not have API server log access. Use failurePolicy: Fail temporarily to make webhook failures visible at pod creation time.
TC3
🔍 CATEGORY 5: TS CONTROL PLANE — Issue TC3
Config Not Syncing — VirtualService Changes Not Applied to Sidecars

🔍 Symptom: A VirtualService was updated (route added, weight changed) 10 minutes ago, but sidecars are still using the old configuration. istioctl proxy-config routes shows stale routes. The update was applied successfully (kubectl apply returned OK), istiod is running, but the configuration is not being pushed to Envoy sidecars. The xDS connection is established (proxy shows SYNCED) but config version hasn't changed.

  kubectl apply -f updated-virtualservice.yaml
  virtualservice.networking.istio.io/anihpj-api-vs configured
  (applied 10 minutes ago)

  istioctl proxy-config routes anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep "weight"
  weight: 100    ← OLD config! Should be 90/10 split!

  istioctl proxy-status anihpj-web-xxx.anihpj
  SYNCED   istiod-xxx   1.22.1   (no config version change)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. VirtualService applied to wrong namespace: kubectl apply -f vs.yaml without -n anihpj applied to default namespace. The sidecar is in anihpj — it never sees the VS. Check: kubectl get vs -A | grep anihpj-api.
  2. istiod discoverySelectors filtering namespace: meshConfig.discoverySelectors restricts which namespaces istiod watches. If anihpj is not in the selector, VS changes in that namespace are ignored.
  3. Sidecar resource egress restriction blocking config: The workload's Sidecar resource restricts egress hosts — the updated VS destination host is not in the allowed list. Envoy doesn't receive routes for that host.
  4. xDS stream stalled: The gRPC stream between Envoy and istiod is established but not receiving updates. Proxy shows SYNCED but config version is stale. Restart the Envoy sidecar or istiod to reset the stream.
  5. VS host doesn't match Gateway host: The VS was updated but its hosts field no longer matches any Gateway's hosts. istiod doesn't send routes to gateways for unmatched hosts.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Config version mismatch — istiod has newer config but Envoy has stale version; xDS incremental update failed
  2. Multiple istiod replicas — one replica has updated config, the other has stale; sidecar connected to stale replica
  3. Config rejected by Envoy — istiod sent the config but Envoy rejected it due to validation error; keeps old config
  4. Rate limiting on xDS pushes — too many config changes; istiod throttles updates to prevent overload
  5. etcd watch not triggering — Kubernetes API watch on VS resource didn't fire; istiod unaware of the change
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First config update — team assumes changes are instant: Config propagation takes 5-15 seconds. Team checks immediately and thinks it didn't work.
  2. kind cluster with slow API server: Resource-constrained kind — API watch events delayed; config propagation takes longer.
  3. kubeadm cluster with discoverySelectors: Team restricted istiod to specific namespaces for performance — forgot to include anihpj.
  4. New team applying YAML without -n flag: kubectl defaults to default namespace — VS created in wrong namespace; sidecars in anihpj never see it.
  5. Copy-pasted Sidecar resource blocking config: Sidecar resource copied from another service — egress hosts don't include updated VS destination.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vs --all-namespaces | grep <vs-name> Verify the VS exists in the CORRECT namespace. Wrong namespace = sidecars never see it.
istioctl proxy-config routes <pod> -n <ns> -o json | grep -A5 "<route-name>" Shows the ACTUAL routes in Envoy. Compare against what you expect from the VS YAML.
kubectl logs -n istio-system deploy/istiod --tail=50 | grep -i "push\|config\|ads" istiod logs show config pushes to sidecars. Look for "ADS: config updated" or "push: new routes."
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The VirtualService was applied to the WRONG namespace (default instead of anihpj, or vice versa). Istio resources are namespace-scoped — a VS in default namespace is not processed by sidecars in the anihpj namespace. Additionally, meshConfig.discoverySelectors may restrict which namespaces istiod watches — if anihpj is excluded, VS changes are completely ignored.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify VS exists in the correct namespace kubectl get vs -n anihpj If missing, apply with the correct namespace: kubectl apply -f vs.yaml -n anihpj.
2. Check discoverySelectors in mesh config kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep -A10 "discoverySelectors" Ensure anihpj namespace is in the selector, or remove discoverySelectors entirely for full mesh discovery.
3. Check Sidecar resource egress hosts kubectl get sidecar -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "egress:" Ensure the updated VS host is in the Sidecar's allowed egress list.
4. Force config refresh by restarting sidecar kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj Forces Envoy to establish a fresh xDS stream and receive the latest configuration from istiod.
5. Wait 15 seconds and re-check Config propagation takes 5-15 seconds under normal conditions. Always wait before concluding config is stale.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Always specify -n <namespace> when applying Istio resources. kubectl defaults to default namespace. Istio resources in the wrong namespace are completely invisible to workloads in other namespaces.
Check proxy-config routes — not the VS YAML. The VS YAML is your intent. The Envoy route table is reality. If they don't match, something is preventing config propagation.
Config propagation takes 5-15 seconds. Be patient. istiod watches Kubernetes API, computes new config, and pushes to all affected sidecars. This takes time — especially in large meshes. Wait before investigating.
Use istioctl analyze to catch namespace issues. istioctl analyze -n anihpj Detects misconfigured VS, missing hosts, and namespace-related configuration errors before you spend time debugging propagation.

🔬 Category 6: Troubleshooting Data Plane & Runtime (10 Issues)TD1-TD10

🟣 Data Plane Issues — Envoy Sidecar, iptables, Traffic Capture, and Runtime Failures

When the data plane fails, individual services go dark while the control plane remains healthy. Sidecar crashes, iptables misconfiguration, and runtime errors are isolated to specific workloads — making them harder to detect but easier to contain. These issues require deep Envoy knowledge and runtime debugging skills.

📌 TD1–TD2: Envoy Sidecar Runtime Issues

TD1
🔬 CATEGORY 6: TS DATA PLANE — Issue TD1
Envoy Sidecar OOMKilled — Proxy Consuming Too Much Memory

🔍 Symptom: The istio-proxy container in anihpj-web pods is being OOMKilled repeatedly. The pod shows 1/2 Running with high restart counts on the istio-proxy container. The Envoy sidecar is consuming excessive memory — possibly because it knows about too many services (no Sidecar resource scoping), has large configuration (many VirtualServices/DestinationRules), or has a memory leak from custom WasmPlugin filters.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS      AGE
  anihpj-web-xxx    1/2     Running   15 (30s ago)  10m

  kubectl describe pod anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep -A5 "istio-proxy.*OOMKilled"
  istio-proxy:
    State:          Running (OOMKilled 15 times)
    Last State:     Terminated (OOMKilled, exit code 137)

  kubectl top pod anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj --containers
  NAME           CONTAINER      CPU    MEMORY
  anihpj-web-xxx anihpj-web     50m    200Mi
  anihpj-web-xxx istio-proxy    30m    512Mi   ← At limit! Default is ~128Mi!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No Sidecar resource — Envoy knows about ALL services: Without a Sidecar resource, Envoy creates clusters for EVERY service in the mesh. In a 100-service mesh, that's 100+ clusters consuming memory. Create a Sidecar resource with egress: [{hosts: ["./*", "istio-system/*"]}] to limit scope.
  2. Large configuration pushed to Envoy: Many VirtualServices, DestinationRules, and EnvoyFilters generate large Envoy configurations. Each route, cluster, and endpoint consumes memory. Reduce configuration complexity or increase proxy memory.
  3. WasmPlugin memory leak: Custom WASM filters can leak memory. Check if memory grows over time (leak) vs is immediately high (large config). Disable WasmPlugins to test.
  4. Access logging consuming memory: Envoy access logging buffers logs in memory before flushing. High traffic + verbose logging = memory pressure. Disable access logging or reduce log format.
  5. Default proxy memory too low: Default istio-proxy memory limit is 128Mi-256Mi. Production mesh with 50+ services needs 256Mi-512Mi. Increase via pod annotation: sidecar.istio.io/proxyMemory: "512Mi".
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Metrics/Stats collection memory — Prometheus scraping Envoy stats generates memory overhead
  2. Connection tracking memory — thousands of concurrent connections; each tracked in memory
  3. TLS session cache — mTLS connections cache session data; large cache consumes memory
  4. Envoy version bug — specific Envoy versions have known memory leaks; upgrade to latest patch
  5. gRPC stream memory — long-lived gRPC streaming connections accumulate memory over time
