kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy -- curl localhost:15000/stats | grep "cpu" Envoy CPU stats show throttled time. Non-zero = proxy is CPU-limited and requests are being delayed.
istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n <ns> | grep "downstream_rq_time" Request latency percentiles. P99 > 100ms at moderate load = proxy is bottlenecked.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Envoy sidecar's CPU limit is too low for the actual traffic volume. Default limits (100m-500m CPU) are designed for low-to-moderate traffic. At production RPS with mTLS encryption, access logging, and complex routing rules, Envoy needs 1-2 full CPU cores. When throttled, every request experiences additional latency as Envoy waits for CPU time — the sidecar becomes the application bottleneck.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Increase proxy CPU limit sidecar.istio.io/proxyCPU: "2000m" Pod annotation. Start at 1000m (1 core) for moderate traffic. Use 2000m for high RPS (>1000 req/s).
2. Disable or sample access logging in production meshConfig.accessLogFile: "" Access logging is the #1 CPU consumer after request processing. Disable for normal operation; enable only during debugging.
3. Simplify routing rules Reduce VirtualService match conditions. Use simple prefix matches instead of regex. Fewer rules = less CPU per request.
4. Consider PERMISSIVE mTLS for internal traffic STRICT mTLS doubles CPU usage for encryption. If internal network is trusted, PERMISSIVE reduces CPU while still allowing mTLS where needed.
5. Monitor proxy CPU and set alerts kubectl top pod <pod> -n <ns> --containers | grep istio-proxy Alert if proxy CPU exceeds 80% of limit for >5 minutes. Proactive monitoring prevents throttling before users notice latency.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Default proxy CPU (100m-500m) is for demos. Production needs 1-2 cores. Envoy does real work: mTLS, routing, logging, stats. At production RPS, it needs significant CPU. Treat it like any other critical service component.
CPU throttling causes latency, not errors. When CPU-throttled, Envoy still processes requests — just slowly. You'll see high P99 latency, not 503s. This makes throttling harder to detect than OOMKilled.
Access logging is the easiest CPU optimization. Disabling access logging can reduce proxy CPU by 30-50%. Use Envoy stats for aggregated metrics instead of per-request logs.
Benchmark proxy CPU on your 6-cluster lab. Load test anihpj-api with different proxy CPU limits. Find the sweet spot where P99 latency stays under 50ms at your expected production RPS.
SW23
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW23
CORS Policy Not Working — Cross-Origin Requests Blocked by Istio

🔍 Symptom: The anihpj-web frontend (served from jobpost.com) makes AJAX calls to anihpj-api (api.jobpost.com). Browsers block these cross-origin requests with CORS errors. The Gateway or VirtualService doesn't add CORS headers, and Envoy blocks the preflight OPTIONS request. The browser shows "No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource."

  curl -H "Origin: https://jobpost.com" -X OPTIONS https://api.jobpost.com/api/jobs -v
  HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden   ← Envoy blocks preflight!
  (No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header)

  kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "cors\|Cors\|CORS"
  (no CORS configuration in VirtualService!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No CORS policy in VirtualService: Istio can handle CORS via corsPolicy in VirtualService HTTP routes. Without it, Envoy blocks cross-origin requests by default. Add corsPolicy with allowed origins, methods, and headers.
  2. OPTIONS preflight not matched by any route: Browsers send OPTIONS preflight requests before cross-origin calls. If no VirtualService route matches OPTIONS, Envoy returns 403. Add a match for OPTIONS method.
  3. CORS headers stripped by sidecar: Backend application adds CORS headers, but Envoy sidecar strips them because numTrustedProxies is not configured correctly.
  4. CORS allowOrigin wrong: allowOrigins: [exact: "https://jobpost.com"] but the browser sends Origin: https://www.jobpost.com (with www). Origin mismatch — CORS not applied.
  5. Multiple VirtualServices — CORS on wrong one: CORS policy is on the VS bound to gateways: [mesh] but cross-origin traffic comes through gateways: [istio-ingressgateway] — different VS.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Browser caching preflight — fixed CORS but browser cached old failure; clear cache or use incognito
  2. allowCredentials not set — with credentials: include, browser requires Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
  3. CORS policy on catch-all route — OPTIONS preflight matched by catch-all without CORS before reaching CORS route
  4. Gateway stripping Origin header — cloud LB or CDN strips Origin before it reaches Istio
  5. AuthorizationPolicy blocking OPTIONS — OPTIONS request doesn't have JWT token; blocked by authz before CORS evaluated
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First CORS setup on Istio: Team adds CORS headers in the application (Django) but doesn't know Istio strips/overrides them.
  2. kind cluster with frontend on different port: Frontend on localhost:3000, API on localhost:8080 — treated as cross-origin by browsers.
  3. kubeadm cluster with CDN: Frontend served from CDN domain, API from kubeadm domain — cross-origin between domains.
  4. New team debugging CORS in browser: CORS errors show in browser console — team debugs application code instead of Istio VirtualService.
  5. Copy-pasted VirtualService without CORS — template VS doesn't include corsPolicy section.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get vs <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A15 "corsPolicy:" Check if corsPolicy is configured. Missing = Envoy blocks cross-origin requests. Check allowed origins, methods, headers.
curl -H "Origin: <origin>" -X OPTIONS -v <url> Test preflight request. 403 = Istio blocking. 200 with CORS headers = CORS working. No CORS headers = check VS.
kubectl logs <gateway-pod> -n istio-system | grep -i "cors\|origin\|preflight" Gateway logs show if CORS requests are being processed or blocked by RBAC/CORS filter.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No corsPolicy is configured in the VirtualService for the API endpoint. Istio's Envoy enforces CORS at the proxy level — without explicit corsPolicy configuration, cross-origin requests (especially OPTIONS preflight) are blocked with 403. Application-level CORS headers are ignored because Envoy's CORS filter operates before the request reaches the backend.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add corsPolicy to VirtualService HTTP route corsPolicy: {allowOrigins: [{exact: "https://jobpost.com"}], allowMethods: ["GET","POST","OPTIONS"], allowHeaders: ["Authorization","Content-Type"], allowCredentials: true, maxAge: "24h"} Configure allowed origins, methods, headers, and preflight cache duration.
2. Add OPTIONS route or ensure corsPolicy is on matching route Make sure the route with corsPolicy matches OPTIONS requests. Put CORS route BEFORE catch-all.
3. Verify CORS headers in response curl -H "Origin: https://jobpost.com" -X OPTIONS -v https://api.jobpost.com/api/jobs 2>&1 | grep "Access-Control" Should see Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, and Access-Control-Allow-Headers.
4. Handle CORS on the correct VirtualService If cross-origin traffic comes through the ingress gateway, CORS must be on the VS bound to the gateway, not just the mesh-internal VS.
5. Test from browser after fixing Clear browser cache (especially preflight cache) or use incognito mode. Verify cross-origin AJAX calls succeed.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Istio handles CORS at the proxy level. Application CORS headers are ignored. Envoy's CORS filter evaluates before the request reaches your backend. Configure CORS in VirtualService, not in Django/nginx.
OPTIONS preflight must match a route with corsPolicy. If the catch-all route (no CORS) matches OPTIONS before the CORS route, preflight is blocked. Put CORS routes FIRST.
Use allowOrigins with exact match, not regex, for production. Regex origins can be too permissive. Exact match on specific domains is more secure and predictable.
Browser preflight cache can hide fixes. Use curl to verify first. Always test CORS with curl before testing in the browser. Browsers cache successful preflight responses for maxAge seconds and may hide issues.
SW24
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW24
AuthorizationPolicy Not Applied to TCP Traffic — L4 Policies Ignored

🔍 Symptom: An AuthorizationPolicy is created to control access to the anihpj-db PostgreSQL service (TCP port 5432). But the policy has no effect — all services can still connect to the database. The policy was written for HTTP (with paths and methods) but PostgreSQL is a TCP service. TCP traffic requires different AuthorizationPolicy rules — no HTTP-level conditions like paths, headers, or methods are available.

  kubectl get authorizationpolicy db-access -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 "rules:"
  rules:
  - to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["POST"]      ← HTTP method on TCP service!
        paths: ["/api/*"]      ← Paths don't exist for TCP!

  kubectl exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -- psql -h anihpj-db -U postgres -c "SELECT 1"
  ?column? = 1   ← Web can still access DB — policy not enforced for TCP!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. HTTP-specific rules on TCP service: methods, paths, and headers are HTTP-only conditions. TCP services don't have these concepts — the rules never match. TCP AuthorizationPolicy must use only ports and from conditions.
  2. Service port not named with protocol prefix: Istio determines the protocol from the port name. If port 5432 is named tcp-db it's treated as TCP. If named http-db, Istio expects HTTP traffic — mismatch causes policy to not apply.
  3. AuthorizationPolicy not selecting the correct workload: The selector.matchLabels doesn't match the database pod labels. Policy targets the wrong pods — database is unprotected.
  4. TCP traffic not going through Envoy: The database connection may bypass the sidecar if iptables rules don't capture port 5432. Check traffic interception for TCP ports.
  5. Multiple AuthorizationPolicies — one ALLOW with no rules permits everything: An ALLOW with empty rules: [{}] permits all traffic — overrides restrictive TCP policy.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. TCP AuthorizationPolicy requires mTLS — plaintext TCP connections have no principal; policy can't evaluate
  2. Port number wrong in policy — policy targets port 5432 but actual database port is 5433
  3. Database connection pooling — connection from sidecar appears as localhost; policy sees wrong source
  4. Envoy TCP proxy filter not loaded — custom EnvoyFilter removed TCP inspection from the filter chain
  5. AuthorizationPolicy version doesn't support TCP — older Istio versions had limited TCP authz support
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First TCP AuthorizationPolicy: Team copies HTTP policy template — paths and methods don't apply to TCP; policy silently does nothing.
  2. kind cluster with PostgreSQL: Database port named postgresql — Istio treats as plain TCP; HTTP rules don't apply.
  3. kubeadm cluster with mixed protocols: HTTP API + TCP database in same namespace — team applies HTTP-style policies to both.
  4. New team unaware TCP AuthorizationPolicy differs from HTTP: Assumes AuthorizationPolicy works the same for all protocols.
  5. Copy-pasted AuthorizationPolicy from HTTP API to TCP database — paths, methods, headers don't apply to TCP.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get svc <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A3 "port:" Port name starting with tcp- = TCP protocol. HTTP-only authz rules (paths, methods) don't apply.
kubectl get authorizationpolicy -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A15 "rules:" TCP policies should only have from and to: [{operation: {ports: ["5432"]}}]. No paths, methods, or headers.
kubectl logs <db-pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy | grep -i "rbac\|tcp\|denied" Envoy logs show if TCP AuthorizationPolicy is being evaluated. No RBAC entries = policy not applied to TCP traffic.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The AuthorizationPolicy uses HTTP-specific conditions (methods: ["POST"], paths: ["/api/*"]) on a TCP service (PostgreSQL port 5432). TCP services don't have HTTP methods, paths, or headers — these conditions never match TCP traffic. The policy silently does nothing. TCP AuthorizationPolicy must use only from (source) and ports conditions — no HTTP-level operations.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Rewrite policy with TCP-appropriate conditions Use from: [{source: {principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/anihpj-api"]}}] and to: [{operation: {ports: ["5432"]}}]. No paths, methods, or headers.
2. Name Service port with tcp- prefix Ensure port name is tcp-postgresql. Istio uses the prefix to determine protocol — http- prefix on TCP port causes mismatched expectations.
3. Verify selector matches database pods kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-db Policy selector must match database pod labels exactly. Zero matches = policy not applied.
4. Enable mTLS for principal-based TCP authz TCP principal evaluation requires mTLS. Without STRICT or PERMISSIVE, TCP connections have no SPIFFE identity.
5. Test TCP policy enforcement kubectl exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -- nc -zv anihpj-db 5432 Should timeout or connection refused if policy blocks web→db. Should succeed if policy allows web→db.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
TCP AuthorizationPolicy is simpler than HTTP — only ports, principals, namespaces, and IPs. No paths, no methods, no headers. If your policy has these, it's an HTTP policy applied to TCP — it won't work.
Port name prefix determines protocol detection. http-*, grpc-*, http2-* = HTTP. tcp-*, tls-* = TCP/TLS. All others default to TCP. Name your ports correctly.
TCP AuthorizationPolicy requires mTLS for principal-based rules. Without mTLS, TCP connections have no identity. Principal-based ALLOW/DENY silently does nothing for plaintext TCP.
Database access control through Istio is a key ICA exam scenario. Practice TCP AuthorizationPolicy for PostgreSQL on your 6-cluster lab. Allow only anihpj-api → anihpj-db:5432 and verify web is blocked.
SW25
🔐 CATEGORY 4: SECURING WORKLOADS — Issue SW25
End-to-End mTLS Broken by Gateway TLS Termination

🔍 Symptom: The ingress gateway terminates TLS (SIMPLE mode) and forwards HTTP to backend services. But the mesh is configured with STRICT mTLS — the backend Envoy expects mTLS from ALL clients including the gateway. The gateway sends plaintext HTTP after TLS termination — the backend Envoy rejects the connection because it requires mTLS. End-to-end encryption from client to backend is broken: client→gateway is TLS (encrypted), gateway→backend is plaintext (not encrypted).

  curl https://jobpost.com/api/jobs   ← Client→Gateway: TLS ✅
  HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable   ← Gateway→Backend: mTLS fails!

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep -i "mtls\|peer"
  [error] mTLS required but client (gateway) presented no certificate
  [error] incoming connection from gateway rejected: STRICT mTLS enforced
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Gateway TLS SIMPLE termination → plaintext to backend: After terminating TLS, the gateway forwards HTTP (plaintext) to the backend. Backend STRICT mTLS rejects plaintext. Gateway must either use ISTIO_MUTUAL to backend or the backend must allow PERMISSIVE for gateway traffic.
  2. Gateway not part of the mesh: The gateway pod doesn't have an Envoy sidecar — it's just the gateway Envoy. It doesn't have a workload certificate — can't do mTLS to backend. Gateway must be configured for ISTIO_MUTUAL to backend services.
  3. PeerAuthentication STRICT on backend but not excluding gateway: Backend requires mTLS from ALL sources. Gateway is not excluded — its plaintext traffic is rejected. Add portLevelMtls PERMISSIVE for gateway traffic or configure gateway→backend mTLS.
  4. DestinationRule for backend doesn't specify ISTIO_MUTUAL: The DR for the backend service should have trafficPolicy.tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL to tell the gateway to use mTLS when connecting to the backend.
  5. Gateway terminates TLS but doesn't re-originate: End-to-end encryption requires: Gateway terminates client TLS → Gateway originates mTLS to backend. Missing the "originate mTLS" step = plaintext to backend.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Gateway SA not authorized in backend AuthorizationPolicy — backend allows specific principals; gateway SA not included
  2. Gateway cert expired — gateway can't establish mTLS to backend because its cert is invalid
  3. Different trust domains — gateway in istio-system, backend in anihpj; trust domain mismatch for mTLS
  4. Gateway deployment uses custom SA without mTLS certs — custom SA doesn't have workload identity
  5. Multiple gateways chained — first gateway terminates TLS; second gateway expected to do mTLS but receives plaintext
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First TLS termination + mTLS setup: Team configures gateway TLS but doesn't realize STRICT mTLS on backend will reject the gateway's plaintext traffic.
  2. kind cluster with STRICT mTLS mesh: All services require mTLS — gateway traffic blocked because termination→plaintext breaks end-to-end encryption.
  3. kubeadm cluster with compliance requirement: End-to-end encryption required by policy — current setup breaks compliance because gateway→backend is plaintext.
  4. New team debugging 503 from gateway: Checks VirtualService, DestinationRule, and Gateway config — doesn't check PeerAuthentication on backend services.
  5. Security audit finding plaintext internal traffic — gateway TLS termination created an encryption gap inside the mesh.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get peerauthentication -n <ns> -o yaml | grep "mode:" STRICT mode on backend = gateway plaintext traffic rejected. PERMISSIVE or port exception needed for gateway path.
kubectl get dr <backend-dr> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A5 "tls:" Should have mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL to tell the gateway to use mTLS when connecting to the backend.
kubectl logs <backend-pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy | grep -i "peer.*cert\|mtls.*required\|plaintext" Backend Envoy logs show if the gateway connection is being rejected for missing mTLS certificate.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The ingress gateway terminates client TLS (SIMPLE mode) and forwards plaintext HTTP to backend services. But the backend PeerAuthentication is STRICT — requiring mTLS from ALL clients. The gateway's plaintext traffic is rejected. End-to-end encryption requires the gateway to RE-ORIGINATE mTLS to the backend: Gateway terminates client TLS → Gateway originates ISTIO_MUTUAL to backend. Without this, the gateway→backend segment is unencrypted and rejected by STRICT mTLS.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Configure DestinationRule with ISTIO_MUTUAL for backend trafficPolicy: {tls: {mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL}} Tells the gateway Envoy to establish mTLS when connecting to the backend service.
2. Or set PeerAuthentication PERMISSIVE for gateway traffic port portLevelMtls: {<backend-port>: {mode: PERMISSIVE}}. Allows both mTLS and plaintext on the backend port. Simpler but less secure.
3. Verify gateway can establish mTLS to backend kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway | grep -i "mtls\|tls.*backend\|ISTIO_MUTUAL" Gateway logs should show mTLS negotiation with backend — not "plaintext" or "no certificate."
4. Test end-to-end encryption Client→Gateway: TLS (external cert). Gateway→Backend: mTLS (Istio certs). Verify with tcpdump that no segment is plaintext.
5. Monitor for encryption gaps with Kiali Kiali shows lock icons for encrypted traffic. 🔒 on gateway→backend connection confirms ISTIO_MUTUAL is working.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
TLS termination + STRICT mTLS = guaranteed failure. Always. Gateway terminates TLS → plaintext to backend. Backend STRICT mTLS → rejects plaintext. You MUST configure ISTIO_MUTUAL on the DestinationRule for the backend.
End-to-end encryption: Client→Gateway (TLS) + Gateway→Backend (mTLS). Two separate encryption segments. The Gateway is the bridge — it must terminate one and originate the other.
ISTIO_MUTUAL on DestinationRule tells the source to use mTLS. This is how you configure the GATEWAY (source) to use mTLS when connecting to the BACKEND (destination). The DR is applied to the destination but configures the source's behavior.
This is a top ICA exam scenario — gateway TLS + mesh mTLS. Practice on your 6-cluster lab: configure gateway SIMPLE TLS → backend STRICT mTLS → observe 503 → add ISTIO_MUTUAL DR → verify end-to-end encryption. Master this flow.
TC6
🔍 CATEGORY 5: TS CONTROL PLANE — Issue TC6
Istio DNS Proxying Not Working — Service Discovery Fails for Unknown Hosts

🔍 Symptom: Istio's DNS proxying feature (ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE) is enabled to capture DNS queries from applications and resolve ServiceEntry hosts. But applications can't resolve external hostnames defined in ServiceEntries. DNS queries are not being captured, or the DNS proxy returns NXDOMAIN. The application falls back to standard DNS which can't resolve mesh-registered external services.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-api -- nslookup api.payment-gateway.com
  Server: 10.96.0.10 (CoreDNS)
  ** server can't find api.payment-gateway.com: NXDOMAIN

  kubectl get se payment-gateway -n anihpj
  NAME              HOSTS                             LOCATION        RESOLUTION
  payment-gateway   ["api.payment-gateway.com"]       MESH_EXTERNAL   DNS
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. DNS proxying not enabled in mesh config: Istio's DNS proxy must be explicitly enabled via meshConfig.defaultConfig.proxyMetadata.ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE: "true". Without it, DNS queries go directly to CoreDNS — ServiceEntry hosts are unknown.
  2. DNS capture only works for DNS over UDP/TCP: The iptables redirect only captures standard DNS (port 53 UDP/TCP). If the application uses DNS-over-HTTPS or DNS-over-TLS, the DNS proxy doesn't intercept it.
  3. ServiceEntry resolution DNS not matching: SE has resolution: DNS but the hostname requires resolution: STATIC with explicit IPs. DNS resolution for the external host fails through standard DNS.
  4. DNS proxy port conflict: The DNS proxy listens on port 15053. If another process on the pod uses this port, the proxy can't start — DNS capture silently fails.
  5. DNS capture only works on new pods: DNS proxy is configured at pod startup via iptables. Existing pods created before DNS proxy was enabled don't have DNS capture — must restart pods.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. DNS proxy only resolves ServiceEntry hosts — non-mesh external hosts still fail through standard DNS
  2. CoreDNS caching negative responses — NXDOMAIN cached before DNS proxy was enabled
  3. DNS over TCP not captured — only UDP DNS is redirected by iptables; TCP DNS queries bypass proxy
  4. NetworkPolicy blocking port 15053 — DNS proxy cannot communicate with istiod for resolution
  5. DNS capture annotation typo — ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE vs ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE (case sensitive)
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First DNS proxy setup: Team creates ServiceEntry but doesn't enable DNS proxying — application uses CoreDNS which doesn't know about mesh-registered hosts.
  2. kind cluster DNS configuration: Kind's CoreDNS setup differs from kubeadm — DNS capture behavior may vary.
  3. kubeadm cluster with custom DNS: Custom CoreDNS configuration may not forward unknown hosts correctly — DNS proxy bypassed.
  4. New team confusing ServiceEntry with DNS registration: ServiceEntry registers the host in Istio — but DNS resolution requires DNS proxy to be enabled separately.
  5. DNS proxy enabled but pods not restarted — existing pods don't have iptables rules for DNS capture.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep "DNS_CAPTURE" Must show ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE: "true". Missing or false = DNS proxy not enabled.
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy -- iptables -t nat -L -n | grep "15053\|DNS" Verify iptables has REDIRECT rules for DNS traffic (port 53) to the proxy port (15053).
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy -- curl localhost:15053/dns -d '{"host":"api.payment-gateway.com"}' Test the DNS proxy directly. Should return the resolved IP from the ServiceEntry or mesh registry.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Istio's DNS proxying is not enabled. ServiceEntry registers external hosts in the mesh registry, but DNS resolution requires the DNS proxy to intercept application DNS queries and resolve them using the mesh registry. Without ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE: "true" in the mesh config, DNS queries go to CoreDNS — which has no knowledge of ServiceEntry hosts and returns NXDOMAIN.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Enable DNS proxying in mesh config meshConfig.defaultConfig.proxyMetadata.ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE: "true" Edit the istio ConfigMap. Add DNS_CAPTURE and DNS_AUTO_ALLOCATE for automatic address allocation.
2. Restart all pods to apply DNS capture kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj DNS iptables rules are configured at pod startup. Existing pods must be restarted to get DNS capture.
3. Verify DNS resolution for ServiceEntry hosts kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj -c anihpj-api -- nslookup api.payment-gateway.com Should resolve to an auto-allocated IP (240.240.x.x) or the configured static address.
4. Check ServiceEntry resolution mode Use resolution: DNS for dynamic hostnames (DNS proxy queries CoreDNS). Use resolution: STATIC with explicit endpoints if DNS resolution fails.
5. Test DNS proxy directly for debugging kubectl exec <pod> -c istio-proxy -- curl localhost:15053/dns -d '{"host":"api.payment-gateway.com"}' If the proxy returns an IP, DNS capture is working. If connection refused, proxy is not running.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
ServiceEntry + DNS proxy = application-transparent external service access. ServiceEntry alone lets Envoy route. DNS proxy lets the APPLICATION resolve the hostname. Both are needed for transparent external access.
DNS proxy requires pod restart after enabling. The iptables DNS redirect is set up by istio-init at pod startup. Enabling DNS proxy in mesh config doesn't affect running pods.
Auto-allocated IPs (240.240.0.0/16) are virtual — they're not real network addresses. Istio allocates virtual IPs for DNS resolution. These IPs are only meaningful inside the pod's network namespace — don't try to ping them.
Test DNS proxy on your 6-cluster lab with the payment-gateway ServiceEntry. Enable DNS proxy, create ServiceEntry for api.payment-gateway.com, and verify anihpj-api can resolve and connect to it. This is a key ICA service discovery scenario.
TD6
🔬 CATEGORY 6: TS DATA PLANE — Issue TD6
TCP Connection Pool Exhausted — Ephemeral Ports Running Out

🔍 Symptom: Under high load, the anihpj-web frontend gets "Cannot assign requested address" (EADDRNOTAVAIL) errors when connecting to anihpj-api. The Envoy sidecar has exhausted all available ephemeral ports for upstream connections. TCP connections are in TIME_WAIT state, consuming ports that can't be reused immediately. This is a kernel-level port exhaustion issue, not an Envoy configuration problem.

  kubectl exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- ss -s
  Total: 16384
  TCP:   16345 (established 200, closed 45, timewait 16100)
  (Almost all ports in TIME_WAIT!)

  cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range
  32768   60999   ← Only ~28K ports available!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No HTTP keep-alive — new connection per request: If maxRequestsPerConnection is set to 1, Envoy opens a new TCP connection for every HTTP request — rapidly exhausting ephemeral ports under high RPS. Set to 0 (unlimited reuse).
  2. TIME_WAIT sockets not reused: Linux holds closed connections in TIME_WAIT for 60-120 seconds. At 1000 connections/second, ~60K-120K ports are locked in TIME_WAIT — exceeding the ~28K ephemeral port range.
  3. Ephemeral port range too small: Default range is 32768-60999 (~28K ports). For high-connection services, this is insufficient. Expand to 1024-65535 (~64K ports).
  4. Too many upstream clusters: Each upstream service creates separate connection pools. 50 services × 100 connections = 5000 concurrent connections — consuming 20% of ephemeral ports just for steady state.
  5. Connection idle timeout too short: Connections closed and recreated frequently — each close creates a TIME_WAIT socket. Increase idle timeout to keep connections alive longer.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. tcp_tw_reuse not enabled — kernel can't reuse TIME_WAIT sockets for new connections
  2. Connection pool maxConnections too high — allows too many concurrent connections; port pool fragmented
  3. Health checks at high frequency — probes create/destroy connections; TIME_WAIT accumulation
  4. Node-level port exhaustion — not just Envoy; all pods on the node share the kernel port space
  5. IPv4 vs IPv6 — IPv6 has no ephemeral port shortage; issue only affects IPv4 connections
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. High RPS on kind cluster: Load testing at 5000 RPS on kind — ephemeral ports exhausted; application fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL.
  2. kubeadm cluster with default kernel settings: Never tuned ip_local_port_range — hitting the ~28K limit unexpectedly at scale.
  3. New team debugging "Cannot assign requested address": Assumes it's a DNS or routing issue — actually kernel port exhaustion from high connection churn.
  4. Large mesh without Sidecar resources: 100+ clusters × default connections per cluster = massive port consumption.
  5. Connection pool defaults not adjusted for production RPS — test environment values carried to production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy -- ss -s Shows total TCP sockets. If TIME_WAIT count is near the ephemeral port range limit, port exhaustion is imminent.
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range Shows the ephemeral port range. ~28K default may be insufficient for high-connection services.
istioctl proxy-config stats <pod> -n <ns> | grep "upstream_cx_total\|upstream_cx_overflow" Upstream connection overflow = connections rejected due to port/connection limit exhaustion.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Envoy sidecar creates a new TCP connection for every HTTP request (no keep-alive), rapidly consuming ephemeral ports. Each closed connection sits in TIME_WAIT state for 60-120 seconds. At high RPS, the ~28K ephemeral port range is exhausted — new connections fail with EADDRNOTAVAIL. The fix involves: enabling HTTP keep-alive, expanding the ephemeral port range, and enabling tcp_tw_reuse.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Enable HTTP keep-alive with unlimited requests per connection connectionPool: {http: {maxRequestsPerConnection: 0}} One connection handles unlimited HTTP requests — no new connections per request. Dramatically reduces connection churn.
2. Expand ephemeral port range (node-level) sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="1024 65535" Increases available ports from ~28K to ~64K. Requires privileged container or node-level configuration.
3. Enable tcp_tw_reuse for TIME_WAIT socket reuse sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 Allows the kernel to reuse TIME_WAIT sockets for new connections to the same destination. Reduces port pressure.
4. Reduce upstream clusters with Sidecar resource Fewer upstream services = fewer connection pools = fewer concurrent connections. Create Sidecar resource to limit known services.
5. Increase connection idle timeout connectionPool: {tcp: {idleTimeout: 3600s}} Keep idle connections alive longer. Reduces connection open/close cycles and TIME_WAIT accumulation.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
"Cannot assign requested address" = ephemeral port exhaustion. Always. This error has exactly one cause at the kernel level. Don't debug the application or Envoy — check ss -s for TIME_WAIT count.
HTTP keep-alive is the #1 fix — single biggest impact. One connection handles unlimited requests instead of one-per-request. This eliminates 95% of connection churn and TIME_WAIT accumulation.
Sysctl changes require privileged containers or node-level DaemonSet. Envoy containers typically can't modify kernel parameters. Use a DaemonSet with hostNetwork or configure node sysctl at the infrastructure level.
Sidecar resource is the indirect fix — fewer clusters = fewer connections. Going from 100 clusters to 10 reduces concurrent connections by 90%. Port pressure drops proportionally.
TD7
🔬 CATEGORY 6: TS DATA PLANE — Issue TD7
Envoy Hot Restart Fails — Sidecar Loses Configuration After Crash

🔍 Symptom: The Envoy sidecar crashes (OOM, CPU kill) and restarts, but after restart it loses its configuration and can't reconnect to istiod. The pod shows 1/2 Ready indefinitely — the application container is fine, but the Envoy sidecar can't bootstrap. The hot restart feature (which preserves connections during restart) fails, causing the Envoy to lose its xDS connection and cached configuration.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  anihpj-api-xxx    1/2     Running   5 (30s ago)

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy --tail=20
  [error] Hot restart failed: cannot find parent process
  [error] Bootstrap failed: lost configuration from previous instance
  [warning] Connecting to istiod for fresh bootstrap config
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Envoy OOMKilled — no hot restart possible: When Envoy is killed by OOM, the parent process is terminated forcefully. Hot restart requires the parent process to still be running to pass configuration and connections to the new Envoy instance.
  2. Pod restart (not just Envoy restart): If the entire pod restarts (not just the Envoy process), both containers restart — hot restart across pod boundaries doesn't exist. Envoy starts fresh with no cached configuration.
  3. istiod unreachable during restart: Envoy tries to bootstrap from istiod after losing hot restart state. If istiod is unreachable (network, DNS, or istiod itself down), Envoy can't get fresh config — stays not-ready.
  4. Shared memory segment corrupted: Hot restart uses shared memory to pass state. If the shared memory segment is corrupted or permissions are wrong, hot restart fails.
  5. Envoy version mismatch during hot restart: The new Envoy binary is a different version than the old one — hot restart between different versions is not supported. Configuration format may differ.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Disk space full — Envoy can't write hot restart files to /tmp or shared memory
  2. Container restartPolicy not Always — container exits and doesn't restart; pod stays in error state
  3. SELinux/AppArmor blocking shared memory — security module prevents Envoy from accessing hot restart SHM
  4. PID namespace conflict — Envoy can't find parent process in different PID namespace
  5. Custom Envoy bootstrap config breaks hot restart — non-standard bootstrap may not configure hot restart correctly
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First Envoy crash in production: Team has never seen an Envoy restart — doesn't know about hot restart or bootstrap from istiod.
  2. kind cluster OOM kills: Resource-constrained kind nodes — Envoy OOMKilled regularly; hot restart fails each time.
  3. kubeadm cluster with infrequent restarts: Envoy runs for months without restarting — when it finally restarts, team has forgotten the bootstrap process.
  4. New team debugging 1/2 pod state: Sees Envoy container restarting but doesn't know to check istiod reachability for bootstrap.
  5. Multi-container pod with shared process namespace — Envoy can't find its parent PID due to shared namespace.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy --tail=50 | grep -i "hot\|restart\|bootstrap\|parent" Envoy logs show hot restart status. "Hot restart failed" = parent process not available; fresh bootstrap required.
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> | grep -A5 "istio-proxy.*OOMKilled\|Exit Code" Exit code 137 = OOMKilled. Hot restart not possible after OOM — fresh bootstrap from istiod.
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod istiod must be Running for Envoy to bootstrap after losing hot restart state. If istiod is down, bootstrap fails.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Envoy was OOMKilled (exit code 137), which forcefully terminates the process — hot restart is not possible because the parent process is gone. Envoy must bootstrap fresh from istiod. If istiod is unreachable during the restart window, Envoy can't get new configuration and stays not-ready (1/2). The fix involves preventing OOMKills (increase memory limits, add Sidecar resource to reduce clusters) and ensuring istiod is always available for bootstrap.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Prevent OOMKills — increase proxy memory limit sidecar.istio.io/proxyMemory: "512Mi" OOMKilled Envoy can't hot restart. Increasing memory prevents the crash in the first place.
2. Ensure istiod is reachable for bootstrap kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod At least one istiod replica must be Running. Verify network connectivity from the pod to istiod:15012.
3. Add Sidecar resource to reduce Envoy memory footprint Limit Envoy to only necessary services. Reduces cluster count and memory usage — prevents OOMKills.
4. Restart the pod if hot restart fails kubectl delete pod <pod> -n anihpj Forces a clean start with fresh bootstrap from istiod. The pod should come back 2/2 Ready within 30 seconds.
5. Monitor Envoy restart events and OOMKills Alert on Envoy container restarts. Investigate every OOMKill — don't let it become routine. Each OOMKill risks configuration loss.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
OOMKilled Envoy = no hot restart. Fresh bootstrap from istiod is the only recovery. Hot restart requires the parent Envoy process to still be alive. OOMKill terminates the parent — there's nothing to restart from.
1/2 Ready with Envoy restarting = check istiod first. If Envoy can't reach istiod for bootstrap, it stays not-ready indefinitely. Always verify istiod health before debugging the sidecar.
Preventing OOMKills is better than recovering from them. Increase proxy memory, use Sidecar resources, disable access logging. Every OOMKill risks configuration loss and application downtime during bootstrap.
Practice Envoy restart scenarios on your 6-cluster lab. Kill the istio-proxy process, watch the hot restart attempt, observe bootstrap from istiod. Understanding this flow is critical for data plane troubleshooting on the ICA exam.
TC7
🔍 CATEGORY 5: TS CONTROL PLANE — Issue TC7
Mutating Webhook Injection Failure — New Pods Not Getting Sidecar

🔍 Symptom: New pods in the namespace labeled with istio-injection: enabled are not getting the istio-proxy sidecar. Pods start with 1/1 Ready instead of 2/2. The Istio mutating webhook should inject the sidecar automatically, but it's not being invoked. The pod spec shows no sidecar container. Existing pods with sidecars are fine — only new pods are affected.

  kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  anihpj-api-new    1/1     Running   0    ← No sidecar!
  anihpj-api-old    2/2     Running   0    ← Has sidecar ✅

  kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector -o yaml
  (no admissionReviewVersions — webhook not called!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Namespace label incorrect: The namespace must have istio-injection: enabled (not "enabled" as a string, not "true"). Label key must be exactly istio-injection. Use istio-injection=enabled (no value field — just label).
  2. istiod webhook service not reachable: The API server must be able to reach the istiod webhook service. If the service endpoint is down, the webhook is called but fails — pods may be created without injection if failurePolicy: Ignore.
  3. Webhook configuration missing or deleted: The istio-sidecar-injector MutatingWebhookConfiguration could be accidentally deleted or the CA bundle has expired.
  4. Istio namespace not properly configured: The namespace needs both the injection label AND no istio-injection: disabled annotation that overrides the label.
  5. Webhook namespace selector excludes the target namespace: The MutatingWebhookConfiguration has namespaceSelector that excludes the target namespace — injection is never triggered.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Pod annotation istio-sidecar-injector.istio.io/inject: "false" overrides namespace label
  2. istiod certificate expired — API server doesn't trust webhook TLS; webhook calls fail
  3. API server not configured to call admission webhooks — --enable-admission-plugins missing MutatingAdmissionWebhook
  4. Webhook timeout too short — injection takes longer than webhook timeout; request fails silently (failurePolicy: Ignore)
  5. Network policy blocking API server → istiod webhook port (15017) — webhook cannot reach istiod
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First Istio install — forgot to label namespace: Team installs Istio but doesn't label namespaces with istio-injection=enabled.
  2. kind cluster API server connectivity: Kind's API server may have different network paths to the webhook — injection silently fails.
  3. kubeadm cluster with custom CA: Webhook CA bundle must be updated after Istio install — expired or wrong CA bundle breaks webhook trust.
  4. New team doesn't know sidecar injection is webhook-based: Thinks sidecar is "built-in" to pods — doesn't check webhook or namespace labels.
  5. Minikube namespace reset — cluster rebuild didn't reapply namespace labels.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get ns <ns> -o yaml | grep "istio-injection" Must show istio-injection: enabled. Missing or "disabled" = no injection. Check for both label and annotation.
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector -o yaml | grep -A2 "caBundle\|failurePolicy\|namespaceSelector" Verify webhook exists, CA bundle is valid, failurePolicy is set, and namespaceSelector includes the target namespace.
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod istiod must be Running and healthy. Webhook service endpoint must exist and be reachable from the API server.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The namespace is not labeled with istio-injection: enabled. Istio's mutating webhook uses a namespaceSelector to only invoke injection for labeled namespaces. Without this label, the webhook is never called — pods are created without the istio-proxy sidecar. The fix is to label the namespace and restart deployments to trigger new pod creation with sidecar injection.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Label the namespace for injection kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection=enabled --overwrite Adds the injection label. The webhook namespaceSelector matches this label — injection is triggered for new pods.
2. Verify webhook configuration kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector -o yaml | grep -A5 "namespaceSelector" Should have matchExpressions for istio-injection: enabled. If missing, the webhook is incorrectly configured.
3. Restart deployments to inject sidecars kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj Existing pods won't get sidecars retroactively. Rolling restart creates new pods — webhook injects sidecar.
4. Check webhook service and istiod health kubectl get svc istiod -n istio-system; kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=istiod --tail=20 Webhook service must exist and istiod must be processing injection requests without errors.
5. Verify injection with describe kubectl describe pod <new-pod> -n anihpj | grep -A5 "istio-proxy\|Init Containers" New pods should show istio-init container and istio-proxy sidecar after labeling and restart.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
istio-injection=enabled is a LABEL, not an annotation. Label goes on the NAMESPACE, not individual pods. Pod-level override is via annotation sidecar.istio.io/inject with "true"/"false".
Existing pods never get sidecars retroactively. Restart required. Sidecar injection happens at pod creation time via the webhook. Running pods must be recreated to get sidecars.
Check failurePolicy: Ignore — it hides webhook failures. If the webhook fails silently (timeout, unreachable), failurePolicy: Ignore allows pods to be created without injection. Check API server audit logs for webhook errors.
Label all application namespaces as part of Istio installation. On your 6-cluster lab, label all application namespaces with istio-injection=enabled as part of the setup script. Never forget this step.
TD8
🔬 CATEGORY 6: TS DATA PLANE — Issue TD8
Sidecar Traffic Interception Not Working — Application Bypasses Envoy

🔍 Symptom: The application in the pod is supposed to have ALL traffic intercepted by the Envoy sidecar via iptables. But the application bypasses the sidecar and connects directly to other services. Traffic is not being observed by Envoy — metrics, tracing, and policies don't apply. The application connects directly to pod IPs (not through Envoy), bypassing all Istio traffic management and security policies.

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- iptables -t nat -L -n
  Chain ISTIO_OUTPUT (0 references)  ← ISTIO_OUTPUT not referenced!
  Chain OUTPUT (policy ACCEPT)
  target     prot opt source    destination
  (no ISTIO_OUTPUT redirect — traffic goes directly out!)

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-api -- curl anihpj-db:5432 -v
  Connected to anihpj-db:5432   ← Direct connection — not through Envoy!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Traffic interception mode wrong: Istio supports REDIRECT and TPROXY modes. If the mode is wrong for the kernel version, iptables rules may not be applied correctly — no traffic redirection.
  2. Init container (istio-init) failed or didn't run: The iptables rules are set up by the istio-init container. If istio-init fails or is missing, the sidecar container runs but there are no iptables rules.
  3. Pod has annotations to exclude ports from interception: traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInboundPorts or traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeOutboundPorts may exclude the critical ports.
  4. Application uses non-standard network path: Go applications with sidecarless networking, Unix domain sockets, or direct pod-to-pod IP connections may bypass iptables entirely.
  5. CNI plugin interference: Some CNIs (Calico with eBPF, Cilium with eBPF) bypass iptables entirely — Istio's iptables-based interception doesn't work. Requires TPROXY mode or CNI-specific configuration.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. iptables rules overwritten by other init containers — later init container removes or overwrites Istio rules
  2. NET_ADMIN capability missing — istio-init can't modify iptables without NET_ADMIN capability
  3. IPv6-only cluster — Istio interception rules are IPv4 only; IPv6 traffic bypasses Envoy entirely
  4. Sidecar started but iptables not yet applied — race condition between Envoy start and iptables setup
  5. Custom DNS resolution — application resolves service to pod IP and connects directly; iptables only intercepts service IP
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First Istio install on eBPF-based CNI: Team installs Istio on Cilium/Calico eBPF — iptables interception doesn't work; needs explicit configuration.
  2. kind cluster with different kernel: Kind nodes may have different iptables support — REDIRECT vs TPROXY mode matters.
  3. kubeadm cluster with custom init containers: Application has multiple init containers — one of them messes up iptables rules set by istio-init.
  4. New team doesn't know about istio-init container: Sees Envoy running but doesn't check if istio-init ran successfully or even exists.
  5. Minikube with none driver — host networking bypasses all iptables rules.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy -- iptables -t nat -L -n | grep "ISTIO" Verify ISTIO_INBOUND, ISTIO_OUTPUT, ISTIO_REDIRECT chains exist and are referenced by INPUT/OUTPUT. No ISTIO chains = no interception.
kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.initContainerStatuses[?(@.name=="istio-init")].state}' istio-init must show completed=true. If missing or failed, iptables rules were never set up.
kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -E "traffic.sidecar.istio.io/(include|exclude)" Check for port exclusion annotations. Excluded ports are not intercepted — traffic bypasses Envoy.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The istio-init container failed to set up iptables rules, or it didn't run at all. Without the iptables rules, the application's network traffic goes directly to the network without being redirected to the Envoy sidecar. istio-init requires the NET_ADMIN capability to modify iptables. If istio-init exits with an error (missed capability, unsupported kernel, CNI conflict), Envoy still starts but has no traffic to proxy.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify istio-init completed successfully kubectl get pod <pod> -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.status.initContainerStatuses[?(@.name=="istio-init")].state.terminated.exitCode}' Exit code should be 0. Non-zero = iptables setup failed. Check istio-init logs for details.
2. Check iptables chains in the pod kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- iptables -t nat -L -n -v Must show ISTIO_OUTPUT referenced from OUTPUT chain with REDIRECT rules to port 15001.
3. Remove port exclusion annotations if they block critical ports Port exclusions (excludeOutboundPorts, excludeInboundPorts) bypass Envoy. Only exclude ports that genuinely should bypass the mesh.
4. For eBPF-based CNIs, switch to TPROXY mode sidecar.istio.io/interceptionMode: TPROXY TPROXY works with eBPF-based CNIs (Cilium, Calico eBPF) where REDIRECT mode doesn't capture traffic.
5. Restart pod to re-trigger istio-init kubectl delete pod <pod> -n anihpj Deleting the pod forces a full restart — istio-init runs again and sets up iptables rules.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
No iptables ISTIO rules = no traffic interception = no mesh. Period. If iptables -t nat -L doesn't show ISTIO chains, the application is not in the mesh. All Istio policies, metrics, and security are bypassed.
istio-init is just as important as istio-proxy. Check both. The init container sets up the network rules. If istio-init fails silently (exit code 0 but no rules), your debugging should start there.
eBPF-based CNIs break iptables interception. Know your CNI. Cilium eBPF and Calico eBPF don't use iptables for policy — Istio's iptables-based interception doesn't work. Use TPROXY or disable eBPF for mesh workloads.
Test interception on your 6-cluster lab: exec into a pod and check iptables. On each cluster, verify ISTIO rules exist. Try curl to another service — traffic should appear in Envoy access logs (kubectl logs -c istio-proxy).
TD9
🔬 CATEGORY 6: TS DATA PLANE — Issue TD9
Envoy Filter Chain Not Applied — Istio Config Exists but Envoy Ignores It

🔍 Symptom: An EnvoyFilter was created to add custom HTTP headers or modify the filter chain. The EnvoyFilter CR exists and is applied — kubectl get envoyfilter shows it — but the Envoy proxy doesn't pick up the changes. Traffic flows normally as if the EnvoyFilter doesn't exist. No errors in istiod, no errors in Envoy logs — the config simply isn't applied to the sidecar.

  kubectl get envoyfilter add-custom-header -n anihpj
  NAME                 AGE
  add-custom-header    10m   ← CR exists, but not applied!

  istioctl proxy-config filters anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj | grep "custom-header"
  (no custom-header filter found in Envoy config!)

  kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=istiod | grep -i "envoyfilter.*anihpj\|add-custom-header"
  (no mention of the EnvoyFilter in istiod logs!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Workload selector doesn't match any pod: spec.workloadSelector.labels must match pod labels exactly. If the selector is wrong (wrong namespace, wrong label), the filter is never applied to any Envoy.
  2. Filter insert position invalid: EnvoyFilter specifies insertPosition as FIRST, LAST, BEFORE, or AFTER a specific filter. If the referenced filter doesn't exist in the chain, the filter is silently not inserted.
  3. Filter patch context wrong: context: SIDECAR_INBOUND vs GATEWAY vs SIDECAR_OUTBOUND — if the context doesn't match the traffic direction, the filter is applied to the wrong listener and has no effect.
  4. Filter configuration schema invalid: The filter config has the right structure for EnvoyFilter CR but wrong structure for the actual Envoy filter — Envoy rejects it silently. No validation error from istioctl.
  5. Multiple EnvoyFilters with patch operations — later patch overwrites earlier: Another EnvoyFilter with the same priority or filter chain removes or overrides the first filter.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. EnvoyFilter priority conflict — another EF with same priority for same filter chain; merge behavior undefined
  2. Pilot agent not pushing updated config — xDS connection healthy but filter delta not included in LDS update
  3. Filter typed_config uses deprecated API — Envoy version doesn't support the filter's API version (v2 vs v3)
  4. AuthorizationPolicy blocks filter — authz policy executed before custom filter; request never reaches filter
  5. EnvoyFilter references a listener that doesn't exist — wrong listener name or port; filter never attached
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First EnvoyFilter attempt: Team copies a GATEWAY EnvoyFilter example but applies it to SIDECAR — wrong context; filter never applied.
  2. kind cluster with limited testing: EnvoyFilter created and applied but not verified — team assumes it works because CR accepted.
  3. kubeadm cluster with multiple teams: Team A creates EnvoyFilter; Team B's filter with same priority overrides it; neither knows about the other.
  4. New team unaware that istioctl proxy-config is needed to verify EnvoyFilter: Checks kubectl but never verifies actual Envoy config.
  5. EnvoyFilter is the most misused Istio CR — often created and never verified.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get envoyfilter -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A5 "workloadSelector\|insertPosition\|context" Verify selector matches pods, insert position targets an existing filter, and context matches traffic direction.
istioctl proxy-config listeners <pod> -n <ns> -o json | jq '.[].filterChains[].filters[].name' Shows the actual filter chain in Envoy. Check if the custom filter appears — if not, the EnvoyFilter didn't apply.
kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=istiod --tail=100 | grep -i "envoyfilter\|rejected\|invalid\|patch" istiod logs should show EnvoyFilter processing. If no mention, the filter isn't even being considered (selector mismatch).
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The EnvoyFilter's workloadSelector doesn't match any pod. An EnvoyFilter CR being accepted by Kubernetes doesn't mean it's applied to Envoy. The workloadSelector must match pod labels in the namespace. If no labels match, istiod never pushes the filter configuration to any Envoy — and there's no error generated. The filter exists as a Kubernetes resource but has zero effect in the data plane.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify workload selector matches pods kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-api The labels in workloadSelector must match the labels returned by this command. Zero matches = filter not applied.
2. Check filter insert position Ensure the named filter (BEFORE/AFTER) exists in the chain. Use istioctl proxy-config listeners to list actual filters.
3. Verify EnvoyFilter context SIDECAR_INBOUND (incoming traffic to app), SIDECAR_OUTBOUND (outgoing traffic from app), GATEWAY (ingress/egress). Must match traffic direction.
4. Confirm Envoy picks up the filter istioctl proxy-config listeners <pod> -n anihpj -o json | grep "custom-header" The custom filter name should appear in the listener's filter chain. If not, the EnvoyFilter was silently dropped.
5. Check for conflicting EnvoyFilters kubectl get envoyfilter --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -B5 -A10 "priority\|workloadSelector" Look for other EnvoyFilters affecting the same workloads. Higher priority filters override lower ones. Same priority → undefined merge.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
EnvoyFilter CR accepted ≠ EnvoyFilter applied. Always verify with istioctl proxy-config. Kubernetes accepting the CR means the schema is valid. It says nothing about whether the filter actually reaches Envoy.
Workload selector mismatch is the silent killer of EnvoyFilters. No error, no warning, no log — the filter just quietly does nothing. Always verify pod labels match before creating the EnvoyFilter.
EnvoyFilter is the "escape hatch" — use it last, verify it first. Try VirtualService, DestinationRule, or EnvoyFilter patches before raw EnvoyFilters. When you must use EnvoyFilter, verify it with istioctl proxy-config immediately.
Practice EnvoyFilter debugging on your 6-cluster lab. Create an EnvoyFilter with wrong selector → observe it's not applied → fix the selector → verify with istioctl proxy-config. This is a must-know ICA data plane scenario.
TD10
🔬 CATEGORY 6: TS DATA PLANE — Issue TD10
Envoy Log Level Not Changing — Debug Mode Can't Be Enabled

🔍 Symptom: While debugging a traffic issue, you need to increase Envoy's log level to debug or trace. You set the annotation sidecar.istio.io/logLevel: debug and restart the pod. But Envoy continues logging at info level only — the debug log level is ignored. Envoy logs show no additional detail. The proxy-level log is stuck at the default info level regardless of annotation changes.

  kubectl get pod anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -o yaml | grep "logLevel"
  sidecar.istio.io/logLevel: "debug"    ← Annotation is set!

  kubectl logs anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy --tail=10
  [2025-01-15T10:00:00.000Z] "GET /api/jobs HTTP/1.1" 200 ...
  (Only info-level access logs — no debug output!)

  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request POST 'log?level=debug'
  curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 15000: Connection refused
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Annotation on Running pod — log level changes require pod restart: The sidecar.istio.io/logLevel annotation is read at pod startup. Adding/changing it on a running pod doesn't affect the already-running Envoy — need to restart the pod.
  2. Proxy Admin Interface not enabled: Runtime log level change via pilot-agent requires the admin interface (port 15000). If it's disabled or misconfigured, pilot-agent can't change log level at runtime.
  3. Log level set on the wrong container: Annotation is on the application container's pod spec but not in the right location for the sidecar injector to read it.
  4. Mesh-wide log level override: meshConfig.defaultConfig.proxyLogLevel is set to info — this overrides individual pod annotations. Mesh-wide config wins over per-pod.
  5. Envoy component log level not changed: logLevel only changes the overall log level. Individual components (router, filter, upstream) have their own log levels — unchanged, they stay at info.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Pod annotation typo — sidecar.istio.io/loglevel (lowercase L) instead of logLevel (camelCase); annotation silently ignored
  2. Access logging is separate from log level — debug doesn't enable access logs; need accessLogFile or accessLogFormat
  3. Envoy crashed and restarted with old config — new debug-level config wasn't saved before crash
  4. Log output redirected to different location — debug logs exist but not in stdout; written to file or /dev/null
  5. Istio version bug — certain versions have known issues with runtime log level changes via annotation
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First time debugging with log level: Team adds annotation but doesn't restart pod — debug level not applied; confused why nothing changed.
  2. kind cluster with resource constraints: Debug logging at trace level generates massive logs — pod OOMKilled from log volume.
  3. kubeadm cluster with centralized logging: Debug logs sent to external aggregator — team checks kubectl logs but logs are in aggregator.
  4. New team doesn't know about meshConfig override: Changes pod annotation but meshConfig defaultConfig.proxyLogLevel overrides it.
  5. Minikube with old Istio — annotation syntax changed between versions; old syntax ignored.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep "proxyLogLevel" Mesh-wide proxyLogLevel overrides per-pod annotations. Set to info = debug annotation ignored at pod level.
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request GET 'logging' Shows current log levels for all Envoy components. Compare with the annotation. If mismatch, annotation not applied.
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request POST 'logging?level=debug' Runtime log level change via pilot-agent admin interface. This works without pod restart — test if admin interface is reachable.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The sidecar.istio.io/logLevel annotation was added to a running pod. This annotation is read by the sidecar injector at pod creation time — it doesn't take effect on running pods. Additionally, the mesh-wide meshConfig.defaultConfig.proxyLogLevel may be set to info, overriding individual pod settings. The fix requires either restarting the pod (so the injector reads the annotation) or changing the log level at runtime via the pilot-agent admin interface (GET/POST /logging).
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set annotation and restart the pod (preferred for persistent change) kubectl patch deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"annotations":{"sidecar.istio.io/logLevel":"debug"}}}}}}' Patch the deployment template. Rolling restart will create new pods with debug log level from annotation.
2. Use runtime log level change (no restart needed) kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request POST 'logging?level=debug' Changes log level immediately without pod restart. But it's lost on pod restart — use for temporary debugging.
3. Check mesh-wide proxy log level setting If meshConfig.defaultConfig.proxyLogLevel: info is set, remove it or set to debug to allow per-pod annotations to take effect.
4. Set component-specific log levels for targeted debugging kubectl exec <pod> -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request POST 'logging?router=debug&filter=trace' Only increase log level for specific Envoy components (router, filter, upstream) — avoids log volume overload.
5. Verify log level is applied kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request GET 'logging' Shows current log levels. Verify debug/trace is active for expected components before proceeding with debugging.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Runtime log level change via pilot-agent is the fastest debugging tool. No pod restart needed. pilot-agent request POST 'logging?level=debug' takes effect immediately. Use for quick debugging, then reset to info.
Debug log level on ALL components generates massive log volume. Be selective. Use component-specific levels: router=debug,filter=trace. Debug-all in production can cause OOMKills from log volume.
Annotation vs runtime: annotation persists across restarts; runtime change is temporary. Use annotation for persistent log level (deployment-wide). Use runtime for quick one-off debugging. Know when to use each.
Practice log level changes on your 6-cluster lab before the ICA exam. Set debug via annotation (restart pod), verify with pilot-agent GET logging, change at runtime, set back to info. Speed matters on the exam.
TC8
🔍 CATEGORY 5: TS CONTROL PLANE — Issue TC8
istioctl not Connected to Cluster — CLI Can't Reach API Server

🔍 Symptom: istioctl analyze, istioctl proxy-config, or istioctl x describe commands fail with "Unable to connect to the Istio control plane" or "The connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused". The operator can run kubectl get pods successfully but istioctl commands fail. The kubeconfig context is set, Kubectl works, but istioctl can't use the kubeconfig.

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system
  NAME                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  istiod-xxx               1/1     Running   0   ← Works fine!

  istioctl proxy-config routes anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj
  Error: unable to connect to Istio control plane: ... connection refused

  echo $KUBECONFIG
  /wrong/path/kubeconfig   ← Wrong kubeconfig path!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Wrong kubeconfig context: kubectl uses a different kubeconfig context than istioctl. The KUBECONFIG or ~/.kube/config may have multiple contexts — istioctl is using the wrong one.
  2. KUBECONFIG environment variable pointing to wrong file: The KUBECONFIG env var is set to a non-existent or wrong kubeconfig file. kubectl may fall back to ~/.kube/config but istioctl may not.
  3. istioctl not finding kubeconfig: If the kubeconfig is in a non-standard location and KUBECONFIG is not set, istioctl can't find it. Use --kubeconfig <path> flag.
  4. Pod ID provided with wrong namespace: istioctl proxy-config <pod> -n <ns> requires the correct namespace. Wrong namespace = pod not found = misleading "can't connect" error.
  5. istioctl version incompatible with cluster: istioctl v1.20 connecting to Istio v1.18 — API changes between versions cause connection failures. istioctl and istiod must be compatible versions.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Local firewall blocking istioctl → API server — kubectl may use cached connection; istioctl has different network behavior
  2. istioctl corrupted binary — incomplete download or wrong architecture (amd64 vs arm64)
  3. Multiple kubeconfig files merged — KUBECONFIG with colon-separated paths; wrong order
  4. istioctl uses different authentication — kubectl uses oidc-login; istioctl doesn't support the same auth plugin
  5. istioctl cached old connection info — stale discovery address; restart istioctl or clear cache
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First istioctl usage on new machine: KUBECONFIG not configured; kubectl works via cloud CLI but istioctl doesn't.
  2. kind cluster kubeconfig in non-standard location: Kind writes kubeconfig to ~/.kube/config but KUBECONFIG points elsewhere.
  3. kubeadm cluster with multiple contexts: Team manages 6 clusters (kind-cl1, kind-cl2, kubeadm) — wrong context selected for istioctl.
  4. New team confused by kubectl working but istioctl failing: Assumes "if kubectl works, istioctl should work" — doesn't check kubeconfig differences.
  5. istioctl installed via brew/choco — version mismatch with cluster istiod; connection fails silently.
🔍 What to Look At:
echo $KUBECONFIG; kubectl config current-context Verify KUBECONFIG points to a valid file and the current context matches the cluster you want to query.
istioctl version Shows local istioctl version and remote istiod version (if connected). If remote version shows "unknown", istioctl can't reach istiod.
istioctl analyze --kubeconfig ~/.kube/config Explicitly passing the kubeconfig path isolates whether it's a kubeconfig/context issue.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The KUBECONFIG environment variable is pointing to a wrong or non-existent kubeconfig file. kubectl may fall back to ~/.kube/config, but istioctl strictly uses the KUBECONFIG setting. With no valid kubeconfig, istioctl tries localhost:8080 as default (old kubectl proxy default) — which fails. The fix is to set KUBECONFIG correctly or use --kubeconfig <path> flag.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set correct KUBECONFIG or use --kubeconfig flag export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config or istioctl analyze --kubeconfig ~/.kube/config Point istioctl to the valid kubeconfig file. Test with istioctl version first.
2. Switch to correct context for multi-cluster setups kubectl config use-context kind-cka-lab On your 6-cluster lab, ensure the current context matches the target cluster before running istioctl commands.
3. Verify istioctl and istiod version compatibility istioctl version Local and remote versions should match (same major.minor). v1.20 client with v1.18 istiod may have API incompatibilities.
4. Use --context flag for contextual kubectl access istioctl analyze --context kind-cka-lab Pass the context directly to bypass KUBECONFIG issues entirely.
5. Download matching istioctl version for the cluster curl -L https://istio.io/downloadIstio | ISTIO_VERSION=<version> sh - Always use istioctl version matching the cluster's istiod version. istioctl is backward-compatible but not upward-compatible.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
istioctl version is the connectivity smoke test. Run it first. If istioctl version shows "unable to connect" for the remote version, istioctl has no connectivity to the cluster. Fix kubeconfig before anything else.
kubectl working ≠ istioctl working. Different kubeconfig resolution. kubectl merges KUBECONFIG in order and has fallbacks. istioctl uses the first value and doesn't fall back. Always set KUBECONFIG explicitly.
On the ICA exam, you get one environment. But in practice, multi-cluster is common. Know how to use --context, --kubeconfig, and KUBECONFIG to switch between your 6 clusters quickly.
Install matching istioctl version on all your lab machines. On your 6-cluster lab, ensure each cluster's matching istioctl is available. Use ksw context switcher + istioctl version check before starting any session.
TC9
🔍 CATEGORY 5: TS CONTROL PLANE — Issue TC9
Mesh Config Changes Not Propagating — istio ConfigMap Updated but No Effect

🔍 Symptom: The istio ConfigMap in istio-system namespace was updated with new mesh-level settings (access logging, tracing, or protocol detection). But the changes don't take effect on existing pods. New pods pick up the changes, but running pods use the old configuration. The mesh-wide settings like disablePolicyChecks, outboundTrafficPolicy, or enableTracing are not reflected in the Envoy proxies.

  kubectl edit cm istio -n istio-system
  # Changed enableTracing: false → true

  istioctl proxy-config bootstrap anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj | grep -i "tracing"
  "tracing": null   ← Still disabled — ConfigMap change not picked up!

  kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=istiod --tail=20 | grep "istio.*cm\|config.*update"
  (No indication istiod detected the ConfigMap change)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Mesh config changes only apply to new pods: The mesh config from the ConfigMap is pushed to Envoy proxies at pod startup. Existing proxies don't get the updated config until the pod restarts or istiod restarts.
  2. istiod not watching the ConfigMap: istiod watches the istio ConfigMap for changes. If the watch connection breaks (API server timeout, istiod restart), changes are not detected — istiod keeps the old cached config.
  3. ConfigMap YAML syntax error after edit: A typo or YAML indentation error in the ConfigMap causes istiod to reject the entire mesh config — falls back to defaults silently. The edit appears to succeed but the config is invalid.
  4. Mesh config key wrong: The config must be under data.mesh key. If the entry is under data.meshConfig or data.config, istiod doesn't read it — changes are ignored.
  5. istiod restart required for certain config changes: Some mesh config changes (like defaultConfig changes) require istiod to restart to pick up the new defaults. ConfigMap update alone doesn't trigger a restart.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. ConfigMap cached by local filesystem — istiod reads from disk cache, not from API server
  2. Multiple istiod replicas — one replica picked up change; other replicas still pushing old config
  3. Proxy-side config caching — Envoy caches bootstrap config; doesn't re-request unless LDS connection breaks
  4. Config change depends on another change — trace sampling rate also needed; trace enabled but sampling 0 = no traces
  5. RBAC change prevents istiod from reading ConfigMap — istiod SA no longer has get/list/watch on configmaps in istio-system
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First mesh config change: Team edits ConfigMap and expects immediate effect — doesn't know changes only apply to new pods.
  2. kind cluster with frequent istiod restarts: Kind restarts istiod frequently — ConfigMap watch breaks; changes lost until next istiod restart.
  3. kubeadm cluster with long-running pods: Pods run for months — mesh config changes never applied until pod restart months later.
  4. New team edits ConfigMap in wrong editor: VS Code YAML auto-format breaks the mesh config structure — YAML is valid but semantically wrong.
  5. ConfigMap diff shows change accepted but istioctl proxy-config shows old values — team confused by the discrepancy.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | yq eval Validate YAML syntax. A single indent error can cause istiod to reject the entire mesh config.
kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=istiod --tail=50 | grep -i "configmap\|mesh.*config\|invalid\|error" istiod logs should show ConfigMap reload events. No mention = istiod didn't detect the change.
istioctl proxy-config bootstrap <pod> -n <ns> -o json | grep "<config-key>" Compare the proxy's actual config with the ConfigMap values. Mismatch = change not propagated.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Mesh config changes from the istio ConfigMap are pushed to Envoy proxies at pod startup only. Existing pods retain the old mesh config until they restart. Unlike xDS changes (which are pushed dynamically), mesh-level bootstrap config is static — set once at proxy bootstrap. The ConfigMap change is valid and istiod picks it up, but it only affects NEW proxies. For existing pods, a rollout restart or individual pod restart is required.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Restart pods to pick up new mesh config kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj Rolling restart creates new pods that get the updated mesh config from istiod. Zero-downtime propagation.
2. Validate ConfigMap YAML before applying kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | yq eval YAML syntax error = istiod silently rejects the config. Always validate after editing.
3. Verify istiod detected the change kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=istiod --since=5m | grep -i "configmap\|mesh.*update" istiod should log ConfigMap change detection. No log = istiod didn't detect the change (watch broken).
4. Restart istiod if config change doesn't propagate kubectl rollout restart deploy istiod -n istio-system Forces istiod to re-read the ConfigMap. All connected proxies get new config on reconnection.
5. Use kubectl apply with prepared YAML instead of kubectl edit kubectl edit can introduce formatting errors. Prepare the full ConfigMap YAML and use kubectl apply for safer changes.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
Mesh config = bootstrap config = requires pod restart. xDS = dynamic = takes effect immediately. Know the difference. VirtualService changes are dynamic (xDS). Mesh config changes (tracing, access logging, protocol detection) require pod restart.
Always validate ConfigMap YAML after kubectl edit. A single cat ~ mistake can silently invalidate the config. Use yq or istioctl validate to verify syntax.
istiod restart is the nuclear option — but sometimes necessary. If ConfigMap changes don't propagate after pod restarts, restart istiod. It forces a fresh read of the ConfigMap and re-pushes to all proxies.
Test mesh config propagation on your 6-cluster lab. Change enableTracing in ConfigMap → restart anihpj-api → verify with istioctl proxy-config bootstrap. This is a key ICA control plane scenario.
TC10
🔍 CATEGORY 5: TS CONTROL PLANE — Issue TC10
Gateway Pod Not Scheduling — istio-ingressgateway Pending Indefinitely

🔍 Symptom: The istio-ingressgateway deployment shows 0/1 Ready pods — the pod is stuck in Pending state. After Istio installation, the gateway should be available to handle ingress traffic, but it never starts. kubectl describe pod shows scheduling failures: insufficient CPU/memory, node taints/tolerations, or node affinity conflicts. No external traffic can reach the mesh.

  kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway
  NAME                                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  istio-ingressgateway-xxx               0/1     Pending   0

  kubectl describe pod istio-ingressgateway-xxx -n istio-system | grep -A10 "Events:"
  Warning  FailedScheduling  0/3 nodes available: 1 node(s) had taint {...},
    2 Insufficient cpu, 3 Insufficient memory
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Insufficient cluster resources: The default istio-ingressgateway deployment requests 2GB memory and 2 CPU. On resource-constrained clusters (kind, minikube, small kubeadm), there aren't enough resources — pod stays Pending.
  2. Node taints not tolerated: Nodes have taints (e.g., node-role.kubernetes.io/master:NoSchedule) and the gateway deployment doesn't have matching tolerations. No nodes available for scheduling.
  3. Node affinity/anti-affinity conflicts: The gateway has node affinity rules that don't match any node labels, or pod anti-affinity prevents co-location with other pods.
  4. PVC or PV not available for gateway: If the gateway uses persistent storage (for SSL certificates) and the PVC can't be bound, the pod stays Pending.
  5. Single-node cluster with control-plane taint: On single-node clusters (kind, minikube), the only node has a control-plane taint. Without proper tolerations, the gateway can't schedule.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Image pull failure — pod stuck in Pending/ContainerCreating because gateway image can't be pulled
  2. ServiceAccount missing or insufficient RBAC — gateway SA doesn't have permissions to mount secrets
  3. PodSecurityPolicy/PodSecurity admission denies gateway pod — security context violations prevent scheduling
  4. CNI not ready — network plugin not initialized on node; pod can't get IP address
  5. Topology spread constraints prevent scheduling — required zone/region labels don't exist on nodes
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First Istio install on kind: Kind cluster with 4GB RAM — gateway requests 2GB; insufficient resources; pod stays Pending.
  2. kubeadm cluster with tainted nodes: Production nodes are tainted for specific workloads — gateway can't schedule without tolerations.
  3. New team doesn't check Events in describe pod: Sees Pending but doesn't read Events — the exact reason for scheduling failure is right there.
  4. Minikube with Docker driver — single node with limited resources; gateway competes with core services.
  5. Istio demo profile vs default profile — demo installs lighter gateway; default installs resource-heavy gateway.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <gateway-pod> -n istio-system | tail -30 The Events section explains exactly why the pod can't schedule — taints, resource shortages, affinity violations, or PVC issues.
kubectl top nodes Shows current node resource usage. If all nodes are at capacity, the gateway can't schedule. Consider reducing resource requests.
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.taints}' List all node taints. The gateway deployment must have matching tolerations for every taint on candidate nodes.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The cluster has insufficient resources or node taints prevent the gateway pod from scheduling. The default istio-ingressgateway deployment requests significant resources (2 CPU, 2GB memory) and has limited tolerations. On resource-constrained clusters (kind, minikube) or clusters with tainted nodes, the gateway can't find a suitable node. The fix involves reducing resource requests, adding tolerations, or modifying node affinity to match available nodes.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Check Events in pod description for the exact reason kubectl describe pod <gateway-pod> -n istio-system The Events tell you exactly why: taint, resource shortage, affinity, or PVC. Don't guess — read Events first.
2. Reduce resource requests for resource-constrained clusters Patch the deployment to lower CPU/memory requests: resources: {requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}}. On kind/minikube, reduce significantly.
3. Add tolerations for tainted nodes If the only available nodes have taints, add tolerations: [{operator: Exists}] to the gateway deployment to allow scheduling on any node.
4. Verify node affinity matches available nodes Check node labels and gateway affinity rules. If the gateway requires node-type: gateway but no nodes have this label, add the label or remove the affinity.
5. Use Istio demo profile for learning environments istioctl install --set profile=demo -y Demo profile uses lighter resource requirements and adds tolerations for single-node clusters. Better for kind/minikube.
💡 Personal Mesh Advice:
