kubectl describe pod is your scheduling troubleshooter. Read Events FIRST. Every scheduling failure reason is in the Events section. Taints, resources, affinity, PVC — it tells you exactly what to fix.
On kind and minikube, always use demo profile or reduce resource requests. Default gateway requests 2 CPU/2GB. Kind with 4GB total can't accommodate this alongside istiod and application pods.
Single-node clusters need tolerations for control-plane taint. node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule blocks all pods without tolerations. The gateway must tolerate this on single-node setups.
Practice gateway troubleshooting on your 6-cluster lab. On kind-cka-lab, deliberately reduce gateway resources too low → observe OOM → increase. On kubeadm, add a taint → observe Pending → add toleration. Know the recovery flows cold for the ICA exam.

📦 Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Lab ScenariosS1-S20

🟢 anihpj/jobpost — Full-Stack Django + PostgreSQL on Istio Service Mesh

What is anihpj/jobpost? A Django-based job board application where employers post jobs and applicants apply. It consists of a Django web server, PostgreSQL database, and Redis cache — all running on the Istio service mesh. Each scenario deploys a part of this app with intentional mesh misconfigurations — your job is to find and fix them. ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Check the cluster requirement at the top of each scenario before applying! All clusters have Istio pre-installed.

S1
🧪 SCENARIO S1 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Injection Debug

Deploy anihpj Web — Fix Missing Istio Sidecar (1/1 Instead of 2/2)

The Problem: You deploy the anihpj/jobpost Django web frontend in the anihpj namespace. The pod starts but shows 1/1 READY instead of the expected 2/2 — the Envoy sidecar (istio-proxy) was never injected. mTLS fails, metrics don't appear in Prometheus, and Kiali shows the service outside the mesh. The namespace is missing the istio-injection=enabled label — the MutatingWebhook never fires for this namespace. Your job: find why the sidecar is missing and fix it so all pods get injected.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Dedicated Istio mesh practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj Web Frontend (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is a Django job board app running on Istio service mesh. Employers post jobs, applicants apply. The Django web frontend serves the UI and REST API. It MUST have the Envoy sidecar injected to participate in the mesh — without it: no mTLS, no traffic management, no observability. The web pod starts as 1/1 — the sidecar was never injected because the namespace label is missing.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S1): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns anihpj (BUG: no label!)
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml         ← Django web frontend (3 replicas)
├── 02-web-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
└── 03-gateway-virtualservice.yaml ← Istio Gateway + VirtualService for ingress
BASH — Create Namespace + Deploy anihpj Web (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S1: Sidecar Not Injected — Namespace Missing Label
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE (BUG: deliberately WITHOUT the injection label)
kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 2. DEPLOY THE DJANGO WEB FRONTEND
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
    version: v1
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-web
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        env:
        - name: DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE
          value: anihpj.settings
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          value: postgres://anihpj:secret123@anihpj-db:5432/jobpost
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 80
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: anihpj-gateway
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 80
      name: http
      protocol: HTTP
    hosts:
    - "jobpost.com"
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - "jobpost.com"
  gateways:
  - anihpj-gateway
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-web
        port:
          number: 80
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n anihpj
✗2. All pods show 1/1 READY instead of expected 2/2 — no istio-proxy sidecar injected!
✗3. Check proxy status: istioctl proxy-status → No anihpj-web proxies listed!
✗4. mTLS between services fails — the web pod has no Envoy to handle mTLS. Kiali shows web service outside the mesh.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check namespace labels: kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels
→ LABELS: kubernetes.io/metadata.name=anihpj (NO istio-injection!)
2Check the MutatingWebhookConfiguration: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector -o yaml | grep -A5 namespaceSelector
→ namespaceSelector: matchLabels: istio-injection: enabled (webhook only fires for labeled namespaces!)
3Check if istiod is running: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod
→ istiod is Running ✅ (control plane is healthy — it's the namespace label that's missing)
4Describe a pod to confirm no sidecar: kubectl describe pod -n anihpj anihpj-web-xxx | grep -A2 Containers
→ Containers: anihpj-web (only 1 container — no istio-proxy!)
5Root cause: Namespace "anihpj" is missing the label istio-injection=enabled. The MutatingWebhook only fires for namespaces with this label — without it, pods are created without the Envoy sidecar.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod shows 1/1 → Sidecar not injected
②
Check ns label → istio-injection MISSING
③
Check webhook nsSelector → requires label
④
Label namespace → istio-injection=enabled
⑤
Rollout restart → new pods get sidecars → 2/2 ✅

Tenet: On Istio, the sidecar is NEVER injected automatically — a mutating admission webhook (istio-sidecar-injector) must be triggered. The webhook's namespaceSelector only matches namespaces with the label istio-injection: enabled. Without this label, the webhook never fires and pods are created without the istio-proxy container. Existing pods are NEVER retroactively injected — you must restart them after labeling the namespace. This is the #1 "my app isn't in the mesh" issue on the ICA exam.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-x 1/1 Running 0 3m anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-y 1/1 Running 0 3m anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-z 1/1 Running 0 3m
$ kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels NAME STATUS AGE LABELS anihpj Active 5m kubernetes.io/metadata.name=anihpj ← MISSING: istio-injection=enabled!
$ istioctl proxy-status NAME CDS LDS EDS RDS istio-ingressgateway-xxx SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED ← No anihpj-web proxies listed! They are NOT in the mesh.
$ kubectl describe pod anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-x -n anihpj | grep -A3 Containers Containers: anihpj-web: Container ID: containerd://abc123 Image: nginx:alpine ← Only 1 container. No istio-proxy!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection=enabled namespace/anihpj labeled
$ kubectl rollout restart deploy anihpj-web -n anihpj deployment.apps/anihpj-web restarted
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-web-9f3g7h6j-k 2/2 Running 0 45s anihpj-web-9f3g7h6j-m 2/2 Running 0 40s anihpj-web-9f3g7h6j-n 2/2 Running 0 35s ✅ 2/2 READY — Sidecar injected!
$ istioctl proxy-status NAME CDS LDS EDS RDS anihpj-web-9f3g7h6j-k.anihpj SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED anihpj-web-9f3g7h6j-m.anihpj SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED anihpj-web-9f3g7h6j-n.anihpj SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED ✅ All proxies SYNCED — web is now IN the mesh!
🔧
BASH — Label namespace + restart (existing pods never get sidecars retroactively) 
# Step 1: Label the namespace for Istio sidecar injection
# The MutatingWebhook only fires for namespaces with this label
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# Step 2: Verify the label was applied
kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels | grep istio-injection

# Step 3: Restart ALL deployments in the namespace
# ⚠️ Existing pods NEVER get sidecars retroactively — must be recreated!
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj

# Step 4: Wait for rollouts to complete
kubectl rollout status deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 5: Verify sidecars are now injected (2/2 READY)
kubectl get pods -n anihpj

# Step 6: Verify Envoys are connected to the control plane
istioctl proxy-status

# Optional: Check the sidecar container is present
kubectl get pod -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[*].name}'
✓

✅ Verify — Sidecars Are Injected And Mesh Is Operational

After labeling the namespace with istio-injection=enabled and restarting the deployment, all new pods are created with the istio-proxy sidecar injected by the MutatingWebhook. kubectl get pods -n anihpj shows 2/2 READY for all replicas, and istioctl proxy-status confirms all Envoy proxies are SYNCED across CDS, LDS, EDS, and RDS. The web frontend is now fully participating in the Istio service mesh — mTLS works, metrics flow to Prometheus, and Kiali shows the service inside the mesh.

💡 Key takeaway: Sidecar injection is triggered by the istio-sidecar-injector MutatingWebhook only at pod creation time. The webhook's namespaceSelector matches namespaces with istio-injection=enabled. Without this label, the webhook silently skips the namespace. Existing pods are never retroactively injected — label first, then rollout restart. Always verify with istioctl proxy-status after injection.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside (pods, services, gateway, virtualservice)
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Remove the injection label from the namespace (if not deleting the namespace)
# kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection-

# Verify all resources are gone
kubectl get all -n anihpj
S2
🧪 SCENARIO S2 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Init Debug

Deploy anihpj API — Fix istio-init CrashLoopBackOff (Pod Security Blocking NET_ADMIN)

The Problem: You labeled the anihpj namespace with istio-injection=enabled and deployed the Django REST API backend. But the pods are stuck in Init:CrashLoopBackOff. The istio-init container fails because the cluster enforces Pod Security Admission Restricted profile — which blocks the NET_ADMIN capability needed by istio-init to configure iptables. The application container never starts. The error: "iptables: Permission denied (you must be root)" appears in istio-init logs. Without istio-cni, sidecar injection on PSA-restricted clusters is impossible.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Dev cluster with PSA Restricted enabled
1

📋 Deploy anihpj API With PSA Restricted (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is a Django job board running on Istio. The API backend (anihpj-api) serves REST endpoints at /api/jobs, /api/applications. It MUST have the Envoy sidecar for mTLS, metrics, and traffic routing. But the minikube cluster enforces Pod Security Admission Restricted — the NET_ADMIN capability istio-init needs is BLOCKED. The API pods are stuck in Init:CrashLoopBackOff — the entire API layer is DOWN.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S2): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml           ← ns anihpj with PSA Restricted label
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml      ← Django REST API deployment (2 replicas)
├── 02-api-service.yaml         ← ClusterIP Service (port 8080)
└── 03-api-virtualservice.yaml  ← Istio VirtualService for /api routes
BASH — Create PSA-Restricted Namespace + Deploy API (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S2: istio-init Crash — Pod Security Blocks NET_ADMIN
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE WITH PSA RESTRICTED (BUG: Blocks NET_ADMIN for istio-init!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  labels:
    istio-injection: enabled
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
EOF

# 2. DEPLOY THE DJANGO REST API BACKEND
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-api
    version: v1
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        env:
        - name: DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE
          value: anihpj.settings
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          value: postgres://anihpj:secret123@anihpj-db:5432/jobpost
      # BUG: No securityContext with NET_ADMIN — istio-init will be BLOCKED by PSA Restricted!
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-api
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-api
  ports:
  - name: http-api
    port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - anihpj-api
  http:
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /api
    route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api
        port:

⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n anihpj
✗2. All pods stuck in Init:CrashLoopBackOff — istio-init container keeps failing!
✗3. Check istio-init logs: kubectl logs -n anihpj anihpj-api-xxx -c istio-init → "iptables: Permission denied (you must be root)"
✗4. The application container never starts — init containers must complete first. API is completely DOWN. No mTLS, no metrics, no routing.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check init container status: kubectl describe pod -n anihpj anihpj-api-xxx | grep -A10 "istio-init"
→ State: Waiting (CrashLoopBackOff), Reason: Error, Exit Code: 1
2Read istio-init logs: kubectl logs -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api -c istio-init
→ "iptables: Permission denied (you must be root)" — NET_ADMIN capability blocked!
3Check Pod Security labels on namespace: kubectl get ns anihpj -o yaml | grep pod-security
→ enforce: restricted — PSA Restricted blocks NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN, privileged containers!
4Verify istio-cni is NOT installed: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep istio-cni
→ No istio-cni pods found! Without CNI plugin, istio-init MUST have NET_ADMIN.
5Root cause: Pod Security Admission Restricted profile blocks NET_ADMIN capability needed by istio-init. Without istio-cni (which handles traffic capture at the node level), sidecar injection is impossible on PSA-restricted clusters. The fix is to install istio-cni OR relax the PSA enforcement.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod Init:CrashLoopBackOff → Check init container
②
istio-init logs → Permission denied (iptables)
③
Check PSA labels → enforce: restricted
④
PSA Restricted blocks NET_ADMIN → need istio-cni
⑤
Install istio-cni → restart pods → Init completes → API ready ✅

Tenet: Pod Security Admission (PSA) Restricted is the Kubernetes replacement for PodSecurityPolicy. It blocks ALL privileged operations including NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN, and running as root. istio-init requires NET_ADMIN to configure iptables for traffic capture — PSA Restricted silently blocks this. The solution is istio-cni: a DaemonSet that runs on every node and handles traffic capture at the node level (before the pod network namespace is created), eliminating the need for NET_ADMIN in the pod. Newer Istio versions default to istio-cni for this exact reason. NEVER disable PSA — install istio-cni instead.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-api-6d4f8c9b-x 0/2 Init:CrashLoopBackOff 5 (30s ago) 3m anihpj-api-6d4f8c9b-y 0/2 Init:Error 4 (45s ago) 3m
$ kubectl logs -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api -c istio-init iptables: Permission denied (you must be root) iptables-restore: line 12 failed Error: iptables setup failed exit status 1
$ kubectl get ns anihpj -o yaml | grep pod-security pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted ← PSA Restricted blocks NET_ADMIN!
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep istio-cni ← No output — istio-cni is NOT installed!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ istioctl install --set components.cni.enabled=true --set profile=default -y ✔ Istio core installed ✔ Istiod installed ✔ CNI installed ✔ Ingress gateways installed ✔ Installation complete
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep istio-cni istio-cni-node-xxxxx 1/1 Running 0 30s istio-cni-node-yyyyy 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ istio-cni DaemonSet is now running!
$ kubectl delete pod -n anihpj --all && kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-api-9f3g7h6j-k 2/2 Running 0 45s anihpj-api-9f3g7h6j-m 2/2 Running 0 40s ✅ 2/2 READY — istio-init completed successfully with CNI!
🔧
BASH — Install istio-cni (handles traffic capture at node level, no NET_ADMIN needed) 
# Step 1: Install istio-cni component (DaemonSet on every node)
# This handles iptables rules at the NODE level — pods don't need NET_ADMIN
istioctl install --set components.cni.enabled=true --set profile=default -y

# Step 2: Verify CNI pods are running on each node
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=istio-cni-node

# Step 3: Check CNI DaemonSet is deployed
kubectl get daemonset -n kube-system istio-cni-node

# Step 4: Delete existing pods so they restart with CNI support
kubectl delete pods --all -n anihpj

# Step 5: Watch pods come up (istio-init should complete successfully now)
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w

# Step 6: Verify sidecars are injected and connected
istioctl proxy-status | grep anihpj
✓

✅ Verify — istio-init Completes and API Pods Are Running

After installing istio-cni, traffic capture is handled by the CNI DaemonSet at the node level — istio-init no longer needs NET_ADMIN in the pod's security context. The PSA Restricted profile no longer blocks the init container because istio-cni configures the pod's network namespace before the container starts. Pods now show 2/2 READY — the API is fully operational inside the mesh with mTLS, metrics, and routing.

💡 Key takeaway: On PSA-restricted clusters, istio-cni is REQUIRED for sidecar injection. The CNI plugin runs as a privileged DaemonSet on each node and handles iptables while creating the pod's network namespace — the pod itself never needs NET_ADMIN. Starting with Istio 1.20+, istio-cni is the default installation mode. Never disable PSA enforcement — use istio-cni instead. Also check for istio-cni DaemonSet logs if injection still fails after installation.

kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Remove the PSA label from namespace (if reusing the namespace)
# kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-

# Verify all resources are gone
kubectl get all -n anihpj

🧪 SCENARIO S3 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Profile Debug

Route API to External Payment Gateway — Fix Missing Egress Gateway on demo Profile

The Problem: You deployed Istio using the demo profile for quick testing. Now production requires the anihpj-api to call an external payment gateway (api.payment-gateway.com) through an Egress Gateway for security and auditing. You create a ServiceEntry and configure the Egress Gateway, but traffic to the external service fails with 503. The issue: the demo profile does NOT include the Egress Gateway component — it's a minimal profile for demos only. The Gateway resource references an egress gateway that doesn't exist.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1) — Multi-cluster mesh node 1
1

📋 Install Istio demo Profile + Configure Egress (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost processes payments through api.payment-gateway.com. For security compliance, ALL external traffic must exit through the Istio Egress Gateway (for auditing, TLS origination, and monitoring). The ops team configured ServiceEntry + Gateway + VirtualService for egress, but the API calls to the payment gateway fail with 503. The demo profile was used for initial setup and doesn't include egress gateway pods — traffic has nowhere to go.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S3): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Django API (calls payment gateway)
├── 02-serviceentry.yaml           ← ServiceEntry for api.payment-gateway.com
├── 03-egress-gateway.yaml         ← Gateway for egress (BUG: no egress pods!)
├── 04-egress-virtualservice.yaml  ← VirtualService routing to external host
└── 05-destinationrule.yaml        ← DestinationRule for TLS origination
BASH — Install demo profile + Deploy app + Configure Egress (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S3: Egress Gateway Missing — demo Profile Incomplete
# ============================================

# 1. INSTALL ISTIO WITH demo PROFILE (BUG: demo = minimal, no egress gateway!)
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y

# 2. CREATE NAMESPACE AND DEPLOY API
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-api
        image: curlimages/curl
        command: ["sleep", "3600"]
EOF

# 3. CONFIGURE SERVICEENTRY FOR EXTERNAL PAYMENT GATEWAY
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: payment-gateway
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.payment-gateway.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
EOF

# 4. CREATE EGRESS GATEWAY (BUG: references gateway that doesn't exist!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: istio-egressgateway
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  selector:
    istio: egressgateway    # ❌ BUG! No pods with this label in demo profile!
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
    hosts:
    - api.payment-gateway.com
    tls:
      mode: PASSTHROUGH
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: egress-payment-gw
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.payment-gateway.com
  gateways:
  - istio-egressgateway
  - mesh
  http:
  - match:
    - gateways:
      - mesh
      port: 443
    route:
    - destination:
        host: istio-egressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local
        port:
          number: 443
  - match:
    - gateways:
      - istio-egressgateway
      port: 443
    route:
    - destination:
        host: api.payment-gateway.com
        port:
          number: 443
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: egress-payment-gw-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: istio-egressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    tls:
      mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Test external call: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api -- curl -kv https://api.payment-gateway.com
✗2. Returns HTTP 503 Service Unavailable — the egress gateway is unreachable!
✗3. Check Gateway pods: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway → No resources found!
✗4. Payment processing is completely DOWN — the job board can't process any transactions!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check installed Istio profile: istioctl profile dump
→ Shows 'demo' profile — egressGateways: enabled: false!
2Check egress gateway deployment: kubectl get deploy -n istio-system | grep egress
→ No egress gateway deployment found — demo profile doesn't deploy it!
3Check Gateway resource status: kubectl describe gateway istio-egressgateway -n istio-system
→ Gateway CR exists but no pods match selector istio=egressgateway
4List available Istio profiles: istioctl profile list
→ demo, minimal, default, empty, preview, external, ambient — 'default' has egress gateway!
5Root cause: Istio was installed with 'demo' profile which has egress gateway DISABLED. The Gateway CR references pods with label istio=egressgateway but no such pods exist. Must upgrade to 'default' profile or explicitly enable the egress gateway component.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
External call fails 503 → Check egress path
②
kubectl get pods → No egressgateway pods
③
istioctl profile dump → demo profile
④
demo disables egress → need default profile
⑤
Upgrade to default → egress pods created → 200 OK ✅

Tenet: Istio profiles define which components are installed. The demo profile is for quick demos — it includes ingress gateway and istiod but NOT the egress gateway. For production, always use default profile (includes both ingress and egress gateways) or explicitly enable components. The ICA exam frequently tests profile differences — know that demo = minimal (no egress), default = production (ingress + egress), minimal = just istiod. Always verify installed components with istioctl profile dump before configuring Gateways.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://api.payment-gateway.com 503
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway No resources found in istio-system namespace. ← Egress gateway pods do NOT exist!
$ kubectl get deploy -n istio-system | grep egress ← No output — egress gateway deployment was never created!
$ istioctl profile dump | grep -A5 egressGateways egressGateways: - enabled: false ← DISABLED in demo profile! name: istio-egressgateway
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ istioctl install --set profile=default -y ✔ Istio core installed ✔ Istiod installed ✔ Ingress gateways installed ✔ Egress gateways installed ← NOW included! ✔ Installation complete
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE istio-egressgateway-7d8f9c5b-x 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ Egress gateway is now Running!
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://api.payment-gateway.com 200 ✅ Payment gateway reachable through egress!
🔧
BASH — Upgrade from demo to default profile (adds egress gateway) 
# Step 1: Upgrade Istio from demo to default profile
# istioctl install preserves existing config and adds missing components
istioctl install --set profile=default -y

# Step 2: Verify egress gateway pods are running
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway

# Step 3: Verify the Gateway resource now has matching pods
kubectl get gateway istio-egressgateway -n istio-system

# Step 4: Restart the API pod to pick up new egress config
kubectl rollout restart deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj

# Step 5: Test external connectivity through egress gateway
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api -- curl -sk https://api.payment-gateway.com/health

# Step 6: Check egress gateway logs for traffic
kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway --tail=20
✓

✅ Verify — Egress Gateway Routes External Traffic Correctly

After upgrading to the default profile, the egress gateway deployment is created with pods matching the istio=egressgateway selector. The Gateway CR now binds to actual pods. Traffic flows: anihpj-api → mesh → istio-egressgateway → api.payment-gateway.com. All external traffic is audited, TLS-originated at the egress, and monitored through Kiali. The payment gateway returns HTTP 200 — the job board can now process payments securely.

💡 Key takeaway: Istio profiles control component enablement. demo = ingress only, default = ingress + egress, minimal = istiod only. Always check installed components with istioctl profile dump before assuming a Gateway component exists. You can also enable individual components without changing profiles: istioctl install --set components.egressGateways[0].enabled=true.

Canary Upgrade Gone Wrong — Sidecars Stuck on Old Revision After istiod Upgrade

The Problem: The ops team performed a canary upgrade of istiod from revision 1-18 to 1-20. The new istiod-1-20 is Running and healthy. But pods in the anihpj namespace are still connected to the OLD istiod-1-18 — they show STALE xDS configuration and aren't picking up new VirtualService changes. The namespace is labeled with istio.io/rev: 1-18 instead of 1-20. The MutatingWebhook injects sidecars configured to connect to the old revision, and existing pods never migrate.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 4 (kind-cl2) — Multi-cluster mesh node 2
1

📋 Canary Upgrade istiod + Deploy App on Old Revision (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is running on Istio 1.18. The platform team performs a canary upgrade: deploy new istiod-1-20 alongside istiod-1-18, then migrate namespaces one-by-one. They deploy anihpj-db (PostgreSQL StatefulSet) into the namespace — but forgot to update the revision label. The database pods get sidecars configured for istiod-1-18. When istiod-1-18 is eventually decommissioned, the database sidecars go STALE — xDS stops updating, new mTLS certs can't be fetched, and the database becomes unreachable. The entire job board loses its database.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S4): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml           ← ns with OLD revision label (BUG!)
├── 01-db-statefulset.yaml      ← PostgreSQL StatefulSet
├── 02-db-service.yaml          ← ClusterIP Service (port 5432)
└── 03-peerauthentication.yaml  ← STRICT mTLS for database
BASH — Canary upgrade + Deploy DB on old revision (BUG inside)

# SCENARIO S4: Canary Upgrade — Namespace Still on Old Revision
# ============================================

# 1. SIMULATE CANARY UPGRADE: Deploy new istiod revision alongside old

# 2. CREATE NAMESPACE WITH OLD REVISION LABEL (BUG: should be 1-20!)

  labels:

    istio-injection: enabled
EOF

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check proxy status: istioctl proxy-status | grep anihpj
✗2. Database sidecar shows istiod-1-18 as control plane — NOT the new 1-20!
✗3. Check namespace revision label: kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels | grep istio.io/rev → 1-18 (WRONG!)
✗4. If istiod-1-18 is decommissioned, the database sidecar goes STALE — mTLS certs expire, VirtualService changes stop applying, the database becomes unreachable.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check both istiod revisions: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod
→ istiod-1-18 Running, istiod-1-20 Running — canary in progress!
2Check which revision the sidecar uses: istioctl proxy-config bootstrap anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj | grep discoveryAddress
→ discoveryAddress: istiod-1-18.istio-system.svc:15012 (OLD revision!)
3Check namespace revision label: kubectl get ns anihpj -o yaml | grep istio.io/rev
→ istio.io/rev: 1-18 — BUG! Should be 1-20 after canary migration!
4Check MutatingWebhook revision selector: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration -o yaml | grep -B5 -A10 "istio.io/rev"
→ Webhook uses namespace's istio.io/rev label to select which istiod to inject!
5Root cause: During canary upgrade, the namespace label istio.io/rev was NOT updated from 1-18 to 1-20. Sidecars connect to istiod-1-18, and when that revision is decommissioned, all sidecars in this namespace lose their control plane — xDS stops, mTLS certs expire, and the mesh breaks for this namespace.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Canary upgrade → two istiod revisions running
②
Check proxy-status → sidecar on istiod-1-18
③
Check ns label → istio.io/rev: 1-18
④
Webhook uses rev label for injection config
⑤
Update label → restart pods → 1-20 ✅

Tenet: Canary upgrades of istiod use revision labels to control which sidecars connect to which control plane. The namespace label istio.io/rev: <rev> tells the MutatingWebhook which istiod revision to configure injected sidecars for. During canary migration, you update this label AND restart pods. Forgetting either step leaves sidecars on the old revision — when the old istiod is removed, those sidecars become orphaned. This is the #1 canary upgrade failure on the ICA exam.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ istioctl proxy-status | grep anihpj anihpj-db-0.anihpj istiod-1-18 SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED ← Connected to OLD istiod-1-18, not the new 1-20!
$ kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels | grep istio anihpj Active 10m istio-injection=enabled,istio.io/rev=1-18,kubernetes.io/metadata.name=anihpj ← REVISION IS 1-18! Should be 1-20!
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE istiod-1-18-7d8f9c5b-x 1/1 Running 0 2d istiod-1-20-9f3g7h6j-y 1/1 Running 0 10m ← Both revisions running — canary in progress
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl label ns anihpj istio.io/rev=1-20 --overwrite namespace/anihpj labeled
$ kubectl rollout restart statefulset anihpj-db -n anihpj statefulset.apps/anihpj-db restarted
$ istioctl proxy-status | grep anihpj anihpj-db-0.anihpj istiod-1-20 SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED ✅ Now connected to NEW istiod-1-20!
🔧
BASH — Migrate namespace to new istiod revision 
# Step 1: Update namespace revision label to new istiod
kubectl label ns anihpj istio.io/rev=1-20 --overwrite

# Step 2: Verify the label was updated
kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels | grep istio.io/rev

# Step 3: Restart ALL workloads to pick up new sidecar config
# ⚠️ Existing pods stay on old revision until restarted!
kubectl rollout restart statefulset anihpj-db -n anihpj

# Step 4: Wait for pods to be ready with new sidecars
kubectl rollout status statefulset anihpj-db -n anihpj

# Step 5: Verify sidecars now connect to new istiod revision
istioctl proxy-status | grep anihpj

# Step 6: Once all namespaces are migrated, decommission old istiod
# kubectl delete istiooperator installed-state-1-18 -n istio-system
✓

✅ Verify — Database Sidecar Connected to New istiod Revision

After updating the namespace label to istio.io/rev: 1-20 and restarting the StatefulSet, the new database pod gets a sidecar configured to connect to istiod-1-20. istioctl proxy-status confirms the sidecar is SYNCED on the new revision. The database continues serving traffic with updated mTLS certificates, VirtualService changes propagate correctly, and the mesh remains operational even after istiod-1-18 is decommissioned.

💡 Key takeaway: Canary upgrades in Istio use revision-based sidecar injection. Each istiod revision is a separate deployment with its own service (e.g., istiod-1-20). Namespaces are labeled with the revision they should use. Both the label update AND pod restart are required for migration. The MutatingWebhook uses istio.io/rev to configure the sidecar's discovery address. Without updating the label, new pods still connect to the old revision.

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Deploy Full Stack + Delete Webhook (CONTAINS THE BUG)

After the cleanup, they deploy the full application stack: web frontend, API backend, and PostgreSQL database. Every pod starts as 1/1 — no sidecars anywhere. ⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check ALL pods: kubectl get pods -n anihpj
✗2. Every pod shows 1/1 — web (3×), api (2×), db (1×) — NO sidecar in any pod!
✗3. Check webhook: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector → NOT FOUND!
✗4. NO errors anywhere — istiod is Running, namespace is labeled, pods are healthy. But there is ZERO mesh functionality: no mTLS, no routing rules, no metrics.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check namespace label: kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels | grep istio-injection
→ istio-injection=enabled ✅ (label is correct — this is NOT the issue!)
2Check istiod health: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod
→ istiod Running ✅ (control plane is healthy — this is NOT the issue!)
3Check MutatingWebhookConfiguration EXISTS: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration | grep istio
→ No resources found! The webhook was DELETED!
4Check API server admission chain: Without the webhook, the API server NEVER calls istiod for pod creation — pods are created without sidecars with ZERO errors or warnings.
→ Kubernetes doesn't know the webhook is supposed to exist — silent failure!
5Root cause: The istio-sidecar-injector MutatingWebhookConfiguration was accidentally deleted. Without this webhook, the Kubernetes API server never intercepts pod creation to inject the sidecar. All pods are created normally — without istio-proxy. This is the most dangerous Istio failure because there are ZERO errors: istiod is healthy, namespaces are labeled, pods are running — but the mesh simply doesn't exist.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
All pods 1/1 → No sidecar ANYWHERE
②
ns label correct + istiod healthy → Check webhook
③
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration → MISSING!
④
Webhook deleted → API server never calls istiod
⑤
Reinstall webhook → Restart pods → 2/2 ✅

Tenet: The istio-sidecar-injector MutatingWebhookConfiguration is the SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE for sidecar injection. It tells the Kubernetes API server: "when a pod is created in a namespace with istio-injection: enabled, call istiod to inject the sidecar." Without it, the API server NEVER calls istiod. No errors are generated because the webhook simply isn't in the admission chain. This is the hardest Istio failure to detect because everything looks healthy — you only notice when mesh features don't work. Always verify the webhook exists as part of cluster health checks: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-api-6d4f8c9b-x 1/1 Running 0 3m anihpj-api-6d4f8c9b-y 1/1 Running 0 3m anihpj-db-0 1/1 Running 0 3m anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-x 1/1 Running 0 3m anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-y 1/1 Running 0 3m anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-z 1/1 Running 0 3m ← ALL pods 1/1 — NO sidecar injected ANYWHERE!
$ kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration | grep istio ← No resources found! Webhook was deleted!
$ kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels | grep istio-injection anihpj Active 10m istio-injection=enabled ← Namespace label is CORRECT — webhook is the missing piece!
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE istiod-7d8f9c5b-x 1/1 Running 0 2d ← istiod is healthy — but the API server never calls it for injection!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ istioctl install --set profile=default -y ✔ Istio core installed ✔ Istiod installed ✔ Ingress gateways installed ✔ Egress gateways installed ✔ Installation complete ← This recreates the webhook automatically!
$ kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector NAME WEBHOOKS AGE istio-sidecar-injector 4 10s ✅ Webhook restored!
$ kubectl rollout restart deploy,statefulset -n anihpj && sleep 30 && kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-api-9f3g7h6j-k 2/2 Running 0 45s anihpj-api-9f3g7h6j-m 2/2 Running 0 40s anihpj-db-0 2/2 Running 0 35s anihpj-web-8e4f9g2h-p 2/2 Running 0 50s anihpj-web-8e4f9g2h-q 2/2 Running 0 48s anihpj-web-8e4f9g2h-r 2/2 Running 0 45s ✅ ALL pods 2/2 — Sidecars injected everywhere!
🔧
BASH — Recreate the MutatingWebhookConfiguration (reinstall Istio) 
# Step 1: Reinstall Istio to recreate the webhook
# istioctl install is idempotent — it will recreate missing components
istioctl install --set profile=default -y

# Step 2: Verify the webhook is back
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector

# Step 3: Check webhook configuration details
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector -o yaml | grep -A10 namespaceSelector

# Step 4: Restart ALL deployments and statefulsets in the namespace
# ⚠️ Existing pods NEVER get sidecars retroactively!
kubectl rollout restart deploy,statefulset -n anihpj

# Step 5: Wait for all rollouts to complete
kubectl rollout status deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj
kubectl rollout status deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj
kubectl rollout status statefulset/anihpj-db -n anihpj

# Step 6: Verify ALL pods now have sidecars (2/2)
kubectl get pods -n anihpj

# Step 7: Verify all proxies are connected to istiod
istioctl proxy-status | grep anihpj
✓

✅ Verify — Entire Application Stack Is Now Inside the Mesh

After reinstalling Istio (which recreates the istio-sidecar-injector MutatingWebhookConfiguration) and restarting all pods, every pod now shows 2/2 READY. The entire anihpj/jobpost stack is inside the mesh: mTLS encrypts all inter-service traffic, VirtualService routing is enforced, metrics flow to Prometheus, and Kiali visualizes the full service topology. The webhook is now part of the API server's admission chain — new pods automatically get sidecars.

💡 Key takeaway: The MutatingWebhookConfiguration is the bridge between Kubernetes and Istio. Without it, the API server has no way to call istiod for injection. Always include kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector in your Istio health check runbook. This is the #1 "everything looks fine but nothing works" issue. The webhook can be deleted by cluster cleanup scripts, accidental kubectl delete, or failed Istio uninstalls. istioctl install is idempotent and will recreate it safely.

# DO NOT delete: mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector

🧪 SCENARIO S6 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config CNI Debug

Deploy anihpj Database — Fix Traffic Bypassing Sidecar (Excluded Port Bug)

The Problem: You deployed Istio with the CNI plugin and added port exclusion annotations to prevent health-check interference. But you accidentally excluded port 5432 (PostgreSQL) from sidecar interception. The anihpj-db StatefulSet deploys successfully (2/2 READY), mTLS is configured as STRICT, and AuthorizationPolicy restricts access to only anihpj-api. But other pods can still access the database directly on port 5432 — the traffic bypasses Envoy completely. The `traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInboundPorts` annotation contains `5432` by mistake. mTLS and AuthorizationPolicy are silently bypassed — the database is exposed with NO mesh security.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 5 (kind-cl3) — Multi-cluster mesh node 3
1

📋 Deploy Database With Bad Port Exclusion (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost stores ALL user data, job listings, and applications in PostgreSQL. Security requires STRICT mTLS on the database port and an AuthorizationPolicy that allows ONLY the API backend. The ops team added an exclusion annotation for the health-check port (8080) but accidentally typed 5432 instead of 8080. Now port 5432 traffic completely bypasses the Envoy sidecar — no mTLS, no authz, no metrics. The production database has a gaping security hole — any pod in the mesh can connect directly to PostgreSQL without authentication.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S6): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-db-statefulset.yaml         ← PostgreSQL with BUG: excludeInboundPorts: 5432
├── 02-db-service.yaml             ← ClusterIP Service (port 5432)
├── 03-peerauthentication.yaml     ← STRICT mTLS for database
└── 04-authorizationpolicy.yaml    ← ALLOW only anihpj-api → anihpj-db
BASH — Deploy DB with port exclusion bug (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S6: CNI Port Exclusion — Database Traffic Bypasses Sidecar
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE WITH INJECTION
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# 2. DEPLOY POSTGRESQL WITH BAD PORT EXCLUSION
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  serviceName: anihpj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-db
      annotations:
        # ❌ BUG! 5432 should NOT be excluded — it's the database port!
        traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInboundPorts: "5432"
        # Intended to exclude health port 8080, but typed 5432 by mistake
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: anihpj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
          name: tcp-postgresql
        - containerPort: 8080
          name: http-health
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-db
  ports:
  - name: tcp-postgresql
    port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: db-mtls-strict
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-access
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals:
        - cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/anihpj-api
    to:
    - operation:
        ports:
        - "5432"
EOF

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Deploy a test pod: kubectl run test-pod --rm -i --image=postgres:15-alpine --restart=Never -n anihpj -- env PGPASSWORD=secret123 psql -h anihpj-db -U anihpj -d jobpost -c "SELECT 1"
✗2. The test pod CAN connect to the database — despite AuthorizationPolicy only allowing anihpj-api!
✗3. Check Envoy logs: kubectl logs anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep 5432 → No traffic on port 5432 in Envoy!
✗4. mTLS STRICT and AuthorizationPolicy are silently bypassed — database is exposed with ZERO mesh security on port 5432.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod annotations: kubectl get pod anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 annotations
→ traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInboundPorts: "5432" — PORT 5432 IS EXCLUDED!
2Check iptables rules: kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- iptables -t nat -L -n | grep 5432
→ No REDIRECT rule for port 5432 — traffic goes directly to postgres, bypasses Envoy!
3Verify AuthZ policy exists: kubectl get authorizationpolicy db-access -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 rules
→ Policy looks correct (allows only anihpj-api) — but it's NEVER evaluated because traffic bypasses Envoy!
4Check PeerAuthentication: kubectl get peerauthentication db-mtls-strict -n anihpj
→ STRICT mTLS is configured — but port 5432 traffic bypasses Envoy, so mTLS is NEVER applied!
5Root cause: The annotation traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInboundPorts: "5432" tells istio-init to skip iptables for port 5432. Traffic on this port goes directly to PostgreSQL — Envoy never sees it. mTLS and AuthorizationPolicy only apply to traffic that passes THROUGH Envoy. The exclusion was meant for port 8080 (health checks), but 5432 was typed by mistake. This is a critical security vulnerability — any pod can connect to the database with zero mesh security.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Test pod connects despite AuthZ → Policy bypassed
②
Check Envoy logs → No 5432 traffic seen
③
Check pod annotations → excludeInboundPorts: 5432
④
Port excluded → iptables skips it → Envoy bypassed
⑤
Fix annotation → restart pod → Envoy intercepts → AuthZ enforced ✅

Tenet: Port exclusion annotations tell istio-init to NOT set up iptables redirect rules for specific ports. Traffic on excluded ports goes directly to the application container — Envoy never sees it. This means mTLS, AuthorizationPolicy, metrics, and tracing are ALL bypassed for excluded ports. Port exclusions are powerful but dangerous — a single typo can create a gaping security hole. Always verify excluded ports are truly non-critical (health probes, metrics endpoints). Never exclude your main service port. Use kubectl exec -c istio-proxy -- iptables -t nat -L to verify which ports are being intercepted.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl run test-pod --rm -i --image=postgres:15-alpine --restart=Never -n anihpj -- env PGPASSWORD=secret123 psql -h anihpj-db -U anihpj -d jobpost -c "SELECT 1" ?column? ---------- 1 (1 row) ← Test pod CAN connect! AuthZ policy is BYPASSED!
$ kubectl logs anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy --tail=50 | grep "5432\|postgres" ← No traffic on port 5432 in Envoy logs — Envoy never sees database connections!
$ kubectl get pod anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}' | grep exclude "traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInboundPorts":"5432" ← PORT 5432 IS EXCLUDED from sidecar interception!
$ kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- iptables -t nat -L ISTIO_INBOUND -n | grep 5432 ← No REDIRECT for port 5432 — traffic goes DIRECTLY to postgres!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch statefulset anihpj-db -n anihpj --type=json -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/metadata/annotations/traffic.sidecar.istio.io~1excludeInboundPorts"}]' statefulset.apps/anihpj-db patched
$ kubectl rollout restart statefulset anihpj-db -n anihpj && sleep 30 && kubectl run test-pod --rm -i --image=postgres:15-alpine --restart=Never -n anihpj -- env PGPASSWORD=secret123 psql -h anihpj-db -U anihpj -d jobpost -c "SELECT 1" psql: error: connection to server at "anihpj-db" (10.96.x.x), port 5432 failed: FATAL: no pg_hba.conf entry for host... ← Test pod is BLOCKED! AuthorizationPolicy now enforced through Envoy! ✅
🔧
BASH — Fix port exclusion (only exclude health ports, not service ports) 
# Step 1: Remove the bad port exclusion annotation
kubectl patch statefulset anihpj-db -n anihpj --type=json -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/metadata/annotations/traffic.sidecar.istio.io~1excludeInboundPorts"}]'

# Step 2: Or replace with the CORRECT exclusion (health port only, not database port)
# kubectl patch statefulset anihpj-db -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"annotations":{"traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInboundPorts":"8080"}}}}}'

# Step 3: Restart the StatefulSet to recreate pod with fixed annotations
kubectl rollout restart statefulset anihpj-db -n anihpj

# Step 4: Wait for the pod to be ready with new iptables rules
kubectl rollout status statefulset anihpj-db -n anihpj

# Step 5: Verify iptables now redirects port 5432 to Envoy
kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- iptables -t nat -L ISTIO_INBOUND -n | grep 5432

# Step 6: Test that AuthZ is now enforced (test pod should be BLOCKED)
kubectl run test-pod --rm -i --image=postgres:15-alpine --restart=Never -n anihpj -- env PGPASSWORD=secret123 psql -h anihpj-db -U anihpj -d jobpost -c "SELECT 1"
✓

✅ Verify — Database Traffic Now Goes Through Envoy With Full Mesh Security

After removing the port exclusion annotation and restarting the StatefulSet, istio-init configures iptables to redirect port 5432 traffic to Envoy. Now ALL database connections pass through the sidecar: mTLS encrypts every connection, AuthorizationPolicy enforces that ONLY anihpj-api can connect, and metrics flow to Prometheus. The test pod is BLOCKED — the security hole is closed. The database is fully protected by the Istio service mesh.

💡 Key takeaway: Port exclusion annotations (traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInboundPorts and excludeOutboundPorts) create deliberate holes in the mesh. Traffic on excluded ports completely bypasses Envoy — no mTLS, no AuthorizationPolicy, no metrics, no tracing. Only exclude ports that genuinely should NOT be in the mesh (health probes, metrics scraping endpoints). A single typo in excluded ports can create a massive security vulnerability. Always verify with iptables -t nat -L that your service ports ARE being intercepted.

# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Verify all resources are gone
kubectl get all -n anihpj

🧪 SCENARIO S7 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config ControlPlane Debug

Deploy 50 Services — Fix istiod OOMKilled and STALE Proxies After Memory Exhaustion

The Problem: You deploy the full anihpj/jobpost microservices architecture with 50 services. After applying all VirtualServices, DestinationRules, and AuthorizationPolicies, istiod crashes with OOMKilled. All 50 sidecar proxies go STALE — xDS updates stop, new routes aren't pushed, mTLS certificates can't be renewed. The mesh appears to work (proxies use cached config) but new configuration changes don't propagate. istiod's default memory limit of 2048Mi is insufficient for a 50-service mesh with complex policies. The control plane is overwhelmed by the config push.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Resource-constrained kind cluster
1

📋 Deploy 50 Services With Heavy Config + Low istiod Memory (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is scaling up to a full microservices architecture: 50 services including web, api, payments, notifications, search, analytics, and 45 backend workers. Each service has VirtualService, DestinationRule, and AuthorizationPolicy. The ops team deployed everything at once — istiod tries to push ALL config to ALL 50 proxies simultaneously and runs out of memory. istiod is OOMKilled, restarts, tries again, and crashes again. The control plane is in a death spiral — 50 proxies are STALE with no config updates.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S7): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml       ← Django web (1 replica)
├── 02-services-bulk.yaml        ← 10 bulk services simulating 50-service load
└── 03-istiod-patch.yaml         ← istiod with BUG: memory limit 256Mi (too low!)
BASH — Deploy bulk services + Reduce istiod memory (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S7: istiod OOMKilled — Proxies Go STALE
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# 2. PATCH ISTIOD WITH LOW MEMORY LIMIT (BUG: 256Mi is way too low for 50 services!)
kubectl patch deployment istiod -n istio-system --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"256Mi"},{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/memory","value":"128Mi"}]'

# 3. DEPLOY WEB FRONTEND + 10 BULK SERVICES (simulating 50-service load)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-web
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

# 4. CREATE 10 SERVICES WITH VIRTUALSERVICES AND DESTINATIONRULES
# (This simulates a 50-service mesh load on istiod)
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
cat << EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: service-${i}
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: ${i}080
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1

metadata:
  name: vs-${i}
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - service-${i}
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: service-${i}
        port:
          number: ${i}080
      weight: 100
  - match:
    - headers:
        x-version:
          exact: v2
    route:
    - destination:
        host: service-${i}
        port:
          number: ${i}080
      weight: 100
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: dr-${i}
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: service-${i}
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:

        maxConnections: 100
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 100
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 10
    loadBalancer:

EOF
done
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check istiod: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod
✗2. istiod shows RESTARTS: 3, 5, 8... — keeps crashing and restarting!
✗3. Check proxy status: istioctl proxy-status → ALL proxies show STALE across CDS, LDS, EDS, RDS!
✗4. New VirtualService changes don't propagate — proxies use cached config. mTLS certificates can't renew — mesh will eventually break completely when certs expire.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check istiod restart count: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod
→ RESTARTS: 8 — istiod is in a crash loop!
2Check why istiod crashed: kubectl describe pod -n istio-system istiod-xxx | grep -A5 "Last State"
→ Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137 — istiod ran out of memory!
3Check current memory limit: kubectl get deploy istiod -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A2 "memory"
→ limits: memory: 256Mi — far too low for 50 services with complex policies!
4Check config volume: kubectl get vs,dr,se,pa --all-namespaces | wc -l
→ 40+ Istio CRs — each must be pushed to every proxy via xDS. 256Mi can't handle this.
5Root cause: istiod's memory limit was reduced to 256Mi (from the default 2048Mi). With 50 services and complex routing policies, istiod needs at least 2Gi to push config to all proxies. The low memory limit causes OOMKill during xDS push, restarting istiod, which then tries to push to all 50 proxies again — creating a death spiral. Proxies go STALE because istiod can't complete the push before crashing.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Proxies STALE → istiod not pushing config
②
Check istiod → High restarts → OOMKilled
③
Check memory limit → 256Mi (too low)
④
Mesh size needs ~2Gi for 50 services
⑤
Increase to 4Gi → restart istiod → proxies SYNCED ✅

Tenet: istiod memory requirements scale with mesh size. Each service, VirtualService, DestinationRule, and AuthorizationPolicy consumes memory for the xDS cache. The default 2048Mi is adequate for ~100 services with moderate config. A rule of thumb: ~20-40Mi per service for the xDS cache, plus base overhead of ~500Mi. When istiod OOMKills, ALL proxies lose config updates and eventually go STALE. Increase istiod memory BEFORE scaling the mesh — never let istiod crash-loop.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE istiod-7d8f9c5b-x 1/1 Running 8 (30s ago) 10m ← RESTARTS: 8 — istiod keeps crashing!
$ kubectl describe pod -n istio-system istiod-7d8f9c5b-x | grep -A5 "Last State" Last State: Terminated Reason: OOMKilled Exit Code: 137 Started: ... Finished: ... ← OOMKilled — istiod ran out of memory!
$ istioctl proxy-status NAME CDS LDS EDS RDS anihpj-web-xxx.anihpj STALE STALE STALE STALE ← ALL proxies STALE — no config updates from istiod!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch deploy istiod -n istio-system --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"4096Mi"}]' deployment.apps/istiod patched
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE istiod-9f3g7h6j-y 1/1 Running 0 60s ✅ istiod stable — no more OOMKills!
$ istioctl proxy-status NAME CDS LDS EDS RDS anihpj-web-xxx.anihpj SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED SYNCED ✅ All proxies SYNCED — config flowing again!
🔧
BASH — Increase istiod memory to handle mesh scale 
# Step 1: Increase istiod memory limit to 4Gi
kubectl patch deploy istiod -n istio-system --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"4096Mi"},{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/memory","value":"2048Mi"}]'

# Step 2: Wait for new istiod pod to be ready
kubectl rollout status deploy/istiod -n istio-system

# Step 3: Verify istiod is stable (no restarts in last 2 min)
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod

# Step 4: Verify proxies reconnect and sync
istioctl proxy-status

# Step 5: Check istiod logs for successful xDS pushes
kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=istiod --tail=20 | grep "ads\|push"
✓

✅ Verify — istiod Stable, All Proxies SYNCED

After increasing istiod's memory limit to 4Gi, the control plane has enough memory to maintain the xDS cache for all 50 services and push config to every proxy. istiod stops crash-looping — RESTARTS stays at 0. All proxies reconnect and istioctl proxy-status shows SYNCED across CDS, LDS, EDS, RDS. New VirtualService changes propagate within seconds. The mesh is fully operational with a healthy control plane.

💡 Key takeaway: istiod is the single point of config distribution for the ENTIRE mesh. If istiod OOMKills, ALL proxies go STALE within minutes. Memory requirements scale with: number of services, complexity of routing rules, number of AuthorizationPolicies, and proxy count. Production rule of thumb: 4Gi for up to 200 services. Monitor istiod memory usage with Prometheus (container_memory_working_set_bytes) and set alerts at 80% of limit. Use Sidecar resources to limit the config scope per proxy and reduce istiod memory pressure.

# Restore istiod memory to defaults
kubectl patch deploy istiod -n istio-system --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"2048Mi"}]'

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj

🧪 SCENARIO S8 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Gateway Debug

Expose anihpj Web Externally — Fix Ingress Gateway EXTERNAL-IP Stuck Pending

The Problem: You deployed Istio on a bare-metal kubeadm cluster and want to expose the anihpj web frontend to external users via jobpost.com. The Gateway and VirtualService are configured correctly, but the ingress gateway Service shows EXTERNAL-IP: <Pending> indefinitely. The Istio installation used the default profile which creates the gateway Service as type: LoadBalancer — but bare-metal clusters have NO load balancer controller. External traffic can't reach the mesh because the gateway has no external IP. The entire job board is inaccessible from the internet.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Bare-metal production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Install Istio default Profile + Deploy Web + Gateway (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is launching to the public! The web frontend needs to be accessible at jobpost.com. The ops team installed Istio with the default profile and configured Gateway + VirtualService for external access. But the kubeadm cluster is bare-metal — there's no cloud load balancer controller. The ingress gateway Service type LoadBalancer stays Pending forever. The job board launch is blocked — nobody can access the site from the internet.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S8): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml         ← Django web frontend (2 replicas)
├── 02-web-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
├── 03-gateway.yaml                ← Istio Gateway for jobpost.com

BASH — Install Istio + Deploy app + Configure Gateway (BUG: LB on bare metal)

# SCENARIO S8: Ingress Gateway Pending — No LB on Bare Metal
# ============================================

# 1. INSTALL ISTIO WITH DEFAULT PROFILE (BUG: gateway type=LoadBalancer on bare metal!)
istioctl install --set profile=default -y

# 2. CREATE NAMESPACE AND DEPLOY WEB
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

kind: Deployment

spec:

  namespace: anihpj
spec:

  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
---

kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: anihpj-gateway
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 80
      name: http
      protocol: HTTP
    hosts:
    - "jobpost.com"
---

kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - "jobpost.com"

        port:
          number: 80

⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check gateway service: kubectl get svc -n istio-system istio-ingressgateway
✗2. EXTERNAL-IP shows <Pending> — no IP assigned, has been Pending for hours!
✗3. Test external access: curl -H "Host: jobpost.com" http://<node-ip>:<nodeport> → works via NodePort but no stable external IP!
✗4. The job board launch is BLOCKED — DNS can't point to a Pending IP. Users can't access the site.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check gateway Service type: kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -o yaml | grep type
→ type: LoadBalancer — bare metal has NO load balancer controller!
2Check if MetalLB or cloud LB is installed: kubectl get pods -n metallb-system 2>/dev/null || echo "No MetalLB"
→ No MetalLB installed — kubeadm is bare metal without any LB solution!
3Check NodePort alternative: kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A3 "nodePort"
→ NodePort 32380 is auto-assigned — we CAN use NodePort or change to ClusterIP!
4Check if ingress gateway pods are running: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway
→ Pod is Running ✅ — gateway works, just no external IP!
5Root cause: The default Istio profile creates the ingress gateway Service as type: LoadBalancer. On bare-metal clusters (kubeadm, kind, minikube without tunnel), there is NO cloud load balancer controller to provision an external IP. The Service stays Pending indefinitely. Solutions: change to NodePort (and use node IP + port), install MetalLB, or use ClusterIP with an external reverse proxy.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Gateway EXTERNAL-IP Pending → Check Service type
②
type: LoadBalancer → No cloud LB controller
③
Check environment → Bare-metal kubeadm
④
Options: NodePort, MetalLB, or ClusterIP+proxy
⑤
Switch to NodePort → curl nodeIP:nodePort → 200 ✅

Tenet: The Istio ingress gateway Service type must match your infrastructure. LoadBalancer requires a cloud provider (AWS, GCP, Azure) or an on-prem solution like MetalLB. On bare-metal clusters, use NodePort (access via node IP:port) or ClusterIP (with an external reverse proxy like HAProxy/Nginx in front). You can change the Service type without reinstalling Istio: kubectl patch svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'. For production bare-metal, install MetalLB to get real LoadBalancer IPs.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) istio-ingressgateway LoadBalancer 10.96.100.1 <Pending> 80:32380/TCP ← EXTERNAL-IP Pending — no load balancer on bare metal!
$ curl -H "Host: jobpost.com" http://10.96.100.1 ← Works via ClusterIP internally, but no external access!
$ kubectl get pods -n metallb-system 2>&1 No resources found in metallb-system namespace. ← No MetalLB or cloud LB controller installed!

$ kubectl patch svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}' service/istio-ingressgateway patched
$ NODE_IP=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses[0].address}'); NODE_PORT=$(kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}'); curl -H "Host: jobpost.com" http://${NODE_IP}:${NODE_PORT} <!DOCTYPE html>... ← Works! Web frontend accessible via NodePort!
🔧
BASH — Change Service type to NodePort (or install MetalLB) 
# Step 1: Change the gateway Service from LoadBalancer to NodePort
kubectl patch svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'

# Step 2: Get the assigned NodePort and node IP
NODE_PORT=$(kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[?(@.port==80)].nodePort}')
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
echo "Access the web app at: http://${NODE_IP}:${NODE_PORT}"
echo "Add header: Host: jobpost.com"

# Step 3: Test external access via NodePort
curl -H "Host: jobpost.com" http://${NODE_IP}:${NODE_PORT}

# Step 4: (Production) Install MetalLB for real LoadBalancer IPs on bare metal
# kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/metallb/metallb/v0.14.3/config/manifests/metallb-native.yaml
✓

✅ Verify — Gateway Accessible Externally via NodePort

After switching the ingress gateway Service to NodePort, the gateway is accessible on every node's IP at the assigned port. External traffic flows: User → NodeIP:NodePort → istio-ingressgateway → Gateway → VirtualService → anihpj-web. The job board is now accessible externally. For production, install MetalLB to get real LoadBalancer IPs — or place an external load balancer (HAProxy, Nginx, F5) in front of the NodePort.

💡 Key takeaway: type: LoadBalancer only works if your cluster has a load balancer controller (cloud LB, MetalLB, or similar). Bare-metal clusters require either NodePort (access via node IP:30000-32767) or MetalLB (provides real LoadBalancer IPs on-prem). You can change the gateway Service type at any time without downtime. For ICA exam scenarios, know how to quickly switch between Service types when the gateway shows Pending EXTERNAL-IP.

🧹

# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Restore gateway service type to default
kubectl patch svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj

🧪 SCENARIO S9 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Config Debug

Debug anihpj 503 Errors — Fix MeshConfig accessLogFile Empty (No Envoy Logs)

The Problem: Users report intermittent HTTP 503 errors on the anihpj web frontend. You need to debug by checking Envoy access logs, but kubectl logs anihpj-web-xxx -c istio-proxy shows no per-request logs — only startup messages. The MeshConfig has accessLogFile: "" (empty string) which DISABLES Envoy access logging. Without access logs, you can't see request paths, response codes, upstream cluster routing, or latency. Debugging 503s is impossible — you're flying blind. The ops team disabled logging during installation to "save resources" and forgot to re-enable it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Dev cluster for testing
1

📋 Deploy Web With Access Logging Disabled (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is experiencing 503 errors in production. The SRE team needs to check Envoy access logs to see which requests are failing and where they're being routed. But someone set accessLogFile: "" in the MeshConfig to reduce disk I/O during a previous performance issue and forgot to re-enable it. Now kubectl logs -c istio-proxy is empty — no request data at all. The team can't debug the 503s and users are complaining.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S9): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml         ← Django web frontend (2 replicas)
├── 02-web-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
└── 03-meshconfig-patch.yaml       ← MeshConfig with BUG: accessLogFile: ""
BASH — Disable access logging + Deploy app (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S9: MeshConfig accessLogFile Empty — No Envoy Logs
# ============================================

# 1. DISABLE ACCESS LOGGING IN MESHCONFIG (BUG: can't debug traffic!)
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml | sed 's/accessLogFile:.*/accessLogFile: ""/' | kubectl apply -f -

# 2. CREATE NAMESPACE AND DEPLOY WEB
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-web
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---

kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj

EOF

# 3. GENERATE SOME TRAFFIC
kubectl run load-gen --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -n anihpj -- sh -c 'for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s anihpj-web; done'
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Generate traffic: kubectl exec anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -c anihpj-web -- curl localhost
✗2. Check Envoy logs: kubectl logs anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy --tail=20
✗3. Shows ONLY startup messages — NO HTTP request logs (no GET, POST, 200, 503)!
✗4. When users report 503 errors, you have ZERO visibility into which requests are failing, what upstream cluster is targeted, or what response codes Envoy is returning.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check MeshConfig accessLogFile: kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep accessLogFile
→ accessLogFile: "" — EMPTY STRING disables access logging!
2Check Envoy access log status in proxy config: istioctl proxy-config bootstrap anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep -A5 accessLog
→ accessLog: [] — No access log configuration pushed to Envoy!
3Verify MeshConfig was applied: kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A2 "accessLog"
→ accessLogFile: "" — Confirmed disabled at mesh level!
4Check if pods have restarted to pick up config: kubectl get pods -n anihpj
→ AGE: 5m — MeshConfig changes only apply to NEW pods!
5Root cause: The MeshConfig has accessLogFile: "" which completely disables Envoy access logging. Without it, Envoy logs only startup/bootstrap messages — no per-request HTTP logs. This was done to save disk I/O but makes production debugging impossible. The fix is to set accessLogFile: "/dev/stdout" and restart pods to pick up the new mesh config.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
No access logs → Check MeshConfig
②
accessLogFile: "" → Logging disabled
③
Set to /dev/stdout → Mesh config updated
④
Restart pods → MeshConfig only applies at startup
⑤
kubectl logs -c istio-proxy → Full HTTP logs visible ✅

Tenet: Envoy access logging is controlled by the MeshConfig accessLogFile setting. An empty string ("") means disabled. The standard value is "/dev/stdout" which sends logs to the container's stdout (visible via kubectl logs). MeshConfig changes only apply to NEW pods — existing pods must be restarted. For per-workload overrides, use the sidecar.istio.io/proxyLogLevel annotation. Always keep access logging enabled in non-production; it's your primary debugging tool for traffic issues.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj -c istio-proxy --tail=10 2025-01-15T10:00:00.000Z info FLAG: --concurrency="2" 2025-01-15T10:00:00.000Z info FLAG: --serviceCluster="istio-proxy" ... (startup messages only — NO HTTP request logs!)
$ kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep accessLogFile accessLogFile: "" ← Empty string = access logging DISABLED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml | sed 's/accessLogFile: ""/accessLogFile: "\/dev\/stdout"/' | kubectl apply -f - && kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj configmap/istio configured deployment.apps/anihpj-web restarted
$ kubectl exec anihpj-web-yyy -n anihpj -c anihpj-web -- curl -s localhost && kubectl logs anihpj-web-yyy -n anihpj -c istio-proxy --tail=3 [2025-01-15T11:00:00.000Z] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 - via_upstream - "-" 0 615 2 1 "10.1.0.5" "curl/8.x" "abc-123" "anihpj-web:80" "10.1.0.10:80" ✅ Full HTTP access logs now visible! Method, path, status code, upstream, latency — everything!
🔧
BASH — Set accessLogFile to /dev/stdout and restart pods 
# Step 1: Enable access logging in MeshConfig
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml | sed 's|accessLogFile: ""|accessLogFile: "/dev/stdout"|' | kubectl apply -f -

# Step 2: Verify the change was applied
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep accessLogFile

# Step 3: Restart pods to pick up new MeshConfig
# ⚠️ MeshConfig changes only apply to NEW pods — existing pods keep old config!
kubectl rollout restart deploy anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 4: Generate test traffic
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -c anihpj-web -- curl -s localhost

# Step 5: Verify access logs are now visible
kubectl logs deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -c istio-proxy --tail=5
✓

✅ Verify — Envoy Access Logs Now Show Full Request Details

After setting accessLogFile: "/dev/stdout" in the MeshConfig and restarting the deployment, every HTTP request passing through Envoy is logged with: timestamp, method, path, response code, upstream cluster, bytes sent/received, latency, and client IP. kubectl logs -c istio-proxy now shows detailed per-request logs — the SRE team can finally debug the 503 errors.

💡 Key takeaway: Access logging is your #1 debugging tool for Istio traffic issues. Never disable it in non-production environments. The MeshConfig accessLogFile controls logging globally. You can also set accessLogFormat for JSON output and accessLogEncoding for structured logging. For high-traffic production, use sampling or OTEL-based access logging instead of file-based to avoid I/O bottlenecks. MeshConfig changes require pod restart — they don't propagate dynamically like VirtualService changes.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Re-enable access logging to default (good practice for future scenarios)
kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml | sed 's|accessLogFile:.*|accessLogFile: "/dev/stdout"|' | kubectl apply -f -

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj
