🧪 SCENARIO S10 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Upgrade Debug

Upgrade Istio 1.18 to 1.20 — Fix In-Place Upgrade Blocked by Revision Conflict

The Problem: You need to upgrade Istio from 1.18 to 1.20 on the production cluster. The recommended canary upgrade uses revision labels, but you attempt an in-place upgrade with istioctl upgrade. The upgrade fails with: "revision conflict: an IstioOperator with the same name already exists". The old IstioOperator resource for revision 1-18 blocks the new 1-20 installation. In-place upgrades require removing the old operator first or using the correct upgrade flags. The mesh is stuck on 1.18 while security patches for 1.20 are waiting.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1) — Multi-cluster mesh node 1
1

📋 Install Istio 1.18 + Attempt In-Place Upgrade (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is running on Istio 1.18 in production. A critical CVE requires upgrading to Istio 1.20 within 48 hours. The ops team attempts an in-place upgrade with istioctl upgrade but hits a revision conflict — in-place upgrades are risky and often fail when IstioOperator resources conflict. The upgrade is blocked — the mesh is vulnerable and the clock is ticking.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S10): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Django API backend (1 replica)
├── 02-api-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 8080)
└── istio-system/                   ← IstioOperator with BUG: revision conflict
BASH — Install 1.18 + Attempt blocked upgrade (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S10: IstioOperator Upgrade Blocked — Revision Conflict
# ============================================

# 1. INSTALL ISTIO 1.18 (simulates existing production installation)
istioctl install --set revision=1-18 --set profile=default -y

# 2. CREATE NAMESPACE WITH 1-18 REVISION AND DEPLOY API
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio.io/rev=1-18 istio-injection=enabled
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-api
  ports:
  - port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
EOF

# 3. ATTEMPT IN-PLACE UPGRADE (BUG: this fails with revision conflict!)
# istioctl upgrade --set profile=default -y
# Error: revision conflict — an IstioOperator "installed-state-1-18" already exists
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Attempt upgrade: istioctl upgrade --set profile=default -y
✗2. Fails with: "an IstioOperator with the name installed-state-1-18 already exists"
✗3. Check existing IstioOperator: kubectl get istiooperator -A → shows installed-state-1-18
✗4. The upgrade is BLOCKED — Istio 1.18 stays in place. CVE window is shrinking with no upgrade path available.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1List existing IstioOperator resources: kubectl get istiooperator -A
→ installed-state-1-18 in istio-system — blocks in-place upgrade!
2Check upgrade error details: The in-place upgrade tries to create a NEW IstioOperator but one already exists
→ istioctl upgrade is for in-place upgrades but conflicts with existing revision-based operator!
3Check the correct upgrade path: Canary upgrade (new revision) is preferred over in-place
→ Use istioctl install --set revision=1-20 to add new revision alongside existing one!
4Verify existing istiod is healthy: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod
→ istiod-1-18 is Running — can add 1-20 as canary without disrupting existing mesh!
5Root cause: istioctl upgrade attempts an in-place replacement of the existing IstioOperator, but the existing revision-based operator (installed-state-1-18) blocks it. The correct approach is a canary upgrade: install new revision 1-20 alongside 1-18, migrate namespaces by updating revision labels, then decommission 1-18. Use istioctl install --set revision=1-20 (NOT istioctl upgrade) for canary upgrades.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
istioctl upgrade fails → Revision conflict
②
Check IstioOperator → installed-state-1-18
③
In-place blocked → Use canary instead
④
istioctl install --set revision=1-20 → succeeds
⑤
Migrate ns labels → decommission 1-18 → upgrade complete ✅

Tenet: Istio supports two upgrade strategies: in-place (istioctl upgrade) and canary (revision-based). In-place upgrades replace the existing control plane directly — faster but riskier. Canary upgrades deploy a new istiod revision alongside the old one and migrate workloads gradually — safer for production. When in-place is blocked by existing IstioOperator resources, fall back to canary: istioctl install --set revision=<new>, migrate namespaces by updating istio.io/rev labels, then decommission the old revision. On the ICA exam, canary upgrade is the recommended approach for production environments.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ istioctl upgrade --set profile=default -y Error: failed to install: an IstioOperator with the name "installed-state-1-18" already exists in namespace "istio-system" ← In-place upgrade BLOCKED by existing revision operator!
$ kubectl get istiooperator -A NAMESPACE NAME AGE istio-system installed-state-1-18 2d ← Existing 1-18 operator blocks in-place upgrade!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ istioctl install --set revision=1-20 --set profile=default -y ✔ Istio core installed ✔ Istiod installed ✔ CNI installed ✔ Ingress gateways installed ✔ Installation complete ✅ Canary revision 1-20 installed alongside 1-18!
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE istiod-1-18-7d8f9c5b-x 1/1 Running 0 2d istiod-1-20-9f3g7h6j-y 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ Both revisions running — can now migrate namespaces!
🔧
BASH — Canary upgrade: add new revision + migrate namespaces 
# Step 1: Install new istiod revision (canary — runs alongside existing)
istioctl install --set revision=1-20 --set profile=default -y

# Step 2: Verify both revisions are running
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod

# Step 3: Migrate namespace to new revision
kubectl label ns anihpj istio.io/rev=1-20 --overwrite

# Step 4: Restart workloads to pick up new sidecar config
kubectl rollout restart deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj

# Step 5: Verify sidecars connect to new istiod
istioctl proxy-status | grep anihpj

# Step 6: After all namespaces migrated, decommission old revision
# istioctl uninstall --revision=1-18 -y
✓

✅ Verify — Canary Upgrade Successful, Both Revisions Running

Instead of the blocked in-place upgrade, the canary upgrade successfully deployed istiod-1-20 alongside istiod-1-18. Both revisions run simultaneously — the existing mesh on 1-18 continues unaffected while the namespace is migrated to 1-20. After updating the revision label and restarting the deployment, istioctl proxy-status confirms the API sidecar is now connected to istiod-1-20. The upgrade is complete without downtime — the CVE is patched and the job board stays online.

💡 Key takeaway: istioctl upgrade attempts in-place replacement and often conflicts with existing IstioOperator resources. For production upgrades, always prefer canary upgrades with istioctl install --set revision=<new>. This deploys a parallel control plane, allowing namespace-by-namespace migration with zero downtime. The old revision can be decommissioned after all namespaces are migrated. This is a critical ICA exam concept — know the difference between in-place and canary upgrade strategies.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Decommission the canary revision (if done testing)
# istioctl uninstall --revision=1-20 -y
# Or keep default revision clean:
# istioctl uninstall --revision=1-18 -y

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj
S11
🧪 SCENARIO S11 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Route Debug

Deploy anihpj Web v1/v2 — Fix Canary Traffic All Going to v1 (Route Order Bug)

The Problem: You deploy anihpj-web v2 alongside v1 for a canary release. The VirtualService is configured to send 90% traffic to v1 and 10% to v2. But ALL traffic goes to v1 — v2 receives ZERO requests. The issue: the catch-all route (no match conditions, destination v1) is listed BEFORE the header-match route (x-version: v2). Istio evaluates routes in order and the first match wins — the catch-all matches EVERY request. The specific canary route is never reached. Traffic management is completely broken.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Dedicated Istio mesh practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy Web v1 + v2 With Broken Route Order (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is releasing a new UI (v2) alongside the current production UI (v1). The plan is a canary: 90% v1, 10% v2. The ops team created two Deployments (v1 and v2), a DestinationRule for subsets, and a VirtualService with weighted routing. But the VirtualService routes are in the WRONG order — the catch-all (v1) comes first, so it matches every request before the canary route (v2 with x-version header) is ever evaluated. The v2 canary receives ZERO traffic — the release is silently blocked.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S11): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-web-deployment-v1.yaml      ← anihpj-web v1 (nginx:alpine)
├── 02-web-deployment-v2.yaml      ← anihpj-web v2 (nginx:alpine)
├── 03-web-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
├── 04-destinationrule.yaml        ← subsets: v1, v2
└── 05-virtualservice.yaml         ← VS with BUG: catch-all before canary route!
BASH — Deploy v1/v2 with broken route order (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S11: VirtualService Route Order — Catch-All Before Specific
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# 2. DEPLOY v1 AND v2
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-v1
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
    version: v1
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
      version: v1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-v2
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
    version: v2
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
      version: v2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: anihpj-web
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - anihpj-web
  http:
  # ❌ BUG! Catch-all route FIRST — matches EVERY request before canary route!
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-web
        subset: v1
      weight: 100
  # Canary route — NEVER REACHED because catch-all matches everything first!
  - match:
    - headers:
        x-version:
          exact: v2
    route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-web
        subset: v2
      weight: 100
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Send canary traffic: kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web-v1 -n anihpj -c web -- curl -s -H "x-version: v2" anihpj-web
✗2. All requests go to v1 — even with x-version: v2 header!
✗3. Check v2 access logs: kubectl logs deploy/anihpj-web-v2 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy → ZERO requests!
✗4. The canary receives NO traffic — v2 deployment is running but completely invisible. Release is blocked.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check VirtualService routes: kubectl get vs anihpj-web-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A20 "http:"
→ Route 0 is catch-all (no match) → v1. Route 1 has x-version match → v2.
2Understand route ordering: Istio evaluates VirtualService routes in ORDER — first match wins
→ The catch-all at index 0 matches EVERY request. Route 1 is NEVER evaluated!
3Verify with istioctl: istioctl proxy-config routes anihpj-web-v1-xxx -n anihpj | grep -A5 "virtual_hosts"
→ Only one route is active — the catch-all. The canary route exists but has no matches.
4Check v1 vs v2 traffic: kubectl logs deploy/anihpj-web-v1 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep "GET" | wc -l vs v2
→ v1: 100 requests, v2: 0 requests — confirmed!
5Root cause: The VirtualService routes are in the wrong order. The catch-all route (no match conditions, destination v1) is listed BEFORE the specific canary route (header x-version: v2, destination v2). Istio's first-match semantics mean the catch-all matches every request, and the canary route is never reached. The fix: swap the order — put the specific route FIRST, catch-all LAST.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
All traffic to v1 → Canary not working
②
Check VS routes → Catch-all before specific
③
Istio uses first-match → Catch-all wins always
④
Swap route order → specific first, catch-all last
⑤
Canary now receives traffic → 10% to v2 ✅

Tenet: Istio VirtualService routes are evaluated in array order — first match wins. This is fundamentally different from traditional load balancers where "longest prefix match" or "most specific wins." In Istio, if the catch-all is first, it ALWAYS wins. The rule: most specific routes FIRST, catch-all LAST. This applies to prefix matching too: put /api/v2 before /api. Route ordering is the #1 VirtualService mistake — always verify with istioctl proxy-config routes.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ for i in $(seq 1 10); do kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web-v1 -n anihpj -c web -- curl -s -H "x-version: v2" anihpj-web | grep -o "v[12]"; done v1 v1 v1 v1 v1 v1 v1 v1 v1 v1 ← ALL 10 requests go to v1! Canary header IGNORED!
$ kubectl logs deploy/anihpj-web-v2 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy --tail=5 ← ZERO HTTP request logs — v2 receives no traffic!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get vs anihpj-web-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | sed '0,/catch-all.*matches/d' | kubectl apply -f - && kubectl edit vs anihpj-web-vs -n anihpj # (Swap routes: specific canary route FIRST, catch-all LAST)
$ for i in $(seq 1 10); do kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web-v1 -n anihpj -c web -- curl -s -H "x-version: v2" anihpj-web | grep -o "v[12]"; done v2 v2 v2 v2 v2 v2 v2 v2 v2 v2 ✅ ALL 10 requests now go to v2! Canary header RESPECTED!
🔧
BASH — Edit VirtualService to put specific routes before catch-all 
# Step 1: Edit the VirtualService
kubectl edit vs anihpj-web-vs -n anihpj

# Step 2: Swap the http routes array so the SPECIFIC route comes FIRST:
# http:
#   - match:                        ← THIS ROUTE FIRST (specific)
#     - headers:
#         x-version:
#           exact: v2
#     route:
#     - destination:
#         host: anihpj-web
#         subset: v2
#   - route:                        ← THIS ROUTE LAST (catch-all)
#     - destination:
#         host: anihpj-web
#         subset: v1

# Step 3: Verify the updated route order
kubectl get vs anihpj-web-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A30 "http:"

# Step 4: Test that canary header now routes to v2
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web-v1 -n anihpj -c web -- curl -s -H "x-version: v2" anihpj-web
✓

✅ Verify — Canary Traffic Now Routes Correctly to v2

After swapping the VirtualService route order (specific canary route FIRST, catch-all LAST), requests with x-version: v2 header are correctly routed to the v2 subset. The catch-all route only matches requests that don't have the canary header. Traffic flows as intended: 100% of canary-header requests → v2, all other requests → v1. The canary release is now operational.

💡 Key takeaway: Istio VirtualService routes use array-order first-match semantics — NOT longest-prefix or most-specific. Always put specific routes (with match conditions) BEFORE catch-all routes. This is the opposite of some traditional load balancers. Route ordering is tested on the ICA exam — knowing that the first match wins is critical. Use istioctl proxy-config routes to verify the effective route order in Envoy.

kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj

🧪 SCENARIO S12 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Gateway Debug

Expose anihpj Web via HTTPS — Fix Gateway 404 (TLS Hosts Mismatch)

The Problem: You configured TLS for the anihpj web frontend with a Gateway and VirtualService. Users access https://jobpost.com but get HTTP 404. The TLS certificate is valid, the Gateway is listening on port 443, but the hosts field in the Gateway has "jobpost.com" while the VirtualService has "www.jobpost.com". The Gateway-VirtualService binding requires the host to match EXACTLY in both resources. Envoy receives the TLS handshake on the Gateway but can't match it to any VirtualService — it returns 404 because NO route matches the host.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Deploy Web + Gateway With Hosts Mismatch (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is going live with HTTPS. The ops team created a TLS secret, Gateway on port 443, and VirtualService for routing. But during configuration, the Gateway host was set to jobpost.com while the VirtualService host was set to www.jobpost.com — a subtle copy-paste error. HTTPS returns 404 for ALL requests — the site appears broken to users.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S12): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml         ← Django web (1 replica)
├── 02-web-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
├── 03-tls-secret.yaml             ← TLS cert for jobpost.com
├── 04-gateway.yaml                ← Gateway: hosts ["jobpost.com"]
└── 05-virtualservice.yaml         ← VS: hosts ["www.jobpost.com"] (BUG: mismatch!)
BASH — Deploy app + TLS Gateway with host mismatch (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S12: Gateway TLS Hosts Mismatch — 404
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# Create self-signed TLS cert for testing
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout /tmp/tls.key -out /tmp/tls.crt -subj "/CN=jobpost.com"
kubectl create secret tls jobpost-tls --key=/tmp/tls.key --cert=/tmp/tls.crt -n anihpj

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web; namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1; selector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj-web}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: anihpj-web}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web; image: nginx:alpine; ports: [{containerPort: 80}]
---
apiVersion: v1; kind: Service
metadata: {name: anihpj-web, namespace: anihpj}
spec: {selector: {app: anihpj-web}, ports: [{port: 80}]}
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: Gateway
metadata: {name: anihpj-gateway, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  selector: {istio: ingressgateway}
  servers:
  - port: {number: 443, name: https, protocol: HTTPS}
    tls: {mode: SIMPLE, credentialName: jobpost-tls}
    hosts: ["jobpost.com"]    # Gateway accepts jobpost.com
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata: {name: anihpj-web-vs, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  hosts: ["www.jobpost.com"]  # ❌ BUG! VS expects www.jobpost.com — MISMATCH!
  gateways: [anihpj-gateway]
  http:
  - route:
    - destination: {host: anihpj-web, port: {number: 80}}
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Test HTTPS: curl -kv --resolve jobpost.com:443:<INGRESS_IP> https://jobpost.com
✗2. Returns HTTP 404 Not Found — TLS handshake succeeds but NO route matches!
✗3. The Gateway accepts the connection but can't find a VirtualService for the host!
✗4. Users see a blank 404 page — the job board is inaccessible even though TLS is working.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Gateway hosts: kubectl get gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 hosts
→ hosts: ["jobpost.com"] — Gateway accepts this host
2Check VirtualService hosts: kubectl get vs anihpj-web-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep hosts
→ hosts: ["www.jobpost.com"] — VS expects DIFFERENT host!
3Check gateway logs: kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway | grep 404
→ "404 NR" (No Route) — Gateway can't match host to any VirtualService!
4Compare hosts exactly: Gateway="jobpost.com" vs VS="www.jobpost.com" — NOT the same!
→ Host matching in Istio is EXACT string comparison — "jobpost.com" ≠ "www.jobpost.com"
5Root cause: The Gateway and VirtualService have DIFFERENT host values. The Gateway accepts TLS for "jobpost.com" but the VirtualService only handles "www.jobpost.com". Since no VirtualService matches "jobpost.com", Istio returns 404 NR (No Route). Both must match exactly, or use wildcards (*.jobpost.com).
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
HTTPS returns 404 → TLS OK, routing broken
②
Check Gateway hosts vs VS hosts → MISMATCH
③
Gateway accepts jobpost.com → VS expects www.jobpost.com
④
Fix VS host to match Gateway → jobpost.com
⑤
curl https://jobpost.com → 200 ✅

Tenet: Istio Gateway-VirtualService binding uses exact host matching. The host in the Gateway's server block must match the host in the VirtualService — "jobpost.com" ≠ "www.jobpost.com". Use wildcards (*.jobpost.com) in BOTH resources for flexible matching. The 404 NR (No Route) error from the ingress gateway is the telltale sign of a host mismatch. Always verify hosts are identical between Gateway and VirtualService.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -kv --resolve jobpost.com:443:10.96.100.1 https://jobpost.com 2>&1 | grep "< HTTP" < HTTP/2 404 ← 404 NR — Gateway has NO matching VirtualService for host "jobpost.com"!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch vs anihpj-web-vs -n anihpj --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/hosts/0","value":"jobpost.com"}]' virtualservice.networking.istio.io/anihpj-web-vs patched
$ curl -kv --resolve jobpost.com:443:10.96.100.1 https://jobpost.com 2>&1 | grep "< HTTP" < HTTP/2 200 ✅
🔧
BASH — Patch VS to match Gateway host
# Step 1: Patch VirtualService to match Gateway host
kubectl patch vs anihpj-web-vs -n anihpj --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/hosts/0","value":"jobpost.com"}]'
# Step 2: Verify both resources now have matching hosts
kubectl get gateway,vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep hosts
# Step 3: Test HTTPS access
curl -k --resolve jobpost.com:443:$(kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}') https://jobpost.com
✓

✅ Verify — HTTPS Returns 200, Host Match Resolved

After patching the VirtualService host to jobpost.com (matching the Gateway), HTTPS requests are properly routed to the web frontend. The Gateway accepts the TLS connection for jobpost.com and finds the matching VirtualService — routing works correctly. The job board is accessible via HTTPS.

💡 Key takeaway: Gateway and VirtualService hosts must match EXACTLY. Use kubectl get gateway,vs -o yaml | grep hosts to compare. For multiple hosts, use wildcards: *.jobpost.com in BOTH resources. The 404 NR error in ingress gateway logs is the signature of a host mismatch. This is a common ICA exam pitfall.

Deploy anihpj API With Circuit Breaker — Fix All Requests Returning 503

The Problem: You configured a DestinationRule circuit breaker to protect the API backend from overload. But the maxConnections is set to 1 and http1MaxPendingRequests is set to 0 — the circuit breaker allows only ONE concurrent connection and ZERO pending requests. Any second request immediately gets HTTP 503 Service Unavailable. Under normal load with multiple users, almost ALL requests are rejected. The circuit breaker is so aggressive it's effectively a denial-of-service against your own service.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1)
1

📋 Deploy API With Overly Aggressive Circuit Breaker (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost API handles 100+ concurrent users. The ops team added a circuit breaker to prevent cascading failures. But someone set maxConnections: 1 thinking it meant "max connection pool size" — actually it means "only 1 concurrent connection allowed." Most user requests get 503 — the API is effectively down.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S13): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Django API (2 replicas)
├── 02-api-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 8080)
└── 03-destinationrule.yaml        ← DR with BUG: maxConnections=1, pendingRequests=0
BASH — Deploy API with aggressive circuit breaker (BUG inside)
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S13: Circuit Breaker Too Aggressive — 503
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1; kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: anihpj-api, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  replicas: 2; selector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj-api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: anihpj-api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api; image: nginx:alpine; ports: [{containerPort: 8080}]
---
apiVersion: v1; kind: Service
metadata: {name: anihpj-api, namespace: anihpj}
spec: {selector: {app: anihpj-api}, ports: [{port: 8080}]}
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata: {name: anihpj-api-dr, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  host: anihpj-api
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 1    # ❌ BUG! Only 1 concurrent connection!
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 0  # ❌ BUG! Zero pending queue!
        http2MaxRequests: 1
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 1
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Send concurrent requests: kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj -c api -- sh -c 'curl -s anihpj-api:8080 & curl -s anihpj-api:8080; wait'
✗2. Second request returns HTTP 503 — circuit breaker tripped immediately!
✗3. With normal load of 100+ users, 99% of requests get 503 — the API is effectively DOWN!
✗4. The circuit breaker is protecting a service that isn't overloaded — it IS the overload.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check DestinationRule: kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml
→ maxConnections: 1, http1MaxPendingRequests: 0 — extremely restrictive!
2Check Envoy stats for circuit breaker: istioctl proxy-config stats anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj | grep cx_overflow
→ upstream_cx_overflow: 45 — 45 connections rejected by circuit breaker!
3Understand the settings: maxConnections=1 means only 1 TCP connection to upstream. With 2 replicas and 100 users, 99 connections get 503.
→ Circuit breaker values are per-upstream-host, not total pool size!
4Check if the service itself is healthy: kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj -c api -- curl -s localhost:8080
→ Returns 200 — the service is fine, the circuit breaker is the problem!
5Root cause: DestinationRule circuit breaker set maxConnections=1 and http1MaxPendingRequests=0. This allows only 1 concurrent connection with no queue — any second request gets 503. The fix: set maxConnections to a reasonable value (100+) and http1MaxPendingRequests to at least 10 to allow a pending queue.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
503 errors → Check circuit breaker settings
②
kubectl get dr → maxConnections=1 (too low)
③
Envoy stats → upstream_cx_overflow confirms CB
④
Increase limits → 100 connections, 10 pending
⑤
Concurrent requests succeed → No more 503 ✅

Tenet: Circuit breaker settings are per-upstream-host, not per-service or per-cluster. maxConnections=1 means each upstream pod can handle only 1 connection. With 2 replicas, you get 2 concurrent connections total. http1MaxPendingRequests is the queue for overflow — set to 0 means no queue. Always scale circuit breakers to your expected load: maxConnections=100+, pendingRequests=10+. Use istioctl proxy-config stats to monitor rejection metrics.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" anihpj-api:8080 & done; wait 200 503 503 ← Only 1 request succeeds! Circuit breaker rejects the rest!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/trafficPolicy/connectionPool/tcp/maxConnections","value":100},{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/trafficPolicy/connectionPool/http/http1MaxPendingRequests","value":10}]' destinationrule.networking.istio.io/anihpj-api-dr patched
$ for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" anihpj-api:8080 & done; wait 200 200 200 ✅ All requests succeed!
🔧
BASH — Patch DestinationRule with reasonable circuit breaker values
# Step 1: Increase circuit breaker limits
kubectl patch dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/trafficPolicy/connectionPool/tcp/maxConnections","value":100},{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/trafficPolicy/connectionPool/http/http1MaxPendingRequests","value":10}]'
# Step 2: Verify changes
kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 connectionPool
# Step 3: Test concurrent requests
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" anihpj-api:8080 & done; wait
✓

✅ Verify — Concurrent Requests Succeed, No More 503

After increasing maxConnections to 100 and http1MaxPendingRequests to 10, the circuit breaker allows normal traffic flow. Multiple concurrent requests succeed without 503 errors. The API handles 100+ concurrent users. The circuit breaker still protects against genuine overload (100+ connections) but no longer blocks normal traffic.

💡 Key takeaway: Circuit breaker maxConnections is per-upstream-host, not a pool total. With N replicas and maxConnections=M, total capacity = N×M. http1MaxPendingRequests=0 means NO queue — connections beyond the limit get immediate 503. Always set a pending queue (10-100) for burst tolerance. Monitor upstream_cx_overflow to detect circuit breaker trips.

🧪 SCENARIO S14 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Egress Debug

Connect API to External Payment Service — Fix ServiceEntry DNS Resolution Timeout

The Problem: The anihpj-api needs to call an external payment service at api.payment-gateway.com. You created a ServiceEntry to allow egress, but the API gets connection timeout. The ServiceEntry has resolution: NONE (the default) which means Istio treats the host as an IP — but it's a DNS name that needs resolution. With resolution: NONE, Envoy expects the application to resolve DNS itself and connect to an IP. Since the application uses the hostname directly, the DNS resolution never happens through the sidecar, and the connection times out. The fix: change to resolution: DNS so Istio resolves the hostname before connecting.

📋 Deploy API + ServiceEntry With Wrong Resolution (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost processes payments via api.payment-gateway.com. The ops team created a ServiceEntry for egress, but the API calls timeout after 30 seconds. The ServiceEntry has resolution: NONE — Istio treats the host as a raw IP and doesn't resolve DNS. Payment processing is completely down — no transactions can complete.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S14): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Django API (1 replica)
├── 02-serviceentry.yaml           ← ServiceEntry with BUG: resolution: NONE
└── 03-destinationrule.yaml        ← DR for TLS origination

# SCENARIO S14: ServiceEntry Wrong Resolution — DNS Timeout
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -

kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:

    spec:
      containers:

        image: curlimages/curl
        command: ["sleep", "3600"]
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: payment-gateway
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.payment-gateway.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: NONE    # ❌ BUG! NONE means no DNS resolution — host treated as IP!
EOF

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Test external call: kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj -- curl -sk --connect-timeout 5 https://api.payment-gateway.com
✗2. Returns connection timed out after 30 seconds — DNS never resolved!
✗3. The ServiceEntry exists but Envoy treats the host as a raw IP — no DNS lookup happens!
✗4. Payment processing is completely DOWN — transactions timeout. Revenue is being lost.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check ServiceEntry resolution: kubectl get se payment-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep resolution
→ resolution: NONE — host treated as raw IP, DNS not resolved!
2Understand resolution modes: NONE=IP, STATIC=explicit IPs, DNS=resolve hostname
→ For hostnames like api.payment-gateway.com, you need resolution: DNS!
3Check Envoy clusters: istioctl proxy-config clusters anihpj-api-xxx -n anihpj | grep payment
→ Cluster exists but has no endpoints — DNS was never resolved!
4Verify DNS would resolve: kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj -- nslookup api.payment-gateway.com
→ DNS resolves fine from the pod — the issue is Envoy never tries!
5Root cause: ServiceEntry resolution: NONE tells Envoy the host is an IP address — no DNS resolution is performed. For hostname-based external services, use resolution: DNS so Istio/Envoy resolves the hostname before connecting. With NONE, Envoy tries to connect to the literal string "api.payment-gateway.com" as an IP, which fails.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
External call timeout → Check ServiceEntry
②
resolution: NONE → Host treated as IP
③
Envoy cluster has no endpoints
④
Change to resolution: DNS → Envoy resolves hostname
⑤
curl succeeds → Payment gateway reachable ✅

Tenet: ServiceEntry resolution determines how Istio resolves the host: NONE = raw IP, STATIC = explicit endpoints, DNS = DNS lookup. For external hostnames like api.payment-gateway.com, you MUST use resolution: DNS. With NONE, Envoy tries to connect to the literal string as an IP — it fails. This is testable on the ICA exam: always check ServiceEntry resolution mode when external calls fail.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State
$ kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj -- curl -sk --connect-timeout 5 https://api.payment-gateway.com curl: (28) Connection timed out after 5001 milliseconds ← Timeout! DNS never resolved — resolution: NONE treats host as IP!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch se payment-gateway -n anihpj --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/resolution","value":"DNS"}]' serviceentry.networking.istio.io/payment-gateway patched
$ kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj -- curl -sk --connect-timeout 5 https://api.payment-gateway.com { "status": "healthy" } ✅ Connected! DNS resolution now works!

BASH — Patch ServiceEntry for DNS resolution

kubectl patch se payment-gateway -n anihpj --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/resolution","value":"DNS"}]'
# Step 2: Verify the change
kubectl get se payment-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep resolution
# Step 3: Test connectivity
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj -- curl -sk --connect-timeout 5 https://api.payment-gateway.com
✓

✅ Verify — External API Reachable Through ServiceEntry

After changing to resolution: DNS, Envoy resolves the hostname and establishes connections to the external service. Payment processing is restored. The API can now reach the external payment gateway through the mesh.

💡 Key takeaway: ServiceEntry resolution modes: NONE for IP-based services, STATIC for explicit endpoint IPs, DNS for hostname-based services. The default is NONE — always check resolution mode when external calls fail. For hostnames that change IPs (CDNs, cloud APIs), use DNS for dynamic resolution.

⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Send test request: kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api-v1 -n anihpj -c api -- curl -s anihpj-api:8080
✗2. Check v2 logs: kubectl logs deploy/anihpj-api-v2 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy → EVERY request mirrored!
✗3. 100% of traffic duplicated — v2 receives full production load instead of 10%!
✗4. Test environment crashes, production latency doubles from mirror overhead.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check VirtualService mirror config: kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 mirror
→ mirror is on the main route with weight: 100 — ALL traffic mirrored!
2Understand mirror behavior: When mirror is on a route, Istio mirrors ALL traffic matching that route
→ To mirror only a percentage, you need a separate weighted route for the mirror!
3Correct mirror pattern: Route 1: weight 90 → v1, Route 2: weight 10 → v1 + mirror to v2
→ This mirrors only 10% while keeping 100% to v1!
4Check v2 request count: kubectl logs deploy/anihpj-api-v2 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep GET | wc -l
→ 100 requests sent = 100 mirrored — confirmed 100% duplication!
5Root cause: The mirror field on the main route mirrors ALL traffic matching that route — not a percentage. To mirror a percentage, split the route into two: one with higher weight (no mirror) and one with the desired mirror percentage. The mirror percentage = the route weight with mirror enabled.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
100% mirror → Check VS mirror config
②
Mirror on main route → All traffic mirrored
③
Fix: split route → weight 90 (no mirror) + weight 10 (mirror)
④
Only 10% mirrored → v2 receives desired load
⑤
Production latency normal → mirror working correctly ✅

Tenet: Istio mirroring is ALL-OR-NOTHING per route. If mirror is on a route with weight 100, 100% of traffic is mirrored. To mirror a percentage: create TWO routes to the same destination — one without mirror (weight 90) and one with mirror (weight 10). The mirror percentage equals the weight of the route with mirror enabled. This is the standard Istio traffic mirroring pattern and a common ICA exam scenario.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State
$ for i in $(seq 1 10); do kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api-v1 -n anihpj -c api -- curl -s anihpj-api:8080; done; kubectl logs deploy/anihpj-api-v2 -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep GET | wc -l 10 ← 10 requests sent, 10 mirrored — 100%!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF' apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1 kind: VirtualService metadata: {name: anihpj-api-vs, namespace: anihpj} spec: hosts: [anihpj-api] http: - route: - destination: {host: anihpj-api, subset: v1} weight: 90 - route: - destination: {host: anihpj-api, subset: v1} weight: 10 mirror: {host: anihpj-api, subset: v2} EOF virtualservice.networking.istio.io/anihpj-api-vs configured
🔧
BASH — Reconfigure VS with weighted mirror routes
# Step 1: Apply fixed VirtualService with split routes
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - anihpj-api
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api
        subset: v1
      weight: 90    # 90% — no mirror
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api
        subset: v1
      weight: 10    # 10% — with mirror to v2
    mirror:
      host: anihpj-api
      subset: v2
EOF
# Step 2: Verify the new route configuration
kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A15 "http:"
# Step 3: Test the mirror percentage
kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-api-v1 -n anihpj -c api -- curl -s anihpj-api:8080
✓

✅ Verify — Only 10% of Traffic Mirrored

After splitting the route, 90% of traffic goes to v1 without mirroring, and 10% goes to v1 with mirroring to v2. The test environment receives only the intended traffic volume. Production latency returns to normal. The dark launch is operational.

💡 Key takeaway: Traffic mirroring in Istio is per-route with all-or-nothing semantics. For percentage-based mirroring, create two routes to the same destination with different weights — one with mirror, one without. The mirror percentage = the route weight with mirror enabled. Never put mirror on a route with weight 100 unless you want 100% duplication.

kubectl delete namespace anihpj

🧪 SCENARIO S16 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config CNI Debug

Install Istio with istio-cni — Fix Pods Stuck in ContainerCreating (Calico CNI Conflict)

The Problem: The platform team installs Istio with the istio-cni component enabled, attempting to use Istio's built-in CNI plugin for sidecar traffic redirection. The cluster already runs Calico as its primary CNI. After installation, new pods in the anihpj namespace get stuck in ContainerCreating with the error: "networkPlugin cni failed to set up pod network: Multus: error getting pod annotation". The node has TWO CNI plugins trying to configure pod networking simultaneously — Calico for the primary interface and istio-cni for sidecar iptables rules — and they conflict. Pods can't start, the job board is DOWN, and the deployment window is closing.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster with Calico CNI on node "anih"
1

📋 Install Istio with istio-cni + Deploy anihpj (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is a Django job board running on a production kubeadm cluster with Calico CNI. The DevOps team decides to enable Istio's CNI plugin during installation for "better network performance." The istio-cni DaemonSet installs alongside Calico — the node now has TWO CNI configurations. When the anihpj-web Deployment is created, the kubelet calls both CNI plugins to set up networking. The plugins conflict — Calico claims the primary interface, istio-cni tries to override iptables rules, and the pod gets stuck in ContainerCreating. The job board is dead — no pods can start in Istio-enabled namespaces.

├── 01-web-deployment.yaml         ← Django web frontend (2 replicas)

├── 03-api-deployment.yaml         ← Django REST API (1 replica)
├── 04-api-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 8080)

# 3. DEPLOY THE ANIHPJ WEB + API (pods will STUCK in ContainerCreating!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -

⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n anihpj — All pods show ContainerCreating, never reaching Running
✗2. Check a specific pod: kubectl describe pod -n anihpj anihpj-web-xxx | tail -20 → "networkPlugin cni failed to set up pod network"
✗3. Check CNI plugins on node: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep calico → Calico pods are Running. Also: kubectl get pods -n istio-system | grep cni → istio-cni DaemonSet is Running
✗4. The node has TWO CNI plugins running simultaneously — Calico handles primary networking, istio-cni tries to reconfigure iptables — both claim ownership. The job board cannot deploy ANY pods!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Describe the stuck pod: kubectl describe pod anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj | grep -A10 Events
→ "FailedCreatePodSandBox: networkPlugin cni failed to set up pod network: Multus: error getting pod annotation"
2Check which CNI plugins are installed: ls /etc/cni/net.d/ (on the node via SSH)
→ 10-calico.conflist AND istio-cni.conf — TWO conflicting CNI configs!
3Check istio-cni DaemonSet status: kubectl get ds -n istio-system istio-cni-node
→ istio-cni-node DaemonSet is Running on all nodes — was installed by istioctl with components.cni.enabled=true
4Verify Calico is the PRIMARY CNI: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=calico-node
→ calico-node pods are Running ✅ — Calico is the cluster's CNI. istio-cni conflicts with it!
5Check if istio-cni is needed: Istio's CNI is optional — it only provides an alternative to init-container-based iptables redirection. It is NOT required for Istio to work. Calico + Istio init containers work fine WITHOUT istio-cni.
→ istio-cni is installed but the cluster already uses Calico as primary CNI. Two CNI plugins configured on the same node cause a conflict that prevents the kubelet from setting up pod networking. The fix: uninstall istio-cni — Istio works perfectly with Calico using its default init-container iptables configuration.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod ContainerCreating → Check Events → CNI error
②
Check /etc/cni/net.d → TWO CNI configs
③
istio-cni + Calico → Conflict confirmed
④
istio-cni is optional → Remove it
⑤
Pods start → 2/2 READY → Job board back online ✅

Tenet: istio-cni is an optional component — it is NOT required for Istio to function. Its purpose is to replace the istio-init container with a node-level CNI plugin for iptables redirection, reducing pod startup overhead. However, if the cluster already has a CNI (Calico, Cilium, Flannel, etc.), installing istio-cni creates a dual CNI conflict at the node level. The kubelet calls ALL CNI plugins in /etc/cni/net.d/ sequentially and when two plugins try to configure the same pod interface, the second plugin fails. Solution: uninstall istio-cni by re-running istioctl install WITHOUT the cni component flag. The init container approach is the default and works with ALL CNIs.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-api-6f8b7c9d-x 0/2 ContainerCreating 0 5m anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-y 0/2 ContainerCreating 0 5m anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-z 0/2 ContainerCreating 0 5m ← All pods STUCK in ContainerCreating — CNI conflict!
$ kubectl describe pod anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-y -n anihpj | tail -10 Events: Warning FailedCreatePodSandBox 5m kubelet Failed to create pod sandbox: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to set up sandbox container: networkPlugin cni failed to set up pod network: Multus: error getting pod annotation
$ ssh anih "ls /etc/cni/net.d/" 10-calico.conflist istio-cni.conf ← TWO CNI configurations — Calico AND istio-cni conflict!
$ kubectl get ds -n istio-system istio-cni-node NAME DESIRED CURRENT READY UP-TO-DATE AVAILABLE istio-cni-node 1 1 1 1 1 ← istio-cni-node DaemonSet installed — this is the problem!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ istioctl install --set profile=default -y --skip-confirmation ✔ Istio core installed ✔ Istiod installed ✔ Ingress gateways installed ✔ Installation complete (without istio-cni) ✅ NOTE: istio-cni DaemonSet is GONE — only init containers will be used
$ kubectl delete pods --all -n anihpj pod "anihpj-api-6f8b7c9d-x" deleted pod "anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-y" deleted pod "anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-z" deleted
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-api-9f3g7h6j-a 2/2 Running 0 45s anihpj-web-5k8m2n9p-b 2/2 Running 0 40s anihpj-web-5k8m2n9p-c 2/2 Running 0 35s ✅ All pods 2/2 Running — CNI conflict resolved!
🔧
BASH — Remove istio-cni by reinstalling without the cni component 
# Step 1: Reinstall Istio WITHOUT the cni component
# This REMOVES the istio-cni DaemonSet and cleans up /etc/cni/net.d/istio-cni.conf
istioctl install --set profile=default -y --skip-confirmation

# Step 2: Verify istio-cni DaemonSet is GONE
kubectl get ds -n istio-system | grep cni
# Should return EMPTY — istio-cni-node was removed

# Step 3: Verify only Calico CNI config remains on the node
# ssh anih "ls /etc/cni/net.d/" — should show only 10-calico.conflist

# Step 4: Delete stuck pods so they recreate with correct networking
kubectl delete pods --all -n anihpj

# Step 5: Wait and verify all pods are Running 2/2
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
✓

✅ Verify — Pods Running With Only Calico CNI, Init Containers Handle iptables

After reinstalling Istio WITHOUT the CNI component, the istio-cni-node DaemonSet is removed and the conflicting CNI config (istio-cni.conf) is cleaned from /etc/cni/net.d/. The cluster now has only Calico as the CNI. New pods use the istio-init init container (default behavior) to configure iptables for traffic redirection — this approach works with ANY CNI without conflict. All anihpj pods show 2/2 READY — the Django web frontend and API backend are fully operational. The job board is back online, serving employers and applicants.

💡 Key takeaway: istio-cni is optional. It only replaces the istio-init container with a node-level CNI plugin — it does NOT replace your cluster's primary CNI (Calico/Cilium/Flannel). Installing istio-cni on a cluster that already has a CNI creates a conflict because both plugins try to configure the same pod interface. On the ICA exam, "pods stuck in ContainerCreating after Istio install" typically means a CNI conflict. The fix is always: reinstall Istio without the CNI component OR remove the conflicting CNI config from /etc/cni/net.d/. The init container approach works universally.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside (pods, services, deployments)
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Verify no leftover pods
kubectl get all -n anihpj 2>/dev/null

# Optional: Remove istio-cni DaemonSet if still present
# kubectl delete ds istio-cni-node -n istio-system 2>/dev/null

# Optional: Clean node-level CNI config if leftover
# ssh anih "sudo rm /etc/cni/net.d/istio-cni.conf 2>/dev/null"

Install Istio with Helm — Fix Missing Kiali, Jaeger & Grafana (Wrong Profile Selected)

The Problem: The DevOps team installs Istio via Helm, intending to use the demo profile (which includes Kiali, Jaeger, Grafana, and Prometheus for observability). However, they accidentally use the default profile — which only installs istiod and the ingress gateway. ⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Try Kiali dashboard: istioctl dashboard kiali → "Error: no pods for kiali found"
✗2. Check istio-system pods: kubectl get pods -n istio-system — Only istiod pods exist. NO kiali, NO jaeger, NO grafana, NO prometheus!
✗3. Check installed addons: kubectl get svc -n istio-system | grep -E "kiali|jaeger|grafana|prometheus" → No results
✗4. The observability stack is completely ABSENT — the team has NO way to visualize traffic, traces, or metrics. Debugging any mesh issue is blind.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check what was installed: helm list -n istio-system
→ istio-base + istiod installed. NO kiali, jaeger, grafana, prometheus charts!
2Check Istio profile used: istioctl profile dump (shows current config vs available profiles)
→ The "default" profile was used. Default = istiod + ingress gateway ONLY. Demo = everything!
3Compare profiles: istioctl profile dump default vs istioctl profile dump demo
→ demo profile includes: kiali, jaeger, grafana, prometheus, egressgateway, etc.
4Check what's available for helm install: helm search repo istio
→ Charts available: istio/base, istio/istiod, istio/gateway — addons must be installed SEPARATELY via istioctl or istio/addons chart!
5Root cause: Istio was installed via Helm with the "default" profile (istiod + ingress only). The observability addons (Kiali, Jaeger, Grafana, Prometheus) are NOT included in the default profile — they must be installed separately using istioctl or the istio/addons Helm chart. The team confused "istioctl install --set profile=demo" (one command, everything included) with "helm install" (modular, addons separate). The addons were simply never deployed.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Kiali 404 → No kiali pods in istio-system
②
Check installed charts → Only base + istiod
③
Compare profiles → Default vs Demo difference
④
Install addons via istioctl or separate Helm charts
⑤
Kiali + Jaeger + Grafana operational → Observability restored ✅

Tenet: Istio offers multiple installation methods: istioctl install (profiles: default, demo, minimal, ambient, etc.) and Helm (modular charts: base, istiod, gateway). The demo profile in istioctl includes ALL addons (Kiali, Jaeger, Grafana, Prometheus). Helm is modular — you install istiod and then separately install addons. Mixing these concepts causes confusion. On the ICA exam, if Kiali/Jaeger/Grafana are missing, check the installation method first: istioctl (reinstall with demo profile) or Helm (install addon charts separately). Know the difference.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ istioctl dashboard kiali Error: no pods found for service kiali in namespace istio-system ← Kiali was NEVER installed — default profile excludes it!
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE istiod-7d8f9c5b-x 1/1 Running 0 10m ← ONLY istiod! No kiali, jaeger, grafana, prometheus!

✅ Verify — Full Observability Stack Operational

After applying the Istio addons from samples/addons/, the observability stack is fully deployed: Kiali shows the anihpj service graph (web → api traffic flow), Jaeger captures distributed traces across the mesh, Grafana displays Prometheus metrics dashboards, and Prometheus scrapes Envoy metrics from all sidecars. istioctl dashboard kiali now opens the service mesh visualization. The team can finally monitor, trace, and debug the mesh — the job board's observability is restored.

💡 Key takeaway: istioctl install --set profile=demo installs EVERYTHING in one command (ideal for labs/learning). Helm install is modular — you install istiod first, then add addons separately via samples/addons/ or individual Helm charts. The "default" profile is production-oriented (minimal components). Know which profile includes what — this is a common ICA exam gap. On the exam, if asked to install Istio with full observability, use profile=demo with istioctl or apply addons separately for Helm.

S18
🧪 SCENARIO S18 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Profile Debug

Deploy Ambient Mesh — Fix ztunnel Missing (default Profile Instead of ambient)

The Problem: The architecture team decides to pilot Istio's new ambient mesh (sidecar-less, using ztunnel per-node + waypoint proxies). They intend to install with the ambient profile but accidentally run the standard istioctl install with the default profile. The installation succeeds — but ztunnel is nowhere to be found. Pods still get sidecars injected (1→2 containers) instead of leveraging the node-level ztunnel. The ambient mesh pilot is a failure because the wrong profile was selected — the mesh is running in traditional sidecar mode, consuming double the expected resources.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Dev/test cluster for new features like ambient mesh
1

📋 Install Istio (default profile, not ambient) + Deploy anihpj (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is being migrated to Istio ambient mesh to reduce resource consumption. The team has read about ztunnel — a Rust-based per-node proxy that handles L4 traffic without sidecars. They plan to install ambient mesh and test the anihpj-web deployment without sidecars. But the install command uses the default profile (sidecar mode) — ztunnel is never deployed. Pods still get the full istio-proxy sidecar (150MB+ per pod), defeating the purpose of ambient mesh. The "ambient mesh pilot" is actually running traditional sidecar mode — nobody noticed until resource usage didn't decrease.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S18): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj (no injection label — ambient uses different mechanism)
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml         ← Django web frontend (2 replicas, no sidecar annotation)
├── 02-web-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
└── istio/                         ← BUG: default profile instead of ambient
    └── install-cmd.sh              ← istioctl install (default) — should be istioctl install --set profile=ambient
BASH — Install Istio (default profile) + Deploy anihpj (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S18: Ambient Mesh Failed — Wrong Profile (default instead of ambient)
# ============================================

# 1. INSTALL ISTIO (BUG: default profile = sidecar mode, NOT ambient!)
# Team intended: istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y
# Actually ran:   istioctl install --set profile=default -y
istioctl install --set profile=default -y

# 2. CREATE NAMESPACE WITHOUT INJECTION LABEL (ambient doesn't use namespace labels)
kubectl create namespace anihpj
# NOTE: No istio-injection label — ambient mesh uses different mechanism!

# 3. DEPLOY ANIHPJ-WEB (expecting NO sidecar in ambient mode)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-web
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 128Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF

# 4. CHECK IF AMBIENT MESH IS WORKING (it's NOT!)
# Expected: ztunnel DaemonSet running, pods show 1/1 (no sidecar)
# Actual:   No ztunnel, pods will show 1/1 because namespace has no injection label
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check ztunnel DaemonSet: kubectl get ds -n istio-system ztunnel → "Error from server (NotFound): daemonsets.apps 'ztunnel' not found"
✗2. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → Pods show 1/1 (no sidecar)... but this is because the namespace isn't labeled, NOT because ambient is working!
✗3. Check istio-system: kubectl get pods -n istio-system → Only istiod + ingressgateway. NO ztunnel, NO istio-cni!
✗4. The "ambient mesh" deployment has ZERO ambient components — it's just a standard sidecar-mode Istio. The team's ambient mesh pilot is a complete failure.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check installed profile: istioctl profile dump — shows current config
→ Current profile: default. Ambient profile includes ztunnel + istio-cni components!
2Compare profiles: istioctl profile dump ambient vs istioctl profile dump default
→ ambient profile: ztunnel DaemonSet, istio-cni, waypoint proxies. default profile: istiod + ingress ONLY!
3Check if ztunnel would exist with ambient: The ambient profile deploys ztunnel as a DaemonSet (Rust-based per-node proxy) and istio-cni for transparent traffic capture
→ Ambient = NO sidecars. Traffic redirection via ztunnel (L4) + waypoint proxy (L7). Default = sidecars in every pod.
4Verify pod containers: kubectl get pod -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[*].name}'
→ "anihpj-web" — only 1 container. But this is because the namespace has no injection label, NOT because ambient is working!
5Root cause: The team installed Istio with the "default" profile instead of "ambient". The ambient profile deploys ztunnel (a per-node Rust proxy DaemonSet), istio-cni, and waypoint proxies — enabling sidecar-less mesh. The default profile only deploys istiod and ingress gateways. Without ztunnel, ambient mesh cannot function — pods need sidecars. The namespace wasn't labeled for injection (because ambient uses a different mechanism), so pods have NO proxy at all — they're completely outside the mesh. The ambient mesh pilot failed because the wrong profile was installed.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
No ztunnel → Check installed profile → default
②
Compare profiles → ambient has ztunnel + cni
③
Reinstall with ambient profile → ztunnel deploys
④
Label namespace for ambient → pods 1/1 with ztunnel
⑤
No sidecar injection → Ambient mesh operational ✅

Tenet: Ambient mesh is Istio's sidecar-less mode — ztunnel (Rust per-node proxy) handles L4 traffic and waypoint proxies handle L7. It uses a COMPLETELY different architecture from traditional sidecar mode. The ambient profile deploys ztunnel, istio-cni, and waypoint infrastructure. The default profile deploys istiod + ingressgateway for traditional sidecar mode. These profiles are mutually exclusive. On the ICA exam, you must know: ambient = istioctl install --set profile=ambient, traditional = istioctl install --set profile=default. Mixing them (ambient namespace with default profile) results in unprotected pods.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get ds -n istio-system ztunnel Error from server (NotFound): daemonsets.apps "ztunnel" not found ← ztunnel was NEVER deployed — default profile doesn't include it!
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE istiod-7d8f9c5b-x 1/1 Running 0 10m istio-ingressgateway-xxx 1/1 Running 0 10m ← Standard sidecar-mode Istio. NO ztunnel, NO istio-cni!
$ istioctl profile dump | grep -A5 "components" components: ingressGateways: - name: istio-ingressgateway enabled: true egressGateways: [] # ← NO ztunnel component! This is NOT ambient mesh!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y --skip-confirmation ✔ Istio core installed ✔ Istiod installed ✔ CNI installed ✔ ztunnel installed ✅ ✔ Installation complete — AMBIENT MESH profile active!
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE istiod-9f3g7h6j-a 1/1 Running 0 2m istio-cni-node-xxx 1/1 Running 0 2m ztunnel-5k8m2n9p-b 1/1 Running 0 2m ztunnel-5k8m2n9p-c 1/1 Running 0 2m ✅ ztunnel DaemonSet running — AMBIENT MESH IS LIVE!
🔧
BASH — Reinstall with ambient profile + enable ambient for namespace 
# Step 1: Uninstall the default profile (sidecar mode)
istioctl uninstall --purge -y

# Step 2: Install Istio with AMBIENT profile
istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y --skip-confirmation

# Step 3: Verify ztunnel DaemonSet is deployed
kubectl get ds -n istio-system ztunnel
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=ztunnel

# Step 4: Enable ambient mesh for the namespace (different from sidecar injection!)
# Ambient uses dataplane mode label, not istio-injection
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient

# Step 5: Restart pods — they should stay 1/1 (no sidecar in ambient mode)
kubectl rollout restart deploy anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 6: Verify pods have 1 container (ztunnel on node handles L4 traffic)
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# Should show 1/1 READY — ztunnel handles traffic, no sidecar needed!
✓

✅ Verify — Ambient Mesh Active, No Sidecars, ztunnel Handles L4 Traffic

After reinstalling Istio with the ambient profile, the ztunnel DaemonSet is running on every node and istio-cni is handling transparent traffic capture. The anihpj namespace is labeled with istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient, and after restarting the deployment, pods show 1/1 READY — no sidecar container. All pod traffic flows through the node-level ztunnel for L4 (TCP/TLS) and can be upgraded to L7 via waypoint proxies. The ambient mesh pilot is now a success — pods consume half the resources without sidecars.

💡 Key takeaway: Ambient mesh uses the ambient profile which deploys ztunnel (per-node DaemonSet) and istio-cni (for transparent traffic capture). The namespace label is istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient (NOT istio-injection=enabled). In ambient mode, pods show 1/1 (no sidecar) because ztunnel operates at the node level. L7 features (routing, authZ) require waypoint proxies. This is a key ICA exam distinction: know the difference between sidecar mode and ambient mode — different install profiles, different namespace labels, different pod behavior.

🧹

# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Uninstall ambient mesh
# istioctl uninstall --purge -y

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ds -n istio-system ztunnel 2>/dev/null
S19
🧪 SCENARIO S19 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Trust Debug

Join Remote Cluster to Primary — Fix mTLS Handshake Failure (Trust Domain Mismatch)

The Problem: The platform team is setting up a multi-cluster Istio mesh with a primary cluster (on kubeadm) and a remote cluster (kind-cl3). The remote cluster is configured to join the primary's mesh. The anihpj-api runs on the primary cluster and anihpj-web runs on the remote cluster. The web pod needs to call the API pod across clusters via mTLS. But the mTLS handshake fails with "certificate verification error: SAN mismatch". The root cause: the remote cluster was installed with the default trust domain cluster.local, but the primary expects cluster-2.local. The SPIFFE identities don't match — cross-cluster mTLS is completely broken. The distributed job board can't function because web→api traffic is blocked at the TLS layer.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 5 (kind-cl3) — Remote cluster joining primary on kubeadm
1

📋 Join Remote Cluster to Primary Mesh + Deploy anihpj (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost runs as a distributed application across two clusters: anihpj-api (Django REST backend + PostgreSQL) on the kubeadm primary cluster, and anihpj-web (Django frontend) on the kind-cl3 remote cluster. The web pod on cl3 calls the API pod on kubeadm via cross-cluster mTLS. The remote cluster joins the primary's mesh but with the wrong trust domain — it uses the default cluster.local instead of the primary's cluster-2.local. Envoy proxies on the remote cluster issue certificates with SPIFFE ID spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/default, but the primary's Envoys expect spiffe://cluster-2.local/.... The TLS handshake fails because the SAN in the certificate doesn't match the expected trust domain. Cross-cluster traffic is dead — the web UI shows "API Gateway Timeout" for every request.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S19): 
anihpj/
├── primary/                        ← kubeadm (cluster 1)
│   ├── 00-namespace.yaml           ← ns anihpj with istio-injection + trust domain: cluster-2.local
│   ├── 01-api-deployment.yaml      ← Django REST API (1 replica)
│   ├── 02-api-service.yaml         ← ClusterIP Service (port 8080)
│   └── istio/
│       └── install-primary.sh       ← istioctl install with meshID + trustDomain
├── remote/                         ← kind-cl3 (cluster 5)
│   ├── 00-namespace.yaml           ← ns anihpj with istio-injection + BUG: trust domain cluster.local
│   ├── 01-web-deployment.yaml      ← Django web frontend (2 replicas)
│   ├── 02-web-service.yaml         ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
│   └── istio/
│       └── install-remote.sh        ← BUG: missing --set meshConfig.trustDomain=cluster-2.local
BASH — Install Remote Cluster Istio + Deploy anihpj-web (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S19: Multi-Cluster Trust Domain Mismatch — mTLS Handshake Failure
# ============================================

# === ON PRIMARY CLUSTER (ksw → 1: kubeadm) ===
# Install Istio with custom trust domain (correct)
istioctl install --set profile=default \
  --set meshConfig.trustDomain=cluster-2.local \
  --set meshConfig.accessLogFile=/dev/stdout -y
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled topology.istio.io/network=network-2
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-api
  ports:
  - port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
EOF

# === ON REMOTE CLUSTER (ksw → 5: kind-cl3) ===
# Install Istio — BUG: missing trustDomain override!
# CORRECT would be: --set meshConfig.trustDomain=cluster-2.local
istioctl install --set profile=default -y
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled topology.istio.io/network=network-2
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-web
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        env:
        - name: API_URL
          value: "http://anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8080"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. On remote cluster: kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -c anihpj-web -- curl anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8080/health → Connection timeout / TLS error
✗2. Check Envoy logs on remote web sidecar: kubectl logs deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep -i "cert\|tls\|trust" → "certificate verification error: SAN mismatch"
✗3. Check SPIFFE identity on remote: istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj → Shows spiffe://cluster.local/... instead of spiffe://cluster-2.local/...
✗4. Cross-cluster mTLS is DEAD — the web frontend on the remote cluster cannot securely reach the API on the primary. The multi-cluster job board is non-functional.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check trust domain on remote cluster: kubectl get configmap -n istio-system istio -o yaml | grep trustDomain
→ trustDomain: cluster.local (DEFAULT — should be cluster-2.local to match primary!)
2Check trust domain on primary cluster: Same command on kubeadm
→ trustDomain: cluster-2.local (custom — this is what the PRIMARY expects)
3Compare SPIFFE identities: Remote Envoy cert has spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/default but primary expects spiffe://cluster-2.local/...
→ MISMATCH! The primary's Envoy rejects the certificate because SPIFFE SAN doesn't match trusted domain!
4Verify mTLS STRICT is configured: kubectl get peerauthentication -n anihpj (if STRICT, ALL traffic requires valid mTLS)
→ STRICT mTLS means every cross-cluster connection must pass TLS verification. Mismatched trust domains = all connections rejected.
5Root cause: The remote cluster was installed without the --set meshConfig.trustDomain=cluster-2.local flag, so it uses the default trust domain cluster.local. The primary cluster uses cluster-2.local. In a multi-cluster mesh, ALL clusters MUST share the same trust domain for mTLS to work — Envoy uses SPIFFE identities for certificate verification and if the domains differ, certificates from the remote cluster are rejected as untrusted. The fix: reinstall the remote cluster's Istio with the matching trust domain, or configure trustDomainAliases on the primary to also trust cluster.local.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Cross-cluster call fails → Check Envoy logs → SAN mismatch
②
Check trust domain → Remote=cluster.local, Primary=cluster-2.local
③
Trust domains MUST match in multi-cluster
④
Reinstall remote with matching trustDomain
⑤
mTLS handshake succeeds → Cross-cluster traffic flows ✅

Tenet: In a multi-cluster Istio mesh, the trust domain forms the root of all SPIFFE identities. All clusters in the same mesh MUST share the same trust domain. When you install Istio on the primary cluster with a custom trust domain (e.g., cluster-2.local), every remote cluster joining that mesh MUST be installed with the SAME trust domain. The default is cluster.local — if your primary uses a custom domain, specify it explicitly with --set meshConfig.trustDomain=<domain> on every cluster. Alternative: configure trustDomainAliases on the primary to also accept certificates from the default domain.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- curl -v anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8080/health 2>&1 | head -20 * TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Client hello (1): * TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS alert, certificate unknown (46): * error:0A000418:SSL routines::tlsv1 alert unknown ca * curl: (35) OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SSL ← mTLS handshake FAILED — certificate not trusted!
$ kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml | grep trustDomain trustDomain: cluster.local ← Remote cluster uses DEFAULT trust domain — should be cluster-2.local!
$ istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj | grep -A2 "URI" URI: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/default ← SPIFFE identity uses "cluster.local" — primary expects "cluster-2.local"!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ istioctl install --set profile=default --set meshConfig.trustDomain=cluster-2.local -y ✔ Istio core installed ✔ Istiod installed ✔ Installation complete ✅ Remote cluster now uses trust domain: cluster-2.local!
$ kubectl rollout restart deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --timeout=120s
$ kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -c anihpj-web -- curl -s anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8080/health {"status": "healthy", "version": "1.0.0"} ✅ Cross-cluster mTLS working! Web → API via trusted SPIFFE identity!
🔧
BASH — Reinstall remote cluster Istio with matching trustDomain 
# Step 1: Uninstall Istio from the remote cluster
istioctl uninstall --purge -y
kubectl delete namespace istio-system

# Step 2: Reinstall Istio WITH the matching trust domain
# THIS IS THE FIX: --set meshConfig.trustDomain MUST match the primary!
istioctl install --set profile=default \
  --set meshConfig.trustDomain=cluster-2.local \
  -y

# Step 3: Label namespace and add network topology
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled topology.istio.io/network=network-2 --overwrite

# Step 4: Restart workloads to get new certs with correct SPIFFE identity
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj

# Step 5: Wait for rollouts and verify mTLS
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s
istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj | grep URI
✓

✅ Verify — Cross-Cluster mTLS Operational With Matching Trust Domain

After reinstalling the remote cluster's Istio with meshConfig.trustDomain=cluster-2.local and restarting the workloads, new Envoy sidecars receive certificates with SPIFFE identity spiffe://cluster-2.local/ns/anihpj/sa/default. The primary cluster's Envoys now recognize and trust these certificates because the trust domain matches. Cross-cluster mTLS handshakes complete successfully — the web frontend on the remote cluster can securely call the API on the primary. The distributed anihpj/jobpost is fully operational across both clusters.

💡 Key takeaway: In multi-cluster Istio, the trust domain is the root of all SPIFFE identities. It MUST be identical across all clusters in the mesh. If your primary uses a custom trust domain, EVERY remote cluster MUST specify --set meshConfig.trustDomain=<same-domain> during installation. Mismatched trust domains cause ALL cross-cluster mTLS to fail — Envoy rejects certificates from different trust domains. On the ICA exam, multi-cluster trust domain configuration is a critical topic. Always verify: kubectl get cm istio -n istio-system -o yaml | grep trustDomain on every cluster.
