kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Uninstall Istio from remote cluster
# istioctl uninstall --purge -y
# kubectl delete namespace istio-system

# On primary cluster, clean up api namespace
# ksw 1
# kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S20
🧪 SCENARIO S20 — Category 1: Install/Upgrade/Config Rollback Debug

Rollback Istio 1.22 to 1.20 — Fix Revision Label Preventing Downgrade

The Problem: The ops team performs a canary upgrade from Istio 1.20 to 1.22 by installing the new revision and migrating the anihpj namespace via istio.io/rev=1-22. After the upgrade, they discover that Istio 1.22 introduces a regression — circuit breakers are too aggressive, causing 503 errors on the anihpj-api service. They need to roll back to 1.20. But when they change the namespace label back to istio.io/rev=1-20 and restart the pods, the istio-proxy sidecars fail to start with: "error adding pod to controller: revision 1-20 pod injection failed." The istiod-1-20 control plane was decommissioned during the upgrade — only istiod-1-22 exists. The rollback is blocked because the old revision's control plane was prematurely removed. The team is stuck on the broken 1.22 with no rollback path.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 4 (kind-cl2) — Multi-cluster mesh node simulating production upgrade
1

📋 Canary Upgrade to 1.22 + Prematurely Decommission 1.20 (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is running on Istio 1.20 in production on kind-cl2. The platform team performs a canary upgrade: install istiod-1-22 alongside istiod-1-20, migrate the anihpj namespace to the new revision, verify the API health, then — in a rush to clean up — prematurely decommission istiod-1-20. Hours later, users report 503 errors on the API (Istio 1.22 regression). The team tries to roll back by changing istio.io/rev=1-20 but istiod-1-20 is GONE. New pods can't get sidecars because the mutating webhook finds no istiod for revision 1-20. The rollback is impossible — the job board is stuck on a broken Istio with no path back.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S20): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj (revision label: istio.io/rev=1-22)
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Django REST API (1 replica, affected by 1.22 regression)
├── 02-api-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 8080)
├── 03-web-deployment.yaml         ← Django web frontend (2 replicas)
├── 04-web-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
└── istio/                         ← Canary upgrade + premature decommission
    ├── 01-install-1-20.sh          ← Original 1.20 install
    ├── 02-canary-upgrade-1-22.sh   ← Add 1-22 revision
    └── 03-decommission-1-20.sh     ← BUG: Premature cleanup of 1-20!
BASH — Canary upgrade to 1.22 + Premature cleanup of 1.20 (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S20: Rollback Blocked — Revision 1-20 Decommissioned Prematurely
# ============================================

# 1. INSTALL ISTIO 1.20 (simulates existing production)
istioctl install --set revision=1-20 --set profile=default -y

# 2. CREATE NAMESPACE AND DEPLOY ANIHPJ ON 1.20
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio.io/rev=1-20 istio-injection=enabled
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-api
  ports:
  - port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-web
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF

# 3. CANARY UPGRADE TO 1.22
istioctl install --set revision=1-22 --set profile=default -y
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio.io/rev=1-22 --overwrite
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj

# 4. PREMATURELY DECOMMISSION 1.20 (BUG: this breaks rollback!)
istioctl uninstall --revision=1-20 -y
# istiod-1-20 is NOW GONE — rollback is impossible!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Users report 503 errors on anihpj-api — Istio 1.22 has a regression with circuit breakers
✗2. Attempt rollback: kubectl label ns anihpj istio.io/rev=1-20 --overwrite && kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj
✗3. New pods show 1/1 instead of 2/2 — istio-proxy sidecar NOT injected! Events: "revision 1-20 pod injection failed"
✗4. The rollback is DEAD — istiod-1-20 was prematurely removed. The job board is stuck on broken 1.22 with NO downgrade path!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check available istiod revisions: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod
→ ONLY istiod-1-22 is Running. istiod-1-20 was decommissioned — it no longer exists!
2Check pod events for injection failure: kubectl describe pod -n anihpj anihpj-api-xxx | tail -15
→ "error adding pod to controller: revision 1-20 pod injection failed: no running istiod revision found"
3Check IstioOperator resources: kubectl get istiooperator -n istio-system
→ Only installed-state-1-22 exists. installed-state-1-20 was REMOVED during decommission!
4Check namespace revision label: kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels | grep istio.io/rev
→ istio.io/rev=1-20 — pointing to a revision that NO LONGER EXISTS!
5Root cause: The canary upgrade to 1.22 was followed by PREMATURE decommissioning of istiod-1-20. The team removed the old control plane before verifying that 1.22 was stable. When 1.22 proved to be problematic (regression causing 503s), the rollback to 1.20 was impossible because the 1.20 control plane no longer exists. The namespace label points to revision 1-20 but there is no istiod to handle it. Lesson: ALWAYS keep the previous revision running until the new revision is verified stable for at least 24-48 hours. Never decommission the old control plane immediately after migration.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
503 on API → 1.22 regression confirmed
②
Attempt rollback → Pods 1/1, no sidecar
③
Check istiod pods → Only 1-22 exists
④
istiod-1-20 was decommissioned → Rollback blocked
⑤
Reinstall 1-20 → Switch label → Rollback succeeds ✅

Tenet: Canary upgrades in Istio work by running MULTIPLE istiod revisions simultaneously. The namespace label istio.io/rev determines which revision's sidecars get injected. Never decommission the old revision immediately after migration — keep it running as a rollback safety net. If the new revision proves problematic, simply change the namespace label back to the old revision and restart pods. If the old revision was decommissioned, you must REINSTALL it (istioctl install --set revision=1-20) before you can roll back. This is a critical production practice for the ICA exam: canary = safe, in-place + immediate decommission = dangerous.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl label ns anihpj istio.io/rev=1-20 --overwrite kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj namespace/anihpj labeled deployment.apps/anihpj-api restarted deployment.apps/anihpj-web restarted
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-api-6f8b7c9d-x 1/1 Running 0 2m anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-y 1/1 Running 0 2m anihpj-web-7d8f9c5b-z 1/1 Running 0 2m ← 1/1 — NO SIDECAR! istiod-1-20 doesn't exist to inject proxies!
$ kubectl describe pod anihpj-api-6f8b7c9d-x -n anihpj | tail -5 Events: Warning Failed istio-sidecar-injector error adding pod to controller: revision 1-20 pod injection failed: no running istiod revision found ← istiod-1-20 was DECOMMISSIONED — rollback is impossible!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ istioctl install --set revision=1-20 --set profile=default -y ✔ Istio core installed ✔ Istiod installed ✔ Installation complete ✅ istiod-1-20 control plane RESTORED!
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE istiod-1-20-9f3g7h6j-x 1/1 Running 0 2m istiod-1-22-7d8f9c5b-y 1/1 Running 0 2h ✅ Both revisions running — rollback to 1-20 now possible!
$ kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-api-5k8m2n9p-a 2/2 Running 0 45s anihpj-web-9f3g7h6j-b 2/2 Running 0 40s anihpj-web-9f3g7h6j-c 2/2 Running 0 35s ✅ 2/2 READY — Rollback to 1.20 SUCCESSFUL! Job board back online!
🔧
BASH — Reinstall the old revision's control plane + roll back 
# Step 1: Reinstall istiod-1-20 (the old revision was prematurely decommissioned)
istioctl install --set revision=1-20 --set profile=default -y

# Step 2: Verify BOTH revisions are now running
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod
# Should show: istiod-1-20 AND istiod-1-22

# Step 3: Roll back the namespace label to the old (stable) revision
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio.io/rev=1-20 --overwrite

# Step 4: Restart all deployments so new pods get 1.20 sidecars
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n anihpj

# Step 5: Wait for pods to be ready with 1.20 sidecars (2/2)
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s
kubectl get pods -n anihpj

# Step 6: Verify sidecars are connected to istiod-1-20
istioctl proxy-status | grep anihpj
✓

✅ Verify — Rollback to 1.20 Successful, Both Revisions Running

After reinstalling istiod-1-20 and switching the namespace label back, all anihpj pods restart with 2/2 READY — the sidecars are now connected to the stable istiod-1-20 control plane. The 1.22 regression is mitigated — circuit breakers no longer cause 503 errors. Both istiod revisions run simultaneously (1-20 active, 1-22 idling), providing a safe path to troubleshoot the 1.22 issue without disrupting production. The rollback succeeded because the old revision was reinstalled — a lesson in never prematurely decommissioning a control plane revision during canary upgrades.

💡 Key takeaway: Canary upgrade rollback requires the PREVIOUS revision's control plane to still be running. If it was decommissioned, you must reinstall it before the namespace can roll back. The sequence: istioctl install --set revision=<old> → kubectl label ns <ns> istio.io/rev=<old> --overwrite → kubectl rollout restart deploy. Always keep the old revision for 24-48 hours after upgrading. On the ICA exam, "pod sidecar not injected after rollback" = old istiod revision was decommissioned. This is a crucial production readiness concept.

🔀 Category 2: Traffic Ingress/Egress/Routing Lab ScenariosS21-S40

🟢 anihpj/jobpost — Istio Traffic Management

Traffic routing is the core of Istio. These scenarios cover VirtualService misconfigurations, Gateway TLS issues, DestinationRule circuit breakers, ServiceEntry resolution, and traffic mirroring. Each scenario deploys part of the anihpj/jobpost app with intentional traffic routing bugs — your job is to find and fix them. ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Check the cluster requirement at the top of each scenario before applying! All clusters have Istio pre-installed.

S21
🧪 SCENARIO S21 — Category 2: Traffic Routing Subset Debug

Deploy anihpj-api v1/v2/v3 — Fix Traffic Going to Wrong Subset (Label Mismatch)

The Problem: You deploy three versions of anihpj-api (v1=stable, v2=canary, v3=experimental) with a DestinationRule defining subsets and a VirtualService routing /test traffic to the v3 experimental subset. But ALL traffic goes to v1 — the subset routing is completely ignored. The DestinationRule defines subsets with label version: v1, version: v2, version: v3, but the actual pods are labeled with app-version: v1, app-version: v2, app-version: v3. The label key mismatch means NO pods match ANY subset — Istio falls back to the default Service endpoint (v1 only). The A/B testing pipeline is completely broken.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Istio mesh practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj-api v1/v2/v3 with Broken Subset Routing (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is releasing API v3 with experimental ML-powered job recommendations. The ops team created three Deployments (v1, v2, v3) and configured a DestinationRule with subsets. The plan: route 90% to v1 (stable), 10% to v2 (canary), and /test traffic to v3 (experimental). But during label assignment, the team used app-version on pods while the DestinationRule references version. Istio's subset matching uses exact label key matching — the mismatch means ZERO pods match any subset. Traffic falls back to the default Service endpoint, which only has v1 pods registered. The v3 experimental API is deployed but completely invisible to the mesh.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S21): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-api-deployment-v1.yaml      ← Stable API v1 (app-version: v1)
├── 02-api-deployment-v2.yaml      ← Canary API v2 (app-version: v2)
├── 03-api-deployment-v3.yaml      ← Experimental API v3 (app-version: v3)
├── 04-api-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 8080)
├── 05-destinationrule.yaml        ← DR with BUG: subsets use version: label
└── 06-virtualservice.yaml         ← VS routes /test → subset: v3
BASH — Deploy 3 API versions with subset label mismatch (BUG inside) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S21: Subset Label Mismatch — Traffic Goes to Wrong Version
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE AND LABEL FOR INJECTION
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# 2. DEPLOY 3 API VERSIONS (BUG: pods use app-version, DR expects version!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-v1
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-api
    app-version: v1    # ❌ BUG! Pod labels use "app-version"
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
      app-version: v1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
        app-version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        lifecycle:
          postStart:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'v1 (STABLE) - Pod: '$HOSTNAME > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html; mkdir -p /usr/share/nginx/html/test; cp /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/test/index.html"]
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-v2
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-api
    app-version: v2
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
      app-version: v2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
        app-version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        lifecycle:
          postStart:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'v2 (CANARY) - Pod: '$HOSTNAME > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html; mkdir -p /usr/share/nginx/html/test; cp /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/test/index.html"]
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-v3
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-api
    app-version: v3
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
      app-version: v3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
        app-version: v3
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        lifecycle:
          postStart:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'v3 (EXPERIMENTAL) - Pod: '$HOSTNAME > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html; mkdir -p /usr/share/nginx/html/test; cp /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/test/index.html"]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-api
  ports:
  - port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
---
# DestinationRule: subsets use "version" label (BUG: pods have "app-version"!)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: anihpj-api
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1    # ❌ Pods have app-version: v1, not version: v1!
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
  - name: v3
    labels:
      version: v3
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - anihpj-api
  http:
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /test
    route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api
        subset: v3    # Should route /test → v3 experimental
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api
        subset: v1
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api
        subset: v2
      weight: 10
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Test /test route: curl -s anihpj-api:8080/test → Response from v1, not v3!
✗2. Check subset endpoints: istioctl proxy-config endpoints deploy/anihpj-api-v1 -n anihpj --subset v3 → "subset v3 not found"
✗3. Check pod labels: kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels | grep anihpj-api → All pods have app-version=v1/v2/v3, NOT version!
✗4. The v3 experimental API is deployed but receives ZERO traffic — the subset routing is completely broken because no pods match the DestinationRule's label selectors.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check DestinationRule subsets: kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 labels
→ subsets use labels: version: v1/v2/v3
2Check actual pod labels: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-api --show-labels
→ Pods have app-version: v1/v2/v3 — NOT version!
3Compare label keys: DestinationRule matches version, pods expose app-version — these are different label keys!
→ Subset label selectors use EXACT key matching. "version" ≠ "app-version"!
4Check Envoy clusters: istioctl proxy-config clusters deploy/anihpj-api-v1 -n anihpj | grep subset
→ Subset clusters exist but have ZERO endpoints — no pods match the labels!
5Root cause: The DestinationRule subsets use label key "version" (v1, v2, v3) but the actual pods are labeled with "app-version" (v1, v2, v3). Istio's subset matching uses exact label key matching — "version" and "app-version" are different keys, so ZERO pods match any subset. Traffic falls back to the default Service endpoint, which only routes to pods matching the Service selector (app=anihpj-api) — which is only the v1 pods. The fix: update the DestinationRule to use the correct label key "app-version" instead of "version".
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
/test → v1 (wrong!) → Subset routing broken
②
Check DR labels → version: v3
③
Check pod labels → app-version: v3
④
Mismatch! version ≠ app-version
⑤
Fix DR labels → /test now reaches v3 ✅

Tenet: DestinationRule subsets use label selectors to group pods. The selector uses EXACT label key matching — if the key in the DestinationRule doesn't match the key on the pod, the pod is NOT included in the subset. This is the #1 cause of "my subsets don't work" on the ICA exam. Always verify: kubectl get pods -l <label-key>=<label-value> --show-labels and compare with kubectl get dr <name> -o yaml | grep labels. If the subsets have zero endpoints, check label key spelling, case, and naming conventions.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -s anihpj-api:8080/test v1 /test — Welcome to anihpj API v1 ← Expected: v3! But got v1 — subset routing FAILED!
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-api --show-labels NAME READY STATUS LABELS anihpj-api-v1-xx 2/2 Running app=anihpj-api,app-version=v1 anihpj-api-v1-yy 2/2 Running app=anihpj-api,app-version=v1 anihpj-api-v2-zz 2/2 Running app=anihpj-api,app-version=v2 anihpj-api-v3-ww 2/2 Running app=anihpj-api,app-version=v3 ← Pods have "app-version" — NOT "version"!
$ kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 labels labels: version: v1 labels: version: v2 labels: version: v3 ← DR expects "version" — label key MISMATCH!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl delete dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF' apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1 kind: DestinationRule metadata: name: anihpj-api-dr namespace: anihpj spec: host: anihpj-api subsets: - name: v1 labels: app-version: v1 - name: v2 labels: app-version: v2 - name: v3 labels: app-version: v3 EOF
$ curl -s anihpj-api:8080/test v3 /test — Welcome to anihpj API v3 (EXPERIMENTAL) ✅ /test now routes to v3 — subset routing FIXED!
🔧
BASH — Recreate DestinationRule with correct label key 
# Step 1: Delete and recreate DestinationRule with CORRECT label key
kubectl delete dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: anihpj-api
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      app-version: v1    # ✅ FIXED! Matches pod labels
  - name: v2
    labels:
      app-version: v2
  - name: v3
    labels:
      app-version: v3
EOF

# Step 2: Verify subsets now have endpoints
istioctl proxy-config endpoints deploy/anihpj-api-v1 -n anihpj --subset v3

# Step 3: Test /test route goes to v3
curl -s anihpj-api:8080/test
✓

✅ Verify — Subset Routing Operational, All 3 Versions Receiving Traffic

After updating the DestinationRule subsets to use app-version (matching the pod labels), all three subsets now have endpoints. The VirtualService correctly routes /test traffic to the v3 experimental API. The A/B testing pipeline is operational — the ML-powered job recommendation API is now accessible for internal testing.

💡 Key takeaway: DestinationRule subset labels use EXACT key matching against pod labels. If the label key differs (e.g., version vs app-version), the subset will have ZERO endpoints. Always verify with kubectl get pods --show-labels and compare with kubectl get dr -o yaml. On the ICA exam, "my subsets have no endpoints" is almost always a label key mismatch.

S22
🧪 SCENARIO S22 — Category 2: Traffic Routing LB Debug

Benchmark anihpj-api Load Balancing — Fix All Traffic Hitting One Pod (ROUND_ROBIN Not Working)

The Problem: The anihpj-api service runs 3 replicas behind Istio. The DestinationRule specifies loadBalancer: simple: ROUND_ROBIN to distribute traffic evenly. But monitoring shows ALL traffic goes to a single pod — the other 2 replicas receive ZERO requests. The issue: the DestinationRule has trafficPolicy nested under a subset instead of at the top-level, and since no subsets are actually used in the VirtualService routes, the LB policy is never applied. Istio defaults to the Envoy default (LEAST_REQUEST) which, combined with HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connections, pins all requests to a single pod.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Istio mesh practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy anihpj-api with Broken LB Policy (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost API handles high traffic from web and mobile clients. The ops team deployed 3 replicas with a DestinationRule configured for ROUND_ROBIN load balancing. But the LB policy is nested inside a subset definition — and the VirtualService routes directly to the host without referencing any subset. Istio ignores the subset-level traffic policy for routes that don't use subsets. Two API pods sit completely idle while one handles 100% of production traffic — latency spikes as the single pod is overwhelmed.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S22): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Django API (3 replicas)
├── 02-api-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 8080)

✗2. Check DestinationRule: kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A20 trafficPolicy → LB is inside subset, not top-level
✗3. Check VirtualService: kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep subset → No subset referenced!
✗4. 2 out of 3 API pods are IDLE — one pod is overwhelmed. Horizontal scaling is completely wasted.

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Envoy LB for the API cluster: istioctl proxy-config clusters deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj --fqdn anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -o json | grep lb_policy
→ "lb_policy": "LEAST_REQUEST" — NOT ROUND_ROBIN!
2Check if subsets are referenced: istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj | grep subset
→ No subset references — VS routes to host directly!
3Check DR topology: LB policy is inside subsets[0].trafficPolicy
→ Only applies when THAT subset is referenced in a route!
4Check Envoy cluster LB config: istioctl proxy-config clusters deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj --fqdn anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -o json | grep -E "(lb_policy|subset)"
→ lb_policy: LEAST_REQUEST — Envoy default because top-level trafficPolicy is missing!
5Root cause: The ROUND_ROBIN setting is nested inside a subset's trafficPolicy, but the VirtualService routes directly to the host without any subset. Istio ignores subset-level policies when the subset is not used. Fix: move trafficPolicy to the top level of the DestinationRule.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
All traffic to one pod → LB not working
②
Check Envoy LB → LEAST_REQUEST (default)
③
DR has LB inside subset only
④
VS doesn't reference subset → Ignored
⑤
Move LB to top-level → ROUND_ROBIN active ✅

Tenet: DestinationRule traffic policies at the subset level only apply when that specific subset is referenced. Traffic policies at the top level apply to ALL traffic to the host. Envoy defaults to LEAST_REQUEST which can pin all connections to one pod with HTTP/1.1 keep-alive. For service-wide LB policies, always use top-level trafficPolicy.

Deploy anihpj-api v1 + v2 — Fix v2 500 Errors Never Ejected (Missing Outlier Detection)

The Problem: You deploy anihpj-api with two versions: v1 (stable, 2 replicas) and v2 (canary, 1 replica — intentionally broken, returns HTTP 500). The ops team configured a DestinationRule with subsets and traffic splitting (90% v1, 10% v2) via VirtualService. But there's a critical bug: the DestinationRule has NO outlierDetection configured. The broken v2 pod returns 500 on every request, but Envoy never ejects it. ~10% of production traffic keeps failing with 500 errors. The circuit breaker that should automatically eject unhealthy pods was never configured — the team assumed Istio handles it by default. It doesn't. Your job: find why v2 is still receiving traffic despite continuous 500 errors, add outlier detection to the DestinationRule, and verify v2 gets ejected so all traffic flows to v1.

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Verify v2 returns 500: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" anihpj-api:8080/ — run multiple times
→ ~10% return 500 (v2), ~90% return 200 (v1) — v2 is broken but still in the pool!
2Check DestinationRule for outlierDetection: kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml
→ trafficPolicy has loadBalancer: ROUND_ROBIN but NO outlierDetection block at all!

→ No outlier_detection section in Envoy config — Istio never pushed any!

5Root cause: The DestinationRule has subsets (v1, v2) and a loadBalancer policy, but outlierDetection is COMPLETELY MISSING. Istio does NOT enable circuit breaking by default — you must explicitly configure it. Without outlierDetection, Envoy has no mechanism to detect that v2 is returning 500 errors and eject it from the load balancing pool. The broken canary receives traffic indefinitely. Fix: add outlierDetection to the DestinationRule with proper thresholds (consecutive5xxErrors: 5, interval: 10s, baseEjectionTime: 30s, maxEjectionPercent: 50).
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
~10% 500 errors → v2 still in pool
②
Check DR → subsets exist, no outlierDetection
③
Check Envoy → v2 HEALTHY, never ejected
④
Istio does NOT auto-enable circuit breakers!
⑤
Add outlierDetection → v2 ejected → 100% 200 ✅

Tenet: Istio does NOT enable outlier detection (circuit breaking) by default. You must explicitly add outlierDetection to the DestinationRule's trafficPolicy. Without it, Envoy treats all endpoints equally — a pod returning 500 errors forever will keep receiving traffic. This is a critical production gap: always configure outlier detection alongside any canary deployment. The key settings: consecutive5xxErrors (how many errors before ejection), interval (evaluation window), baseEjectionTime (how long to eject), and maxEjectionPercent (cap on ejected pods to prevent complete outage).

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl delete dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF' apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1 kind: DestinationRule metadata: name: anihpj-api-dr namespace: anihpj spec: host: anihpj-api subsets: - name: v1 labels: version: v1 - name: v2 labels: version: v2 trafficPolicy: loadBalancer: simple: ROUND_ROBIN outlierDetection: consecutive5xxErrors: 5 interval: 10s baseEjectionTime: 30s maxEjectionPercent: 50 EOF
$ # Wait ~10 seconds for v2 to accumulate 5 consecutive 5xx errors... $ for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" anihpj-api:8080/; done | sort | uniq -c 20 200 ✅ ALL 20 requests return 200! v2 has been ejected — traffic goes only to v1!
$ istioctl proxy-config endpoints deploy/anihpj-api-v1 -n anihpj --subset v2 -o json | grep healthStatus "health_status": "EJECTED" ✅ v2 endpoint is now EJECTED — circuit breaker is working!

BASH — Recreate DestinationRule with outlier detection enabled 
# Step 1: Delete and recreate DestinationRule WITH outlier detection
kubectl delete dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: anihpj-api
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      simple: ROUND_ROBIN
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5    # ✅ Eject after 5 consecutive 5xx errors
      interval: 10s              # ✅ Check every 10 seconds
      baseEjectionTime: 30s      # ✅ Eject for 30 seconds minimum
      maxEjectionPercent: 50     # ✅ Cap: never eject more than 50% of pods
EOF

# Step 2: Wait ~10-15 seconds for v2 to accumulate errors and get ejected
sleep 15

# Step 3: Verify v2 is now ejected
istioctl proxy-config endpoints deploy/anihpj-api-v1 -n anihpj --subset v2 -o json | grep healthStatus

# Step 4: Confirm all traffic now returns 200
for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" anihpj-api:8080/; done | sort | uniq -c
✓

✅ Verify — v2 Ejected, All Traffic Goes to v1, Zero 500 Errors

After adding outlierDetection to the DestinationRule, Envoy now monitors v2 for 5xx errors. Within 10-15 seconds, v2 accumulates 5 consecutive 500 errors and is ejected from the load balancing pool. All 100% of traffic now routes to v1 — the API returns 200 consistently. The canary deployment is safely contained: v2 is isolated and can be debugged without affecting production traffic.

💡 Key takeaway: Istio does NOT auto-enable circuit breaking. You must explicitly add outlierDetection to the DestinationRule. Always configure it alongside canary deployments so broken versions are automatically ejected. Production-safe defaults: consecutive5xxErrors: 5, interval: 10s, baseEjectionTime: 30s, maxEjectionPercent: 50. Never set maxEjectionPercent to 100 — that risks a complete outage if all pods experience transient errors.

Load Test anihpj-api — Fix 503 Under Concurrent Load (Connection Pool Too Small)

The Problem: The anihpj-api handles job searches with bursts of up to 50 concurrent requests during peak hours. Under load testing with 20 concurrent connections, the API returns HTTP 503 for every request beyond the first 5. The DestinationRule has maxConnections: 5 and http1MaxPendingRequests: 0 — meaning only 5 TCP connections are allowed simultaneously with NO queue. The 6th concurrent connection gets an immediate 503. The API has plenty of pod capacity but the connection pool is severly bottlenecked.

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost experiences traffic spikes during morning job searches. A dev optimizes the DestinationRule with maxConnections: 5 to "prevent overload." During peak, only 5 users can access the API simultaneously — the rest get 503. 90% of morning traffic is rejected.

anihpj/

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE AND LABEL FOR INJECTION

# 2. DEPLOY API WITH TINY CONNECTION POOL (BUG: maxConnections=5, no queue!)

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:

  namespace: anihpj

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: anihpj-api
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 5           # ❌ BUG! Only 5 connections!
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 0  # ❌ BUG! No pending queue!

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. 10 concurrent requests: seq 1 10 | xargs -P10 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" anihpj-api:8080/ → First 5 = 200, rest = 503!
✗2. Check Envoy overflow stats: istioctl proxy-config stats deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj | grep overflow → High upstream_rq_pending_overflow count!
✗3. Check pods are idle: kubectl top pods -n anihpj → Pods have very low CPU/memory usage — they're not the bottleneck!
✗4. 90% of traffic is rejected at 20 concurrent users — the connection pool is the bottleneck, not the application.

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check DestinationRule connection pool: kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A10 connectionPool
→ maxConnections: 5, http1MaxPendingRequests: 0 — only 5 concurrent connections!
2Check Envoy circuit breaker stats: istioctl proxy-config stats deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj | grep "cx_overflow\|pending_overflow"
→ upstream_cx_overflow: 95 — 95 connections were rejected at the pool!
3Check active connections vs limit: istioctl proxy-config clusters deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj --fqdn anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -o json | grep -E "(max_connections|active)"
→ max_connections: 5, active: 5 — pool is saturated, all new connections rejected!
4Check pending requests queue: istioctl proxy-config stats deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj | grep "upstream_rq_pending"
→ upstream_rq_pending_overflow: 95 — NO queue to absorb burst (http1MaxPendingRequests: 0)!
5Root cause: maxConnections: 5 restricts the pool to only 5 simultaneous TCP connections. http1MaxPendingRequests: 0 means there is NO pending request queue — the 6th connection gets immediate 503. The API has 3 replicas with plenty of capacity, but the connection pool creates an artificial bottleneck. Fix: increase maxConnections to 100 and set http1MaxPendingRequests to 50 to absorb traffic bursts.

①
50% 503 → Pool exhausted
②
DR: max 5, queue 0
③
Pods idle → Pool is bottleneck
④
Increase to 100 + queue 50
⑤
All requests succeed ✅

Tenet: Connection pool limits must match capacity. maxConnections ≥ peak concurrency. http1MaxPendingRequests > 0 for burst absorption.

🧪 SCENARIO S25 — Category 2: Traffic Routing Hash Debug

Configure Session Affinity for anihpj-api — Fix All Users Going to Random Pods (Wrong Hash Header)

The Problem: The anihpj-api needs session affinity — the same user should always reach the same pod for cached job search results. The ops team configured consistent hash load balancing to route by the X-User-ID HTTP header. But users report that their session is constantly lost — each request goes to a different pod. The DestinationRule has httpHeaderName: "x-user-id" (lowercase) but the application sends X-User-ID (mixed case). Envoy's consistent hash header matching is case-sensitive. The hash never matches — Envoy falls back to random selection.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Deploy API with Broken Consistent Hash (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost API caches job search results per user. Session affinity via X-User-ID header ensures same user → same pod → warm cache. But DR uses lowercase "x-user-id" while app sends "X-User-ID" — Envoy hash is case-sensitive. Every request hits a different pod with cold cache.

anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml (3 replicas)
├── 02-api-service.yaml
└── 03-destinationrule.yaml (BUG: httpHeaderName: "x-user-id")
BASH — Case mismatch in hash header (BUG)

  namespace: anihpj

# Consistent hash on header — CASE MISMATCH!
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: anihpj-api
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      consistentHash:
        httpHeaderName: "x-user-id"  # ❌ App sends "X-User-ID"!

⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Same user 5x: for i in $(seq 1 5); do curl -s -H "X-User-ID: user-123" anihpj-api:8080/; done → Different pod each time! No session affinity.
✗2. Check DR hash header: kubectl get dr anihpj-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep httpHeaderName → "x-user-id" (lowercase)
✗3. Check what app actually sends: curl -v -H "X-User-ID: user-123" anihpj-api:8080/ 2>&1 | grep "> X-User" → App sends "X-User-ID" (mixed case)
✗4. Users report lost sessions — cached job search results are useless. Cache hit ratio is 0% because every request hits a different cold pod.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Verify Envoy hash configuration: istioctl proxy-config clusters deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj --fqdn anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -o json | grep -A10 consistentHash
→ httpHeaderName: "x-user-id" — Envoy is looking for lowercase header!
2Check actual header in request: curl -v -H "X-User-ID: user-123" anihpj-api:8080/ 2>&1 | grep "> X-User"
→ App sends "X-User-ID" (mixed case) — NOT "x-user-id"!
3Check HTTP header case sensitivity: HTTP header names are case-insensitive by spec, but Envoy's consistent hash header matching is case-sensitive by implementation!
→ "X-User-ID" ≠ "x-user-id" — Envoy treats them as different strings!
4Check hash behavior without matching header: istioctl proxy-config endpoints deploy/anihpj-api -n anihpj --subset v1 -o json
→ Without matching header, Envoy falls back to random selection — no session affinity!
5Root cause: Envoy's consistent hash HTTP header matching is CASE-SENSITIVE. The DestinationRule specifies "x-user-id" (lowercase) but the application sends "X-User-ID" (mixed case). Since the hash never matches any header, Envoy falls back to random pod selection — completely defeating session affinity. Fix: update the DestinationRule httpHeaderName to exactly match the application's header casing: "X-User-ID".
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Same user → diff pods → Hash broken
②
DR: "x-user-id" vs App: "X-User-ID"
③
Envoy hash = case-sensitive!
④
Fix: match exact casing
⑤
Same user → same pod ✅

Tenet: Envoy's consistent hash header matching is CASE-SENSITIVE. "X-User-ID" ≠ "x-user-id". Always verify exact header casing from your application.

🧪 SCENARIO S26 — Category 2: Traffic Routing Gateway Debug

Deploy Public + Internal Admin Gateways — Fix Admin API Exposed to Public Internet

The Problem: The platform team deploys two Istio Gateways: a public gateway for the anihpj job board and an internal admin gateway for the Django admin panel. The admin Gateway is supposed to be accessible only from internal cluster IPs (10.96.0.0/12). But during configuration, the ops team accidentally set the admin Gateway's selector to istio: ingressgateway — the SAME label as the public gateway. The admin VirtualService is bound to this gateway, and since both Gateways bind to the same ingress gateway pod, the Django admin panel is now accessible from the public internet on port 8443. Any external user who discovers port 8443 can access /admin — a critical security breach. Your job: find why the admin panel is publicly accessible, deploy a dedicated internal gateway, and fix the selector.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Deploy Public API + Internal Admin with Leaked Gateway Selector (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost has two web interfaces: the public job board at jobpost.com (port 443) and the internal Django admin panel at admin.jobpost.internal (port 8443). The security policy requires the admin panel to be accessible ONLY from within the cluster. The ops team created two Gateway resources — one for public traffic and one for admin. But in a copy-paste error, the admin Gateway's selector was left as istio: ingressgateway instead of a dedicated internal label. Both Gateways now bind to the same istio-ingressgateway pod. The Django admin panel with full CRUD access to the job database is exposed on the public internet.

├── 01-public-api-deployment.yaml  ← Public job board API (2 replicas)
├── 02-admin-api-deployment.yaml   ← Internal Django admin (1 replica)
├── 03-public-api-service.yaml     ← ClusterIP for public API (port 8080)
├── 04-admin-api-service.yaml      ← ClusterIP for admin API (port 8081)
├── 05-public-gateway.yaml         ← Public Gateway (443, selector: istio=ingressgateway)
├── 06-admin-gateway.yaml          ← Admin Gateway (8443, BUG: same selector!)

✗1. Check Gateway selectors: kubectl get gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 selector → BOTH show istio: ingressgateway — admin Gateway has the SAME selector as public!
✗2. Check which gateway pod has both routes: istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system | grep -E "jobpost.com|admin" → Admin route is in the public ingress gateway pod!
✗3. The admin VirtualService is bound to anihpj-admin-gateway which uses the public ingress gateway pod — the admin panel is served from the public gateway!
✗4. Any external user who discovers port 8443 can access the Django admin panel — full CRUD access to the job database is exposed to the public internet.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1List all Gateways and their selectors: kubectl get gateway -n anihpj -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,SELECTOR:.spec.selector
→ Both show istio:ingressgateway — admin Gateway has NO dedicated selector!
2Check the public ingress gateway pod routes: istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system --name http.8443 2>/dev/null | head -20
→ Port 8443 admin route is SERVED by the public ingress gateway pod!
3Verify there's no separate admin gateway pod: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway
→ Only ONE istio-ingressgateway pod exists — serving BOTH public AND admin traffic!
4Check if admin Gateway should use a different label: kubectl get gateway anihpj-admin-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 selector
→ selector: istio: ingressgateway — should be istio: internal-gateway for isolation!
5Root cause: The admin Gateway's selector is istio: ingressgateway — the SAME label as the public Gateway. Istio binds both Gateways to the same ingress gateway pod because the selector matches. There is no separate internal gateway pod deployed. The admin panel, which should only be accessible internally, is now served by the public ingress gateway pod on port 8443. Fix: deploy a dedicated internal gateway pod with label istio: internal-gateway, then update the admin Gateway selector to istio: internal-gateway.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Admin accessible externally → Gateway leak
②
Check selectors → Both use ingressgateway
③
Only ONE gateway pod running
④
Deploy dedicated internal gateway pod
⑤
Fix selector → Admin isolated ✅

Tenet: Each Istio Gateway binds to an Envoy pod whose labels match the Gateway's selector. If two Gateways use the same selector, they bind to the SAME gateway pod — all routes are served from one pod. For security isolation (public vs internal), deploy SEPARATE gateway pods with different labels and use distinct selectors. The ingress gateway pod is just an Envoy proxy — you can deploy as many as you need with different labels.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get gateway -n anihpj -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,SELECTOR:.spec.selector NAME SELECTOR anihpj-admin-gateway map[istio:ingressgateway] anihpj-public-gateway map[istio:ingressgateway] ← BOTH Gateways use the SAME selector — admin is NOT isolated!
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway -o wide NAME READY IP NODE istio-ingressgateway-7d8f9c5b-x 1/1 10.96.1.45 anih ← Only ONE gateway pod — serving BOTH public AND admin traffic!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=internal-gateway NAME READY IP NODE istio-internal-gateway-3k9m2n8p-z 1/1 10.96.2.12 anih ✅ Dedicated internal gateway pod DEPLOYED — admin traffic now isolated!
$ kubectl get gateway -n anihpj -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,SELECTOR:.spec.selector NAME SELECTOR anihpj-admin-gateway map[istio:internal-gateway] anihpj-public-gateway map[istio:ingressgateway] ✅ Admin Gateway now uses DEDICATED selector — internal traffic isolated!
🔧
BASH — Deploy internal gateway pod + update admin Gateway selector 
# Step 1: Deploy a dedicated internal gateway pod with custom label
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: istio-internal-gateway
  namespace: istio-system
  labels:
    app: istio-internal-gateway
    istio: internal-gateway
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: istio-internal-gateway
      istio: internal-gateway
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: istio-internal-gateway
        istio: internal-gateway
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: istio-proxy
        image: auto
EOF

# Step 2: Update admin Gateway selector to dedicated internal label
kubectl patch gateway anihpj-admin-gateway -n anihpj --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/selector","value":{"istio":"internal-gateway"}}]'

# Step 3: Verify admin Gateway now uses its own pod
kubectl get gateway -n anihpj -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,SELECTOR:.spec.selector

# Step 4: Verify admin routes moved to internal gateway pod
istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/istio-internal-gateway -n istio-system | grep admin
✓

✅ Verify — Admin Panel Isolated on Internal Gateway, Not Publicly Accessible

After deploying a dedicated internal gateway pod with label istio: internal-gateway and updating the admin Gateway selector, the admin panel is now served exclusively by the internal gateway pod. The public ingress gateway no longer serves admin routes on port 8443. External users cannot reach the Django admin panel — it is accessible only from within the cluster via the internal gateway pod's IP.

💡 Key takeaway: Gateway isolation is achieved through SELECTOR labels. Each Gateway binds to Envoy pods matching its selector. For security isolation (public vs internal/admin), deploy separate gateway pods with distinct labels. Never use the same selector for public and internal Gateways — all routes will be served from the same pod, exposing internal services to the public internet.

Deploy HTTPS Gateway for anihpj — Fix TLS Certificate Not Found (Secret Name Mismatch)

The Problem: The ops team creates a self-signed TLS certificate for the anihpj job board and stores it in a Kubernetes Secret named jobpost-tls-secret. They configure an Istio Gateway with TLS mode SIMPLE and set credentialName: jobpost-tls-cert. But the Gateway fails to serve HTTPS — curl returns "connection refused" or "SSL handshake failed." The Secret exists in the cluster, the certificate is valid, and the Gateway is deployed — but the credentialName in the Gateway doesn't match the actual Secret name. Istio can't find the TLS certificate, so the Gateway listener never activates. The job board is inaccessible over HTTPS.

1

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost is going live! The security team generates a TLS certificate using OpenSSL and stores it in a Kubernetes Secret named jobpost-tls-secret. The platform team configures the Gateway with TLS mode SIMPLE, referencing credentialName: jobpost-tls-cert. During the launch, the first user visits https://jobpost.com — and gets "Secure Connection Failed." The Gateway's HTTPS listener never started because Istio can't find a Secret named jobpost-tls-cert. The job board launch is delayed while the team scrambles to figure out why TLS isn't working.

├── 01-web-deployment.yaml         ← Django web frontend (2 replicas)

├── 03-tls-secret.yaml             ← TLS Secret: jobpost-tls-secret (CORRECT name)
├── 04-gateway.yaml                ← Gateway with BUG: credentialName: jobpost-tls-cert (WRONG!)

kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# 2. CREATE SELF-SIGNED TLS CERTIFICATE
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout /tmp/jobpost.key -out /tmp/jobpost.crt \
  -subj "/CN=jobpost.com/O=anihpj"

# 3. STORE TLS CERT IN SECRET (CORRECT name: jobpost-tls-secret)
kubectl create secret tls jobpost-tls-secret \
  --cert=/tmp/jobpost.crt --key=/tmp/jobpost.key \
  -n anihpj

    targetPort: 8080
---

kind: Gateway
metadata:

✗1. Check Gateway status: kubectl describe gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj | tail -10 → No errors visible in Gateway resource itself.
✗2. Check ingress gateway logs: kubectl logs deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system | grep -i "secret\|tls\|cert" | tail -5 → "secret 'jobpost-tls-cert' not found in namespace 'anihpj'"
✗3. Check available Secrets: kubectl get secrets -n anihpj | grep tls → Shows jobpost-tls-secret, NOT jobpost-tls-cert!
✗4. HTTPS listener never activates — users get "SSL handshake failed" or "connection refused." The Gateway is deployed but TLS is broken.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Gateway TLS config: kubectl get gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 tls
→ credentialName: jobpost-tls-cert
2Check actual Secret names: kubectl get secrets -n anihpj --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/tls
→ jobpost-tls-secret (NOT jobpost-tls-cert!)
3Check ingress gateway logs for TLS errors: kubectl logs deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system --tail=50 | grep -i secret
→ "secret 'jobpost-tls-cert' not found" — Istio can't find the Secret!
4Compare names side by side: Gateway expects jobpost-tls-cert, Secret is jobpost-tls-secret — the suffix doesn't match!
→ "cert" ≠ "secret" — one character difference, TLS completely broken!
5Root cause: The Gateway's tls.credentialName is "jobpost-tls-cert" but the Kubernetes Secret is named "jobpost-tls-secret". Istio's Gateway controller looks for a Secret matching the credentialName exactly in the Gateway's namespace. When it can't find it, the HTTPS listener never activates — the port is open but no TLS handshake can complete because there's no certificate to present. Fix: update the Gateway's credentialName to match the actual Secret name: "jobpost-tls-secret".
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
HTTPS fails → TLS cert issue
②
Check Gateway → credentialName: X
③
Check Secrets → named Y, not X!
④
Mismatch → Gateway can't find cert
⑤
Fix credentialName → HTTPS works ✅

Tenet: The Gateway's credentialName must EXACTLY match the Kubernetes Secret name in the Gateway's namespace. Istio's gateway controller watches for Secrets matching the credentialName — if it can't find one, the TLS listener silently fails. Always verify: kubectl get secrets -n <ns> | grep tls and compare with kubectl get gateway -n <ns> -o yaml | grep credentialName.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 tls tls: credentialName: jobpost-tls-cert mode: SIMPLE ← Gateway expects Secret named "jobpost-tls-cert"
$ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/tls NAME TYPE DATA AGE jobpost-tls-secret kubernetes.io/tls 2 5m ← Secret is named "jobpost-tls-secret" — MISMATCH!
$ kubectl logs deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system --tail=20 | grep -i secret warning envoy config StreamAggregatedResources gRPC config stream closed warning tls secret "jobpost-tls-cert" not found in namespace "anihpj" ← Istio explicitly logs: Secret NOT FOUND!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj --type=json \ -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/servers/0/tls/credentialName","value":"jobpost-tls-secret"}]' gateway.networking.istio.io/anihpj-gateway patched
$ kubectl logs deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system --tail=5 | grep -i secret info tls Secret "jobpost-tls-secret" loaded successfully ✅ TLS Secret FOUND — HTTPS listener NOW ACTIVE!
🔧
BASH — Fix credentialName to match actual Secret name 
# Step 1: Patch the Gateway to use the correct Secret name
kubectl patch gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/servers/0/tls/credentialName","value":"jobpost-tls-secret"}]'

# Step 2: Verify the Gateway picked up the Secret (check logs)
kubectl logs deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system --tail=10 | grep -i secret

# Step 3: Verify the Gateway now shows the correct credential
kubectl get gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep credentialName

# Step 4: Test HTTPS (optional — requires port-forward or NodePort)
# curl -k https://jobpost.com/
✓

✅ Verify — TLS Secret Found, HTTPS Listener Active

After patching the Gateway's credentialName to jobpost-tls-secret, Istio's gateway controller finds the TLS Secret and activates the HTTPS listener. The ingress gateway logs confirm the Secret was loaded successfully. The job board is now accessible over HTTPS with the self-signed certificate.

💡 Key takeaway: The Gateway's credentialName is the EXACT name of a Kubernetes Secret in the same namespace. Always create the Secret FIRST, then verify the Gateway references it correctly with kubectl get secrets -n <ns> | grep tls and kubectl get gateway -o yaml | grep credentialName. A single character mismatch silently breaks TLS — no error in kubectl describe gateway, only in the ingress gateway pod logs.

🧪 SCENARIO S28 — Category 2: Traffic Routing SNI Debug

Configure SNI Passthrough for Two Backends — Fix All Traffic Going to Wrong Service (Wildcard Collision)

The Problem: The ops team configures an Istio Gateway with TLS PASSTHROUGH mode to route traffic to two backend services — the public job board API and an internal metrics dashboard — both behind a single port 443. SNI passthrough should route api.jobpost.com → anihpj-api and metrics.jobpost.internal → anihpj-metrics based on the TLS SNI hostname. But the Gateway has both servers configured with hosts: ["*"]. When both servers match everything, Istio routes ALL traffic to the first server — the metrics dashboard receives API traffic, and the API receives nothing. SNI routing is completely broken because the Gateway can't distinguish between the two backends.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Deploy Two Backends with SNI Passthrough — Both Hosts Wildcard (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost has two backend services that need TLS termination at the backend (not at the Gateway): the public API (api.jobpost.com) and an internal metrics dashboard (metrics.jobpost.internal). The team configures TLS PASSTHROUGH mode so Envoy forwards the raw TLS stream to the backend without decrypting. But when configuring the Gateway servers, both were set to hosts: ["*"] — the wildcard matches everything. SNI routing is based on the first matching server, so ALL TLS connections are forwarded to the FIRST server (metrics), regardless of the SNI hostname. The public API is completely unreachable — all traffic is being sent to the metrics dashboard.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S28): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Public API (2 replicas, port 8443)
├── 02-metrics-deployment.yaml     ← Metrics dashboard (1 replica, port 8443)
├── 03-api-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP for API (port 8443)
├── 04-metrics-service.yaml        ← ClusterIP for metrics (port 8443)
├── 05-gateway.yaml                ← Gateway PASSTHROUGH: BOTH hosts: ["*"]!
└── 06-virtualservices.yaml        ← VS for api + VS for metrics
BASH — Deploy SNI Passthrough with both servers using wildcard hosts (BUG) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S28: SNI Passthrough — Wildcard Host Collision
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE AND LABEL FOR INJECTION
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# 2. DEPLOY API + METRICS WITH SNI PASSTHROUGH GATEWAY (BUG: both hosts = *)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
# ─── PUBLIC API ───
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-api
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8443
        lifecycle:
          postStart:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'API BACKEND - Pod: '$HOSTNAME > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html"]
---
# ─── METRICS DASHBOARD ───
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-metrics
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-metrics
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-metrics
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-metrics
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: metrics
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8443
        lifecycle:
          postStart:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'METRICS DASHBOARD - Pod: '$HOSTNAME > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html"]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-api
  ports:
  - port: 8443
    targetPort: 8443
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-metrics
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-metrics
  ports:
  - port: 8443
    targetPort: 8443
---
# Gateway: TLS PASSTHROUGH — BOTH servers use hosts: ["*"] (BUG!)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: anihpj-sni-gateway
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: tls-api
      protocol: TLS
    tls:
      mode: PASSTHROUGH
    hosts:
    - "*"    # ❌ BUG! Wildcard catches ALL SNI hostnames!
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: tls-metrics
      protocol: TLS
    tls:
      mode: PASSTHROUGH
    hosts:
    - "*"    # ❌ BUG! Same wildcard — SNI routing can't distinguish!
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - "api.jobpost.com"
  gateways:
  - anihpj-sni-gateway
  tls:
  - match:
    - port: 443
      sniHosts:
      - api.jobpost.com
    route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-api
        port:
          number: 8443
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-metrics-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - "metrics.jobpost.internal"
  gateways:
  - anihpj-sni-gateway
  tls:
  - match:
    - port: 443
      sniHosts:
      - metrics.jobpost.internal
    route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-metrics
        port:
          number: 8443
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check Gateway server hosts: kubectl get gateway anihpj-sni-gateway -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 hosts → BOTH servers show hosts: "*" — all SNI traffic matches both!
✗2. All TLS connections on port 443 are forwarded to the FIRST server (metrics) — api.jobpost.com traffic goes to the metrics backend!
✗3. The VirtualService for api.jobpost.com is never reached — SNI routing resolves to the first matching Gateway server, which is metrics.
✗4. Public API is completely unreachable — all production traffic is being sent to the internal metrics dashboard.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Gateway server configuration: kubectl get gateway anihpj-sni-gateway -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.servers[*].hosts}'
→ ["*"] ["*"] — BOTH servers use wildcard hosts!
2Check which routes are active on the gateway: istioctl proxy-config listeners deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system --port 443 -o json | grep -A5 name
→ Only the FIRST server's routes are present — second server's routes are shadowed!
3Verify API VirtualService SNI match: kubectl get vs anihpj-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 sniHosts
→ sniHosts: api.jobpost.com — correct, but Gateway server has hosts: "*" which shadow it!
4Check if second server routes are present: istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system --name tls-metrics 2>/dev/null
→ No tls-metrics route found — second Gateway server routes are not configured!
5Root cause: Both Gateway servers use hosts: ["*"] (wildcard). In Istio's TLS PASSTHROUGH mode, when multiple servers on the same port have overlapping hosts, the FIRST matching server wins. Since both match everything, all SNI traffic is routed through the first server (tls-metrics). The second server (tls-api) and its VirtualService are never reached. Fix: set specific hosts for each server — "api.jobpost.com" for the API server and "metrics.jobpost.internal" for the metrics server.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
API unreachable → SNI routing broken
②
Check Gateway → both hosts: "*"
③
First match wins → all to metrics
④
Fix: specific hosts per server
⑤
SNI routes correctly ✅

Tenet: In TLS PASSTHROUGH mode, the Gateway's hosts field determines which SNI hostnames match each server. When multiple servers share the same port, the FIRST server whose hosts match the SNI gets the traffic. Never use hosts: ["*"] on multiple PASSTHROUGH servers on the same port — they will collide. Always use specific hostnames that don't overlap.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get gateway anihpj-sni-gateway -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{range .spec.servers[*]}{.hosts}{"\n"}{end}' ["*"] ["*"] ← BOTH servers match EVERYTHING — SNI routing is impossible!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch gateway anihpj-sni-gateway -n anihpj --type=json \ -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/servers/0/hosts","value":["api.jobpost.com"]},{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/servers/1/hosts","value":["metrics.jobpost.internal"]}]' gateway.networking.istio.io/anihpj-sni-gateway patched
$ kubectl get gateway anihpj-sni-gateway -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{range .spec.servers[*]}{.hosts}{"\n"}{end}' ["api.jobpost.com"] ["metrics.jobpost.internal"] ✅ Specific hosts — SNI routing NOW WORKS!
🔧
BASH — Patch Gateway with specific SNI hosts 
kubectl patch gateway anihpj-sni-gateway -n anihpj --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/servers/0/hosts","value":["api.jobpost.com"]},{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/servers/1/hosts","value":["metrics.jobpost.internal"]}]'

# Verify both servers now have distinct hosts
kubectl get gateway anihpj-sni-gateway -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{range .spec.servers[*]}{.name}{": "}{.hosts}{"\n"}{end}'
✓

✅ Verify — SNI Routing Operational, Each Host Routes to Correct Backend

After setting specific hosts for each Gateway server, SNI passthrough correctly routes api.jobpost.com TLS connections to the API backend and metrics.jobpost.internal to the metrics dashboard. The two servers no longer collide because their host patterns don't overlap.

💡 Key takeaway: In TLS PASSTHROUGH mode, Gateway servers on the same port MUST have non-overlapping hosts. Wildcards ("*") on multiple servers cause the first server to shadow all others. Always use specific, non-overlapping hostnames or use prefix/suffix matching ("*.jobpost.com", "*.jobpost.internal") that don't collide.

🧪 SCENARIO S29 — Category 2: Traffic Routing Listener Debug

Deploy Gateway with HTTP/HTTPS/TCP Listeners — Fix HTTP→HTTPS Redirect Not Working (Missing gateways Field)

The Problem: The ops team configures an Istio Gateway with three listeners: port 80 (HTTP, should redirect to HTTPS), port 443 (HTTPS), and port 5432 (TCP, for PostgreSQL). They create a VirtualService on port 80 that should redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS. But users visiting http://jobpost.com get a blank nginx page instead of being redirected to HTTPS. The HTTP redirect VirtualService has the correct redirect rule but is missing the gateways field — it's not bound to any Gateway. Without a gateway binding, Istio treats the VirtualService as a mesh-internal route, and the Gateway's port 80 listener serves the default Envoy response. The redirect never fires.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "anih"
1

📋 Deploy Gateway with HTTP/HTTPS/TCP — HTTP Redirect VirtualService Missing gateways (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: anihpj/jobpost needs three listeners on the production Gateway: HTTP (port 80) to redirect users to HTTPS, HTTPS (port 443) for secure web traffic, and TCP (port 5432) for direct PostgreSQL access by DBA tools. The team creates the Gateway with all three listeners and a VirtualService for the HTTPS web traffic. They also create a redirect VirtualService for port 80 — but they forget to include the gateways field. The redirect VS has no gateway binding, so Istio ignores it for ingress traffic. Users hitting http://jobpost.com see an empty nginx page instead of the expected 301 redirect to https://jobpost.com. Plain HTTP traffic reaches the site with no encryption.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S29): 
anihpj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← ns anihpj with istio-injection
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml         ← Django web frontend (2 replicas)
├── 02-web-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 8080)
├── 03-gateway.yaml                ← Gateway: 80(HTTP), 443(HTTPS), 5432(TCP)
├── 04-virtualservice-https.yaml   ← VS: jobpost.com → anihpj-web (HTTPS, correct)
└── 05-virtualservice-redirect.yaml ← VS: HTTP→HTTPS redirect (BUG: no gateways!)

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S29: Multiple Listeners — HTTP Redirect Missing gateways Field
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE AND LABEL FOR INJECTION
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# 2. DEPLOY WEB APP + GATEWAY WITH 3 LISTENERS (BUG: redirect VS has no gateways!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        lifecycle:
          postStart:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'SECURE JOB BOARD - Pod: '$HOSTNAME > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html"]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-web
  ports:
  - port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
---
# Gateway: 3 listeners — HTTP(80), HTTPS(443), TCP(5432)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: anihpj-gateway
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 80
      name: http
      protocol: HTTP
    hosts:
    - "jobpost.com"
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
    hosts:
    - "jobpost.com"
    tls:
      mode: SIMPLE
      credentialName: jobpost-tls-secret
  - port:
      number: 5432
      name: tcp-postgres
      protocol: TCP
    hosts:
    - "db.jobpost.internal"
---
# VirtualService: HTTPS traffic to web (CORRECT — has gateways field)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-https
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - "jobpost.com"
  gateways:
  - anihpj-gateway
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-web
        port:
          number: 8080
---
# VirtualService: HTTP→HTTPS redirect (BUG: missing gateways field!)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-redirect-http
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - "jobpost.com"
  # ❌ BUG! No gateways field — this VS is NOT bound to any Gateway!
  # ❌ Without gateways, Istio ignores this for ingress traffic!
  http:
  - redirect:
      uri: https://jobpost.com
      authority: jobpost.com
      redirectCode: 301
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check HTTP redirect VS: kubectl get vs anihpj-redirect-http -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 gateways → No gateways field! The VS is unbound!
✗2. Compare with HTTPS VS: kubectl get vs anihpj-web-https -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 gateways → Has gateways: [anihpj-gateway] ✅ — the HTTPS one works.
✗3. HTTP traffic on port 80 shows default Envoy response (blank page or "no healthy upstream") — the redirect never fires.
✗4. Users visiting http://jobpost.com stay on HTTP — no encryption, no redirect. Plain text traffic flows to the site.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1List VirtualServices and their gateway bindings: kubectl get vs -n anihpj -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GATEWAYS:.spec.gateways
→ anihpj-redirect-http has EMPTY gateways column!
2Check if redirect VirtualService is applied: kubectl describe vs anihpj-redirect-http -n anihpj | grep -i gateway
→ Gateways: <none> — VirtualService is NOT bound to any Gateway!
3Check Gateway's port 80 routes: istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system --name http.80 2>/dev/null
→ No redirect route on port 80 — the Gateway has no VirtualService for this port!
4Compare with the working HTTPS VS: the HTTPS VS has gateways: [anihpj-gateway] — it's properly bound. The redirect VS is missing this field entirely.
→ Without gateways, Istio ignores the VS for ingress; it only applies to mesh-internal traffic!
5Root cause: The HTTP→HTTPS redirect VirtualService is missing the gateways field. Istio uses this field to determine which Gateways the VirtualService applies to. Without it, the VirtualService only applies to mesh-internal sidecar traffic — it is COMPLETELY IGNORED by the ingress gateway. The Gateway's port 80 listener has no VirtualService to handle requests, so Envoy serves its default response. Fix: add gateways: [anihpj-gateway] to the redirect VirtualService.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
HTTP not redirecting → VS not working
②
Check VS gateways → EMPTY!
③
No gateway binding → ignored by ingress
④
Add gateways field
⑤
HTTP→HTTPS redirect works ✅

Tenet: A VirtualService's gateways field determines WHICH gateways it binds to. If omitted, the VirtualService only applies to sidecar (mesh-internal) traffic — it is NEVER applied to ingress gateway listeners. Always include gateways: [<gateway-name>] for VirtualServices that handle ingress traffic. This is a silent failure — the VirtualService is accepted and exists in etcd but is completely ignored by the ingress gateway.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get vs -n anihpj -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GATEWAYS:.spec.gateways NAME GATEWAYS anihpj-redirect-http <none> anihpj-web-https [anihpj-gateway] ← Redirect VS has NO gateway binding — IGNORED by ingress!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch vs anihpj-redirect-http -n anihpj --type=json \ -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/gateways","value":["anihpj-gateway"]}]' virtualservice.networking.istio.io/anihpj-redirect-http patched
$ kubectl get vs -n anihpj -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GATEWAYS:.spec.gateways NAME GATEWAYS anihpj-redirect-http [anihpj-gateway] anihpj-web-https [anihpj-gateway] ✅ Both VS now bound — HTTP→HTTPS redirect ACTIVE!
🔧
BASH — Patch VirtualService with gateways binding 
kubectl patch vs anihpj-redirect-http -n anihpj --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/gateways","value":["anihpj-gateway"]}]'

# Verify redirect route is now on the Gateway
kubectl get vs -n anihpj -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GATEWAYS:.spec.gateways
✓

✅ Verify — HTTP→HTTPS Redirect Active, All Three Listeners Working

After adding gateways: [anihpj-gateway] to the redirect VirtualService, HTTP traffic on port 80 now returns a proper 301 redirect to https://jobpost.com. All three Gateway listeners are now operational: HTTP (80) redirects to HTTPS, HTTPS (443) serves the web frontend, and TCP (5432) routes PostgreSQL traffic.

💡 Key takeaway: The gateways field on a VirtualService is MANDATORY for ingress traffic. Without it, Istio treats the VS as mesh-internal only. This is a common pitfall — the VS is created successfully but silently ignored. Always verify with kubectl get vs -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GATEWAYS:.spec.gateways.
